analyze: Executing this procedure implements Example Org's Secure Development Lifecycle Standard by embedding security, privacy, and supply chain risk management into the acquisition, development, testing, documentation, and disposition of systems, system components, and system services.

Completion produces the evidence artifacts expected of this process — SAST/DAST results per release and dependency and supply-chain scan output — and demonstrates traceability to NIST 800-53, ARC-AMPE, FedRAMP, and HIPAA requirements.

The Application Security team performs this procedure end to end, on a continuous basis, for all systems, components, and services developed in-house or acquired from external developers, including preproduction and test environments and the contracts governing them.
Development teams, the privacy office, the senior official for privacy, system owners, and developers participate in individual steps as directed below.
- Access to the organization's [Ticketing System], [Source Repository], and [CI/CD Pipeline]
- Access to the organization's [SAST Tool], [DAST Tool], [Dependency Scanning Tool], and [Supply Chain Scanning Tool]
- Access to the organization's [Risk Acceptance Form], [POA&M Record], and the applicable System Security and Privacy Plan (SSPP)
- Coordination contact and approval path to the senior official for privacy
- The applicable acquisition contract(s), Statement(s) of Work, and business associate agreement(s) under review
- Developer deliverables required under this procedure (assessment plans, documentation, threat models, evidence packages)
- [Identity Provider] access for verifying developer personnel authorizations

Application Security maintains the formally defined SDLC process document, including information security and privacy considerations at each lifecycle phase (initiation, design, development, implementation, operation, disposal).
Application Security documents the security and privacy roles and responsibilities required at each lifecycle phase in the SDLC process document.
Application Security identifies, by name and contact, the individuals currently holding each documented security and privacy role, and records this roster in the SDLC process document.

Application Security integrates the organizational risk management process into each SDLC phase, embedding risk assessment, Security Impact Analysis (SIA), and Privacy Impact Assessment (PIA) checkpoints into [Ticketing System] workflow templates.

Application Security provides the security and privacy offices a formal review opportunity — via a scheduled gate in [Ticketing System] — to confirm PII protection requirements are considered at every lifecycle phase.
Application Security, with [Infrastructure Team], inventories all preproduction environments (development, test, staging) supporting each system.

Application Security assesses the risk of each preproduction environment and applies protections commensurate with that risk, recording the risk determination and applied protections in the environment's entry in [Ticketing System].
Application Security verifies at each environment change that protections remain aligned with the current risk determination.
Before any live data is placed into a preproduction environment, Application Security obtains written approval via [Ticketing System], documenting the data set, purpose, and requested duration.

Application Security configures the preproduction environment to the same impact or classification level as any live data within it, coordinating with [Infrastructure Team] to enforce matching controls.

Where PII is used in a test environment, Application Security applies the full set of controls required for systems containing PII to that environment and uses synthetic PII to the maximum extent practicable for functional testing.
Application Security limits the creation, collection, use, and disclosure of PII in all development and testing to only what is necessary for the specified, authorized purpose.

Application Security obtains approval from the senior official for privacy before using PII in testing, training, or research, presenting synthetic or de-identified alternatives as the preferred option in each request.
Application Security, with [Infrastructure Team], develops and maintains a technology refresh plan for each system covering its full SDLC.
Application Security reviews and updates the refresh plan at each major lifecycle phase change or system modification.

Application Security reviews each acquisition contract for a system, component, or service and confirms, explicitly or by reference using the organization's standardized contract language, inclusion of: security and privacy functional requirements; strength of mechanism requirements; security and privacy assurance requirements; controls needed to satisfy security and privacy requirements; security and privacy documentation requirements; requirements for protecting that documentation; a description of the development and intended operating environments; allocation of responsibility for information security, privacy, and supply chain risk management; and acceptance criteria.

For each contract or Statement of Work involving development of, or access to, systems containing PII, Application Security confirms the contract includes language requiring adherence to the organization's security and privacy policies and standards (consistent with 45 CFR § 155.260(b)), defines security and privacy roles and responsibilities, and is approved by the system owner.

When the acquisition stores, processes, or transmits PII, Application Security consults the privacy office and confirms the contract includes a list of controls necessary to protect PII (how data is stored, handled, and accessed within the provider environment), enforcement of applicable privacy requirements where appropriate, privacy training and awareness and rules-of-behavior requirements, and PII-specific privacy functional requirements.
Application Security records contract review outcomes in [Ticketing System] and withholds acceptance of any deliverable until required clauses are confirmed.
Application Security requires the developer to provide a description of the functional properties of the security and privacy controls to be implemented.

Application Security reviews the description to confirm it describes only functionality visible at the control interfaces and explicitly excludes internal functionality and data structures, per ARC-AMPE.

Application Security requires the developer to provide design and implementation information for the controls, including security-relevant external system interfaces, high-level design documentation, and source code or hardware schematics, at [Assignment: organization-defined level of detail].
Application Security reviews the submitted information to prove control implementation and records acceptance in [Ticketing System].

Application Security requires the developer to use [Assignment: organization-defined systems engineering methods]; \[Selection (one or more): [Assignment: organization-defined system security engineering methods]; [Assignment: organization-defined privacy engineering methods]\]; and \[Selection (one or more): [Assignment: organization-defined software development methods]; [Assignment: organization-defined testing, evaluation, assessment, verification, and validation methods]; [Assignment: organization-defined quality control processes]\].
Application Security documents the required methods in the acquisition contract and verifies developer adherence during acceptance review.
Application Security requires the developer to deliver the system, component, or service with [Assignment: organization-defined security configurations] implemented.
Application Security designates those configurations as the default baseline for any subsequent reinstallation or upgrade and verifies the default is preserved during upgrade testing.

When classified information traverses networks at a lower classification level, Application Security permits only government off-the-shelf or commercial off-the-shelf information assurance (and information assurance-enabled) IT products that compose an NSA-approved solution.
Application Security verifies each such product has been evaluated and/or validated by NSA or in accordance with NSA-approved procedures, recording the validation reference in the product record.

Application Security limits commercial information assurance (and information assurance-enabled) IT products to those successfully evaluated against a NIAP-approved Protection Profile for the specific technology type, where such a profile exists.

Where no such profile exists but the product relies on cryptographic functionality to enforce its security policy, Application Security requires the cryptographic module to be FIPS-validated or NSA-approved before use.
Application Security requires the developer to produce a plan for continuous monitoring of control effectiveness consistent with the organization's continuous monitoring program.
Application Security reviews the plan against the organizational program and records acceptance or required revisions in [Ticketing System].
Application Security requires the developer to identify the functions, ports, protocols, and services intended for organizational use.
Application Security reviews the inventory against the intended operating environment and documents approval in [Ticketing System] before connection to organizational networks.
Application Security verifies that any IT product implementing Personal Identity Verification (PIV) capability within organizational systems appears on the FIPS 201-approved products list.
Application Security blocks procurement or deployment of non-listed PIV products and records the disposition in [Ticketing System].
For contracts covering operation of a system of records on behalf of the organization, Application Security confirms the contract includes [Assignment: organization-defined Privacy Act requirements].
Application Security records the clause verification in the contract review record in [Ticketing System].
Application Security confirms each acquisition contract includes organizational data ownership requirements.

Application Security confirms the contract requires all data to be removed from the contractor's system and returned to the organization within [Assignment: organization-defined time frame], and tracks that return at contract closeout in [Ticketing System].

Application Security permits a business associate to create, receive, maintain, or transmit electronic protected health information on the organization's behalf only after satisfactory assurances are obtained in accordance with § 164.314(a).

Application Security permits a business associate to engage a subcontractor for such information only when the business associate obtains equivalent satisfactory assurances from the subcontractor, and verifies the flow-down during contract review.
Application Security documents the satisfactory assurances through a written contract or other arrangement meeting the applicable requirements of § 164.314(a).

Application Security confirms each business associate contract requires the business associate to comply with the applicable Security Rule requirements, ensures subcontractors creating, receiving, maintaining, or transmitting electronic protected health information agree to comply by entering a compliant contract or arrangement, and requires reporting of any security incident of which it becomes aware, including breaches of unsecured protected health information as required by § 164.410.

Application Security confirms the same contract requirements apply between the business associate and its subcontractor as between the covered entity and the business associate, per § 164.314(a)(2)(iii).

Application Security obtains or develops administrator documentation describing secure configuration, installation, and operation; effective use and maintenance of security and privacy functions and mechanisms; and known vulnerabilities regarding configuration and use of administrative or privileged functions.

Application Security obtains or develops user documentation describing user-accessible security and privacy functions and how to use them effectively; user interaction methods enabling more secure use and privacy protection; and user responsibilities for maintaining system security and individual privacy.

When documentation is unavailable or nonexistent, Application Security documents each attempt to obtain it and takes [Assignment: organization-defined actions] in response, recording both in [Ticketing System].
Application Security distributes system documentation to [Assignment: organization-defined personnel or roles].
Application Security confirms the documentation describes the system and specifies the purpose, technical operation, access, maintenance, and required training for administrators and users.

Application Security maintains an updated list of related system operations and security documentation, and updates relevant documentation upon changes in system functions or processes, ensuring each document carries a date and version number.
Application Security evaluates whether each document is aligned with the risk management strategy or essential to control implementation or operation, and protects it accordingly.
Application Security applies the FedRAMP Secure Configuration Guide rules for system documentation.

Application Security applies [Assignment: organization-defined systems security and privacy engineering principles] in the specification, design, development, implementation, and modification of the system and its components.
Application Security records the applied principles and their mapping to design decisions in the system design documentation and reviews the mapping at each lifecycle gate.
Application Security implements the security design principle of clear abstractions, verifying during design review that component abstractions are well-defined and consistently maintained.

Application Security implements the security design principle of least common mechanism in [Assignment: organization-defined systems or system components], reviewing designs to limit shared mechanisms.

Application Security implements the security design principles of modularity and layering in [Assignment: organization-defined systems or system components], confirming layered, modular structure in design review.

Application Security implements the security design principle of partially ordered dependencies in [Assignment: organization-defined systems or system components], verifying no circular dependencies exist.

Application Security implements the security design principle of efficiently mediated access in [Assignment: organization-defined systems or system components], confirming all access is mediated without unnecessary overhead.

Application Security implements the security design principle of minimized sharing in [Assignment: organization-defined systems or system components], identifying and reducing shared resources in design review.

Application Security implements the security design principle of reduced complexity in [Assignment: organization-defined systems or system components], simplifying security-relevant design elements wherever feasible.

Application Security implements the security design principle of secure evolvability in [Assignment: organization-defined systems or system components], confirming designs accommodate change without loss of security.

Application Security implements the security design principle of trusted components in [Assignment: organization-defined systems or system components], confirming critical functions rely on trustworthy components.
Application Security implements the security design principle of hierarchical trust in [Assignment: organization-defined systems or system components], structuring trust relationships hierarchically.

Application Security implements the security design principle of inverse modification threshold in [Assignment: organization-defined systems or system components], confirming more trustworthy elements are harder to modify.

Application Security implements the security design principle of hierarchical protection in [Assignment: organization-defined systems or system components], matching protection levels to component trustworthiness.

Application Security implements the security design principle of minimized security elements in [Assignment: organization-defined systems or system components], minimizing the number of security-critical elements.

Application Security implements the security design principle of least privilege in [Assignment: organization-defined systems or system components], consistently with AC-6 and across all aspects of secure system design.

Application Security implements the security design principle of predicate permission in [Assignment: organization-defined systems or system components], confirming permissions are granted only upon defined predicates.

Application Security implements the security design principle of self-reliant trustworthiness in [Assignment: organization-defined systems or system components], minimizing dependence on external trustworthy behavior.

Application Security implements the security design principle of secure distributed composition in [Assignment: organization-defined systems or system components], verifying security holds when components compose across distributed boundaries.

Application Security implements the security design principle of trusted communications channels in [Assignment: organization-defined systems or system components], restricting access to the channel and employing end-to-end protections for data transmitted over it.

Application Security implements the security design principle of continuous protection in [Assignment: organization-defined systems or system components], confirming protections remain effective for the data and resources throughout their lifecycle.

Application Security implements the security design principle of secure metadata management in [Assignment: organization-defined systems or system components], protecting metadata with commensurate controls.

Application Security implements the security design principle of self-analysis in [Assignment: organization-defined systems or system components], confirming components can assess their own trustworthy state.

Application Security implements the security design principle of accountability and traceability in [Assignment: organization-defined systems or system components], enabling tracing of security-relevant subject-object interactions to the entity on whose behalf the action was taken, supported by a trustworthy infrastructure recording details of actions affecting system security.

Application Security implements the security design principle of secure defaults in [Assignment: organization-defined systems or system components], confirming default behavior is secure out of the box.

Application Security implements the security design principle of secure failure and recovery in [Assignment: organization-defined systems or system components], confirming failure states preserve security and recovery restores it.

Application Security implements the security design principle of economic security in [Assignment: organization-defined systems or system components], reducing the cost and complexity of security mechanisms relative to their benefit.

Application Security implements the security design principle of performance security in [Assignment: organization-defined systems or system components], confirming security mechanisms meet performance requirements.

Application Security implements the security design principle of human factored security in [Assignment: organization-defined systems or system components], ensuring security mechanisms are usable by the humans who operate them.

Application Security implements the security design principle of acceptable security in [Assignment: organization-defined systems or system components], aligning security with operator and stakeholder acceptance.
Application Security implements the security design principle of repeatable and documented procedures in [Assignment: organization-defined systems or system components].
Application Security implements the security design principle of procedural rigor in [Assignment: organization-defined systems or system components].

Application Security implements the security design principle of secure system modification in [Assignment: organization-defined systems or system components], accompanying every system change with a Security Impact Analysis (SIA) and a Privacy Impact Assessment (PIA) recorded in [Ticketing System].

Application Security implements the security design principle of sufficient documentation in [Assignment: organization-defined systems or system components], confirming documentation adequacy at each lifecycle gate.
Application Security implements the privacy principle of minimization using [Assignment: organization-defined processes].
Application Security drives those processes from business needs, coordinates their implementation with the senior privacy officer, and confirms consistency with PM-25, PT-2, and SI-12.
Application Security requires the developer to perform configuration management during design, development, implementation, operation, and disposal of the system, component, or service.
Application Security requires the developer to document, manage, and control the integrity of changes to [Assignment: organization-defined configuration items].
Application Security requires the developer to implement only organization-approved changes, verifying each change against the organization's approval record before acceptance.
Application Security requires the developer to document approved changes and their potential security and privacy impacts, and reviews that documentation at delivery.

Application Security requires the developer to track security flaws and flaw resolution within the system, component, or service and report findings to [Assignment: organization-defined personnel or roles].
Application Security requires the developer to enable integrity verification of software and firmware components.
Application Security requires the developer to enable integrity verification of hardware components.

Where no dedicated developer configuration management team exists, Application Security provides an alternate configuration management process using organizational personnel, and documents that arrangement in [Ticketing System].
Application Security requires the developer to employ tools for comparing newly generated versions of security-relevant hardware descriptions, source code, and object code with previous versions.

Application Security requires the developer to maintain the integrity of the mapping between the master build data describing the current version of security-relevant hardware, software, and firmware and the on-site master copy of that data.

Application Security requires the developer to execute procedures ensuring that security-relevant hardware, software, and firmware updates distributed to the organization are exactly as specified by the master copies.

Application Security requires [Assignment: organization-defined security and privacy representatives] to be included in the [Assignment: organization-defined configuration change management and control process].
Application Security requires the developer, at all post-design stages of the SDLC, to develop and implement a plan for ongoing security and privacy control assessments.

Application Security requires the developer to perform unit, integration, system, and regression testing/evaluation at [Assignment: organization-defined frequency to conduct] and at [Assignment: organization-defined depth and coverage].

Application Security requires the developer to produce evidence of the execution of the assessment plan and the results of the testing and evaluation, and retains that evidence with the release record.
Application Security requires the developer to implement a verifiable flaw remediation process and to correct flaws identified during testing and evaluation, tracking closure in [Ticketing System].
Application Security makes no security-relevant modifications to the information systems after the assessment.
Application Security uses non-production data when executing test scripts, or uses a test environment configured to comply with the security controls as though it were a production environment.

Application Security connects all systems supporting development and pre-production testing to an isolated network separated from production systems, permitting network traffic into and out of that environment only to facilitate system testing and restricting it by source and destination access control lists as well as ports and protocols, configured with [Infrastructure Team].
Application Security requires the developer, and runs the organization's [SAST Tool] in [CI/CD Pipeline] per release, to employ static code analysis tools to identify common flaws.
Application Security documents the results of the analysis and retains the SAST results with each release's evidence package.
Application Security requires the developer to perform threat modeling and vulnerability analyses during development and subsequent testing and evaluation.

Application Security requires those analyses to use [Assignment: organization-defined information] (impact, environment of operations, known or assumed threats, acceptable risk levels), employ [Assignment: organization-defined tools and methods], be conducted at [Assignment: organization-defined breadth and depth], and produce evidence meeting [Assignment: organization-defined acceptance criteria].
Application Security reviews the threat model outputs and records acceptance in [Ticketing System].

Application Security requires an independent agent satisfying [Assignment: organization-defined independence criteria] to verify the correct implementation of the developer security and privacy assessment plans and the evidence produced during testing and evaluation.

Application Security verifies the independent agent is provided with sufficient information to complete the verification or granted the authority to obtain it, documenting either condition in [Ticketing System].

Application Security requires the developer to perform a manual code review of [Assignment: organization-defined specific code] using [Assignment: organization-defined processes, procedures, and/or techniques].
Application Security obtains and reviews the review findings before release approval.
Application Security requires the developer to perform penetration testing at [Assignment: organization-defined breadth and depth of testing] under [Assignment: organization-defined constraints].
Application Security retains the penetration test results with the release evidence package.
Application Security requires the developer to perform attack surface reviews at each major development milestone.
Application Security reviews the attack surface findings against the system's threat model and records the outcome in [Ticketing System].

Application Security requires the developer to verify that the scope of testing and evaluation provides complete coverage of the required controls at [Assignment: organization-defined breadth and depth of testing and evaluation].
Application Security reviews the coverage verification before accepting the assessment results.
Application Security requires the developer, and runs the organization's [DAST Tool] in [CI/CD Pipeline] per release, to employ dynamic code analysis tools to identify common flaws.
Application Security documents the results and retains the DAST results with each release's evidence package.
Application Security requires the developer to employ interactive application security testing tools to identify flaws and document the results.
Application Security retains the IAST results with the release evidence package.

Application Security requires the developer to follow a documented development process that explicitly addresses security and privacy requirements, identifies the standards and tools used, documents the specific tool options and tool configurations used, and documents, manages, and ensures the integrity of changes to the process and/or tools.

Application Security reviews the development process, standards, tools, tool options, and tool configurations at [Assignment: organization-defined frequency] — at least annually, or as needed per ARC-AMPE — to determine whether they can satisfy the [Assignment: organization-defined security and privacy requirements].

Application Security requires the developer to define quality metrics at the beginning of the development process and to provide evidence of meeting them at \[Selection (one or more): [Assignment: organization-defined frequency]; [Assignment: organization-defined program review]; upon delivery\].

Application Security requires the developer to select and employ security and privacy tracking tools for use during the development process, and verifies the tooling is in use during milestone reviews.

Application Security performs criticality analysis at [Assignment: organization-defined decision points] in the SDLC and at [Assignment: organization-defined breadth and depth of criticality analysis].
Application Security records the analysis results and uses them to prioritize security and privacy review effort.
Application Security requires the developer to reduce attack surfaces to [Assignment: organization-defined thresholds].
Application Security measures the attack surface against the thresholds at each milestone review before accepting the build.
Application Security requires the developer to implement an explicit process to continuously improve the development process.
Application Security reviews evidence of improvement activity during the periodic development process review (see the SA-15 subsection above).

Application Security requires the developer to perform an automated vulnerability analysis using [Assignment: organization-defined tools], determine the exploitation potential for discovered vulnerabilities, and determine potential risk mitigations for delivered vulnerabilities.

Application Security requires delivery of the tool outputs and analysis results to [Assignment: organization-defined personnel or roles], and retains the dependency and supply-chain scan output with the release evidence.
Application Security requires the developer to use threat modeling and vulnerability analyses from similar systems, components, or services to inform the current development process.
Application Security reviews how prior analyses were incorporated at each design review.
Application Security requires the developer to provide, implement, and test an incident response plan.
Application Security reviews the plan and its test evidence for consistency with the organization's incident response process before acceptance.
Application Security requires the developer to archive the system or component to be released or delivered together with the corresponding evidence supporting the final security and privacy review.
Application Security verifies the archive contents at delivery and retains the archive record in [Ticketing System].
Application Security requires the developer to minimize the use of personally identifiable information in development and test environments.
Application Security audits development and test data stores on a continuous basis for unnecessary PII and directs removal where found.

Application Security requires the developer to provide [Assignment: organization-defined training] on the correct use and operation of the implemented security and privacy functions, controls, and/or mechanisms.
Application Security obtains and retains the training materials and delivery evidence in the system documentation set.

Application Security requires the developer to produce a design specification and security and privacy architecture consistent with the organization's security and privacy architecture (an integral part of the enterprise architecture).

Application Security verifies the specification accurately and completely describes the required security and privacy functionality and the allocation of controls among physical and logical components.

Application Security verifies the specification expresses how individual security and privacy functions, mechanisms, and services work together to provide the required capabilities and a unified approach to protection.

Application Security requires the developer to produce, as an integral part of the development process, a formal policy model describing [Assignment: organization-defined elements of organizational security and privacy policy] to be enforced.
Application Security requires the developer to prove the model is internally consistent and sufficient to enforce those elements when implemented, and reviews the proof before acceptance.
Application Security requires the developer to define security-relevant hardware, software, and firmware and provide a rationale that the definition is complete.

Application Security requires the developer to produce a formal top-level specification of the interfaces to security-relevant hardware, software, and firmware; demonstrate (to the extent feasible via proof, supplemented by informal demonstration) its consistency with the formal policy model and its complete coverage of those interfaces; show it accurately describes the implemented components; and describe internal mechanisms not addressed in the specification.

Application Security requires the developer to produce an informal descriptive top-level specification of those interfaces; demonstrate via [Selection: informal demonstration, convincing argument with formal methods as feasible] its consistency with the formal policy model and via informal demonstration its complete coverage of those interfaces; show it accurately describes those interfaces; and describe internal mechanisms not addressed in the specification.

Application Security requires the developer to design and structure security-relevant hardware, software, and firmware around a complete, conceptually simple protection mechanism with precisely defined semantics, and to internally structure them with specific regard for that mechanism.
Application Security requires the developer to structure security-relevant hardware, software, and firmware to facilitate testing.
Application Security requires the developer to structure security-relevant hardware, software, and firmware to facilitate controlling access with least privilege.
Application Security designs [Assignment: organization-defined critical systems] with coordinated behavior to implement [Assignment: organization-defined capabilities].
Application Security uses different designs for [Assignment: organization-defined critical systems] to satisfy a common set of requirements or provide equivalent functionality.

Application Security requires that the developer of systems, components, or services has appropriate access authorizations as determined by assigned [Assignment: organization-defined official government duties] / the assigned Authorizing Official or designee, verified through [Identity Provider] records before access is granted.

Application Security requires that the developer satisfies personnel screening criteria — [Assignment: organization-defined additional personnel screening criteria] per NIST, consistent with PS-3 per ARC-AMPE — and retains screening attestations in the contract file.
Application Security replaces system components when support for the components is no longer available from the developer, vendor, or manufacturer.

Where replacement is not done, Application Security provides alternative sources for continued support: \[Selection (one or more): in-house support; [Assignment: organization-defined support from external providers]\].

Per ARC-AMPE, where continued use of an unsupported component is required to satisfy mission/business needs, Application Security justifies and documents its approval on a [Risk Acceptance Form] and updates the related POA&M finding in [POA&M Record].

Application Security establishes plans to mitigate or remove the unsupported system, application, operating system, or software once identified, and upgrades, retires, or stops using the element or component before end of life or vendor discontinuation of product support.
Where removal of unsupported components is not feasible, Application Security maintains a governance process to review them and make a risk-based decision on their continued use.

Application Security implements validation of [Assignment: organization-defined information inputs] — per ARC-AMPE, all inputs to web/application servers, database servers, and any system or application input that might receive a crafted exploit aimed at executing code or causing a buffer overflow — checking accuracy, completeness, and validity (character set, length, numerical range, and acceptable values) to ensure inputs match the specified definitions for format and content.

Where PII is entered, Application Security applies validation techniques supporting data quality (ensuring the PII entered is the expected type and format), provides the capability to limit or exclude entering PII within fields that should not contain it (recognizing restricted formats such as a Social Security Number), and takes reasonable steps to ensure PII is complete, accurate, and up to date as required by laws and regulations.

Application Security provides a manual override capability for input validation of [Assignment: organization-defined information inputs], restricts its use to [Assignment: organization-defined authorized individuals], and audits its use.
Application Security reviews and resolves input validation errors within [Assignment: organization-defined time period].
Application Security verifies that the system behaves in a predictable and documented manner when invalid inputs are received.
Application Security accounts for timing interactions among system components in determining appropriate responses for invalid inputs.
Application Security restricts the use of information inputs to [Assignment: organization-defined trusted sources] and/or [Assignment: organization-defined formats].
Application Security prevents untrusted data injections, verifying injection defenses during DAST testing each release.

Application Security generates error messages that provide the information necessary for corrective actions without revealing information that could be exploited (e.g., user name/password combinations, password-reset validation attributes, PII, biometric or authenticator data, sensitive financial records, or content related to internal security functions such as private encryption keys, allow/deny-list rules, and object permission settings).

Application Security restricts display of detailed error messages to [Assignment: organization-defined personnel or roles] — per ARC-AMPE, personnel or roles documented in the applicable System Security and Privacy Plan (SSPP), i.e., authorized individuals with a need for the information in the performance of their duties — and confirms external-facing error handling during DAST testing each release.

Application Security establishes a process to identify and address weaknesses or deficiencies in the supply chain elements and processes of [Assignment: organization-defined system or system component], in coordination with [Assignment: organization-defined supply chain personnel].

Application Security employs [Assignment: organization-defined supply chain controls] to protect against supply chain risks and to limit the harm or consequences from supply chain-related events; these controls are not limited to those defined in ARC-AMPE and may include other NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 supply chain controls as appropriate.

Application Security documents the selected and implemented supply chain processes and controls in \[Selection (one or more): security and privacy plans; supply chain risk management plan; [Assignment: organization-defined document]\].

As Cloud Service Operator where applicable, Application Security documents and maintains supply chain custody — including replacement devices — to ensure the integrity of devices before they are introduced to the boundary, retaining the dependency and supply-chain scan output as supporting evidence.
Application Security employs a diverse set of sources for [Assignment: organization-defined system components and services].
Application Security employs [Assignment: organization-defined controls] to limit harm from potential adversaries identifying and targeting the organizational supply chain.
Application Security ensures the controls included in the contracts of prime contractors are also included in the contracts of subcontractors, verifying flow-down during contract review.
Application Security employs [Assignment: organization-defined acquisition strategies, contract tools, and procurement methods] to protect against, identify, and mitigate supply chain risks.
Application Security employs [Assignment: organization-defined controls] to ensure an adequate supply of [Assignment: organization-defined critical system components].

Application Security assesses the system, system component, or system service prior to selection, acceptance, modification, or update, retaining the dependency and supply-chain scan output as assessment evidence.
Application Security implements a tamper protection program for the system, system component, or system service.
Application Security employs anti-tamper technologies, tools, and techniques throughout the system development life cycle.

Application Security inspects [Assignment: organization-defined systems or system components] for tampering \[Selection (one or more): at random; at [Assignment: organization-defined frequency]; upon [Assignment: organization-defined indications of need for inspection]\].
Application Security records each inspection and its findings in [Ticketing System].
Application Security develops and implements anti-counterfeit policy and procedures that include the means to detect and prevent counterfeit components from entering the system.

Application Security reports counterfeit system components to \[Selection (one or more): source of counterfeit component; [Assignment: organization-defined external reporting organizations]; [Assignment: organization-defined personnel or roles]\].
Application Security trains [Assignment: organization-defined personnel or roles] to detect counterfeit system components, including hardware, software, and firmware.

Application Security maintains configuration control over [Assignment: organization-defined system components] awaiting service or repair and serviced or repaired components awaiting return to service.
Application Security scans for counterfeit system components at [Assignment: organization-defined frequency].

Application Security disposes of [Assignment: organization-defined data, documentation, tools, or system components] using [Assignment: organization-defined techniques and methods] — per ARC-AMPE, in accordance with the latest published NIST SP 800-88, Guidelines for Media Sanitization, with techniques consistent with MP-6 Media Sanitization.
Application Security records the sanitization or disposal outcome in [Ticketing System].

The Application Security team is authorized to perform and accountable for every step of this procedure end to end, including contract review, developer oversight, environment controls, testing, and evidence retention; development teams, the privacy office, the senior official for privacy, system owners, [Infrastructure Team], and external developers act as participants in the specific steps named above.

Exceptions to any step in this procedure require documented approval by Application Security, with risk acceptance recorded on the [Risk Acceptance Form] and, where applicable, the senior official for privacy or the Authorizing Official per the requirement concerned.

Application Security implements the security design principle of accountability and traceability in [Assignment: organization-defined systems or system components], enabling tracing of security-relevant subject-object interactions to the entity on whose behalf the action was taken, supported by a trustworthy infrastructure recording details of actions affecting system security.

Application Security implements the security design principle of secure defaults in [Assignment: organization-defined systems or system components], confirming default behavior is secure out of the box.

Application Security implements the security design principle of secure system modification in [Assignment: organization-defined systems or system components], accompanying every system change with a Security Impact Analysis (SIA) and a Privacy Impact Assessment (PIA) recorded in [Ticketing System].

Application Security implements the security design principle of sufficient documentation in [Assignment: organization-defined systems or system components], confirming documentation adequacy at each lifecycle gate.
Application Security requires the developer to enable integrity verification of software and firmware components.
Application Security requires the developer to enable integrity verification of hardware components.

Where no dedicated developer configuration management team exists, Application Security provides an alternate configuration management process using organizational personnel, and documents that arrangement in [Ticketing System].
Application Security requires the developer to employ tools for comparing newly generated versions of security-relevant hardware descriptions, source code, and object code with previous versions.

Application Security requires the developer to maintain the integrity of the mapping between the master build data describing the current version of security-relevant hardware, software, and firmware and the on-site master copy of that data.

Application Security requires the developer to execute procedures ensuring that security-relevant hardware, software, and firmware updates distributed to the organization are exactly as specified by the master copies.

Application Security requires [Assignment: organization-defined security and privacy representatives] to be included in the [Assignment: organization-defined configuration change management and control process].
Application Security requires the developer to define security-relevant hardware, software, and firmware and provide a rationale that the definition is complete.

Application Security requires the developer to produce a formal top-level specification of the interfaces to security-relevant hardware, software, and firmware; demonstrate (to the extent feasible via proof, supplemented by informal demonstration) its consistency with the formal policy model and its complete coverage of those interfaces; show it accurately describes the implemented components; and describe internal mechanisms not addressed in the specification.

Application Security requires the developer to produce an informal descriptive top-level specification of those interfaces; demonstrate via [Selection: informal demonstration, convincing argument with formal methods as feasible] its consistency with the formal policy model and via informal demonstration its complete coverage of those interfaces; show it accurately describes those interfaces; and describe internal mechanisms not addressed in the specification.

Application Security provides a manual override capability for input validation of [Assignment: organization-defined information inputs], restricts its use to [Assignment: organization-defined authorized individuals], and audits its use.
Application Security reviews and resolves input validation errors within [Assignment: organization-defined time period].
Application Security verifies that the system behaves in a predictable and documented manner when invalid inputs are received.
Application Security accounts for timing interactions among system components in determining appropriate responses for invalid inputs.
Application Security restricts the use of information inputs to [Assignment: organization-defined trusted sources] and/or [Assignment: organization-defined formats].
Application Security prevents untrusted data injections, verifying injection defenses during DAST testing each release.
Application Security employs a diverse set of sources for [Assignment: organization-defined system components and services].
Application Security employs [Assignment: organization-defined controls] to limit harm from potential adversaries identifying and targeting the organizational supply chain.
Application Security ensures the controls included in the contracts of prime contractors are also included in the contracts of subcontractors, verifying flow-down during contract review.
Application Security employs [Assignment: organization-defined controls] to ensure an adequate supply of [Assignment: organization-defined critical system components].

Application Security assesses the system, system component, or system service prior to selection, acceptance, modification, or update, retaining the dependency and supply-chain scan output as assessment evidence.
Application Security trains [Assignment: organization-defined personnel or roles] to detect counterfeit system components, including hardware, software, and firmware.

Application Security maintains configuration control over [Assignment: organization-defined system components] awaiting service or repair and serviced or repaired components awaiting return to service.
Application Security scans for counterfeit system components at [Assignment: organization-defined frequency].

analyze: This procedure directs the Security Program / GRC team through the operational steps required to assess risk, authorize systems to operate, and continuously monitor security and privacy controls under the Example Org Information Security Standard: Risk Assessment & Authorization.
Executing it produces the risk register and the authorization decision record that evidence a current, defensible risk and authorization posture.

The Security Program / GRC team performs this procedure for all Example Org systems in scope of the Standard, coordinating with System Owners, the Authorizing Official, the senior privacy official, independent assessors, and CMS where applicable.
It covers risk assessment, security categorization, control assessment, authorization, continuous monitoring, penetration testing, and contingency-related risk activities on those systems.
- Access to the [GRC / Governance Platform] for maintaining the risk register, authorization decision record, POA&M, and policy documents.
- Access to the [Document Repository] for storing and disseminating policies, procedures, and assessment artifacts.
- A designated senior official assigned as the Authorizing Official for the system and for common controls.
- A designated official accountable for risk assessment and for assessment, authorization, and monitoring policy and procedures.
- An identified security official responsible for security policy development and implementation (HIPAA).
- An engaged senior official for privacy (or designee) for categorization and privacy risk activities.
- An independent assessor or assessment team meeting the CMS Framework for Independent Assessment of Security and Privacy Controls, where applicable.
- A CISO-approved independent penetration testing agent or team.
- The current System Security and Privacy Plan (SSPP), the CMS POA&M template, and the risk acceptance form.
- A ticketing/tracking mechanism ([Ticketing System]) for POA&M entries and finding remediation.

Have the Security Program / GRC team develop and document the risk assessment policy, covering purpose, scope, roles, responsibilities, management commitment, coordination among organizational entities, and compliance, and confirming consistency with applicable laws, executive orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, and guidelines.
Have the Security Program / GRC team develop and document supporting procedures that facilitate implementation of the risk assessment policy and its associated controls.
Have the designated official [Designated Official] manage the development, documentation, and dissemination of the risk assessment policy and procedures.
Disseminate the policy and procedures to the organization-defined personnel or roles via the [Document Repository], and record the dissemination in the [GRC / Governance Platform].
Implement reasonable and appropriate policies and procedures to comply with the applicable standards and requirements, and document any changes to those policies and procedures.
Maintain the policy, procedures, and all documented actions, activities, or assessments in written (electronic is acceptable) form in the [Document Repository].

Review and update the risk assessment policy and procedures at least every one (1) year, and also following assessment or audit findings, security or privacy incidents, or changes to applicable laws, executive orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, or guidelines.
Record each review in the [GRC / Governance Platform].

Retain all required documentation (risk assessment policy, procedures, risk assessments, assessment reports, authorization records) for 6 years from the date of its creation or the date when it last was in effect, whichever is later, in the [Document Repository].
Configure access so the documentation is available to the persons responsible for implementing the procedures to which it pertains.

Periodically review the documentation and update it as needed in response to environmental or operational changes affecting the security of electronic protected health information; log each review and update in the [GRC / Governance Platform].
Have the Security Program / GRC team, working with the System Owner, categorize the system and the information it processes, stores, and transmits.
Involve the senior official for privacy, or their designee, in the categorization process.
Document the security categorization results, including supporting rationale, in the security plan for the system.
Perform an impact-level prioritization of organizational systems to obtain additional granularity on system impact levels, and record the prioritization alongside the categorization.

Submit the categorization decision to the Authorizing Official or the Authorizing Official's designated representative for review and approval, and record the approval in the authorization decision record.

Have the Security Program / GRC team conduct a risk assessment that identifies threats to and vulnerabilities in the system; determines the likelihood and magnitude of harm from unauthorized access, use, disclosure, disruption, modification, or destruction of the system and the information it processes, stores, or transmits, and any related information; and determines the likelihood and impact of adverse effects on individuals arising from the processing of personally identifiable information.
Integrate risk assessment results and risk management decisions from the organization and mission or business process perspectives with the system-level risk assessment.
Document the risk assessment results in the security and privacy plans, the risk assessment report, and the risk register, plus any additional organization-defined documents.
Review the risk assessment results at least every one (1) year or when a significant change occurs.

Update the risk assessment at least every three (3) years for internal, organization-specific authorization, and whenever there are significant changes to the system, its environment of operation, or other conditions that may impact the security or privacy state of the system.
Disseminate the risk assessment results to the organization-defined personnel or roles via the [Document Repository] and record the dissemination.

Assess supply chain risks associated with the organization-defined systems, system components, and system services, and update the supply chain risk assessment at [Supply Chain Risk Assessment Update Frequency], when there are significant changes to the relevant supply chain, or when changes to the system, environments of operation, or other conditions may necessitate a change in the supply chain.

Use all-source intelligence, including publicly available or open-source information, to assist in the analysis of risk — including the risk of vulnerabilities (intentional and unintentional) from development, manufacturing, and delivery processes, people, and the environment — and to inform engineering, acquisition, and risk management decisions.
Determine the current cyber threat environment on an ongoing basis using [Threat Intelligence Sources].
Employ [Analytics Tooling] advanced automation and analytics capabilities to predict and identify risks to the organization-defined systems or system components.

Document and implement a privacy risk management process that assesses privacy risk to individuals resulting from the collection, sharing, storing, transmitting, use, and disposal of personally identifiable information, and record it in the risk register.
Implement security measures sufficient to reduce risks and vulnerabilities to a reasonable and appropriate level, and record the measures applied against the relevant risk register entries.

Apply appropriate sanctions against workforce members who fail to comply with the security policies and procedures of the covered entity or business associate, coordinating with [Human Resources] and documenting each sanction action.

Implement procedures to regularly review records of information system activity, such as audit logs, access reports, and security incident tracking reports, and record the reviews in the [GRC / Governance Platform].
Respond to findings from security and privacy assessments, monitoring, and audits in accordance with organizational risk tolerance.
Follow the FedRAMP Vulnerability Detection and Response and Vulnerability Evaluation and Reporting rules when responding to risk findings.

Before any risk acceptance, discuss the risk acceptance with CMS; then document and track risk-accepted findings in the Plan of Action & Milestones (POA&M), with full detail captured in the risk acceptance form.
Record all response decisions and risk acceptances in the risk register and the [GRC / Governance Platform].

Have the Security Program / GRC team identify critical system components and functions by performing a criticality analysis for the organization-defined systems, system components, or system services at [SDLC Decision Points] in the system development life cycle.
Treat all system components within the CMS Authority to Connect (ATC)/Request to Connect (RTC) boundary as critical, and mark them as such in the criticality analysis and risk register.
Retain the criticality analysis results with the system's security documentation.

Establish (and implement as needed) policies and procedures for responding to an emergency or other occurrence — for example, fire, vandalism, system failure, and natural disaster — that damages systems containing electronic protected health information.
Establish and implement procedures to create and maintain retrievable exact copies of electronic protected health information.
Establish (and implement as needed) procedures to restore any loss of data.

Establish (and implement as needed) procedures to enable continuation of critical business processes for protection of the security of electronic protected health information while operating in emergency mode.
Implement procedures for periodic testing and revision of contingency plans (addressable), and record each test and revision.
Assess the relative criticality of specific applications and data in support of other contingency plan components (addressable), and record the assessment in the risk register.

Have the Security Program / GRC team develop, document, and disseminate to the organization-defined personnel or roles an assessment, authorization, and monitoring policy addressing purpose, scope, roles, responsibilities, management commitment, coordination among organizational entities, and compliance, consistent with applicable laws, executive orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, and guidelines.
Develop and document procedures to facilitate implementation of the assessment, authorization, and monitoring policy and the associated controls.

Designate the official [Designated Official] to manage the development, documentation, and dissemination of the assessment, authorization, and monitoring policy and procedures, and name that official in the appropriate security and privacy documents.
Identify and document the security official responsible for the development and implementation of the required security policies and procedures.

Review and update the assessment, authorization, and monitoring policy and procedures at least every one (1) year, and following assessment or audit findings, security or privacy incidents, or changes to applicable laws, executive orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, or guidelines.

Perform a periodic technical and nontechnical evaluation — based initially upon the implemented standards and subsequently in response to environmental or operational changes affecting the security of electronic protected health information — that establishes the extent to which the entity's security policies and procedures meet the applicable requirements, and record the evaluation results.
Select the appropriate assessor or assessment team for the type of assessment to be conducted.

Develop a control assessment plan describing the scope of the assessment, including the controls and control enhancements under assessment, the assessment procedures to be used to determine control effectiveness, and the assessment environment, assessment team, and assessment roles and responsibilities.
Ensure the control assessment plan is reviewed and approved by the Authorizing Official or designated representative prior to conducting the assessment.
Employ independent assessors or assessment teams to conduct the control assessments, following the CMS Framework for Independent Assessment of Security and Privacy Controls where applicable.

Assess the controls in the system and its environment of operation at [Assessment Frequency] to determine the extent to which the controls are implemented correctly, operating as intended, and producing the desired outcome with respect to meeting established security and privacy requirements.

Conduct a complete independent assessment of all security and privacy controls over a three (3) year period — either via a full controls assessment, annual assessments of the controls designated for years one through three, or per CMS guidance on testing for each significant system change — with the complete and final ATC package delivered to CMS no less than ninety (90) days prior to ATC expiration.

Include, at [Specialized Assessment Frequency], announced or unannounced specialized assessments as part of the control assessments, such as in-depth monitoring, security instrumentation, automated security test cases, vulnerability scanning, malicious user testing, insider threat assessment, performance and load testing, data leakage or data loss assessment, or other organization-defined forms of assessment.

Leverage the results of control assessments performed by organization-defined external organizations on organization-defined systems when the assessment meets organization-defined requirements; for FedRAMP, any FedRAMP-recognized independent assessment service qualifies.
Produce a control assessment report documenting the results of the assessment.

Provide the results of the control assessment in writing, within thirty (30) days after the assessment's completion, to the organization-defined individuals or roles — which for FedRAMP include FedRAMP and agency customers, and for ARC-AMPE include the Business Owner responsible for the system and personnel responsible for reviewing assessment documentation.

Update relevant security and privacy documentation to reflect any changes to the system within thirty (30) days of the changes or within thirty (30) days of the control assessment results, and notify CMS within thirty (30) days whenever updates are made to system security and privacy authorization artifacts or when significant role changes occur.

Develop a plan of action and milestones (POA&M) for the system to document the planned remediation actions to correct weaknesses or deficiencies noted during the assessment of the controls and to reduce or eliminate known vulnerabilities in the system.
Base the POA&M on the CMS Standard for POA&M Management and Reporting using the CMS-provided template, and remediate POA&M entries consistent with SI-2.

Establish and maintain the POA&M throughout the system lifecycle starting with development, including scheduled completion dates, milestones with dates, appropriate risk levels, as-detailed-as-possible weakness descriptions, and all findings whether self-discovered or identified through assessments.

Update the existing POA&M in accordance with the frequency documented in the organization's Information Security Continuous Monitoring (ISCM) strategy, based on findings from control assessments, independent audits or reviews, and continuous monitoring activities.
Deliver a fully updated and accurate POA&M to CMS quarterly on 31 January, 30 April, 31 July, and 31 October.
Ensure the accuracy, currency, and availability of the POA&M using [Automated Mechanism], and track entries in the [Ticketing System].
Assign a senior official as the Authorizing Official for the system, and record the assignment in the authorization decision record.
Assign a senior official as the Authorizing Official for common controls available for inheritance by organizational systems.

Before commencing operations, ensure the Authorizing Official for the system accepts the use of common controls inherited by the system and authorizes the system to operate; record the acceptance and authorization decision.
Ensure the Authorizing Official for common controls authorizes the use of those controls for inheritance by organizational systems, and record the decision.

Update authorizations at [Authorization Update Frequency]; for ARC-AMPE, this means at least every three (3) years for all entities (except Direct Enrollment Technology Providers, which must update at least every one (1) year), when significant security breaches occur, whenever there is a significant change to the system or its operating environment, or prior to expiration of the current authorization.

Notify CMS of significant or major changes to architecture, security and privacy posture, or other items that could cause degradation or unexpected results in security and privacy monitoring, detection, response, and mitigation activities, prior to making the change.
Where a joint authorization applies, employ a joint authorization process for the system that includes multiple Authorizing Officials from the same organization conducting the authorization.

Where an external joint authorization applies, employ a joint authorization process that includes multiple Authorizing Officials with at least one Authorizing Official from an organization external to the organization conducting the authorization.

Develop a system-level continuous monitoring strategy and implement continuous monitoring in accordance with the organization-level continuous monitoring strategy, including the organization's ISCM strategy considerations.
Establish system-level metrics to be monitored, based on the organization's security and privacy goals and ISCM strategy.

Establish frequencies for monitoring and for assessment of control effectiveness; for ARC-AMPE, this includes at least once-a-month scans of operating systems, databases, and web applications, and control effectiveness assessment no less than at least every one (1) year.
Conduct ongoing control assessments in accordance with the continuous monitoring strategy.

Conduct ongoing monitoring of system and organization-defined metrics in accordance with the continuous monitoring strategy, including monitoring of systems, appliances, devices, and applications (including databases).
Perform correlation and analysis of information generated by control assessments and monitoring.
Take response actions to address the results of the analysis of control assessment and monitoring information.

Report the security and privacy status of the system to the organization-defined personnel or roles at least every thirty (30) days (monthly) for ARC-AMPE, and at [Status Reporting Frequency] otherwise.

Maintain continuous monitoring records until released by the investigating authority when subject to a legal investigation (e.g., of an insider threat), and provide oversight of information security and privacy, including Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) as applicable, for each system.
Follow the FedRAMP Continuous Collaborative Monitoring, Significant Change Notification, Vulnerability Detection and Response, and Vulnerability Evaluation and Reporting rules.

Employ independent assessors or assessment teams to monitor the controls in the system on an ongoing basis, following the CMS Framework for Independent Assessment of Security and Privacy Controls where applicable.

Employ trend analyses to determine if control implementations, the frequency of continuous monitoring activities, and the types of activities used in the continuous monitoring process need to be modified based on empirical data.

Make risk monitoring an integral part of the continuous monitoring strategy — including effectiveness monitoring, compliance monitoring, and change monitoring — and update the continuous monitoring strategy to document the processes and guidance for each.
Employ [Validation Actions] to validate that policies are established and implemented controls are operating in a consistent manner.
Ensure the accuracy, currency, and availability of monitoring results for the system using [Automated Mechanism].

Conduct penetration testing at least every one (1) year (for ARC-AMPE) or at [Penetration Test Frequency] otherwise, on the organization-defined systems or system components, in accordance with rules of engagement agreed upon with the penetration testers.
Treat penetration testing as part of vulnerability detection, subject to the FedRAMP Vulnerability Detection and Response rules.

Employ an independent penetration testing agent or team to perform the testing; for ARC-AMPE, the independent penetration agent or team must be approved by the organization's Chief Information Security Officer (CISO) or equivalent.

Penetration-test the documented system and its full boundary as documented in the System Security and Privacy Plan (SSPP) to maintain authorization, and perform additional penetration tests when new risks and threats potentially affecting the system/applications are identified and reported or upon request from CMS.

Agree upon and co-sign the Penetration Testing Rules of Engagement — including the scope of systems or components to be tested and any exclusions — between the system Authorizing Official and the penetration testing organization official before commencing testing.

Include evaluation of embedded structures (e.g., content that can be changed without reloading the anchor content) and interactive content in penetration test scanning, with information sources including systems, appliances, devices, services, and applications (including databases).

Keep penetration test scanning results searchable by the organization and in a CMS-compliant format, and implement organization-directed penetration test information collection rules/requests (e.g., sources, queries, data calls) within the specified timeframe.
Conduct penetration testing on production systems in a manner that minimizes the risk of information corruption or service outage.

Provide penetration testing reports to CMS that summarize findings, articulate the significance, impact, and risk of the findings, and provide remediation plans, including the underlying raw security information/results in unaltered format.
Employ [Red-Team Exercise Frequency] red-team exercises to simulate attempts by adversaries to compromise organizational systems in accordance with applicable rules of engagement.

Employ a penetration testing process that includes [Physical Access Bypass Testing Frequency] announced or unannounced attempts to bypass or circumvent controls associated with physical access points to the facility.

The Security Program / GRC team is authorized to perform and accountable for all steps in this procedure end to end, including policy maintenance, risk assessment execution, assessment coordination, POA&M management, and evidence retention.

The Authorizing Official (a designated senior official) approves categorization decisions, assessment plans, rules of engagement, and authorization decisions; the CISO approves independent penetration testers; and exceptions — including risk acceptances — require discussion with CMS prior to acceptance and approval by the Authorizing Official.
