analyze: This procedure directs the Third-Party Risk team through establishing, approving, documenting, monitoring, and terminating information exchange and vendor relationships so that every external party handling organizational data — including business associates handling electronic protected health information (ePHI) — operates under executed agreements, verified controls, and managed supply chain risk.
Executing it produces the retained evidence of this process: executed business associate agreements and vendor security review records.

The Third-Party Risk team performs this procedure for all internal and external parties that exchange information with, provide system services to, or handle ePHI or other sensitive data on behalf of Example Org, including business associates, subcontractors, external system service providers, and supply chain entities.
Legal counsel, the senior privacy officer, contracting officers, the Authorizing Official, and senior cybersecurity or privacy officials participate in defined steps.
- Access to the organization's contract repository `[Contract Repository]` for storing and retrieving executed agreements
- Access to the vendor inventory and tracking system `[Vendor Management System]`
- Access to the ticketing and workflow system `[Ticketing System]` for recording reviews, approvals, and notifications
- Access to the identity and access management system `[Identity Provider]` for verifying transfer authorizations
- Engagement of legal counsel, the senior privacy officer, and contracting officers for contract review
- Designation of the Authorizing Official with authority to order interconnection termination or suspension
- Designation of the supply chain risk management (SCRM) official(s) and SCRM team members
- The current supply chain risk management policy and supply chain risk management plan
- The current HIPAA Security Rule policy documentation set
Identify each proposed exchange of information between the organizational system and another system, and record it in `[Vendor Management System]`.

Select the appropriate agreement type for the exchange — interconnection security agreement, information exchange security agreement, memorandum of understanding or agreement, service level agreement, user agreement, non-disclosure agreement, or another organization-defined agreement type `[Agreement Type Definition]`.
Draft the agreement with legal counsel and the senior privacy officer, covering the security and privacy obligations of both parties.
Submit the draft to Third-Party Risk for review, then to the designated approver `[Agreement Approver]` for signature.

Do not permit any information sharing to begin until the agreement is fully approved and executed; store the executed agreement in `[Contract Repository]` as part of the vendor security review record.
As part of drafting each agreement, document the interface characteristics of the exchange: protocols, ports, data flows, connection methods, and endpoints for each system.
Document the security and privacy requirements and the specific controls each system must apply to the exchanged information.
Document the responsibilities of each system's owner for operating, monitoring, and securing the interface.
Document the impact level of the information communicated across the interface.
Retain the completed documentation with the executed agreement in `[Contract Repository]`.
Third-Party Risk maintains a review calendar in `[Vendor Management System]` scheduling every information exchange agreement for review at least every one (1) year.
On each scheduled review, verify with the system owner that the interface characteristics, controls, responsibilities, and impact level recorded in the agreement still match the exchange as operated.

Update the agreement whenever significant changes to the system, the organizations, or the nature of the information sharing could affect its validity or security posture, and route the update through the approval step above.
Record the review outcome and date in the vendor security review record in `[Contract Repository]`.

For every agreement involving internal or external parties, enter into an MOU, MOA, Letter of Intent, Computer Matching Agreement, Information Exchange Agreement, or similar instrument that specifically describes the Personally Identifiable Information (PII) covered.

Enumerate in the agreement the purposes for which the PII may be used, and confirm with the senior privacy officer that each purpose is compatible with the purpose for which the PII was originally collected.

When a party proposes a use that is incompatible with the original collection purpose, block the sharing until all of the following are complete: additional notice is provided to the individual, the individual's consent is obtained, and the relevant documents are updated or published.
Record the consent and notice actions in `[Ticketing System]` before releasing the sharing restriction.

Confirm in writing that the Authorizing Official or other senior leadership holds documented authority to order the immediate termination and/or suspension of any interconnection, and record this designation in the security and privacy documentation.
When senior cybersecurity or privacy officials judge that an interconnection presents an unacceptable level of risk, escalate the judgment to the Authorizing Official with supporting rationale.

Upon the Authorizing Official's order, Third-Party Risk coordinates immediate termination or suspension of the interconnection, notifies the connected party per the agreement's terms, and records the action and rationale in `[Ticketing System]`.

Before accepting data transferred between interconnecting systems, open `[Identity Provider]` and verify that the individual or system initiating the transfer holds the requisite authorizations, such as write permissions or privileges, on the receiving system.
Reject any transfer from an individual or system whose authorizations cannot be verified, and record the rejection in `[Ticketing System]`.
Re-verify authorizations whenever the interconnection agreement is reviewed or updated.

Using the systems named in each approved exchange agreement, map any downstream (transitive) exchanges — exchanges those systems in turn conduct with other systems using the organization's information.
Record each identified transitive exchange and its downstream system in `[Vendor Management System]`.

Verify and validate the controls on each identified downstream system; where verification cannot be completed, take measures to ensure the transitive exchange ceases, coordinating with the upstream party per the agreement.
Re-run this mapping during the annual agreement review.

Third-Party Risk, with the security team, maintains written policies and procedures for authorizing access to electronic protected health information, consistent with the applicable requirements of 45 CFR part 164 subpart E.
Store the policies in the HIPAA documentation set and disseminate them to personnel responsible for access administration.
If a health care clearinghouse is part of a larger organization, implement policies and procedures that protect the clearinghouse's ePHI from unauthorized access by the larger organization.
Configure logical segregation in `[Identity Provider]` and the clearinghouse systems so that larger-organization personnel without a documented clearinghouse role cannot access clearinghouse ePHI.
Implement policies and procedures for granting access to ePHI through each access mechanism in use — workstation, transaction, program, process, or other mechanism.
Apply these procedures whenever a new access mechanism is introduced or an existing one changes.
Based on the organization's access authorization policies, establish each user's right of access to a workstation, transaction, program, or process at the time access is requested.
Document each granted right in `[Identity Provider]` and the associated access record.
Review user access rights on the defined review cycle `[Access Review Frequency]` and modify or revoke rights when the user's role changes or the right is no longer required.

Before permitting any business associate to create, receive, maintain, or transmit ePHI on the organization's behalf, obtain satisfactory assurances, in accordance with 45 CFR § 164.314(a), that the business associate will appropriately safeguard the information.

When a business associate proposes to permit a subcontractor to handle ePHI on its behalf, require the business associate to obtain the same satisfactory assurances from the subcontractor before the subcontractor begins handling.
Record the obtained assurances in the vendor security review record.

Document the satisfactory assurances provided by each business associate — and each subcontractor — through a written contract or other arrangement that meets the applicable requirements of § 164.314(a).
Route the contract through legal counsel for review, obtain signatures from the authorized signatories, and store the executed business associate agreement in `[Contract Repository]`.
Do not permit ePHI flows to begin until the executed agreement is on file.
Verify that every business associate contract provides that the business associate will comply with the applicable requirements of the HIPAA Security Rule subpart.

Verify the contract requires the business associate to ensure that any subcontractors that create, receive, maintain, or transmit ePHI on its behalf agree to comply, by entering into a contract or other arrangement that complies with § 164.314.

Verify the contract requires the business associate to report to the organization any security incident of which it becomes aware, including breaches of unsecured protected health information as required by § 164.410.
Where any required term is missing, return the contract to legal counsel for correction before execution.

When reviewing a subcontractor arrangement, verify that the same contract requirements that apply between the organization and its business associate apply in the same manner to the contract or other arrangement between the business associate and its subcontractor.
Obtain a copy or attestation of the subcontractor agreement and file it with the parent business associate agreement in `[Contract Repository]`.
Where a written business associate contract is not used, verify that another arrangement in place meets the requirements of § 164.504(e)(3).
Have legal counsel confirm the alternative arrangement's sufficiency and record the confirmation in the vendor security review record.

Except where limited exceptions apply, verify that the group health plan's plan documents require the plan sponsor to reasonably and appropriately safeguard ePHI created, received, maintained, or transmitted on the plan's behalf.
Amend the plan documents as needed to require the plan sponsor to implement administrative, physical, and technical safeguards protecting the ePHI's confidentiality, integrity, and availability.
Verify the plan documents support the adequate separation required by § 164.504(f)(2)(iii) with reasonable and appropriate security measures.

Verify that any agent to whom the plan provides the information agrees to implement reasonable and appropriate security measures, and that the plan documents require the sponsor to report to the group health plan any security incident of which it becomes aware.

For each provider of external system services, require in the service contract or agreement that the provider comply with organizational security and privacy requirements and employ the organization-defined controls `[External Provider Control Set]`.
Verify the provider's acceptance of these requirements before service activation and record it in the vendor security review record.
Define and document the organization's oversight roles and responsibilities with regard to each external system service, assigning oversight to Third-Party Risk.
Define and document the user roles and responsibilities for personnel consuming the external service.
Store the role definitions with the service agreement in `[Contract Repository]` and update them at each annual review.
Employ the organization's defined processes, methods, and techniques `[Provider Monitoring Methods]` to monitor control compliance by each external service provider on an ongoing basis.
Third-Party Risk records each monitoring activity and its findings as a vendor security review record in `[Contract Repository]`.
Escalate identified compliance gaps to the provider and track remediation in `[Ticketing System]`.
Include in each service contract or agreement language requiring the provider to be subject to U.S. federal laws and regulations protecting PII.
Include language requiring adherence to the organization's security and privacy policies and standards consistent with 45 CFR § 155.260(b).
Include language defining the security and privacy roles and responsibilities of both parties.
Consult legal counsel, the senior privacy officer, and contracting officers about applicable laws, directives, policies, or regulations affecting implementation before finalizing the language.
Before any acquisition or outsourcing of information security services, conduct an organizational assessment of risk and document the assessment outcome.
Verify that the acquisition or outsourcing of dedicated information security services is approved by the organization-defined personnel or roles `[Outsourcing Approver]` before contracting.
File the risk assessment and approval with the vendor security review record.
Require each provider of external system services to identify the functions, ports, protocols, and other services required for the use of such services.
For all external systems where federal customer data is processed or stored, apply this requirement per FedRAMP.
Record the provider's identification in the service agreement documentation and validate it against the interface characteristics documented under the CA-3 steps.

Restrict the location of information processing, information or data, and system services to the organization-defined locations `[Approved Locations]` based on the organization-defined requirements `[Location Requirements]`.

Per FedRAMP, for Certification Classes C and D apply this restriction to information processing, information or data, and system services for all federal customer data; for Certification Class D, restrict locations to within the U.S. or U.S. Territories or geographic locations under U.S. jurisdiction.
Restrict the geographic location of information processing and data storage to facilities located within the legal jurisdictional boundary of the United States.

Ensure PII of the system is processed and stored within the continental U.S., Hawaii, or U.S. Territories; support, development, and IT services may be off-shored only after Third-Party Risk weighs that risk and documents the assessment.
In no case permit safeguards afforded to sensitive information to be less than those mandated by state regulation, federal law, Executive Order, or other authoritative direction.
For organizations processing Federal Tax Information, verify adherence to IRS Publication 1075.

For ARC-AMPE Administering Entities, notify CMS at least sixty (60) days prior to committing to outsourcing information system services outside the U.S., such as by contract award or services purchase, and at least sixty (60) days prior to transmitting data into an external information service environment per Change Notification guidance; record each notification in `[Ticketing System]`.
For encrypted material stored or transmitted through an external system, configure key management so the organization retains exclusive control of the cryptographic keys.
Verify in the provider arrangement that the provider cannot access, export, or escrow the keys, and record the verification in the vendor security review record.
Establish with the external system provider the capability to check the integrity of information while it resides in the external system.
Exercise the integrity-check capability during provider monitoring and record the results in the vendor security review record.

Develop and document a supply chain risk management policy addressing purpose, scope, roles, responsibilities, management commitment, coordination among organizational entities, and compliance, consistent with applicable laws, executive orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, and guidelines.
Develop procedures to facilitate implementation of the policy and the associated SCRM controls.
Disseminate the policy and procedures to the organization-defined personnel or roles `[SCRM Policy Distribution]`.
Ensure the policy and procedures support cybersecurity and privacy safeguards to the greatest extent feasible throughout the system's life cycle and for the information on that system.
Designate the official(s) responsible for managing the development, documentation, and dissemination of the supply chain risk management policy and procedures.
Name the designated official(s) in the appropriate security and privacy documents.
Third-Party Risk schedules review and update of the supply chain risk management policy and procedures at least every one (1) year.

Also review and update following organization-defined events: assessment or audit findings, security or privacy incidents, and changes to applicable laws, executive orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, and guidelines.
Actively monitor for changes to applicable privacy laws and trigger an off-cycle review when a relevant change is identified.
Record each review and update in the HIPAA/SCRM documentation record.

Maintain the policies and procedures implemented to comply with the HIPAA Security Rule in written (which may be electronic) form, and maintain a written (which may be electronic) record of any action, activity, or assessment the rule requires to be documented.
Retain all HIPAA documentation for 6 years from the date of its creation or the date when it last was in effect, whichever is later.
Make the documentation available to those persons responsible for implementing the procedures to which it pertains.
Review the documentation periodically `[HIPAA Documentation Review Frequency]` and update it as needed in response to environmental or operational changes affecting the security of ePHI.

Develop, document, and maintain a plan for managing supply chain risks associated with the research and development, design, manufacturing, acquisition, delivery, integration, operations and maintenance, and disposal of the organization-defined systems, system components, or system services `[Systems in Plan Scope]`.

Address in the plan: risk tolerance, acceptable mitigation strategies or controls, a process for consistently evaluating and monitoring supply chain risk, approaches for implementing and communicating the plan, justification for mitigation measures, associated roles and responsibilities, and requirements for developing trustworthy, secure, privacy-protective, and resilient components and systems.
Third-Party Risk schedules review and update of the supply chain risk management plan at least every one (1) year, or as required to address threat, organizational, or environmental changes.
Record each review and the resulting changes in the plan's version history.
Apply access restrictions in `[Contract Repository]` so the supply chain risk management plan is readable and modifiable only by authorized personnel.
Verify the restrictions during the annual plan review.
Establish a supply chain risk management team consisting of the organization-defined personnel, roles, and responsibilities to lead and support the organization's SCRM activities.

Per ARC-AMPE, include diverse functions on the team: risk executive, information technology, contracting, information security, privacy, mission or business, legal, supply chain and logistics, acquisition, and business continuity.
Refer to NIST SP 800-161 and NISTIR 8276 for guidance on SCRM activities.
Record team membership and responsibilities in the SCRM plan.

Assess and review the supply chain-related risks associated with each supplier or contractor and the system, system component, or system service it provides, on the defined assessment cycle `[Supplier Assessment Frequency]`.
Cover in each assessment: the supplier's security and SCRM processes, foreign ownership, control or influence, and the supplier's ability to assess its subordinate second- and third-tier suppliers.
Record each assessment as a vendor security review record in `[Contract Repository]`.

Employ organizational or independent third-party analysis and/or testing of the organization-defined supply chain elements, processes, and actors associated with the system, system component, or system service `[Supply Chain Elements for Testing]`.
Retain the analysis and testing results with the vendor security review record.

Establish agreements and procedures with each entity involved in the supply chain for the system, system component, or system service, requiring notification of supply chain compromises and of the results of assessments or audits.
Follow the FedRAMP Incident Evaluation and Communication rules for supply chain notifications.
Ensure notifications of supply chain incidents are consistent with the organization's incident handling and incident reporting procedures.

When a supply chain compromise notification is received, Third-Party Risk logs it in `[Ticketing System]`, routes it into the incident handling process, and records the disposition in the vendor security review record.

The Third-Party Risk team is accountable for this process end to end: it executes the reviews, maintains the agreement and vendor records, coordinates monitoring, and answers for the outcome of each step.

Legal counsel, the senior privacy officer, contracting officers, the security and privacy teams, and the SCRM team participate in the steps where named; the Authorizing Official or other senior leadership approves agreements and holds sole authority to order interconnection termination or suspension, and approves any exception to this procedure.

analyze: This procedure provides the step-by-step operational instructions for Infrastructure Security to execute the Example Org Vulnerability & Patch Management Standard: scanning Example Org systems for vulnerabilities, remediating or patching them within defined timeframes, and producing the evidence (scan results with remediation SLAs and the patch compliance report) that demonstrates compliance.

This procedure is performed by Infrastructure Security on all information technology components within the Example Org security boundary, including hosted applications, with participation from System Administrators, the Configuration Management process, and the CIO/CISO for authorizations and exceptions.
- Authorized accounts with privileged access to the [Vulnerability Scanning Tool], credentialed for authenticated scanning on all in-scope components
- Authorized accounts with privileged access to the [Patch Management Tool]
- Access to the [Ticketing System] for remediation tracking
- Access to the [Audit Log Platform] for historic log review
- Access to the [Configuration Management System] for change integration and risk-based exception documentation
- Access to the [POA&M Repository] and the [Document Repository] for evidence retention
- An operational [Vulnerability Disclosure Portal] for receiving external vulnerability reports
- A designated official accountable for the system and information integrity policy and procedures
- Distribution list access to system security personnel and administrators with configuration/patch-management responsibilities

The designated official develops and documents the system and information integrity policy, addressing purpose, scope, roles, responsibilities, management commitment, coordination among organizational entities, and compliance, and ensures consistency with applicable laws, executive orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, and guidelines.
The designated official develops and documents the supporting procedures (including this document) that facilitate implementation of the policy and associated controls.
Disseminate the policy and procedures to organization-defined personnel or roles via the [Document Repository], and confirm receipt by Infrastructure Security and affected system owners.

Review and update the policy and procedures at least every one (1) year, and additionally following assessment or audit findings, security or privacy incidents, and changes to applicable laws, executive orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, or guidelines.

Monitor for changes to applicable privacy laws, regulations, and overarching policy affecting system and information integrity policies no less often than at least every one (1) year, and record the review outcome in the [Document Repository].

Implement and follow the policies and procedures in this document that protect electronic protected health information (ePHI) from improper alteration or destruction, including the vulnerability remediation and patching steps below.

Implement and operate electronic mechanisms (for example, integrity verification features of the [Vulnerability Scanning Tool] and file-integrity monitoring within the [Audit Log Platform]) that corroborate ePHI has not been altered or destroyed in an unauthorized manner.
Maintain all policies, procedures, and records of actions, activities, and assessments required by this procedure in written (electronic) form in the [Document Repository].
Retain all required documentation for 6 years from the date of its creation or the date when it last was in effect, whichever is later.
Make the documentation available in the [Document Repository] to the persons responsible for implementing the procedures to which it pertains.
Review the documentation periodically and update it as needed in response to environmental or operational changes affecting the security of ePHI.

Configure the [Vulnerability Scanning Tool] to scan the system and hosted applications every thirty (30) calendar days, and to launch ad hoc scans when new vulnerabilities potentially affecting the system are identified and reported.

Update the vulnerabilities to be scanned in the [Vulnerability Scanning Tool] prior to each new scan and whenever new vulnerabilities are identified and reported; use a tool with the capability to readily update the vulnerabilities to be scanned.
Verify the scan scope fully covers the ACA boundary and all its components, per the documented breadth and depth of scanning coverage, before launching the scan.

Use scanning tools and techniques that facilitate interoperability by employing standards for enumerating platforms, software flaws, and improper configurations; formatting checklists and test procedures; and measuring vulnerability impact.
Follow the FedRAMP Vulnerability Detection and Response and Vulnerability Evaluation and Reporting rules, and their enhancements, for all vulnerability monitoring and scanning activity.
Retain the raw scan results in an unaltered format in the [Document Repository] as the scan results evidence artifact, tagged with the remediation SLAs applied to each finding.
Run the discovery/enumeration function of the [Vulnerability Scanning Tool] to determine what information about the system is discoverable by external parties.
Review the discovery output for information that should not be exposed.
Take corrective actions (for example, removing exposed services or metadata) for any unacceptable discoverable information, and record the actions in the [Ticketing System].
Implement privileged access authorization to the organization-defined system components used for vulnerability scanning activities, requesting the access through the [Access Request System].
Ensure privileged scan credentials are authorized for all components that support authentication for all scans.
Configure the scanning tool's automated functionality to perform credentialed scans, and ensure the scan credentials comply with organizational credential policy to the extent possible.
Analyze each vulnerability scan report and the results from ongoing vulnerability monitoring, distinguishing legitimate vulnerabilities from false positives.
Compare the results of the current scan against prior scans using the automated comparison mechanism of the [Vulnerability Scanning Tool] to identify new, resolved, and persistent findings.
Correlate output across scanning tools to determine the presence of multi-vulnerability and multi-hop attack vectors, and flag any correlated attack paths as findings in their own right.

For each vulnerability identified in the scan results, query the [Audit Log Platform] to determine whether that vulnerability has been previously exploited within the organization-defined time period.

If evidence of exploitation is found, escalate immediately to Infrastructure Security leadership and open a high-priority incident record in the [Ticketing System] before proceeding with standard remediation.
Maintain the [Vulnerability Disclosure Portal] as a public reporting channel for receiving reports of vulnerabilities in organizational systems and system components.
Monitor the channel on an ongoing basis; triage each inbound report, validate it through an ad hoc scan or analysis, and route confirmed vulnerabilities into the remediation workflow below.

Share information obtained from the vulnerability monitoring process and control assessments with organization-defined personnel or roles — at minimum, affected and related stakeholders — to help eliminate similar vulnerabilities in other systems.
Incorporate all vulnerability scan findings and identified weaknesses into the Plan of Action and Milestones (POA&M) in the [POA&M Repository].
Provide timely responses to informational requests and scheduled Information Security and Privacy Continuous Monitoring (ISCM) submission requirements to CMS as applicable.
Deliver vulnerability scans to CMS quarterly on 31 January, 30 April, 31 July, and 31 October.

Assign each legitimate vulnerability a remediation ticket in the [Ticketing System] with a due date set from the following SLAs, in accordance with the organization's assessment of risk: Critical severity within fifteen (15) calendar days, High severity within thirty (30) calendar days, Moderate severity within ninety (90) calendar days, and Low severity within one (1) year.
Route each ticket to the responsible system administrator for remediation; Infrastructure Security tracks all tickets to closure.
Record the SLA due date and closure date on each ticket so the scan results evidence artifact reflects remediation SLA performance.
Identify and report system flaws through the scanning, alert, and disclosure-channel workflows above, and correct them via the remediation workflow.
Test software and firmware updates related to flaw remediation for effectiveness and potential side effects before installation, using the validation tier of the environment.
Install security-relevant software and firmware updates within thirty (30) days of the release of the updates.
Incorporate all flaw remediation into the organizational configuration management process by raising the corresponding change records in the [Configuration Management System].

Run the automated compliance check in the [Patch Management Tool] at least monthly to determine whether all system components have applicable security-relevant software and firmware updates installed.
Use automated mechanisms for updating security-relevant software and firmware to the maximum extent possible.
Record the results of the monthly compliance check in the patch compliance report and store it in the [Document Repository].
For each flaw, measure the time between flaw identification and flaw remediation using the timestamps in the [Ticketing System].
Compare measured remediation times against the organization-defined benchmarks for taking corrective actions, and escalate any breach of a benchmark to Infrastructure Security leadership.
Employ the automated patch management tools in the [Patch Management Tool] to facilitate flaw remediation across the organization-defined system components.
Patch on at least a monthly basis to ensure all systems within the purview of the organization are up to date with the most current security patches.
Apply each patch first to a lower-tier information technology environment and complete a validation period there before production servers receive the patch.
Where the organization-defined components and updates support it, configure the [Patch Management Tool] to install the security-relevant software and firmware updates automatically.

After an updated version of a software or firmware component has been installed and validated, remove the previous version for all upgraded or replaced components that are no longer required for operation.
Record the removal in the corresponding change record in the [Configuration Management System].
For each remediation failure, missed SLA, or recurring vulnerability, conduct a root cause analysis to identify the underlying cause.
Develop actions to address the root cause, implement them, and monitor those actions for effectiveness in subsequent scan and patch cycles.
If a security patch will not be applied to an information technology component, or a legacy component no longer maintained by the vendor remains in use, conduct a risk analysis of the component.

Document the risk-based decision through the configuration management process in the form of written authorization from the organization's Chief Information Officer (CIO) or designee (for example, the system data owner or CISO), filed in the [Configuration Management System].

Apply the flaw remediation requirements of this procedure to all information technology components for which a patch or work-around exists for each vendor-identified and/or CVE/CWE-identified vulnerability.
Provide timely responses, as defined by the CISO, to informational requests for organizational flaw (patch) status and posture information, drawing on the patch compliance report and scan results.

Receive system security alerts, advisories, and directives from the organization-defined external organizations (for example, vendor advisories and US-CERT/CISA feeds) on an ongoing basis, via the subscription channels configured by Infrastructure Security.
Generate internal security alerts, advisories, and directives as deemed necessary based on scan findings, exploitation evidence, or external advisories.

Disseminate security alerts, advisories, and directives to organization-defined personnel or roles, elements, and/or external organizations — at a minimum, to system security personnel and administrators with configuration/patch-management responsibilities.
Implement security directives in accordance with the established time frames; if a directive cannot be implemented in time, notify the issuing organization of the degree of noncompliance.
Follow the FedRAMP Addressing FedRAMP Communication rules for security alerts, advisories, and directives.
Broadcast security alert and advisory information throughout the organization using the organization-defined automated mechanism ([Broadcast Communication Mechanism]).
Infrastructure Security owns this process end to end: it executes the scans, analysis, remediation tracking, patching, reporting, and evidence production, and answers for the outcome.

System Administrators, the Configuration Management function, and the CIO/CISO participate as named in individual steps, and the CIO or designee (e.g., system data owner or CISO) reviews and approves risk-based exceptions to patching.

analyze: This procedure provides the step-by-step operational instructions for Infrastructure Security to execute Example Org's vulnerability monitoring, flaw remediation, and security alerting requirements as defined in the Example Org Information Security Standard: Vulnerability and Patch Management.
Executing this procedure produces the required evidence artifacts: scan results with remediation SLAs and the patch compliance report.

This procedure is performed by Infrastructure Security on all information technology components within the ACA boundary, including systems, hosted applications, supporting operating systems, telecommunications, and configuration components.
System owners, IT operations, the CIO, and the CISO participate in defined steps as stated below.
- Authorized access to the [Vulnerability Scanning Tool] with administrative rights to configure scan content, schedules, and scan credentials.
- Credentialed scan accounts compliant with organizational access policy, provisioned per [Identity Provider] and authorized for privileged access to all components that support authentication.
- Access to the [Ticketing System] for recording, assigning, and tracking vulnerabilities and flaw remediation work.
- Access to the [Patch Management Tool] and the [Test Environment] for staging and evaluating updates.
- Access to the [Configuration Management Process] for change approval and risk-based authorization records.
- Access to the [Audit Log Platform] for historic log review.
- Access to the [POA&M System] for recording weaknesses and remediation plans.
- Access to the [Automated Compliance Mechanism] for verifying update installation status.
- A designated public vulnerability reporting channel ([Public Reporting Channel]) and monitored intake (e.g., a monitored security mailbox or web form).
- Subscriptions to external alert sources ([External Alert Sources], e.g., CISA, vendor advisories, supply chain partners).
- Current copies of the system and information integrity policy and supporting procedures, available to all personnel with implementation responsibilities.

Infrastructure Security maintains the system and information integrity policy and these implementing procedures in written (electronic is acceptable) form, addressing purpose, scope, roles, responsibilities, management commitment, coordination among organizational entities, and compliance, consistent with applicable laws, regulations, and standards.

Infrastructure Security designates the official responsible for developing, documenting, and disseminating the policy and procedures, and ensures that official is named in the appropriate security and privacy documents.

Infrastructure Security disseminates the policy and procedures to organization-defined personnel and roles, and makes the documentation available to every person responsible for implementing the procedures to which it pertains, via [Document Management System].

Infrastructure Security reviews and updates the policy and procedures at least every one (1) year, and additionally following: assessment or audit findings; security or privacy incidents; and changes to applicable laws, executive orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, or guidelines.
As part of each review, Infrastructure Security monitors for changes to applicable privacy laws, regulations, and overarching policy no less often than annually.

Infrastructure Security reviews the documentation periodically and updates it as needed in response to environmental or operational changes affecting the security of electronic protected health information.

Infrastructure Security retains all documentation produced under this procedure, including a written record of any action, activity, or assessment required to be documented, for 6 years from the date of its creation or the date it was last in effect, whichever is later.

Infrastructure Security maintains policies and procedures governing the integrity of electronic protected health information, ensuring that only authorized changes are made and that destruction occurs only through authorized processes.

Infrastructure Security implements electronic mechanisms to corroborate that electronic protected health information has not been altered or destroyed in an unauthorized manner, including integrity checking and monitoring capabilities configured in [Integrity Monitoring Mechanism].

Infrastructure Security verifies the operation of these mechanisms as part of each monthly vulnerability monitoring cycle and records the verification outcome alongside the scan results with remediation SLAs.

Infrastructure Security executes vulnerability scans of the system and hosted applications every thirty (30) calendar days, per the monthly cadence, and additionally whenever new vulnerabilities potentially affecting the system are identified and reported.

Before each scan, Infrastructure Security updates the vulnerabilities to be scanned in the [Vulnerability Scanning Tool] — both prior to a new scan and when new vulnerabilities are identified and reported — using the tool's vulnerability content update capability, so the tool's scan definitions are current.

Infrastructure Security configures and maintains the scanning tool and techniques to facilitate interoperability among tools and automate parts of the vulnerability management process, using standards for enumerating platforms, software flaws, and improper configurations (e.g., CPE, CVE, CWE), formatting checklists and test procedures, and measuring vulnerability impact (e.g., CVSS).

Infrastructure Security defines and maintains the breadth and depth of scan coverage such that the vulnerability scan fully covers the ACA boundary and all its components; the scan target inventory in the [Vulnerability Scanning Tool] is reconciled against the asset inventory before each monthly scan.

Infrastructure Security ensures privileged access authorization to all components that support authentication for all scans; where automated scanning tool functionality is used, scans must be credentialed, with credentials compliant with organizational policy to the extent possible.

Infrastructure Security conducts all vulnerability monitoring and scanning activities in accordance with the FedRAMP Vulnerability Detection and Response and Vulnerability Evaluation and Reporting rules, including any applicable enhancements.

Infrastructure Security retains the raw scan output in an unaltered format, available to the organization, together with the processed report, as part of the scan results with remediation SLAs evidence.

Infrastructure Security analyzes each vulnerability scan report and the results from vulnerability monitoring, and records the analysis in the [Ticketing System], retaining the raw results unaltered per the preceding subsection.

Infrastructure Security determines what information about the system is externally discoverable (e.g., via [External Discovery Review]) and takes [Assignment: organization-defined corrective actions] for any information that should not be exposed.

Infrastructure Security compares the results of the current scan against the previous scan(s) using [Assignment: organization-defined automated mechanisms] to identify new, persistent, and resolved findings.

For each identified vulnerability on an [Assignment: organization-defined system], Infrastructure Security reviews historic audit logs in the [Audit Log Platform] to determine whether the vulnerability has been previously exploited within an [Assignment: organization-defined time period]; if exploitation is suspected, Infrastructure Security escalates to the incident response process.

Infrastructure Security correlates output across vulnerability scanning tools to determine the presence of multi-vulnerability and multi-hop attack vectors, and documents any identified attack chains as higher-priority findings in the [Ticketing System].

Infrastructure Security creates a remediation ticket in the [Ticketing System] for each legitimate vulnerability, assigns it to the responsible system owner or IT operations team, and sets the remediation SLA per the organizational assessment of risk: Critical severity within fifteen (15) calendar days, High severity within thirty (30) calendar days, Moderate severity within ninety (90) calendar days, and Low severity within one (1) year.
Infrastructure Security incorporates all vulnerability scan findings and weaknesses into the POA&M in [POA&M System].

Infrastructure Security shares information obtained from the vulnerability monitoring process and control assessments with [Assignment: organization-defined personnel or roles] — affected and related stakeholders — to help eliminate similar vulnerabilities (systemic weaknesses or deficiencies) in other systems.

Infrastructure Security delivers vulnerability scans to CMS quarterly on 31 January, 30 April, 31 July, and 31 October, and provides timely responses to informational requests and scheduled ISCM submission requirements as applicable.

Infrastructure Security follows the FedRAMP Vulnerability Detection and Response and Vulnerability Evaluation and Reporting rules in conducting all flaw remediation activities, including the applicable enhancements.
Infrastructure Security identifies, reports, and corrects system flaws: new flaws are logged in the [Ticketing System], reported to the responsible component owner, and tracked to closure.
Flaw remediation requirements apply to all information technology components for which a patch or work-around exists for each vendor-identified and/or CVE/CWE-identified vulnerability.

IT Operations, coordinated by Infrastructure Security, tests security-relevant software and firmware updates (patches, service packs, hot fixes) for effectiveness and potential side effects in the [Test Environment] before installation on production systems.
IT Operations installs security-relevant software and firmware updates within thirty (30) days of the release of the updates, consistent with the ARC-AMPE requirement.

Remediation is completed within the severity timeframes: Critical within fifteen (15) calendar days, High within thirty (30) calendar days, Moderate within ninety (90) calendar days, and Low within one (1) year.

Infrastructure Security incorporates all flaw remediation into the organizational configuration management process in [Configuration Management Process], so that update installation is planned, approved, and recorded as configuration changes.

If a security patch will not be applied to an information technology component, or a legacy component remains in use and is no longer maintained by the vendor, Infrastructure Security conducts a risk analysis and documents the risk-based decision through the configuration management process as written authorization from the CIO or designee.
Infrastructure Security provides timely responses, as defined by the CISO, to informational requests for organizational flaw (patch) status and posture information.

Infrastructure Security measures the time between flaw identification and flaw remediation for each finding in the [Ticketing System], compares it against [Assignment: organization-defined benchmarks], and takes corrective action where benchmarks are exceeded.

For recurring issues, failed remediations, or exploited vulnerabilities, Infrastructure Security conducts a root cause analysis to identify the underlying cause, develops actions to address the root cause, implements the actions, and monitors the implementation for effectiveness.

Infrastructure Security operates the [Automated Compliance Mechanism] to determine whether system components have applicable security-relevant software and firmware updates installed, running the check at least monthly (ARC-AMPE requirement); automated mechanisms are used to the maximum extent possible.

Infrastructure Security employs automated patch management tools ([Patch Management Tool]) to facilitate flaw remediation on [Assignment: organization-defined components], patching on at least a monthly basis so all systems within the organization's purview carry the most current security patches.

Before production servers receive a patch, Infrastructure Security runs a validation period on the lower-tier information technology environment ([Test Environment]) per the deployment rings configured in the [Patch Management Tool].

Infrastructure Security configures [Assignment: organization-defined security-relevant software and firmware updates] to install automatically on [Assignment: organization-defined system components] via the [Patch Management Tool].

After updated versions are installed, IT Operations removes previous versions of [Assignment: organization-defined software and firmware components] that are no longer required for operation, and Infrastructure Security verifies removal in the monthly compliance check.
Infrastructure Security compiles the results of the automated compliance check and patch deployment into the patch compliance report and retains it with the monthly evidence artifacts.

Infrastructure Security subscribes to and receives system security alerts, advisories, and directives from [Assignment: organization-defined external organizations] — including supply chain partners, external mission or business partners, external service providers, CISA, and other organizations defined in the applicable system security and privacy plan — on an ongoing basis.
Infrastructure Security reviews incoming alerts and, as deemed necessary, generates internal security alerts, advisories, and directives.

Infrastructure Security disseminates security alerts, advisories, and directives to [Selection: assigned personnel/roles, elements, and external organizations]; at a minimum, dissemination goes to system security personnel and administrators with configuration/patch-management responsibilities, via [Security Distribution Mechanism].
Infrastructure Security broadcasts security alert and advisory information throughout the organization using [Assignment: organization-defined automated mechanisms].

Infrastructure Security implements received security directives in accordance with the established time frames stated in the directive, or, where compliance is not achievable, notifies the issuing organization of the degree of noncompliance and records the exception in the [Ticketing System].
Infrastructure Security follows the FedRAMP Addressing FedRAMP Communication rules for security alerts, advisories, and directives.
Infrastructure Security establishes and maintains a public reporting channel ([Public Reporting Channel]) for receiving reports of vulnerabilities in organizational systems and system components.

Infrastructure Security monitors the channel, triages each incoming report, validates legitimate findings, and routes them into the remediation workflow in the [Ticketing System] with the applicable severity SLA.
Infrastructure Security acknowledges receipt of external reports and coordinates disclosure per the FedRAMP Vulnerability Evaluation and Reporting rules.

Infrastructure Security is accountable for this process end to end: it executes scanning, analysis, alerting, tracking, evidence production, and reporting, and coordinates IT Operations, system owners, and the [Configuration Management Process] participants for remediation actions.

The CIO (or designee) approves written risk-based authorizations where patches will not be applied or unsupported legacy components remain in use, and the CISO defines timely response expectations for flaw status information requests; exceptions to any step in this procedure require review and approval by Infrastructure Security with escalation to the CIO or CISO as indicated.

analyze: This procedure provides the step-by-step operational instructions that Infrastructure Security and supporting personnel follow to schedule, authorize, perform, monitor, and record maintenance, repair, and replacement activities on Example Org systems, including on-site, off-site, and nonlocal (remote) maintenance.
Executing this procedure produces the evidence artifacts this process is accountable for: **maintenance records with authorization** and **remote maintenance session logs**.

This procedure is performed continuously by Infrastructure Security, which owns the process end to end, with participation from maintenance personnel, escorts, supervisors, and workforce members with access to electronic protected health information (ePHI).
It applies to all organizational systems and components subject to maintenance, repair, or replacement, including facilities housing such systems and any tools used to service them.
- Access to the [Maintenance Management System] for scheduling, recording, and reviewing maintenance actions
- Access to the [Ticketing System] for maintenance authorization and approval workflows
- Access to the [Audit Log Platform]/[SIEM] for logging and reviewing nonlocal maintenance sessions
- A current, approved copy of the *Example Org — System Maintenance Standard* and the maintenance policy maintained under this procedure
- A current list of authorized maintenance organizations and personnel, maintained by Infrastructure Security
- Named [Designated Policy Official] accountable for the maintenance policy and procedures
- Access to the latest published NIST SP 800-88 (media sanitization) and NIST SP 800-63B (authenticator assurance) guidance
- For each production system: the system's Contingency Plan, including its Recovery Time Objective (RTO), and its System Security and Privacy Plan
- For classified systems: documented clearance, access approval, and citizenship verification records

Infrastructure Security develops and documents the maintenance policy, covering purpose, scope, roles, responsibilities, management commitment, coordination among organizational entities, and compliance, and aligns it with applicable laws, regulations, and organizational standards.
Infrastructure Security documents the associated maintenance procedures (this document) to facilitate implementation of the policy and controls.
The [Designated Policy Official] manages the development, documentation, and dissemination of the policy and procedures.
Infrastructure Security disseminates the policy and procedures to all applicable personnel and roles and records dissemination in the [Ticketing System].

Infrastructure Security reviews and updates the policy and procedures at least every one (1) year, per ARC-AMPE, and additionally following [Review Trigger Events] such as assessment or audit findings, security or privacy incidents, or changes to applicable laws, regulations, policies, standards, or guidelines.
Infrastructure Security records each review and update as a maintenance record with authorization in the [Maintenance Management System].

Infrastructure Security schedules every maintenance, repair, and replacement action in the [Maintenance Management System] in accordance with manufacturer or vendor specifications or organizational requirements.
Before work begins, the requester opens a maintenance record in the [Ticketing System] containing the components involved, the scheduled date and time, and the personnel performing the work.
Infrastructure Security reviews and explicitly approves the record on site or remotely, and for work performed off site or on components removed from organizational facilities.
Infrastructure Security monitors the activity while it is in process, whether the system is serviced on site or removed to another location.
On completion, Infrastructure Security reviews the maintenance record against the manufacturer or vendor specifications and organizational requirements before closing the ticket.

[Authorized Approving Personnel] explicitly approves the removal of any system or component from organizational facilities for off-site maintenance, repair, or replacement, and records the approval in the [Ticketing System].
Before removal, Infrastructure Security sanitizes the equipment to remove all organizational information from associated media, using sanitization methods from the latest published NIST SP 800-88.
Infrastructure Security records the sanitization method used and the sanitizing individual in the maintenance record with authorization.
After any maintenance, repair, or replacement action, Infrastructure Security identifies all potentially impacted security controls.
Infrastructure Security checks each identified control to verify it is still functioning properly and records the verification result in the [Ticketing System].

Infrastructure Security ensures each maintenance record includes the required maintenance-related information: date and time, description of maintenance performed, names of individuals performing it, escort name, and components removed or replaced.
Infrastructure Security reviews each completed record for completeness and retains it as a maintenance record with authorization.

Infrastructure Security documents all repairs and modifications to system components on any system where Personally Identifiable Information (PII) is stored or accessed, in the [Maintenance Management System].

Infrastructure Security documents repairs and modifications to security-related physical components of a facility — for example, hardware, walls, doors, and locks — under the facility maintenance documentation procedures.
Infrastructure Security links each such record to the corresponding authorization ticket in the [Ticketing System].
Infrastructure Security schedules, conducts, and documents all maintenance, repair, and replacement actions using the [Maintenance Management System].
Infrastructure Security verifies the [Maintenance Management System] produces up-to-date, accurate, and complete records of all actions requested, scheduled, in process, and completed.
Infrastructure Security corrects any incomplete or inaccurate record before closing the associated action.
Infrastructure Security approves each maintenance tool before use and records the approval in the [Maintenance Management System].
Infrastructure Security controls and monitors the use of all approved maintenance tools.
Infrastructure Security reviews previously approved maintenance tools at least every one (1) year, per ARC-AMPE, and re-approves, updates, or revokes each tool as a result.
Infrastructure Security checks every maintenance tool with information-retention capability to ensure no organizational information is saved on the tool.
Infrastructure Security sanitizes each such tool using approved sanitization methods from the latest published NIST SP 800-88.
Infrastructure Security records the sanitization check and result in the [Maintenance Management System].
Infrastructure Security inspects the maintenance tools used by maintenance personnel for improper or unauthorized modifications.
If an unauthorized modification is found, Infrastructure Security removes the tool from service, records the finding in the [Ticketing System], and initiates remediation before the tool is reused.
Before any media containing diagnostic or test programs is used in a system, Infrastructure Security checks the media for malicious code using the organization's approved anti-malware tooling.

If malware or unauthorized changes are discovered, Infrastructure Security treats the discovery consistent with organizational policies and procedures for incident handling and escalates through the [Ticketing System].
Before maintenance equipment leaves a facility, Infrastructure Security verifies there is no organizational information on the equipment.

If organizational information is present, Infrastructure Security either sanitizes or destroys the equipment using NIST SP 800-88 methods, retains the equipment within the facility, or obtains a written exemption from [Authorized Approving Personnel] explicitly authorizing removal.
For all such tools with information-retention capability, Infrastructure Security checks that no information is saved and sanitizes them per the latest published NIST SP 800-88.
Infrastructure Security restricts access to approved maintenance tools to personnel on the authorized maintenance personnel list.
Infrastructure Security reviews tool access assignments against the authorized list and revokes access for any personnel no longer authorized.
Infrastructure Security monitors all use of maintenance tools that execute with increased privilege through the [Audit Log Platform]/[SIEM].

Infrastructure Security reviews the monitoring output to detect unauthorized access to information and assets that would otherwise be inaccessible to individuals as a result of the increased system privileges.
Infrastructure Security escalates any detected unauthorized access through the [Ticketing System] for incident handling.
Infrastructure Security inspects maintenance tools to ensure the latest software updates and patches are installed.
Infrastructure Security installs updates and patches on organizational systems to minimize vulnerabilities, to the extent possible, with minimal impact to organizational systems.
Infrastructure Security records the patch status of each tool in the [Maintenance Management System].
Infrastructure Security approves each nonlocal maintenance or diagnostic activity before it begins, recording the approval in the [Ticketing System].
Infrastructure Security allows the use of nonlocal maintenance and diagnostic tools only as consistent with organizational policy and as documented in the security plan for the system being serviced.
Infrastructure Security monitors the approved nonlocal activity for the duration of the session.
Infrastructure Security establishes each nonlocal maintenance and diagnostic session using strong authentication in accordance with the latest published NIST SP 800-63B.

If password-based authentication is used during remote maintenance, the maintenance personnel change the passwords immediately following each remote maintenance service, and Infrastructure Security verifies the change.
Infrastructure Security maintains records for all nonlocal maintenance and diagnostic activities — these are the remote maintenance session logs.
Infrastructure Security retains the remote maintenance session logs with the associated authorization records in the [Maintenance Management System].
When nonlocal maintenance is completed, the maintenance personnel terminate the session and all network connections to the system.
Infrastructure Security confirms termination in the session record.
Infrastructure Security sanitizes all media used during remote nonlocal maintenance in accordance with the latest published NIST SP 800-88.
Infrastructure Security records the sanitization action in the remote maintenance session log.

Infrastructure Security configures the [Audit Log Platform]/[SIEM] to log the organization-defined audit events, as defined in the organization's formal audit policy (see AU-2), for all nonlocal maintenance and diagnostic sessions.
Infrastructure Security reviews the audit records of those sessions to detect anomalous behavior.
Infrastructure Security escalates any anomalies through the [Ticketing System] for incident handling.
Before nonlocal maintenance, Infrastructure Security verifies the maintenance is performed from a system implementing a security capability comparable to the system being serviced.
If comparable security cannot be verified, Infrastructure Security removes the component to be serviced prior to nonlocal maintenance and sanitizes it for organizational information.

After service, Infrastructure Security inspects and sanitizes the component for potentially malicious software before reconnecting it, and records the inspection in the [Maintenance Management System].
Infrastructure Security configures nonlocal maintenance sessions to use organization-defined authenticators that are replay resistant.
Infrastructure Security separates the maintenance sessions from other network sessions with the system using physically or logically separated communications paths.
Infrastructure Security verifies the session separation configuration before each approved nonlocal maintenance session begins.
[Authorized Approving Personnel] approves each individual nonlocal maintenance session before it is established, recorded in the [Ticketing System].
Infrastructure Security notifies [Notified Personnel and Roles] of the date and time of planned nonlocal maintenance before the session begins.
Infrastructure Security implements the organization-defined cryptographic mechanisms to protect the integrity and confidentiality of nonlocal maintenance and diagnostic communications.
Infrastructure Security verifies the cryptographic protection is active on every approved nonlocal session.
After completion of each nonlocal maintenance and diagnostic session, Infrastructure Security verifies that the session and network connections have been terminated.
Infrastructure Security records the termination verification in the remote maintenance session log.
Infrastructure Security implements the policies and procedures of this document and the Standard to ensure all workforce members have appropriate access to electronic protected health information.
Infrastructure Security verifies through access reviews that workforce members without appropriate access cannot obtain it.
Infrastructure Security maintains a list of authorized maintenance organizations and personnel, and updates it as authorizations are granted or revoked.

Infrastructure Security executes the established process for maintenance personnel authorization, including authorization and supervision procedures for workforce members who work with ePHI or in locations where it might be accessed.
Infrastructure Security records each authorization decision and its supporting basis in the [Ticketing System].
Before any non-escorted maintenance on the system, Infrastructure Security verifies the personnel possess the required access authorizations and security credentials.
Infrastructure Security applies the established procedures to determine that a workforce member's access to ePHI is appropriate before permitting non-escorted work.

Infrastructure Security designates organizational personnel with the required access authorizations and technical competence to supervise the maintenance activities of personnel who do not possess the required authorizations.
Infrastructure Security ensures supervisors are trained on supervisory and escorting responsibilities before assignment.
Escorts follow the organization-established visitor logging and escort security protocols for the duration of the maintenance activity and record their names in the maintenance record.
Infrastructure Security clearly documents the nationality requirements — or the lack thereof — for maintenance personnel, where applicable, in the authorization record.
Infrastructure Security includes the documented requirements in the list of authorized maintenance organizations and personnel.
Infrastructure Security executes the documented procedures for terminating access to ePHI when a workforce member's employment or other arrangement ends, or as required by clearance determinations.
Infrastructure Security removes the individual from the authorized maintenance personnel list and verifies revocation of associated tool and system access.

Infrastructure Security permits maintenance personnel who lack appropriate security clearances or are not U.S. citizens to work only when escorted and supervised during maintenance and diagnostic activities by approved organizational personnel who are fully cleared, have appropriate access authorizations, and are technically qualified.
Before such maintenance begins, the escort sanitizes all volatile information storage components.
The escort removes, or physically disconnects and secures, all nonvolatile storage media prior to the activity.

Where a component cannot be sanitized, removed, or disconnected, Infrastructure Security develops and implements the organization-defined alternate controls identified in the System Security and Privacy Plan, and records their use in the maintenance record.

Before performing maintenance or diagnostic activities on a system processing, storing, or transmitting classified information, Infrastructure Security verifies the personnel possess security clearances and formal access approvals for at least the highest classification level and for the compartments of information on the system.
Infrastructure Security verifies the personnel are U.S. citizens.

Foreign nationals with appropriate security clearances may conduct maintenance on classified systems only where the systems are jointly owned and operated by the United States and foreign allied governments, or owned and operated solely by foreign allied governments.
Infrastructure Security confirms the approvals, consents, and operational conditions are fully documented within the applicable Memoranda of Agreements before authorizing such work.

Infrastructure Security verifies that non-escorted personnel performing maintenance activities not directly associated with the system but in its physical proximity have the required access authorizations.
Personnel who cannot be verified are escorted per the escort procedures above or removed from the proximity area.
Infrastructure Security identifies the system components for which maintenance support and spare parts must be available, per the Standard.

On failure of a covered component, Infrastructure Security obtains maintenance support and/or spare parts within the applicable Recovery Time Objective (RTO) specified in the system Contingency Plan, consistent with the RTOs defined in CP-7(3) and CP-8.
Infrastructure Security records the failure, the support or parts action, and the elapsed time against the RTO in the [Maintenance Management System].

Infrastructure Security schedules preventive maintenance on the organization-defined system components at the intervals derived from the applicable Recovery Time Objective (RTO) in the system Contingency Plan, consistent with CP-7(3) and CP-8.
Infrastructure Security performs each scheduled preventive maintenance action and documents it as a maintenance record with authorization.
Infrastructure Security performs predictive maintenance on the organization-defined system components at the intervals defined in the Standard.
Infrastructure Security documents each predictive maintenance action in the [Maintenance Management System].

Infrastructure Security transfers the predictive maintenance data to the [Maintenance Management System] using the organization's defined automated mechanisms, and verifies the transfer is complete and accurate.
Infrastructure Security implements the physical access controls of this document and the Standard to limit access to electronic information systems and the facilities in which they are housed.
Infrastructure Security ensures properly authorized access is permitted, using the facility access mechanisms operated with the [Facilities/Physical Security Team].

Infrastructure Security establishes, and implements as needed, the procedures that allow facility access in support of restoration of lost data under the disaster recovery plan and emergency mode operations plan.
Infrastructure Security validates the emergency access procedures during contingency testing and records the validation in the [Ticketing System].
Infrastructure Security implements the policies and procedures of the Standard to safeguard the facility and the equipment therein from unauthorized physical access, tampering, and theft.
Infrastructure Security coordinates with the [Facilities/Physical Security Team] on any detected tampering or theft and escalates through the [Ticketing System] for incident handling.
Infrastructure Security implements the procedures that control and validate a person's access to facilities based on their role or function.
Infrastructure Security applies the visitor control procedures, including visitor logging and escort requirements, to all visitors entering facilities housing systems or ePHI.
Infrastructure Security controls access to software programs for testing and revision, restricting program modification to authorized personnel.
Infrastructure Security maintains all policies and procedures implemented to comply with the rule in written (which may be electronic) form.

Infrastructure Security maintains a written (which may be electronic) record of every action, activity, or assessment required to be documented under this procedure, including the maintenance records with authorization and remote maintenance session logs.
Infrastructure Security retains the required documentation for 6 years from the date of its creation or the date when it last was in effect, whichever is later.
Infrastructure Security makes the documentation available to the persons responsible for implementing the procedures to which it pertains.
Infrastructure Security reviews the documentation periodically at [Review Frequency] and updates it as needed in response to environmental or operational changes affecting the security of ePHI.

Infrastructure Security is authorized and accountable to perform every step of this procedure end to end, including scheduling, approving, monitoring, recording, and reviewing maintenance activities, and owns all handoffs to participants such as maintenance personnel, escorts, supervisors, the [Facilities/Physical Security Team], and the [Maintenance Management System] administrators.

Exceptions — including off-site removal exemptions, alternate controls under MA-5(1), and foreign national maintenance under Memoranda of Agreements — require explicit written approval by [Authorized Approving Personnel], with the [Designated Policy Official] accountable for policy-level exceptions.

This procedure operationalizes the *Example Org — System Maintenance Standard*, which contains the requirement text, control rationale, and authoritative definitions referenced throughout this document.

analyze: This procedure provides the step-by-step operational instructions Site Reliability Engineering follows to execute Example Org's backup, restore, and contingency obligations — maintaining retrievable, protected copies of critical data, standing up alternate processing, storage, and telecommunications capability, and proving through testing that systems can be recovered to a known state.
Executing it produces the required evidence artifacts: **Restore test results** and the **Backup job success report**.

Site Reliability Engineering performs this procedure on all Example Org systems that store, process, transmit, or back up electronic protected health information and other critical mission and business data, together with the alternate storage, processing, and telecommunications sites and providers that support them.
Business Owners, related-plan owners, and external service providers participate in individual steps but do not own them.
- Administrative access to the [Backup Platform] and its job scheduling, encryption, and reporting functions
- Access to the [Document Repository] where the contingency planning policy, Information System Contingency Plan (ISCP), and evidence artifacts are stored
- Access to the [Ticketing System] for tracking corrective actions and approvals
- Access to the [Key Management Service] holding the keys used for backup encryption and integrity signing
- A Business Owner-approved Maximum Tolerable Downtime (MTD) and documented recovery time objectives (RTO) and recovery point objectives (RPO) for each critical system
- Executed agreements (for example, Service Level Agreements) for the alternate storage site, alternate processing site, and alternate telecommunications services
- Contingency training records maintained in the [Training Platform]
- The current ISCP distributed to and acknowledged by key contingency personnel
*[NIST CP-1 | ARC-AMPE CP-1 AE Mandatory | HIPAA 164.316(b)(1)]*
[NIST CP-1 | ARC-AMPE CP-1 AE Mandatory | HIPAA 164.316(b)(1)]

Site Reliability Engineering drafts or updates the contingency planning policy so it explicitly addresses purpose, scope, roles, responsibilities, management commitment, coordination among organizational entities, and compliance, and confirms it is consistent with applicable laws, regulations, and Example Org policies and standards.
Draft companion procedures that facilitate implementation of the policy and its associated contingency planning controls, including this procedure.

Submit the policy and procedures to the [Designated Contingency Plan Official] — the official Example Org has designated to manage their development, documentation, and dissemination — for review and approval.
Have the [Designated Contingency Plan Official] confirm management commitment is documented and coordinate sign-off from organizational entities whose operations the policy affects.
Disseminate the approved policy and procedures to applicable personnel and roles via the [Document Repository], and record the dissemination date and recipient list as evidence.

Maintain all contingency-related policies, procedures, and records of actions, activities, or assessments in written (electronic) form in the [Document Repository], retain them for six (6) years from the date of creation or the date they were last in effect (whichever is later), and make them available to the persons responsible for implementing the procedures they pertain to. *[HIPAA 164.316(b)(1) | HIPAA 164.316(b)(2)(i) | HIPAA 164.316(b)(2)(ii) | HIPAA 164.316(b)(2)(iii)]*

Site Reliability Engineering reviews the contingency planning policy and associated procedures at least annually, on the quarterly process cycle that falls closest to the annual anniversary of the last approval.

Review and update the policy and procedures outside the annual cycle following assessment or audit findings, security or privacy incidents, and changes to applicable laws, executive orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, or guidelines, and in response to environmental or operational changes affecting the security of electronic protected health information.
Record each review in the [Document Repository], noting the reviewer, date, and any updates made.
