Site Reliability Engineering identifies essential mission and business functions supported by each system and documents their associated contingency requirements in the ISCP.

Document recovery objectives, restoration priorities, and metrics for each essential function in the ISCP, using the Business Owner-approved MTD and the derived RTO and RPO (see the Resumption Planning section below).

Document contingency roles, responsibilities, and the assigned individuals — with current contact information — in the ISCP, and include procedures for maintaining essential mission and business functions despite a system disruption, compromise, or failure.
Document in the ISCP how eventual full system restoration will occur without deterioration of the originally planned and implemented controls.

Write and maintain, as part of or alongside the ISCP, the policies and procedures for responding to an emergency or other occurrence (for example, fire, vandalism, system failure, natural disaster) that damages systems containing electronic protected health information, including procedures to restore any loss of data.

Write and maintain procedures enabling continuation of critical business processes for the protection of electronic protected health information while operating in emergency mode, including procedures for obtaining necessary electronic protected health information during an emergency.

Write and maintain procedures that allow facility access in support of restoration of lost data under the disaster recovery plan and emergency mode operations plan in the event of an emergency; coordinate these with the facility access owners.

Document how contingency information is shared among response participants, then submit the completed ISCP to the [ISCP Reviewers and Approvers] for review and approval, and record the approval as evidence.

Coordinate contingency planning activities with incident handling activities by reviewing the ISCP against the cyber incident response plan with the incident handling team and reconciling activation triggers, escalation paths, and communication channels.

Coordinate contingency plan development with the organizational elements responsible for related plans — Business Continuity Plans, Disaster Recovery Plans, Continuity of Operations Plans, Crisis Communications Plans, Critical Infrastructure Plans, Cyber Incident Response Plans, Insider Threat Implementation Plans, and Occupant Emergency Plans — and provide the system contingency plan to the [COOP Program Office] and other defined recipients.

Store the contingency plan in the access-controlled section of the [Document Repository], restrict read and edit permissions to the distribution list, and enable version history to protect it from unauthorized disclosure and modification.

Site Reliability Engineering reviews the contingency plan for the system at least annually, on the quarterly process cycle that falls closest to the annual anniversary of the last review.
Update the plan to address changes to the organization, system, or environment of operation and problems encountered during implementation, execution, or testing.
Incorporate lessons learned from contingency plan testing, training, or actual contingency activities into contingency testing and training plans.
Communicate all contingency plan changes to key contingency personnel and organizational elements on the distribution list, and record the change and communication as evidence.

Site Reliability Engineering conducts capacity planning to confirm that necessary capacity for information processing, telecommunications, and environmental support exists during contingency operations, and records the capacity analysis in the ISCP.

Plan for resumption of all or essential mission and business functions within the time period defined in the service provider and organization Service Level Agreements following contingency plan activation.

Work with the Business Owner to calculate the Maximum Tolerable Downtime, consistent with the mission/business Continuity of Operations Plan, and derive recovery time objectives such that each RTO does not exceed the MTD; document both in the ISCP.

Determine with the designated authority who can activate the contingency plan when to activate it, based on maintaining continuity of critical mission/business processes, and record that activation authority and criteria in the ISCP.
Confirm that planned resumption meets mission/business COOP requirements for the system and document the results in the mission/business Contingency Plan.

Plan for continuance of all or essential mission and business functions with minimal or no loss of operational continuity, sustaining that continuity until full system restoration at primary processing and/or storage sites.

Plan for the transfer of all or essential mission and business functions to alternate processing and/or storage sites with minimal or no loss of operational continuity, sustaining that continuity through system restoration to the primary sites.
Site Reliability Engineering coordinates the contingency plan with the contingency plans of external service providers supporting the system.
Compare each provider's stated recovery capabilities against Example Org's contingency requirements and record the confirmation that requirements can be satisfied.
*[NIST CP-2(8) Moderate, High | ARC-AMPE CP-2(8) AE Mandatory | HIPAA 164.308(a)(7)(ii)(E)]*
[NIST CP-2(8) Moderate, High | ARC-AMPE CP-2(8) AE Mandatory | HIPAA 164.308(a)(7)(ii)(E)]

Site Reliability Engineering identifies the critical system assets supporting all or essential mission and business functions — hardware, software, firmware, information, data, applications, communications, and people.
Maintain an active inventory of those critical assets in the ISCP, verifying it against current environment state each quarterly cycle.
Assess and record the relative criticality of specific applications and data in support of the other contingency plan components.
*[NIST CP-3 | ARC-AMPE CP-3 AE Mandatory | NIST CP-3(1) High | NIST CP-3(2)]*
[NIST CP-3 | ARC-AMPE CP-3 AE Mandatory | NIST CP-3(1) High | NIST CP-3(2)]

Site Reliability Engineering assigns contingency training through the [Training Platform] to system users consistent with their assigned roles and responsibilities, completing it within thirty (30) days of a person assuming a contingency role or responsibility, when required by system changes, and every one (1) year thereafter.
Review and update contingency training content at least every one (1) year and following organization-defined events.
Incorporate simulated events into contingency training to facilitate effective response by personnel in crisis situations.
Employ the mechanisms used in actual operations — the [Backup Platform], [Ticketing System], and operational runbooks — in the training environment to provide a more thorough and realistic exercise.
*[NIST CP-4 | ARC-AMPE CP-4 AE Mandatory | HIPAA 164.308(a)(7)(ii)(D) | NIST CP-4(1) Moderate, High | ARC-AMPE CP-4(1) AE Mandatory | NIST CP-4(2) High | NIST CP-4(3) | NIST CP-4(4) | NIST CP-4(5)]*
[NIST CP-4 | ARC-AMPE CP-4 AE Mandatory | HIPAA 164.308(a)(7)(ii)(D) | NIST CP-4(1) Moderate, High | ARC-AMPE CP-4(1) AE Mandatory | NIST CP-4(2) High | NIST CP-4(3) | NIST CP-4(4) | NIST CP-4(5)]

Site Reliability Engineering tests the contingency plan for the system at least within every one (1) year, executing the test on a quarterly process cycle, using organization-defined tests — including the latest published NIST SP 800-34 and NIST SP 800-84 guidance and any organization-defined functional tests or exercises — to determine the effectiveness of the plan and readiness to execute it.
Coordinate the test with the organizational elements responsible for related plans (COOP, BCP, CIP, DRP, ISCP, CIRP, and OEP) before scheduling.

Test the contingency plan at the alternate processing site, both to familiarize contingency personnel with the facility and available resources and to evaluate the site's capability to support contingency operations.
Execute the test using organization-defined automated mechanisms (for example, orchestrated failover and restore tooling in the [Backup Platform]) and retain the tool output as evidence.
Include a full recovery and reconstitution of the system to a known state as part of the test, and record the results in the **Restore test results** artifact.

Conduct a self-challenge exercise: employ organization-defined mechanisms against the organization-defined system or system component to disrupt and adversely affect it, and execute the plan against the induced disruption.
Include in the test and exercise an evaluation of the capability to meet privacy requirements in a contingency scenario, along with corrective measures addressing any privacy risks identified.
*[NIST CP-4 | ARC-AMPE CP-4 AE Mandatory | HIPAA 164.308(a)(7)(ii)(D)]*
[NIST CP-4 | ARC-AMPE CP-4 AE Mandatory | HIPAA 164.308(a)(7)(ii)(D)]

Site Reliability Engineering reviews the contingency plan test results, determines effectiveness, and initiates corrective actions for identified deficiencies via the [Ticketing System] with assigned owners and deadlines.
Produce an after-action report from the test that identifies improvements to existing processes, procedures, and policies, and fold those improvements into plan updates and the next training cycle.
Make the contingency plan test results and after-action report available to the Business Owner.

*[NIST CP-6 Moderate, High | ARC-AMPE CP-6 AE Mandatory | NIST CP-6(1) Moderate, High | ARC-AMPE CP-6(1) AE Mandatory | NIST CP-6(2) High | NIST CP-6(3) Moderate, High | ARC-AMPE CP-6(3) AE Mandatory]*

Site Reliability Engineering establishes an alternate storage site, including necessary agreements (for example, Service Level Agreements) permitting the storage and retrieval of system backup information.

Identify an alternate storage site sufficiently separated from the primary storage site to reduce susceptibility to the same threats, with the sufficient degree of separation ([Minimum Safe Distance]) determined based on the types of threats of concern to the operation.
Configure the alternate storage site to facilitate recovery operations in accordance with the recovery time and recovery point objectives in the ISCP.
Verify that the alternate storage site provides controls equivalent to those of the primary site (physical, environmental, and logical), and record the equivalence assessment.

Identify potential accessibility problems to the alternate storage site in the event of an area-wide disruption or disaster, outline explicit mitigation actions (for example, duplicating backup information at other geographically diverse alternate storage sites or planning physical access to retrieve backup information if electronic accessibility is disrupted), and document those mitigation actions in the ISCP.
*[NIST CP-7 Moderate, High | FedRAMP CP-7 | ARC-AMPE CP-7 AE Mandatory | NIST CP-7(1) | NIST CP-7(2) | NIST CP-7(3) | NIST CP-7(4) | NIST CP-7(6)]*
[NIST CP-7 Moderate, High | FedRAMP CP-7 | ARC-AMPE CP-7 AE Mandatory | NIST CP-7(1) | NIST CP-7(2) | NIST CP-7(3) | NIST CP-7(4) | NIST CP-7(6)]

Site Reliability Engineering establishes an alternate processing site, including necessary agreements permitting the transfer and resumption of system operations for essential mission and business functions within the defined time period ([Transfer and Resumption Time Period], consistent with the RTO and RPO in the ISCP/COOP) when primary processing capabilities are unavailable.

Verify that the required equipment and supplies are available at the alternate processing site, or that contracts are in place to support delivery within the defined transfer and resumption time period.
Confirm the alternate processing site provides administrative, physical, and technical controls equivalent to those at the primary site, and record the equivalence assessment.
Where Personally Identifiable Information is processed at the alternate site, implement administrative, physical, and technical controls to protect it in accordance with the identified privacy risks.

Identify an alternate processing site sufficiently separated from the primary processing site to reduce susceptibility to the same threats, with the degree of separation determined by the organization based on the types of threats of concern (noting that for hostile cyber attacks the degree of separation between sites is less relevant).

Identify potential accessibility problems to the alternate processing site in an area-wide disruption or disaster, outline explicit mitigation actions, and document the remediation actions in the ISCP.

Ensure the alternate processing site agreements (for example, Service Level Agreements) contain priority-of-service provisions in accordance with availability requirements, including the RTOs specified in the ISCP.
Prepare the alternate processing site — provisioning, configurations, and data replication — so it can serve as the operational site supporting essential mission and business functions.
Plan and prepare for circumstances that preclude returning to the primary processing site, including long-term operations at the alternate site, and document that plan in the ISCP.
*[NIST CP-8 Moderate, High | ARC-AMPE CP-8 AE Mandatory | NIST CP-8(1) | ARC-AMPE CP-8(1) AE Mandatory | NIST CP-8(2) | NIST CP-8(3) High | NIST CP-8(4) High | NIST CP-8(5)]*
[NIST CP-8 Moderate, High | ARC-AMPE CP-8 AE Mandatory | NIST CP-8(1) | ARC-AMPE CP-8(1) AE Mandatory | NIST CP-8(2) | NIST CP-8(3) High | NIST CP-8(4) High | NIST CP-8(5)]

Site Reliability Engineering establishes alternate telecommunications services, including necessary agreements, permitting resumption of system operations for essential mission and business functions within the defined resumption time (as specified by the system RTOs and business function MTD in the contingency plan, ISCP, Business Impact Analysis, or COOP) when primary telecommunications are unavailable at either the primary or alternate processing or storage sites.

Ensure primary and alternate telecommunications service agreements contain priority-of-service provisions in accordance with availability requirements (including the ISCP RTOs, documented in the ISCP remediation/mitigation strategy), and request Telecommunications Service Priority for all telecommunications services used for national security emergency preparedness if the services are provided by a common carrier.

Obtain alternate telecommunications services that reduce the likelihood of sharing a single point of failure with primary telecommunications services, and document the remediation/mitigation strategy in the ISCP.
Obtain alternate telecommunications services from providers separated from the primary service providers to reduce susceptibility to the same threats.

Require primary and alternate telecommunications service providers to have contingency plans; review each provider's plan to ensure it meets Example Org's contingency requirements; and obtain evidence of the providers' contingency testing and training at [Provider Evidence Frequency].
Test the alternate telecommunications services at [Alternate Telecommunications Test Frequency] and retain the test output as evidence.

*[NIST CP-9 | ARC-AMPE CP-9 AE Mandatory | HIPAA 164.308(a)(7)(ii)(A) | HIPAA 164.310(d)(2)(iv) | NIST CP-9(3) High | NIST CP-9(6) | NIST CP-9(7) | NIST CP-9(8) Moderate, High | ARC-AMPE CP-9(8) AE Mandatory]*

[NIST CP-9 | ARC-AMPE CP-9 AE Mandatory | HIPAA 164.308(a)(7)(ii)(A) | HIPAA 164.310(d)(2)(iv) | NIST CP-9(3) High | NIST CP-9(6) | NIST CP-9(7) | NIST CP-9(8) Moderate, High | ARC-AMPE CP-9(8) AE Mandatory]

Site Reliability Engineering configures the [Backup Platform] to conduct backups of user-level information contained in the defined system components, system-level information contained in the system, and system documentation (including security- and privacy-related documentation) at the defined backup frequency — for ARC-AMPE scope, daily incremental backups and weekly full backups while maintaining three (3) generations of backups, at least one of which is available online (a full backup and all related incremental backups).
Verify that the backup configuration creates and maintains retrievable exact copies of electronic protected health information, and record each cycle's outcomes in the **Backup job success report**.

Protect the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of backup information: apply role-based access restrictions in the [Backup Platform], store backups redundantly per the configuration above, and alert on failed jobs through the [Monitoring Platform].

Before any movement of equipment containing electronic protected health information, create a retrievable exact copy of that information; before movement of information system equipment generally, ensure a current, retrievable copy of Personally Identifiable Information is available.
Store backup copies of critical system software and other security-related information in a separate facility or in a fire-rated container that is not collocated with the operational system.
Maintain a redundant secondary system that is not collocated with the primary system and that can be activated without loss of information or disruption to operations.

Enforce dual authorization for the deletion or destruction of [Backup Information in Scope for Deletion Control] using the [Backup Platform]'s dual-approval capability: the requesting engineer raises the deletion request, and a second authorized SRE approver must approve before deletion executes.

Implement cryptographic mechanisms to prevent unauthorized disclosure and modification of backup information (all backup files for ARC-AMPE): enable encryption of backups at the storage location using the methodology referenced for encrypting Personally Identifiable Information, with keys held in the [Key Management Service], and apply digital signatures or cryptographic hashes to protect backup integrity.
*[NIST CP-9(1) Moderate, High | ARC-AMPE CP-9(1) AE Mandatory | NIST CP-9(2) High | NIST CP-9(5) High]*
[NIST CP-9(1) Moderate, High | ARC-AMPE CP-9(1) AE Mandatory | NIST CP-9(2) High | NIST CP-9(5) High]

Site Reliability Engineering tests backup information to verify media reliability and information integrity at least every six (6) months for ARC-AMPE scope, and on the quarterly process cycle for all other in-scope systems — including, for example, decrypting and transporting a random sample of backup files from the alternate storage or backup site and comparing the information to the same information at the primary processing site — and records the results in the **Restore test results** artifact.
Use a sample of backup information in the restoration of selected system functions as part of contingency plan testing.

Transfer system backup information to the alternate storage site within the defined time period ([Transfer Time Period]) and at the defined rate ([Transfer Rate]), consistent with the recovery time and recovery point objectives, and confirm completion in the **Backup job success report**.
*[NIST CP-10 | FedRAMP CP-10 | ARC-AMPE CP-10 AE Mandatory | NIST CP-10(2) Moderate, High | ARC-AMPE CP-10(2) AE Mandatory | NIST CP-10(4) High | FedRAMP CP-10(4) | NIST CP-10(6)]*
[NIST CP-10 | FedRAMP CP-10 | ARC-AMPE CP-10 AE Mandatory | NIST CP-10(2) Moderate, High | ARC-AMPE CP-10(2) AE Mandatory | NIST CP-10(4) High | FedRAMP CP-10(4) | NIST CP-10(6)]

Following a disruption, compromise, or failure, Site Reliability Engineering recovers and reconstitutes the system to a known state within the defined time period ([Recovery and Reconstitution Time Period]) consistent with the recovery time and recovery point objectives defined in the Service Level Agreements and specified in the contingency plan or COOP.

Perform the recovery and reconstitution in a trusted, secure, and verifiable manner: reset all system parameters, reinstall patches, reestablish configuration settings, reinstall application and system software, and fully test the system before returning it to production.

For transaction-based systems (for example, database management systems and transaction processing systems), implement transaction recovery using mechanisms such as transaction rollback and transaction journaling.

Restore system components from configuration-controlled and integrity-protected information representing a known, operational state (for example, versioned golden images and infrastructure-as-code artifacts held under change control) within the defined restoration time periods ([Restoration Time Periods], consistent with the Service Level Agreements).

Protect the system components used for recovery and reconstitution — the golden images, backup media, key material, and reconstitution tooling — with access controls and integrity verification, and record the recovery actions and outcomes in the **Restore test results** artifact.
Site Reliability Engineering is accountable end to end for this procedure: it executes every step, produces the **Restore test results** and **Backup job success report**, and answers for outcomes.

The Business Owner approves the MTD and receives test results; the [Designated Contingency Plan Official] approves policy; the [ISCP Reviewers and Approvers] approve the plan; exceptions to any step require documented approval from Site Reliability Engineering leadership and the [Security Officer].

analyze: This procedure provides the step-by-step operational instructions that IT Asset Management follows to implement Example Org's media protection policy: marking, restricting, physically controlling, and securely storing all digital and non-digital media, and maintaining the governing documentation, until media are sanitized or destroyed using approved methods.
IT Asset Management owns and executes this procedure end to end, with participation from workforce members, system owners, and the Chief Information Officer (CIO) where specified.

It applies to all digital and non-digital media at Example Org — magnetic tapes, external removable hard drives, flash/thumb drives, diskettes, compact disks, digital video disks, and paper/microfilm — including media containing PII or PHI.
- Access to the [Document Management System] where the media protection policy and procedures are published and version-controlled.
- Access to the [Ticketing System] for logging media access requests, marking exemptions, and storage/transport activities.
- A current inventory of digital and non-digital media maintained by IT Asset Management in the [Asset Management System].
- Approved media labeling supplies or coding systems consistent with the markings defined in this procedure.
- Written approval authority held by the Chief Information Officer or their designated representative for media marking exemptions.
- Approved sanitization and destruction equipment, techniques, and procedures consistent with the latest published NIST SP 800-88.
- Access to physical controlled areas where media is stored.

IT Asset Management develops and documents the media protection policy, addressing purpose, scope, roles, responsibilities, management commitment, coordination among organizational entities, and compliance, and ensuring consistency with applicable laws, executive orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, and guidelines.
IT Asset Management documents this procedure and any supporting procedures to facilitate implementation of the media protection policy and its associated controls.

IT Asset Management disseminates the policy and procedures to applicable personnel or roles at the organization, mission/business, and system levels by publishing them in the [Document Management System] and notifying affected personnel through the [Ticketing System].

IT Asset Management designates the official(s) responsible for developing, documenting, and disseminating the media protection policy and procedures, records the designation in writing, and names those officials in the appropriate security and privacy documents.

IT Asset Management reviews and updates the media protection policy and procedures at least every one (1) year, and additionally following organization-defined events such as assessment or audit findings, security or privacy incidents, and changes to applicable laws, executive orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, and guidelines.

IT Asset Management actively monitors for changes to applicable privacy laws, regulations, and overarching policy affecting media protection on a continuous basis, and verifies the policy and procedures support cybersecurity and privacy safeguards throughout the system life cycle.

IT Asset Management reviews the documentation periodically and updates it as needed in response to environmental or operational changes affecting the security of electronic protected health information (ePHI), consistent with HIPAA documentation review requirements.

IT Asset Management maintains the media protection policy and all procedures implemented to comply with applicable requirements in written (which may be electronic) form in the [Document Management System].

IT Asset Management retains that documentation for 6 years from the date of its creation or the date it was last in effect, whichever is later; superseded versions are archived in the [Document Management System] with retention flags set accordingly.

IT Asset Management makes the required documentation available to those persons responsible for implementing the procedures to which it pertains, by granting read access to the published versions in the [Document Management System].

IT Asset Management conducts a risk assessment, on a continuous basis as part of this process, to determine what sensitive information, if any, may be stored on particular media types and which personnel are authorized with a valid need to know that information.

IT Asset Management restricts access to all types of digital and non-digital media (including media containing PII) to organization-defined personnel or roles with a valid need to know, by storing restricted media in controlled areas and granting access only to personnel on the approved access list.

IT Asset Management restricts use of media-writing capabilities by disabling CD/DVD writers and USB ports on organizational systems, allowing access only to authorized individuals with a valid need to know, in compliance with the latest published NIST SP 800-88; changes are executed through the [Endpoint Management System] and tracked in the [Ticketing System].
IT Asset Management implements physical safeguards for all workstations that access ePHI — including positioning, locks, and controlled-area placement — to restrict access to authorized users.

IT Asset Management verifies that all workforce members have appropriate access to ePHI and that workforce members without such access cannot obtain it, by executing authorization and supervision procedures for workforce members working with ePHI, verifying workforce access remains appropriate, and terminating access when employment or other arrangements end or as required by clearance determinations, coordinated with the [Identity Provider].

IT Asset Management protects ePHI from improper alteration or destruction and implements electronic mechanisms to corroborate that ePHI has not been altered or destroyed in an unauthorized manner, by enabling integrity-checking mechanisms (such as checksums or audit logging) in the [Endpoint Management System] and reviewing integrity alerts on a continuous basis.

IT Asset Management marks all system media, including removable media, with labels or approved coding systems indicating the distribution limitations, handling caveats, and applicable security markings (if any) of the information the media holds.

At a minimum, IT Asset Management applies the following markings to each piece of media: creation date; information safeguarding markings (based on applicable record retention regulations); and organization-defined contact information.
IT Asset Management additionally marks backup tapes with the system name.

IT Asset Management marks media containing PII or PHI — or the container for the media if labeling the media itself is not practicable — appropriately and consistent with ACA record retention regulations.

Where media (or hardware components) cannot be marked, IT Asset Management submits a written exemption request through the [Ticketing System]; the exemption applies only to organization-defined types of media that remain within organization-defined controlled areas or a secure environment, and must be specified in writing and approved by the Chief Information Officer or their designated representative before the media is deployed unmarked.

IT Asset Management physically controls and securely stores all digital and non-digital media — magnetic tapes, external removable hard drives, flash/thumb drives, diskettes, compact disks, digital video disks, and paper/microfilm — within organization-defined controlled areas, on a continuous basis.
IT Asset Management protects the media types defined above until the media are destroyed or sanitized, using approved equipment, techniques, and procedures consistent with NIST SP 800-88.

IT Asset Management records every movement of media into, out of, or between controlled areas in the Media transport log, including the media identifier, origin, destination, custodian, and escort or courier.

When media reach the end of their life, IT Asset Management sanitizes or destroys them using approved equipment, techniques, and procedures, and obtains and retains a Certificate of destruction for each sanitization or destruction event, filed in the [Document Management System].

IT Asset Management is authorized to and accountable for performing every step in this procedure end to end, including maintaining the policy, assessing risk, restricting and marking media, controlling storage, and producing the Media transport log and Certificates of destruction.

The Chief Information Officer or their designated representative approves written media marking exemptions, and any exception to this procedure must be documented in the [Ticketing System] and approved by IT Asset Management with CIO (or designated representative) sign-off.
This procedure operationalizes the **Media Handling and Disposal Standard**, which contains the underlying control requirements, the full requirement text, and the rationale for each step above.

analyze: Executing this procedure implements the identification, authentication, authenticator management, session management, and system use notification requirements of the Example Org Authentication & Credential Management Standard, so that only uniquely identified and authenticated users, processes, and devices gain access to Example Org systems and electronic protected health information.

IAM Engineering performs this procedure continuously across all Example Org systems that authenticate users, processes, or devices, including the [Identity Provider], [Directory Service], [MDM Solution], [Ticketing System], and all applications that grant access based on authenticated sessions.
- Administrative access to the [Identity Provider] and [Directory Service] for configuring lockout, session, and authentication policies.
- Administrative access to the [MDM Solution] for device lock, wipe, and biometric configuration.
- Access to the [Ticketing System] for logging lockout releases, authenticator changes, and exception requests.

- The applicable System Security and Privacy Plan(s) defining all organization-defined values referenced below (session limits, re-authentication circumstances, logout messages, device lists, lease durations, and similar).
- Capability to generate the MFA enrolment report and the Authentication policy configuration export.
- Access to the [Password Screening Tool] and the source feed for the compromised password list.
- Access to the [Certificate Authority] / [PKI Management Console] for public key and trust store management.
- The current list of General Services Administration-approved identity, credential, and access management products and services.
Open the [Identity Provider] administrative console and set the invalid logon threshold to five (5) consecutive invalid attempts within a fifteen (15) minute period, per ARC-AMPE.

Configure the lockout action to lock the account or node for a minimum of thirty (30) minutes; where the System Security and Privacy Plan requires administrator release instead, set the lock to persist until released by an administrator.
Configure the [Identity Provider] to notify the system administrator (via the [Ticketing System] or [Security Operations] alerting channel) when the maximum unsuccessful logon attempts is exceeded.
Where the plan specifies an alternative action (logon prompt delay algorithm or other organization-defined action), configure it in the [Identity Provider] exactly as documented in the plan.
Generate the Authentication policy configuration export and retain it as evidence that the threshold, time period, and lockout action are in force.
In the [MDM Solution], identify the mobile devices subject to purging or wiping as defined in the System Security and Privacy Plan.
Configure the device wipe policy to trigger after ten (10) consecutive unsuccessful device logon attempts, per ARC-AMPE, using the purging/wiping techniques defined in the plan.
Apply the policy to the defined device group and confirm enrollment coverage in the [MDM Solution] device inventory.
Record the policy configuration in the Authentication policy configuration export.
In the [Biometric Authentication System], set the limit on consecutive unsuccessful biometric logon attempts to [Biometric Attempt Limit].

In the [Identity Provider], configure the fallback authentication factors (different from the primary factors) that a user may use after the consecutive invalid logon attempt limit has been exceeded, as defined in the System Security and Privacy Plan.
Enforce a separate limit of [Alternative Factor Attempt Limit] consecutive invalid attempts through the alternative factors within [Alternative Factor Time Period].
Verify both limits by test authentication attempts and record the results in the [Ticketing System].

Obtain the approved system use notification text from the System Security and Privacy Plan, confirming it states that users are accessing a system containing U.S. Government information, that usage may be monitored, recorded, and subject to audit, that unauthorized use is prohibited and subject to criminal and civil penalties, and that use indicates consent to monitoring and recording.
Configure the banner in the [Identity Provider] login flow and on operating system login screens via the [Endpoint Management System] so it displays before access is granted.
Configure the banner to remain on screen until the user acknowledges the usage conditions and takes an explicit action to log on or further access the system; do not configure auto-dismissal.

For publicly accessible systems, configure the notification to display under the conditions defined in the System Security and Privacy Plan before granting further access, include a description of the authorized uses of the system, and align any references to monitoring, recording, or auditing with the privacy accommodations that generally prohibit those activities on such systems.
Confirm with the System Owner the elements of the environment that require the System Use Notification control, how notification compliance will be verified, and the periodicity of the check.
If verification is performed as part of a configuration baseline check, include the banner settings in the baseline scan scope in [Configuration Management Tool].
If verification is not part of a baseline check, confirm a documented agreement exists covering how verification results are provided to the System Owner and the verification periodicity.
Execute the verification at the agreed periodicity and provide the results to the System Owner through the agreed channel.

In the [Identity Provider] and [Application Platform], configure concurrent session limits for each account and account type to one (1) session, where a session is an encounter between an end-user interface device and an application, including a network logon.

For any account type requiring more than one (1) concurrent session, confirm the requirement is expressly needed for the performance of job duties and documented in the applicable security and privacy plan before raising the limit.
Record any raised limits and their plan documentation references in the [Ticketing System].

Via the [MDM Solution] and [Endpoint Management Tool], configure the device lock to initiate after fifteen (15) minutes of inactivity, with inactivity covering both remote and internal access connections.
Configure and communicate the requirement that users initiate a device lock before leaving the system unattended; ARC-AMPE requires both the timed lock and the user-initiated lock.
Configure the lock so it is retained until the user reestablishes access using established identification and authentication procedures (password, PIN, or biometric as applicable).
Set the lock screen to conceal all previously visible information with a publicly viewable image.
Verify the settings on a sample of endpoints and record the results in the Authentication policy configuration export.

Maintain, with the System Owner, documented policies and procedures specifying the proper functions to be performed, the manner in which those functions are performed, and the physical attributes of the surroundings of each workstation or workstation class that can access electronic protected health information.

In the [Directory Service] and [Application Platform], implement technical policies and procedures so that systems maintaining electronic protected health information allow access only to those persons or software programs granted access rights as specified in § 164.308(a)(4).
Review workstation access group memberships against the § 164.308(a)(4) access grants and remove any mismatch through the [Ticketing System] access change process.

Establish, and implement as needed, documented procedures for obtaining necessary electronic protected health information during an emergency; store the procedure with the applicable security and privacy plan documentation.
When an emergency access is invoked, follow the procedure and log the event, the requester, and the justification in the [Ticketing System].

Implement the [Encryption Mechanism] to encrypt and decrypt electronic protected health information at rest and in transit, using the latest published FIPS 140-compliant encryption standards for systems containing PII.

In the [Identity Provider] and each application handling authenticated sessions, configure automatic session termination after the trigger events defined in the System Security and Privacy Plan (e.g., periods of user inactivity, targeted responses to certain incident types, time-of-day restrictions), including an electronic procedure that terminates the session after the predetermined time of inactivity.

Configure a logout capability for user-initiated communications sessions on every information resource, as defined in the applicable security and privacy plans, wherever authentication is used to gain access.
Configure the explicit logout message documented in the applicable System Security and Privacy Plan (e.g., "Your session has been terminated") to display when an authenticated session is terminated.
Configure the session-end warning to display an explicit message indicating the session will end in [Time Until Session End], as specified in the applicable security and privacy plans.
Verify each setting by an authenticated test session and record the results in the Authentication policy configuration export.

Develop and document the identification and authentication policy and supporting procedures in written (electronic permitted) form, addressing purpose, scope, roles, responsibilities, management commitment, coordination among organizational entities, and compliance, consistent with applicable laws, directives, regulations, policies, standards, and guidelines.
Disseminate the policy and procedures to the personnel or roles defined in the policy.

Confirm the official designated to manage development, documentation, and dissemination of the policy and procedures is named in the policy; if the designation has changed, update the policy through the document change process.

Review and update the policy and procedures at least every one (1) year and following organization-defined events such as assessment or audit findings, security or privacy incidents, or changes to applicable laws, directives, regulations, policies, standards, or guidelines; review periodically and update as needed in response to environmental or operational changes affecting the security of electronic protected health information.
Retain all documentation produced under this procedure for 6 years from the date of its creation or the date it was last in effect, whichever is later.
Make the documentation available to the persons responsible for implementing the procedures to which it pertains, via the [Document Repository].
Assign a unique name and/or number to each organizational user and to processes acting on their behalf, in the [Directory Service], for identifying and tracking user identity.

Perform identity proofing and authentication compliant with the latest published NIST SP 800-63 Digital Identity Guidelines document suite before issuing system and/or network authenticators and unique user identifiers.
Verify that each person or entity seeking access to electronic protected health information is the one claimed, using the proofed identity bound to the authenticator.

Require user identification for any help desk support transaction that has information security and privacy implications; instruct Help Desk staff to verify the requester's identity against the [Directory Service] before proceeding.

In the [Identity Provider], require multi-factor authentication using two or more different factors (something you know, something you have, or something you are) appropriate to the level of risk for all privileged accounts.
Require multi-factor authentication for all non-privileged account types per ARC-AMPE; note that MFA for consumer accounts is strongly recommended but not currently mandated.
Select only phishing-resistant MFA methods, in accordance with current CISA guidance, for new enrollments and replace non-compliant methods as they are identified.

For local, network, and remote access to privileged and non-privileged accounts, configure MFA such that one factor is provided by a device separate from the system gaining access and that device meets the latest published FIPS 140-compliant cryptography.
Configure replay-resistant authentication mechanisms for access to privileged and non-privileged accounts.
Where shared accounts or authenticators are employed, configure the workflow so each user is individually authenticated before access to the shared account or resource is granted.

Generate the MFA enrolment report from the [Identity Provider], reconcile it against the privileged and non-privileged account inventories, and remediate any unenrolled accounts through the [Ticketing System].
Configure single sign-on in the [Identity Provider] for the system accounts and services defined in the System Security and Privacy Plan.
Configure the federation endpoint to accept and electronically verify Personal Identity Verification-compliant credentials.
Implement the out-of-band authentication mechanisms defined in the System Security and Privacy Plan, triggered under the conditions defined in that plan.

Configure the [Network Access Control] system to uniquely identify and authenticate the devices and/or device types approved for identification and authentication management in the applicable System Security and Privacy Plan before establishing a local, remote, or network connection; at a minimum, use authentication mechanisms based on shared information (MAC or IP address) and access control lists to control remote network access.
Configure bidirectional, cryptographically based authentication for the devices and/or device types requiring it before any local, remote, or network connection is established.

Where addresses are allocated dynamically, standardize dynamic address allocation lease information and lease duration in accordance with [Lease Information and Duration], and audit lease information each time it is assigned to a device via the [DHCP Service] logs.
Where device identification and authentication is based on attestation, configure it to rely on the [Configuration Management Process] as the attesting authority.
As part of initial authenticator distribution, verify the identity of the individual, group, role, service, or device receiving the authenticator before issuing it.

Establish initial authenticator content for any authenticators issued by the organization; change default authenticators (including vendor-supplied passwords) prior to first use and immediately upon system installation.

Maintain administrative procedures, held with the policy documentation, covering initial authenticator distribution, lost or compromised or damaged authenticators, and revocation of authenticators; execute them via the [Ticketing System].

Change or refresh authenticators per the time period defined by authenticator type in [Authenticator Refresh Period] and when the defined events occur; change authenticators immediately when they are no longer valid due to known or suspected compromise.
Confirm each authenticator has sufficient strength of mechanism for its intended use, including compliance with the most recent

analyze: This procedure defines the concrete steps Example Org's Security Program / GRC team follows to categorize systems, assess and respond to risk, obtain and maintain authorization to operate, and continuously monitor control effectiveness, producing an auditable risk register and authorization decision record for each system.

This procedure applies to the Security Program / GRC team, Authorizing Officials, system/business owners, and independent assessors involved in risk assessment and authorization activities for all Example Org information systems that process, store, or transmit organizational or regulated data (including electronic protected health information where applicable).
- Access to the organization's [GRC Platform] where the risk register and authorization decision record are maintained
- Current system inventory, system boundary diagram, and system security plan for the system(s) under review
- A designated Authorizing Official (AO) identified and available to review and approve categorization, assessment, and authorization decisions
- Access to [Vulnerability Scanning Tool] for scheduled scans and to [Penetration Testing Vendor] engagement records
- An approved Rules of Engagement template for penetration testing
- [Ticketing System] access for tracking POA&M remediation items and risk response actions
- Prior risk assessment, POA&M, control assessment, and continuous monitoring documentation for the system, where they exist
- Executive/management approval to commit resources to the assessment and authorization activity

Security Program / GRC drafts a risk assessment policy and a separate assessment, authorization, and monitoring policy, each addressing purpose, scope, roles, responsibilities, management commitment, coordination across teams, and compliance with applicable laws, regulations, and standards.
Security Program / GRC drafts implementing procedures for each policy sufficient to operationalize the associated controls.
Security Program / GRC designates an official accountable for developing, documenting, and disseminating each policy and its procedures; record the designation in the [GRC Platform].
Disseminate both policies and procedures to the defined personnel or roles named in each policy via [Ticketing System] or organizational communication channel, and retain acknowledgment records.

Security Program / GRC reviews and updates both policies and procedures on an annual cadence and immediately following triggering events (assessment or audit findings, security or privacy incidents, or changes in applicable laws, regulations, or standards).
Log each review, its outcome, and any updates in the [GRC Platform].

Security Program / GRC identifies and documents the security official responsible for developing and implementing the organization's security policies and procedures; record this designation in the [GRC Platform].
Implement reasonable and appropriate policies and procedures addressing the applicable security rule requirements, factoring in system size, complexity, capabilities, and risk.
Document any change to a policy or procedure at the time it is made, and implement the change consistently with the rule.
Maintain all policies, procedures, and required documentation of actions, activities, and assessments in written or electronic form in the [GRC Platform].
Retain each version of documentation for 6 years from its creation date or the date it was last in effect, whichever is later.
Make current documentation available to the workforce members responsible for implementing the procedures it describes.
Review documentation on an annual cadence and update it in response to environmental or operational changes affecting the security of electronic protected health information.
Implement and maintain policies and procedures designed to prevent, detect, contain, and correct security violations; log violations and corrective actions in the [Ticketing System].
Security Program / GRC, working with the system owner, categorizes the system and the information it processes, stores, and transmits using the organization's categorization methodology.
Document the categorization result and supporting rationale in the system security plan.
Route the categorization decision to the Authorizing Official (or designated representative) for review and approval; record the approval in the [GRC Platform].

Conduct impact-level prioritization across organizational systems to obtain additional granularity on system impact levels, and record prioritization results alongside the categorization in the risk register.

Security Program / GRC conducts a risk assessment identifying threats to and vulnerabilities in the system, and determines the likelihood and magnitude of harm from unauthorized access, use, disclosure, disruption, modification, or destruction of the system and its information.
Determine the likelihood and impact of adverse effects on individuals arising from processing of personally identifiable information as part of the same assessment.
Integrate the system-level risk assessment results with organization- and mission/business-process-level risk management decisions.
Document results in the Information System Risk Assessment (ISRA), Security Assessment Report (SAR), and privacy plans (e.g., PIA) as applicable, and record a summary entry in the risk register.

Review the risk assessment results on an annual cadence or when a significant change occurs, and disseminate results to the Business Owner and other personnel or roles named in the system security plan.

Update the risk assessment at least every three (3) years, before issuing a new internal/organization-specific authorization, or upon significant change to the system, its environment, or other conditions affecting its security or privacy state.
Record each review and update, with date and outcome, in the risk register.

Security Program / GRC documents a privacy risk management process describing how privacy risk to individuals is assessed across the collection, sharing, storing, transmitting, use, and disposal of PII.
Implement the process for each system that handles PII, recording privacy risk findings alongside the ISRA/PIA documentation and in the risk register.
Security Program / GRC, with input from procurement/system owners, assesses supply chain risks associated with defined systems, system components, and system services.
Document supply chain risk findings in the risk register.

Update the supply chain risk assessment on an annual cadence, upon significant change to the relevant supply chain, or when changes to the system or its operating environment necessitate reassessment.
Security Program / GRC gathers all-source intelligence, including publicly available and open-source information, relevant to the system's engineering, acquisition, and risk management decisions.
Use the gathered intelligence to analyze risk of vulnerabilities arising from development, manufacturing, delivery processes, people, and the operating environment.
Incorporate findings into the risk assessment documentation and risk register.
Security Program / GRC monitors [Threat Intelligence Source] on an ongoing basis to determine the current cyber threat environment relevant to the system.
Record significant threat environment changes in the risk register and feed them into the next risk assessment update.
Security Program / GRC employs [Advanced Analytics Tool] capabilities to predict and identify risks to defined systems or system components.
Review generated predictions and record actionable findings in the risk register for follow-up under Risk Response.

Security Program / GRC conducts an accurate and thorough assessment of potential risks and vulnerabilities to the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of electronic protected health information held by the organization.
Implement security measures sufficient to reduce identified risks and vulnerabilities to a reasonable and appropriate level; record measures adopted in the risk register.
Apply sanctions, coordinated with HR, against workforce members who fail to comply with security policies and procedures; log sanctions in the [Ticketing System].
Implement a recurring procedure to review records of information system activity — audit logs, access reports, and security incident tracking reports.

Perform a periodic technical and nontechnical evaluation of the extent to which security policies and procedures meet the security rule's requirements, initially based on the standards implemented and thereafter in response to environmental or operational changes affecting ePHI security.
Document evaluation results in the risk register and route findings requiring remediation into the POA&M process.
Security Program / GRC performs a criticality analysis of defined systems, system components, or system services at defined decision points in the system development life cycle.
Treat all system components within the CMS ATC/RTC boundary (or equivalent State AE/other ARC-AMPE user boundary) as critical by default.
Document identified critical components and functions in the system security plan and risk register.
Security Program / GRC selects the appropriate assessor or assessment team for the type of assessment to be conducted.

Develop a control assessment plan describing the scope of assessment (controls and enhancements under assessment), assessment procedures used to determine control effectiveness, and the assessment environment, team, and roles/responsibilities.
Route the assessment plan to the Authorizing Official (or designated representative) for review and approval prior to conducting the assessment.
Execute the assessment to determine the extent to which controls are implemented correctly, operating as intended, and producing the desired outcome.

For entities under ARC-AMPE, plan and execute a complete independent assessment of all controls over a three (3) year period — either a full reassessment at ATC expiration, annually-designated control subsets across years one through three, or an assessment triggered by CMS guidance for significant system changes — and deliver the final ATC package no less than ninety (90) days prior to ATC expiration.

Where the system is newly implemented or has undergone significant change, ensure an independent assessment of all security and privacy controls is completed before the Authorizing Official issues an authority to operate.

Produce a control assessment report documenting results and distribute it to the Business Owner and personnel responsible for reviewing assessment documentation and updating security/privacy documentation (and to FedRAMP/agency customers where applicable).
Update security and privacy documentation within thirty (30) days of assessment completion, and notify CMS within thirty (30) days of authorization artifact updates or significant role changes.
Record the assessment report location and key findings in the risk register.
Security Program / GRC engages an independent assessor or assessment team, separate from the system implementation team, to conduct the control assessment.
Record the independence determination in the assessment plan.

Security Program / GRC includes specialized assessment activities — announced or unannounced — as part of control assessments on an annual cadence, selecting from in-depth monitoring, security instrumentation, automated security test cases, vulnerability scanning, malicious user testing, insider threat assessment, performance/load testing, or data leakage/loss assessment as applicable to the system.
Document activities performed and results in the control assessment report.

Security Program / GRC identifies whether an external organization's control assessment of the system meets organizational reliance requirements, including leveraging results from any FedRAMP Recognized independent assessment service where applicable.
Document the reliance decision and the external assessment source in the risk register.
Security Program / GRC develops a POA&M for the system documenting planned remediation actions for weaknesses or deficiencies identified during control assessments and known vulnerabilities.
For each item, record a detailed weakness description, risk level, milestones with dates, and scheduled completion date in the [GRC Platform].
Maintain the POA&M throughout the system lifecycle, beginning with development, incorporating all findings — self-discovered or via assessment.

Update the POA&M in accordance with the frequency documented in the organization's Information Security Continuous Monitoring (ISCM) strategy, based on findings from control assessments, independent audits/reviews, and continuous monitoring activities.
Deliver a fully updated and accurate POA&M to CMS quarterly, on January 31, April 30, July 31, and October 31.
Use [GRC Platform] automated mechanisms to maintain the accuracy, currency, and availability of the POA&M.

Security Program / GRC ensures a senior official is assigned as the Authorizing Official (AO) for the system, and a senior official is assigned as the AO for common controls available for inheritance by organizational systems; record designations in the [GRC Platform].

Before operations commence, obtain the system AO's acceptance of inherited common controls and authorization for the system to operate; obtain the common-control AO's authorization for the use of those controls for inheritance.
Record the authorization decision, its date, and supporting rationale in the authorization decision record.

Update the authorization at least every three (3) years for all entities, or at least every one (1) year for Direct Enrollment Technology Providers, and immediately following a significant security breach, a significant change to the system or its operating environment, or prior to expiration of the current authorization.
Notify CMS of significant/major changes prior to making the change.
Log each authorization update in the authorization decision record.

Where required, Security Program / GRC coordinates a joint authorization process involving multiple Authorizing Officials from within the organization; document each AO's decision in the authorization decision record.

Where required, coordinate a joint authorization process involving multiple Authorizing Officials, including at least one from an organization external to the organization conducting the authorization; document the external AO's decision in the authorization decision record.

Security Program / GRC develops a system-level continuous monitoring strategy, consistent with any organization-level strategy, establishing metrics based on organizational security/privacy goals and the ISCM strategy.
Set monitoring frequencies: scan operating systems, databases, and web applications using [Vulnerability Scanning Tool] at least monthly, and assess control effectiveness at least every one (1) year.
Execute ongoing control assessments and metric monitoring per the strategy.
Correlate and analyze information generated by control assessments and monitoring activities; take response actions to address the results, logging actions in the [Ticketing System].
Report the security and privacy status of the system to designated personnel or roles at least every thirty (30) days.

Follow FedRAMP's Continuous Collaborative Monitoring, Significant Change Notification, Vulnerability Detection and Response, and Vulnerability Evaluation and Reporting rules where the system is FedRAMP-authorized.
Maintain continuous monitoring records; if the system becomes subject to a legal investigation (e.g., insider threat), retain records until released by the investigating authority.
Monitor systems, appliances, devices, and applications (including databases), and provide security and privacy oversight — including via [SIEM Platform] where applicable — for each system.
Record monitoring status and reporting history in the risk register.
Security Program / GRC engages independent assessors or an assessment team to monitor system controls on an ongoing basis, separate from the implementation team.

Security Program / GRC performs trend analyses on monitoring data to determine whether control implementations, monitoring frequency, or monitoring activity types require modification based on empirical data.
Document trend analysis conclusions and any resulting strategy changes in the risk register.

Security Program / GRC ensures the continuous monitoring strategy documents processes and guidance defining effectiveness monitoring, compliance monitoring, and change monitoring as a holistic risk monitoring strategy.
Integrate outputs from each monitoring type into the risk register on an ongoing basis.
Security Program / GRC performs [Defined Validation Action] activities to validate that policies are established and implemented controls are operating in a consistent manner across the system.
Record validation results and any inconsistencies identified in the risk register.
Security Program / GRC uses [SIEM Platform]/[GRC Platform] automated mechanisms to ensure the accuracy, currency, and availability of monitoring results for the system.

Security Program / GRC schedules penetration testing at least every one (1) year on the documented system and its full boundary, and additionally when new risks/threats are identified or upon CMS request.
Draft Rules of Engagement specifying the scope of systems/components to be tested and any exclusions.
Obtain co-signature on the Rules of Engagement from the system Authorizing Official and the penetration testing organization official before testing begins.
Coordinate with [Penetration Testing Vendor] to execute testing on production systems in a manner that minimizes risk of information corruption or service outage.
Ensure scanning includes evaluation of embedded structures and interactive content, and information sources cover systems, appliances, devices, services, and applications (including databases).
Fulfill organization-directed information collection requests within the timeframe specified by the requester.
Require results in a searchable, CMS-compliant format.

Receive from [Penetration Testing Vendor] a report summarizing findings, significance, impact, risk, and remediation plans, including underlying raw security information/results in unaltered format, and provide it to CMS.
Follow FedRAMP's Vulnerability Detection and Response rules as part of vulnerability detection activities.
Record test dates, findings, and remediation status in the risk register and POA&M.
Security Program / GRC obtains CISO (or equivalent) approval of the independent penetration testing agent or team before engagement.
Confirm the agent/team is independent of the system implementation team prior to testing.
Security Program / GRC coordinates red-team exercises simulating adversary attempts to compromise organizational systems, in accordance with the applicable Rules of Engagement.
Document exercise scope, findings, and remediation actions in the risk register and POA&M.
Security Program / GRC conducts announced and/or unannounced attempts, on an annual cadence, to bypass or circumvent controls associated with physical access points to the facility.
Document findings and remediation actions in the POA&M.

Security Program / GRC reviews each finding from security and privacy assessments, monitoring, and audits, and determines a response consistent with organizational risk tolerance: mitigate (implement new or strengthened controls), accept (with documented justification/rationale), share/transfer, or avoid.
Follow FedRAMP's Vulnerability Detection and Response and Vulnerability Evaluation and Reporting rules where the system is FedRAMP-authorized.
Before accepting a risk, discuss the proposed acceptance with CMS to reach agreement on approach and mitigations.
Document accepted risks and the full rationale in a risk acceptance form, and track the item in the POA&M and risk register.

Security Program / GRC establishes and, as needed, implements policies and procedures for responding to an emergency or other occurrence (fire, vandalism, system failure, natural disaster) that damages systems containing electronic protected health information.
Establish and implement procedures to create and maintain retrievable exact copies of electronic protected health information.
Establish and implement, as needed, procedures to restore any loss of data from those copies.
Establish and implement, as needed, procedures enabling continuation of critical business processes for protection of ePHI security while operating in emergency mode.
Implement a recurring procedure for periodic testing and revision of the contingency plans; log test dates and revision history in the [GRC Platform].
Assess the relative criticality of specific applications and data to inform and support the other contingency plan components; record the criticality assessment in the risk register.

The Security Program / GRC team owns this procedure end to end — performing categorization, risk assessment, control assessment coordination, POA&M management, continuous monitoring, and authorization support, and maintaining the risk register and authorization decision record.

The Authorizing Official approves categorization decisions, assessment plans, authorization decisions, and risk acceptances; the CISO (or equivalent) approves independent assessor/tester selection; exceptions to this procedure require review and approval by the Authorizing Official or Security Program / GRC leadership.
This procedure implements the **Example Org Risk Assessment and Authorization Standard**, which defines the underlying requirements and rationale for the steps above.
