analyze: Executing this procedure establishes and sustains Example Org's risk assessment, control assessment, continuous monitoring, and authorization operations, producing an accurate, current **risk register** and a defensible **authorization decision record** for every system in scope.

It ensures risks to organizational systems and to electronic protected health information (ePHI) are identified, analyzed, responded to, and formally accepted or authorized by the appropriate officials.

This procedure is performed by the **Security Program / GRC** team, with participation from System Owners, the Authorizing Official, the CISO, the Senior Official for Privacy, and independent assessors, across all Example Org systems that process, store, or transmit organizational or ePHI data.

It covers policy maintenance, risk analysis, security categorization, control assessment, plan of action and milestones (POA&M) management, authorization, continuous monitoring, and penetration testing.
- Access to the [GRC / Document Management System] where policies, procedures, the risk register, the authorization decision record, and HIPAA documentation are maintained.
- Access to the [Ticketing System] for tracking remediation actions and POA&M entries.
- Access to the [Vulnerability Scanning Tool], [SIEM], and [Penetration Test Results Repository].
- A named, appointed Authorizing Official for each system and for common controls, and a named CISO and Senior Official for Privacy.
- A named HIPAA Security Official responsible for security policy development and implementation.

- An established CMS coordination point of contact and access to CMS-provided templates, the CMS Standard for POA&M Management and Reporting, and the CMS Framework for Independent Assessment of Security and Privacy Controls.
- Approved Rules of Engagement templates and executed agreements with [Independent Assessment Provider] and [Independent Penetration Testing Provider].

Have the Security Program / GRC team develop, document, and disseminate an organization-level risk assessment policy in the [GRC / Document Management System] that addresses purpose, scope, roles, responsibilities, management commitment, coordination among organizational entities, and compliance, and is consistent with applicable laws, executive orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, and guidelines.

Designate, by name in the appropriate security and privacy documents, the official within Security Program / GRC who manages the development, documentation, and dissemination of the risk assessment policy and procedures.

Develop, document, and disseminate supporting procedures that facilitate implementation of the risk assessment policy and the associated risk assessment controls; distribute both to organization-defined personnel and roles via the [GRC / Document Management System].
Ensure the policy and procedures support cybersecurity and privacy safeguards to the greatest extent feasible throughout the system life cycle and for the information on each system.

Review and update the risk assessment policy and procedures at least every one (1) year, and additionally following assessment or audit findings, security or privacy incidents, or changes to applicable laws, regulations, policies, standards, or guidelines.

Actively monitor for changes to applicable privacy laws, regulations, and overarching policy that affect risk assessment policies, and review the policies at least every one (1) year to confirm they remain effective; record each review in the policy document's revision history.
Have the Security Program / GRC team implement and maintain policies and procedures to prevent, detect, contain, and correct security violations affecting ePHI.

Conduct an accurate and thorough risk analysis of the potential risks and vulnerabilities to the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of ePHI held by Example Org; document the analysis in the risk assessment report and record identified risks in the risk register.

Identify and implement security measures sufficient to reduce the risks and vulnerabilities identified in the risk analysis to a reasonable and appropriate level; track each measure to closure in the [Ticketing System].

Maintain and apply the sanctions process against workforce members who fail to comply with Example Org security policies and procedures; route confirmed non-compliance cases to [Human Resources] for sanction determination and retain the outcome record.

Regularly review records of information system activity — including audit logs, access reports, and security incident tracking reports — using the [SIEM] and [Log Review Tool], and document the review results for inclusion in the risk register.

Implement reasonable and appropriate policies and procedures to comply with the HIPAA Security Rule; when any policy or procedure is changed, document and implement the change in accordance with the Rule.
Maintain all HIPAA-related policies, procedures, and required records of actions, activities, and assessments in written (electronic) form in the [GRC / Document Management System].
Retain HIPAA Security Rule documentation for 6 years from the date of its creation or the date it was last in effect, whichever is later.
Make the documentation available to the persons responsible for implementing the procedures to which it pertains, via [GRC / Document Management System] access permissions.
Review the documentation at least every one (1) year and update it as needed in response to environmental or operational changes affecting the security of ePHI.
Have the Security Program / GRC team, in coordination with the System Owner, categorize the system and the information it processes, stores, and transmits.
Involve the Senior Official for Privacy, or their designee, in the categorization process.
Document the security categorization results, including supporting rationale, in the system's security plan.
Submit the categorization decision to the Authorizing Official or their designated representative for review and approval; record the approval in the authorization decision record.

Conduct an impact-level prioritization of organizational systems to obtain additional granularity beyond the base impact levels, and record the prioritization results alongside the categorization documentation.

Establish and implement policies and procedures for responding to an emergency or other occurrence (for example, fire, vandalism, system failure, and natural disaster) that damages systems containing ePHI.
Establish and implement procedures to create and maintain retrievable exact copies of ePHI (data backup plan) using the [Backup Solution].
Establish and implement, as needed, procedures to restore any loss of data (disaster recovery plan).
Establish and implement, as needed, procedures to enable continuation of critical business processes for protection of ePHI security while operating in emergency mode.
Assess the relative criticality of specific applications and data in support of the other contingency plan components, and record the criticality assessment with the plan.
Periodically test and revise the contingency plans, document each test's results, and update the plans based on the findings.

Conduct a risk assessment that identifies threats to and vulnerabilities in the system; determines the likelihood and magnitude of harm from unauthorized access, use, disclosure, disruption, modification, or destruction of the system and its information; and determines the likelihood and impact of adverse effects on individuals arising from the processing of personally identifiable information (PII).
Integrate risk assessment results and risk management decisions from the organization and mission/business process perspectives with the system-level risk assessment.
Document the risk assessment results in the security and privacy plans and the risk assessment report, and record identified risks in the risk register.
Document and implement a privacy risk management process that assesses privacy risk to individuals resulting from the collection, sharing, storing, transmitting, use, and disposal of PII.
Review the risk assessment results at least every one (1) year, and when a significant change occurs.

Update the risk assessment at least every three (3) years at a minimum (for internal, organization-specific authorizations), before issuing a new internal organization-specific authorization, or upon significant changes to the system, its environment of operation, or other conditions that may impact the security or privacy state of the system.
Disseminate the risk assessment results to organization-defined personnel or roles via the [GRC / Document Management System] distribution list.
Identify the systems, system components, and system services in scope for supply chain risk assessment per [Systems, Components, and Services in Scope for Supply Chain Risk Assessment].
Assess the supply chain risks associated with the in-scope systems, components, and services.

Update the supply chain risk assessment per [Supply Chain Risk Assessment Update Frequency], when there are significant changes to the relevant supply chain, or when changes to the system, environments of operation, or other conditions may necessitate a change in the supply chain.
Record the results in the supply chain risk assessment section of the risk register.
Obtain and review all-source intelligence — including publicly available or open-source information — using the [Threat Intelligence Service] and [Open-Source Intelligence Collection Process].

Use the intelligence to inform engineering, acquisition, and risk management decisions, including analysis of intentional and unintentional vulnerabilities arising from development, manufacturing, delivery processes, people, and the environment.
Document intelligence-derived findings and their effect on risk decisions in the risk assessment report.
Establish the means for determining the current cyber threat environment per [Threat Environment Determination Means], using the [Threat Intelligence Service].
Monitor the threat environment on an ongoing basis and incorporate current threat data into each risk assessment update and the risk register.

Identify the advanced automation and analytics capabilities in use per [Advanced Analytics Capabilities] and the systems or components they cover per [Systems or Components in Scope for Predictive Analytics].
Apply the capabilities to predict and identify risks to the in-scope systems or components, and feed predicted risks into the risk register and risk assessment report.

Respond to findings from security and privacy assessments, monitoring, and audits in accordance with organizational risk tolerance, selecting to mitigate the risk, accept the risk with appropriate justification, share or transfer the risk, or avoid the risk.
Follow the FedRAMP Vulnerability Detection and Response and Vulnerability Evaluation and Reporting rules when responding to findings.
Before accepting any risk, discuss the risk acceptance with CMS to confirm CMS agrees with the approach and mitigations.
Document and track risk-accepted findings in the POA&M, with full detail captured in the risk acceptance form, and record the accepted risk in the risk register.
Identify the systems, system components, or system services in scope per [Systems, Components, or Services in Scope for Criticality Analysis].
Perform a criticality analysis at the organization-defined decision points in the system development life cycle per [Criticality Analysis Decision Points].
Treat all system components within the CMS Authority to Connect (ATC)/Request to Connect (RTC) boundary as critical in the analysis.
Record the criticality analysis results in the security plan and reflect critical components in the risk register.

Have the Security Program / GRC team develop, document, and disseminate an organization-level assessment, authorization, and monitoring (AAM) policy addressing purpose, scope, roles, responsibilities, management commitment, coordination among organizational entities, and compliance, consistent with applicable laws, regulations, policies, standards, and guidelines.

Designate, by name in the appropriate security and privacy documents, the official within Security Program / GRC who manages the development, documentation, and dissemination of the AAM policy and procedures.
Develop, document, and disseminate procedures that facilitate implementation of the AAM policy and associated controls.
Ensure the AAM policy and procedures support cybersecurity and privacy safeguards to the greatest extent feasible throughout the system life cycle and for the information on each system.

Review and update the AAM policy and procedures at least every one (1) year, and additionally following assessment or audit findings, security or privacy incidents, or changes to applicable laws, regulations, policies, standards, or guidelines.
Actively monitor for changes to applicable privacy laws, regulations, and overarching policy affecting AAM policies, and review at least every one (1) year to ensure the policies remain effective.

Perform a periodic technical and nontechnical evaluation, based initially on the standards implemented under the HIPAA Security Rule, that establishes the extent to which Example Org's security policies and procedures meet the requirements of the Rule.
Repeat the evaluation in response to environmental or operational changes affecting the security of ePHI, and document the evaluation results in the [GRC / Document Management System].
Select the appropriate assessor or assessment team for the type of assessment to be conducted.

Develop a control assessment plan describing the scope of the assessment, including the controls and control enhancements under assessment, the assessment procedures to be used to determine control effectiveness, and the assessment environment, assessment team, and assessment roles and responsibilities.

Submit the control assessment plan to the Authorizing Official or designated representative for review and approval prior to conducting the assessment; retain the approval in the authorization decision record.

Assess the controls in the system and its environment of operation at the frequency specified in the supplemental control requirements and guidance, to determine the extent to which controls are implemented correctly, operating as intended, and producing the desired outcome with respect to meeting established security and privacy requirements.
Complete an independent assessment of all security and privacy controls before the Authorizing Official issues authority to operate for any newly implemented or significantly changed system.

Conduct a complete independent assessment of all security and privacy controls over a three (3) year period, using one of the following approaches: a full controls assessment at the end of the Authority to Connect lifespan (final ATC package delivered no less than ninety (90) days prior to expiration); independent assessments of the annually required controls designated by CMS so all controls are assessed within the three-year period (final ATC package delivered no less than ninety (90) days prior to expiration); or per CMS guidance on required documentation and testing for each significant system change.
Produce a control assessment report documenting the results of the assessment.

Provide the assessment results in writing to the Business Owner responsible for the system and the personnel responsible for reviewing assessment documentation within thirty (30) days after completion, and to FedRAMP and agency customers as applicable.
Update relevant security and privacy documentation to reflect any changes to the system within thirty (30) days of the changes or within thirty (30) days of the control assessment results.
Notify CMS within thirty (30) days whenever updates are made to system security and privacy authorization artifacts or when significant role changes occur.
Engage independent assessors or assessment teams to conduct control assessments, following the CMS Framework for Independent Assessment of Security and Privacy Controls provided for the program.
Document the independence of the assessment team in the control assessment plan and retain the documentation with the assessment report.

Determine the specialized assessment types to perform per [Specialized Assessment Types], selecting from in-depth monitoring, security instrumentation, automated security test cases, vulnerability scanning, malicious user testing, insider threat assessment, performance and load testing, data leakage or data loss assessment, or other defined forms of assessment.
Conduct the specialized assessments at the frequency defined per [Specialized Assessment Frequency] on an announced or unannounced basis per [Specialized Assessment Announcement Basis].
Record specialized assessment results and feed identified weaknesses into the POA&M.
Identify control assessments performed by external organizations per [External Organizations Whose Assessments May Be Leveraged] on the system defined per [System Covered by External Assessment].

Leverage the external assessment results when the assessment meets the requirements defined per [Requirements for Leveraging External Assessments] (for FedRAMP purposes, the external organization is any FedRAMP-recognized independent assessment service).
Document which external assessment results were leveraged, and why they met the leveraging requirements, in the control assessment report.

Develop a POA&M for the system in the [POA&M Management Tool] to document planned remediation actions that correct weaknesses or deficiencies noted during control assessments and reduce or eliminate known vulnerabilities.

Include in each POA&M entry scheduled completion dates, milestones with dates, appropriate risk levels, and weakness descriptions with as much detail as possible, following the CMS Standard for POA&M Management and Reporting and the CMS-provided template.

Include all findings in the POA&M, whether self-discovered or identified through assessments or testing (e.g., security control assessments, penetration tests, automated configuration and vulnerability scans).
Establish the POA&M starting in development and maintain it throughout the system life cycle; remediate POA&M entries consistent with SI-2.

Update the existing POA&M in accordance with the frequency documented in the organization's Information Security Continuous Monitoring strategy, based on findings from control assessments, independent audits or reviews, and continuous monitoring activities.
Deliver to CMS a fully updated and accurate POA&M quarterly on 31 January, 30 April, 31 July, and 31 October.
Ensure the accuracy, currency, and availability of the POA&M using the automated mechanisms defined per [Automated Mechanisms for POA&M Accuracy and Availability].

Assign a senior official as the Authorizing Official for the system and a senior official as the Authorizing Official for common controls available for inheritance by organizational systems; record both designations in the authorization decision record.
Before commencing operations, ensure the Authorizing Official for the system accepts the use of common controls inherited by the system and authorizes the system to operate.
Ensure the Authorizing Official for common controls authorizes the use of those controls for inheritance by organizational systems.

Update authorizations at least every three (3) years (Direct Enrollment Technology Providers must update at least every one (1) year), when significant security breaches occur, whenever there is a significant change to the system or its operating environment, and prior to expiration of the current authorization; record each update in the authorization decision record.

Notify CMS of significant or major changes to architecture, security and privacy posture, or other items that could cause degradation or unexpected results in security and privacy monitoring, detection, response, and mitigation activities prior to making the change.
When a joint authorization applies, employ a joint authorization process for the system that includes multiple authorizing officials from the same organization conducting the authorization.

Where external participation is required, employ a joint authorization process that includes multiple authorizing officials with at least one authorizing official from an organization external to the organization conducting the authorization.
Document each participating authorizing official's authorization decision in the authorization decision record.

Identify by name the security official responsible for the development and implementation of the policies and procedures required by the HIPAA Security Rule, and record the designation in the security plan and the [GRC / Document Management System].

Have the CIO and CISO develop a system-level continuous monitoring strategy, with Example Org as the responsible implementation agent, and implement continuous monitoring in accordance with the organization-level continuous monitoring strategy.
Establish the system-level metrics to be monitored per [System-Level Metrics], based on organization security and privacy goals and in accordance with the organization's ISCM strategy.

Establish the frequencies for monitoring per [Monitoring Frequency] and for assessment of control effectiveness per [Control Effectiveness Assessment Frequency], applying the ARC-AMPE minimums of at least once-a-month scans of operating systems, databases, and web applications for monitoring, and assessment of control effectiveness no less than at least every one (1) year.

Include risk monitoring as an integral part of the continuous monitoring strategy, covering effectiveness monitoring, compliance monitoring, and change monitoring; document in the strategy the processes and guidance for what is considered effectiveness, compliance, and change monitoring as part of a holistic risk monitoring strategy.
Conduct ongoing control assessments in accordance with the continuous monitoring strategy.

Conduct ongoing monitoring of system and defined metrics in accordance with the continuous monitoring strategy, monitoring systems, appliances, devices, and applications (including databases), and providing oversight of information security and privacy, including Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) as applicable, for each system via the [SIEM].
Correlate and analyze information generated by control assessments and monitoring in the [SIEM] and [Analytics Platform].
Take response actions to address the results of the analysis of control assessment and monitoring information, logging response actions in the [Ticketing System].
Report the security and privacy status of the system to the personnel defined per [Security and Privacy Status Reporting Recipients] at least every thirty (30) days (monthly).
When subject to a legal investigation (e.g., of an insider threat), maintain continuous monitoring records until released by the investigating authority.
Follow the FedRAMP Continuous Collaborative Monitoring, Significant Change Notification, Vulnerability Detection and Response, and Vulnerability Evaluation and Reporting rules.

Engage independent assessors or assessment teams to monitor the controls in the system on an ongoing basis, following the CMS Framework for Independent Assessment of Security and Privacy Controls provided for the program.
Retain the independent monitoring results and reports with the system's authorization documentation.

Employ trend analyses on monitoring and assessment data to determine if control implementations, the frequency of continuous monitoring activities, and the types of activities used in the continuous monitoring process need to be modified based on empirical data.
Document proposed modifications and, once approved by Security Program / GRC leadership, update the continuous monitoring strategy accordingly.
Define the validation actions to employ per [Control Consistency Validation Actions].
Employ the actions to validate that policies are established and that implemented controls are operating in a consistent manner, and record validation results for review by Security Program / GRC.
Identify the automated mechanisms to use per [Automated Mechanisms for Monitoring Results].
Use those mechanisms to ensure the accuracy, currency, and availability of monitoring results for the system.
Schedule penetration testing at least every one (1) year to maintain authorization, on the systems or components defined per [Systems or Components in Scope for Penetration Testing].

Conduct penetration testing on the documented system and its full boundary as documented in the System Security and Privacy Plan, and perform additional penetration tests when new risks and threats potentially affecting the system or applications are identified and reported or upon request from CMS.

Agree to the Rules of Engagement before commencing testing, with the rules co-signed by the system Authorizing Official and the penetration testing organization official; include in the Rules of Engagement the scope of systems or components to be tested and any exclusions.

Ensure penetration test scanning includes evaluation of embedded structures (e.g., content that can be changed without reloading the anchor content) and interactive content, and covers information sources including systems, appliances, devices, services, and applications (including databases).

Ensure penetration test scanning results are searchable by the organization and in a format compliant with CMS requirements, and implement or provide organization-directed penetration test information collection rules/requests (e.g., sources, queries, data calls) within the timeframe specified in the request.
Conduct penetration testing on production systems in a manner that minimizes risk of information corruption or service outage.

Provide penetration testing reports to CMS that summarize the findings, articulate the significance, impact, and risk of the findings, provide remediation plans, and include the underlying raw security information/results in unaltered format.
Treat penetration testing as part of vulnerability detection, subject to the FedRAMP Vulnerability Detection and Response rules; record findings in the POA&M.
Engage an independent penetration testing agent or team to perform penetration testing on the system or system components.

Obtain approval of the independent penetration testing agent or team from Example Org's Chief Information Security Officer (CISO) or equivalent before testing begins, and retain the approval record with the test documentation.
Define the red team exercises to employ per [Red Team Exercise Definition].
Employ the exercises to simulate attempts by adversaries to compromise organizational systems in accordance with applicable rules of engagement, and record exercise findings in the POA&M.

Define the frequency of physical access bypass attempts per [Physical Access Bypass Testing Frequency] and select an announced or unannounced basis per [Physical Access Bypass Testing Announcement Basis].

Employ a penetration testing process that includes attempts to bypass or circumvent controls associated with physical access points to the facility at that frequency, and record the results for review by Security Program / GRC.

The **Security Program / GRC** team owns this procedure end to end: it develops and maintains the policies, conducts the risk and control assessments, manages the risk register, POA&M, and authorization decision record, and coordinates all CMS and FedRAMP interactions.

System Owners, the CIO, the CISO, the Senior Official for Privacy, the Authorizing Official(s), independent assessors, and [Human Resources] participate in the specific steps assigned to them above; exceptions to any step in this procedure require review and written approval by Security Program / GRC leadership in consultation with the system Authorizing Official.

This procedure operationalizes the **Risk Assessment and Authorization Standard**, which contains the underlying requirement text, the full control language, and the rationale for each requirement reflected above.

analyze: Executing this procedure embeds information security and privacy controls into every phase of Example Org's system development life cycle — from requirements definition and acquisition through development, testing, operation, and disposal — and produces the evidence required by the Secure Development Lifecycle Standard, including SAST/DAST results per release and dependency and supply-chain scan output.

This procedure is performed by the Application Security team, with participation from Development Teams, the Privacy Office, Procurement/Contracting, System Owners, and supply chain personnel, on all systems, components, and services that Example Org develops, acquires, integrates, or maintains.
It runs continuously across the system development life cycle; each subsection below applies at the life-cycle phase indicated by its steps.
- Named individuals identified for all security and privacy roles in the development life cycle (see Procedure Steps 1), recorded in [Documentation Repository].
- Access to [Source Code Repository], [CI/CD Pipeline], [Ticketing System], [Vulnerability Management Platform], [Documentation Repository], [Risk Acceptance Register], and [POA&M System].
- An executed or in-progress acquisition contract with each developer, containing the security and privacy terms required by Procedure Steps 4 and 9.
- Approval from the Senior Official for Privacy before any PII is used in testing, training, or research.
- A designated independent assessment agent meeting [Independence Criteria] for developer assessment verification.
- Access to the FedRAMP Secure Configuration Guide and the latest published NIST SP 800-88.
- Developer deliverables: functional properties of controls, design documentation, assessment plans, continuous monitoring plan, and training materials as specified below.

Application Security maintains the formally defined, documented system development life cycle in [Documentation Repository], incorporating information security and privacy considerations at each phase.

Application Security documents the security and privacy roles and responsibilities for each life-cycle phase and records the names of the individuals holding those roles; review and update this roster whenever personnel changes occur.
Application Security integrates the organizational risk management process into life-cycle activities by requiring a risk determination at each phase gate, recorded in [Ticketing System].

Before each phase gate, Application Security provides the security and privacy offices an opportunity to review the requirements and confirm that PII protection requirements are appropriately considered; record their sign-off in [Ticketing System].
Application Security classifies each preproduction environment and applies protections commensurate with its risk, documented in [Documentation Repository].
Before any live data is loaded into a preproduction environment, Application Security obtains approval, documents the approval in [Ticketing System], and applies controls over that use.
Set the preproduction environment's protection level to the same impact or classification level as any live data within it; verify this mapping at each environment change.
If PII is used in the test environment, apply the same controls required for systems containing PII to that environment, and use synthetic PII to the maximum extent practicable.
Limit the creation, collection, use, and disclosure of PII in development and test to only what is necessary for the specified, authorized purpose; coordinate with the Senior Official for Privacy.
Obtain the Senior Official for Privacy's approval for any use of PII in testing, training, or research; prefer synthetic or de-identified data and record the approval in [Ticketing System].
Application Security develops and maintains a technology refresh schedule for each system in [Documentation Repository], updated at each life-cycle phase.
Review the refresh schedule at each phase gate and record changes in [Ticketing System].

Application Security, with [Procurement/Contracting], includes in every acquisition contract, explicitly or by reference using standardized contract language: security and privacy functional requirements; strength of mechanism requirements; security and privacy assurance requirements; controls needed to satisfy those requirements; security and privacy documentation requirements; requirements for protecting that documentation; a description of the development environment and intended operating environment; allocation of responsibility for information security, privacy, and supply chain risk management; and acceptance criteria.

For each contract or Statement of Work involving development of, or access to, systems containing PII, include language requiring adherence to Example Org's security and privacy policies and standards (consistent with 45 CFR §155.260(b)), define security and privacy roles and responsibilities, and obtain the System Owner's approval before execution.

For systems, components, or services that store, process, or transmit PII, consult the Privacy Office and include in the contract: a list of security and privacy controls necessary to protect PII (and, if appropriate, enforce applicable privacy requirements); privacy requirements including privacy training and awareness and rules of behavior; and privacy functional requirements.

Before permitting a business associate to create, receive, maintain, or transmit electronic protected health information on Example Org's behalf, obtain satisfactory assurances in accordance with § 164.314(a) that the business associate will appropriately safeguard the information.
Document the satisfactory assurances through a written contract or other arrangement meeting the applicable requirements of § 164.314(a).

Ensure the business associate contract requires the business associate to comply with the applicable requirements of the subpart, to flow down compliant contracts to any subcontractors handling electronic protected health information on its behalf, and to report any security incident of which it becomes aware, including breaches of unsecured protected health information as required by § 164.410.
Apply the same contract requirements to the arrangement between a business associate and its subcontractor; verify flow-down language before the subcontractor begins handling information.
Require the developer to provide a description of the functional properties of the security and privacy controls to be implemented; file it in [Documentation Repository].

Require the developer to provide design and implementation information — security-relevant external system interfaces, high-level design documentation, and source code or hardware schematics — at [Organization-Defined Level of Detail] sufficient to prove control implementation.

Verify that the functional properties description covers only functionality visible at the control interfaces and excludes internal functionality and data structures; reject and return descriptions that expose or rely on internal detail.

Require the developer to follow Example Org's defined systems engineering, security/privacy engineering, software development, testing/evaluation/verification/validation, and quality control methods; record the requirement in the contract per Procedure Steps 4.

Require delivery of the system, component, or service with [Organization-Defined Security Configurations] implemented, and designate those configurations as the default for any subsequent reinstallation or upgrade.

To protect classified information transmitted over networks at a lower classification level, employ only government off-the-shelf or commercial off-the-shelf information assurance (and IA-enabled) products that compose an NSA-approved solution, evaluated and/or validated by NSA or in accordance with NSA-approved procedures.

For commercially provided information assurance products, verify evaluation against a NIAP-approved Protection Profile for the technology type if one exists; if no profile exists and the product relies on cryptographic functionality to enforce its security policy, require a FIPS-validated or NSA-approved cryptographic module.
For Personal Identity Verification (PIV) capability, employ only information technology products on the FIPS 201-approved products list.

Require the developer to produce a plan for continuous monitoring of control effectiveness consistent with Example Org's continuous monitoring program; review and file it in [Documentation Repository].

Require the developer to identify the functions, ports, protocols, and services intended for organizational use; record the list in [Documentation Repository] and verify it against the delivered system at acceptance.
For contracts to operate a system of records on Example Org's behalf, include [Organization-Defined Privacy Act Requirements] in the acquisition contract.

Include organizational data ownership requirements in the acquisition contract, and require all data to be removed from the contractor's system and returned to Example Org within [Data Return Time Frame].

Obtain or develop administrator documentation describing the secure configuration, installation, and operation of the system; the effective use and maintenance of security and privacy functions and mechanisms; and known vulnerabilities regarding configuration and use of administrative or privileged functions.

Obtain or develop user documentation describing user-accessible security and privacy functions and how to use them effectively; methods for user interaction that enable more secure use and protect individual privacy; and user responsibilities for maintaining system security and individual privacy.
When documentation is unavailable or nonexistent, document the attempts to obtain it in [Ticketing System] and take [Organization-Defined Response Actions].
Distribute documentation to [Organization-Defined Personnel or Roles] and maintain an updated list of related system operations and security documentation in [Documentation Repository].
Apply the FedRAMP Secure Configuration Guide rules to configuration documentation and baselines.
Develop system documentation describing the system's purpose, technical operation, access, maintenance, and required training for administrators and users.
Upon changes in system functions or processes, update the relevant documentation, ensuring each document carries a date and version number.
Evaluate documentation against the risk management strategy and its essentiality to security control implementation or operation, and protect it accordingly.
Apply Example Org's defined systems security and privacy engineering principles in the specification, design, development, implementation, and modification of the system and its components.

In design reviews, verify application of the NIST-defined security design principles as applicable: clear abstractions; least common mechanism; modularity and layering; partially ordered dependencies; efficiently mediated access; minimized sharing; reduced complexity; secure evolvability; trusted components; hierarchical trust; inverse modification threshold; hierarchical protection; minimized security elements; least privilege; predicate permission; self-reliant trustworthiness; secure distributed composition; trusted communications channels; continuous protection; secure metadata management; self-analysis; accountability and traceability; secure defaults; secure failure and recovery; economic security; performance security; human factored security; acceptable security; repeatable and documented procedures; procedural rigor; secure system modification; and sufficient documentation.
Verify least privilege is reflected in all aspects of the design, consistent with AC-6.
Verify trusted communications channels restrict access to the channel and employ end-to-end protections for data transmitted over it.

Verify accountability and traceability: security-relevant subject-object interactions must trace to the entity on whose behalf the action is taken, supported by a trustworthy infrastructure recording details of actions affecting system security.
Verify secure defaults are implemented in all shipped configurations.
Require that all system changes are accompanied by a Security Impact Analysis (SIA) and a Privacy Impact Assessment (PIA) before approval; file both in [Ticketing System].
Verify sufficient documentation accompanies each component per Procedure Steps 11.

Implement the privacy principle of minimization using [Organization-Defined Minimization Processes], driven by business needs, coordinated with the Senior Official for Privacy, and consistent with PM-25, PT-2, and SI-12.

Require the developer to perform configuration management during design, development, implementation, operation, and disposal; document, manage, and control the integrity of changes to [Organization-Defined Configuration Items]; implement only Example Org-approved changes; and document approved changes and their potential security and privacy impacts.
Require the developer to track security flaws and flaw resolution within the system, component, or service and report findings to [Organization-Defined Personnel or Roles].
Require the developer to enable integrity verification of software, firmware, and hardware components.
Where no dedicated developer configuration management team exists, Application Security provides an alternate configuration management process using organizational personnel.

Require the developer to employ tools for comparing newly generated versions of security-relevant hardware descriptions, source code, and object code with previous versions, to maintain the integrity of the mapping between master build data for the current version and the on-site master copy, and to execute procedures ensuring updates distributed to Example Org are exactly as specified by the master copies.
Include [Organization-Defined Security and Privacy Representatives] — designated by Application Security — in the configuration change management and control process.
Require the developer, at all post-design stages, to develop and implement a plan for ongoing security and privacy control assessments; review the plan at each assessment cycle.

Require the developer to perform unit, integration, system, and regression testing/evaluation at [Organization-Defined Frequency, Depth, and Coverage], to produce evidence of execution of the assessment plan and the results, and to verify the scope of testing provides complete coverage of required controls at that breadth and depth.
Require the developer to implement a verifiable flaw remediation process and to correct flaws identified during testing and evaluation; track corrections in [Ticketing System].
Prohibit security-relevant modifications of the information system after the assessment; if a modification is required, re-assess before acceptance.
Use non-production data when executing test scripts, or configure the test environment to comply with the security controls as though it were a production environment.

Connect all systems supporting development and pre-production testing to an isolated network separated from production systems; permit network traffic into and out of that environment only to facilitate system testing, restricted by source and destination access control lists as well as ports and protocols.
Require the developer to employ static code analysis tools to identify common flaws and document the results; retain the SAST results per release as evidence in [Documentation Repository].

Require the developer to perform threat modeling and vulnerability analyses during development and subsequent testing and evaluation, using [Organization-Defined Contextual Information] (impact, environment of operations, known or assumed threats, acceptable risk levels), [Organization-Defined Tools and Methods], at [Organization-Defined Breadth and Depth], producing evidence meeting [Organization-Defined Acceptance Criteria].

Require an independent agent satisfying [Independence Criteria] to verify correct implementation of the developer's assessment plans and the evidence produced; confirm the agent is provided sufficient information or granted authority to obtain it.
Require the developer to perform a manual code review of [Organization-Defined Specific Code] using [Organization-Defined Processes, Procedures, and/or Techniques].
Require the developer to perform penetration testing at [Organization-Defined Breadth and Depth] under [Organization-Defined Constraints].
Require the developer to perform attack surface reviews and to employ interactive application security testing tools to identify flaws and document the results.
Require the developer to employ dynamic code analysis tools to identify common flaws and document the results; retain the DAST results per release as evidence in [Documentation Repository].

Require the developer to follow a documented development process that explicitly addresses security and privacy requirements, identifies the standards and tools used, documents the specific tool options and tool configurations used, and documents, manages, and ensures the integrity of changes to the process and/or tools.

Review the development process, standards, tools, tool options, and tool configurations at least every one (1) year or as needed, to determine whether they can satisfy [Organization-Defined Security and Privacy Requirements]; base those requirements on the ARC-AMPE security and privacy controls or their equivalent, including all applicable System Acquisition (SA) and Configuration Management (CM) controls.
Define quality metrics at the beginning of the development process and require evidence of meeting them at [Organization-Defined Frequency], program review, and/or upon delivery.
Require the developer to select and employ security and privacy tracking tools for use during the development process.
Perform criticality analysis at [Organization-Defined Decision Points] in the life cycle at [Organization-Defined Breadth and Depth of Analysis].
Require the developer to reduce attack surfaces to [Organization-Defined Thresholds] and to implement an explicit process to continuously improve the development process.

Perform automated vulnerability analysis using [Organization-Defined Tools]; determine the exploitation potential and potential risk mitigations for discovered vulnerabilities; deliver the tool outputs and analysis results to [Organization-Defined Personnel or Roles].
Retain dependency and supply-chain scan output as evidence in [Documentation Repository].
Require the developer to use threat modeling and vulnerability analyses from similar systems, components, or services to inform the current development process.

Require the developer to provide, implement, and test an incident response plan, and to archive the system or component to be released or delivered together with the corresponding evidence supporting the final security and privacy review.
Require the developer to minimize the use of personally identifiable information in development and test environments.

Require the developer to provide [Organization-Defined Training] on the correct use and operation of the implemented security and privacy functions, controls, and/or mechanisms; schedule delivery before system acceptance.

Require the developer to produce a design specification and security and privacy architecture consistent with Example Org's security and privacy architecture (an integral part of the enterprise architecture), accurately and completely describing required functionality, the allocation of controls among physical and logical components, and how individual functions, mechanisms, and services work together to provide a unified approach to protection.

Require production, as an integral part of development, of a formal policy model describing [Organization-Defined Elements] of organizational security and privacy policy to be enforced, with proof that the model is internally consistent and sufficient to enforce those elements when implemented.
Require the developer to define security-relevant hardware, software, and firmware and provide a rationale that the definition is complete.

Require a formal top-level specification of the interfaces to security-relevant hardware, software, and firmware in terms of exceptions, error messages, and effects, with demonstration of its consistency with the formal policy model, complete coverage of those interfaces, and accuracy as a description of the implemented components, plus description of security-relevant internal mechanisms not addressed in the specification.
Require an informal descriptive top-level specification meeting the same consistency, coverage, accuracy, and internal-mechanism description requirements.

Require that security-relevant hardware, software, and firmware be designed and structured around a complete, conceptually simple protection mechanism with precisely defined semantics, internally structured with specific regard for this mechanism, structured to facilitate testing, and structured to facilitate controlling access with least privilege.

For [Organization-Defined Critical Systems], require coordinated behavior to implement [Organization-Defined Capabilities] and require different designs to satisfy a common set of requirements or provide equivalent functionality.

Before granting developer access, verify with the assigned Authorizing Official (or designee) that the developer of the systems, components, or services has appropriate access authorizations and satisfies personnel screening criteria consistent with PS-3; record the verification in [Ticketing System].
Monitor vendor support status continuously; replace system components when support is no longer available from the developer, vendor, or manufacturer.
Provide alternative sources for continued support for unsupported components, such as in-house support or support from [Organization-Defined External Providers].

Where unsupported components are retained to satisfy mission/business needs, document the justification and approval in a risk acceptance form in [Risk Acceptance Register] and update the related POA&M finding in [POA&M System].

Establish plans to mitigate or remove unsupported systems, applications, operating systems, or software once identified, and upgrade, retire, or stop use of the component before end of life or vendor discontinuation of product support.
If removal is not feasible, Application Security maintains a governance process to review unsupported system components and make a risk-based decision on their continued use.

Check the validity of all information inputs to web/application servers, database servers, and any system or application input that might receive a crafted exploit toward executing code or causing a buffer overflow, verifying that inputs match specified definitions for format and content.

When PII is entered, use validation techniques that support data quality (e.g., ensuring the PII entered is the expected type and format), provide the capability to limit or exclude entering PII in fields that should not contain it, and take reasonable steps to ensure PII is complete, accurate, and up to date as required by laws and regulations.
Provide a manual override capability for input validation of [Organization-Defined Information Inputs], restrict its use to [Organization-Defined Authorized Individuals], and audit its use.
Review and resolve input validation errors within [Input Validation Error Resolution Period].

Verify that the system behaves in a predictable and documented manner when invalid inputs are received, and account for timing interactions among system components in determining appropriate responses for invalid inputs.
Restrict the use of information inputs to [Organization-Defined Trusted Sources] and/or [Organization-Defined Formats], and prevent untrusted data injections.

Generate error messages that provide information necessary for corrective actions without revealing information that could be exploited — such as user name and password combinations, password-reset validation attributes, PII, biometric or authentication data, sensitive financial records, or content related to internal security functions.

Reveal error messages only to [Organization-Defined Personnel or Roles] documented in the applicable System Security and Privacy Plan — authorized individuals with a need for the information in the performance of their duties.

Establish a process, in coordination with [Organization-Defined Supply Chain Personnel], to identify and address weaknesses or deficiencies in the supply chain elements and processes of [Organization-Defined Systems or Components].

Employ [Organization-Defined Supply Chain Controls] to protect against supply chain risks and to limit the harm or consequences from supply chain-related events; these controls are not limited to those defined in ARC-AMPE and may include other NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 supply chain controls as appropriate.
Document the selected and implemented supply chain processes and controls in security and privacy plans, the supply chain risk management plan, and [Other Organization-Defined Documents].
The CSO documents and maintains supply chain custody, including replacement devices, to ensure the integrity of devices before they are introduced to the boundary.

Employ a diverse set of sources for [Organization-Defined System Components and Services], and employ [Organization-Defined Controls] to limit harm from potential adversaries identifying and targeting the organizational supply chain.
Ensure the controls included in the contracts of prime contractors are also included in the contracts of subcontractors.

Employ [Organization-Defined Acquisition Strategies, Contract Tools, and Procurement Methods] to protect against, identify, and mitigate supply chain risks, and employ [Organization-Defined Controls] to ensure an adequate supply of [Organization-Defined Critical System Components].
Assess the system, component, or service prior to selection, acceptance, modification, or update; retain dependency and supply-chain scan output as evidence in [Documentation Repository].
Implement a tamper protection program for the system, component, or service, and employ anti-tamper technologies, tools, and techniques throughout the system development life cycle.

Inspect [Organization-Defined Systems or System Components] at random, at [Inspection Frequency], and/or upon [Organization-Defined Indications of Need for Inspection] to detect tampering; record inspection results in [Ticketing System].
Develop and implement anti-counterfeit policy and procedures that include the means to detect and prevent counterfeit components from entering the system.
Report counterfeit system components to the source of the counterfeit component, [Organization-Defined External Reporting Organizations], and/or [Organization-Defined Personnel or Roles].
Train [Organization-Defined Personnel or Roles] to detect counterfeit system components, including hardware, software, and firmware.
Maintain configuration control over [Organization-Defined System Components] awaiting service or repair and serviced or repaired components awaiting return to service.
Scan for counterfeit system components at [Counterfeit Scan Frequency].

Dispose of [Organization-Defined Data, Documentation, Tools, or System Components] using techniques and methods in accordance with the latest published NIST SP 800-88, Guidelines for Media Sanitization, consistent with MP-6 Media Sanitization; record sanitization results in [Ticketing System].

The Application Security team owns this procedure end to end: it performs the reviews, approvals, and verifications described above, coordinates Development Teams, the Privacy Office, Procurement/Contracting, System Owners, and supply chain personnel as participants, and answers for the outcome and evidence of each step.

Exceptions — including retention of unsupported components and use of live data or PII in preproduction — require Application Security review and, where specified, approval by the Senior Official for Privacy or the Authorizing Official (or designee).
