Sanitize Media at Disposal [NIST 800-53 SR-12 | ARC-AMPE SR-12]

analyze: This procedure provides the step-by-step operational instructions for establishing, authorizing, securing, monitoring, and revoking remote access, wireless access, mobile device access, external system use, and third-party vendor access to Example Org systems.
Executing it produces the evidence artifacts required by the Remote & Third-Party Access Standard: the VPN and remote-access configuration and the Third-party access register.

Network Security performs this procedure end to end on all Example Org remote access methods, wireless networks, mobile devices, external system connections, and publicly accessible systems, with Business Owners, Authorizing Officials, system owners, and Privacy/Counsel participants as noted in individual steps.
It applies to all users — employees, contractors, vendors, and teleworkers — connecting to Example Org systems from non-organizational locations or devices.
- Access to the [VPN Gateway] administration console and the [Network Access Control Point] firewall/policy management interface
- Administrative access to the [Identity Provider] for account creation and recertification
- Administrative access to the [Endpoint Management Platform], [Mobile Device Management (MDM) Platform], and [Wireless Controller]
- Access to the [SIEM] and [Ticketing System] for logging, alerting, and authorization workflow
- The current System Security and Privacy Plan (SSPP) for each in-scope system
- The current VPN and remote-access configuration document and Third-party access register
- Written authorization from the system Business Owner and, where required below, the Authorizing Official (AO)
- The latest published NIST SP 800-46, FIPS 140-compliant encryption standards, and IEEE 802.11 WLAN standard references
- A designated list of officials authorized to order disconnection of remote access or network connections
Inventory every type of remote access in use (e.g., VPN, vendor logon, wireless, teleworking, external system connections) and record each in the VPN and remote-access configuration document.

For each type, document the usage restrictions, configuration and connection requirements, and implementation guidance, using the latest published NIST SP 800-46 guidance as the baseline for teleworking entries.
Network Security reviews and re-approves the document quarterly and upon any change to a remote access method.
Require a connection request for each new remote access type to be submitted through the [Ticketing System], describing the access method, users, and systems involved.
Network Security reviews the request against the documented configuration and connection requirements.
Obtain written authorization from the system Business Owner before enabling the connection.
Record the authorization decision in the VPN and remote-access configuration document; do not enable the connection until authorization is complete.
Where a connection cannot traverse the MPLS service network, configure the [VPN Gateway] to require callback to a pre-registered, authorized location before the session is established.
Require the user to re-authenticate after the callback is completed; do not permit single-factor session continuation.
Document each callback-enabled connection and its authorized locations in the VPN and remote-access configuration document.
For each application or turnkey system requiring vendor logon, assign the vendor a unique User ID and password through the [Identity Provider]; do not share default or shared credentials.
Require vendor access to enter through the standard authentication process — no direct or backdoor entry paths.
Configure the [SIEM] to log each vendor session; record the vendor, User ID, system, and authorization basis in the Third-party access register.
Network Security recertifies every vendor User ID at least every one (1) year; disable any vendor User ID that is not affirmatively recertified.

Before granting network access, verify via the [Endpoint Management Platform] that each device — government-furnished, contractor-furnished, or personal — has, at minimum: up-to-date system patches; current anti-virus software; a host-based intrusion detection system; automatic execution of code disabled; and the latest published FIPS 140-compliant encryption standards.
Configure the [Network Access Control Point] to quarantine or deny connections from devices that fail any check.
Re-verify device compliance quarterly and upon each new connection.

Maintain policies and procedures that follow the latest published NIST SP 800-46 guidelines and define: the forms of permitted remote access; the types of devices permissible for remote access; the types of access granted to remote users; and the handling of remote user account provisioning.
Network Security reviews these policies quarterly and updates them when NIST SP 800-46 is revised.
Configure the [VPN Gateway] and [SIEM] to automatically monitor all remote access methods for session activity, authentication failures, and policy violations.
Configure automated controls to block or terminate sessions that violate the documented usage restrictions.
Network Security reviews monitoring alerts and tuning quarterly.
Configure the [VPN Gateway] to encrypt all remote access sessions using the latest published FIPS 140-compliant encryption standards, protecting both confidentiality and integrity.
Disable legacy or non-compliant cipher suites on the [VPN Gateway].
Verify the cryptographic configuration during the quarterly review of the VPN and remote-access configuration.
Configure firewall policy so that all remote access enters only through the authorized, managed [Network Access Control Point].
Block direct remote access paths that bypass the control point.
Review firewall rules quarterly to confirm no unauthorized ingress paths exist.

Define, in the applicable System Security and Privacy Plan (SSPP), what constitutes a compelling operational need for executing privileged commands or accessing security-relevant information via remote access.

Permit such execution only for the documented compelling operational needs and only in a format that provides assessable evidence — require session logging through the [SIEM] with command-level recording.
Require each instance to be requested via the [Ticketing System] and approved by Network Security before execution.
Document the rationale for permitting remote access to the system in the system's security plan.

Store the VPN and remote-access configuration document and related mechanism details (addresses, ports, methods) in access-controlled [Document Repository] restricted to Network Security and personnel with a documented need to know.
Do not disclose remote access mechanism details in tickets, email, or public channels; share only through the approved controlled channel.
Configure and test a disconnection capability in the [VPN Gateway] that can disable remote access to the system within one (1) hour.
Configure the capability to terminate or suspend network connections (system-to-system interconnections) within one (1) hour upon issuance of an order by an authorized official.
Maintain the list of organization-defined officials authorized to issue such orders, and test the disconnect capability quarterly.
Implement [Assignment: organization-defined mechanisms] to authenticate [Assignment: organization-defined remote commands] executed over remote access.
Record the selected mechanisms and commands in the VPN and remote-access configuration document.

Document, for each workstation or class of workstation that can access electronic protected health information: the proper functions to be performed; the manner in which those functions are to be performed; and the physical attributes of the surroundings of the workstation.
Network Security reviews these workstation specifications quarterly and upon workspace or system changes.
For each type of wireless access, establish configuration requirements, connection requirements, and implementation guidance, recorded alongside the VPN and remote-access configuration.
Require each wireless access type to be authorized through the [Ticketing System] and approved by Network Security prior to allowing connections.
If wireless access is explicitly approved, configure and verify each of the following via the [Wireless Controller] and \[Endpoint Management Platform\]: Disable wireless device SSID broadcasting.
Place access points in secure areas.
Shut down access points when not in use (e.g., nights, weekends).
Implement a stateful inspection firewall between the wireless network and the wired infrastructure.
Utilize Media Access Control (MAC) address authentication.
Utilize static IP addresses rather than DHCP.
Utilize personal firewalls on all wireless clients.
Disable file sharing on all wireless clients.
Deploy intrusion detection agents on the wireless side of the firewall.
Monitor and record wireless activity, with records reviewed on a quarterly basis as part of this procedure's cadence, consistent with the applicable security/privacy plans.
Adhere to the latest published IEEE 802.11 WLAN standard.
Configure the [Wireless Controller] to require authentication of both users and devices before granting wireless access.
Encrypt all communications via the wireless access device using the latest published FIPS 140-compliant encryption standards.
Verify both settings during the quarterly wireless review.

Prior to issuance and deployment, disable wireless networking capabilities embedded within system components that are not intended for use, via the [Endpoint Management Platform] baseline configuration.
Verify the disabled state during device provisioning and the quarterly configuration review.
Identify, by name, the users authorized to independently configure wireless networking capabilities.
Record the authorized list in the VPN and remote-access configuration document and enforce it via role-based permissions in the [Identity Provider].
Network Security revalidates the list quarterly.

Select radio antennas and calibrate transmission power levels on wireless access points via the [Wireless Controller] to reduce the probability that signals can be received outside organization-controlled boundaries.
Validate signal containment during the quarterly wireless review.

Establish configuration requirements, connection requirements, and implementation guidance for organization-controlled mobile devices, including requirements applicable when such devices are outside of controlled areas.
Require the system Business Owner to authorize the use of mobile devices before any connection of a mobile device to organizational systems; record the authorization in the [Ticketing System].
Permit processing, accessing, and storing Personally Identifiable Information (PII) only on organization-owned mobile devices and with organization-owned software; prohibit PII on personal devices.
Configure mobile devices via the [MDM Platform] to protect the storage and transmission of information on the device.
Implement scanning of each device using a virus protection application deployed through the [MDM Platform].

Employ full-device encryption or container-based encryption using the latest published FIPS 140-compliant encryption standards on all approved mobile devices, and encrypt information on all mobile devices that contain PII.
Verify encryption and virus-protection status via the [MDM Platform] quarterly.
Prohibit the use of unclassified mobile devices in facilities containing systems that process, store, or transmit classified information unless specifically permitted by the authorizing official.

For individuals so permitted: prohibit connection of unclassified mobile devices to classified systems; require authorizing official approval for connection of unclassified mobile devices to unclassified systems; and prohibit use of internal or external modems or wireless interfaces within the unclassified mobile devices.

Subject unclassified mobile devices and their stored information to random reviews and inspections by [Assignment: organization-defined security officials]; if classified information is found, follow the incident handling policy.
Restrict the connection of classified mobile devices to classified systems in accordance with [Assignment: organization-defined security policies].

Establish organization-defined terms and conditions for use of external systems, and identify the organization-defined controls asserted to be implemented on external systems, consistent with the trust relationships established with the organizations owning, operating, and/or maintaining those systems.

Ensure the terms and conditions allow authorized individuals to: access the system from external systems; and process, store, or transmit organization-controlled information using external systems — or prohibit the organization-defined prohibited types of external systems.

Ensure the terms and conditions address, at a minimum: the types of applications that can be accessed from external information systems; the maximum FIPS 199 security category of information that can be processed, stored, and transmitted; how other users of the external information system will be prevented from accessing federal information; the use of VPN and stateful inspection firewall technologies; the use of and protection against the vulnerabilities of wireless technologies; the maintenance of adequate physical security controls; the use of virus and spyware protection software; and how often the security capabilities of installed software are to be updated.

Differentiate the interrelated controls as follows: AC-20 governs system access to and from external systems; CA-3 requires documentation of an agreement between the respective system owners when data is exchanged between the CSO and an external system; and SA-9 captures the responsibilities of external system owners, typically in the agreement required by CA-3.

Permit authorized individuals to use an external system to access the system, or to process, store, or transmit organization-controlled information, only after: verification of the implementation of controls on the external system as specified in the organization's security and privacy policies and plans; or retention of an approved system connection or processing agreement with the organizational entity hosting the external system.
Network Security verifies the control implementation or agreement before enabling access and re-verifies quarterly.

Restrict the use of organization-controlled portable storage devices by authorized individuals on external systems using organization-defined restrictions, and permit such use only when all of the following are satisfied: the use is documented within appropriate security/privacy plans; the use is explicitly authorized, in writing, by the Authorizing Official (AO) or designated representative; personally owned devices to which the devices are to be attached comply with organization policies and directives on use of personally owned systems and components; and security and privacy safeguards appropriate for the sensitivity of the data are employed.
Record each written AO authorization in the [Ticketing System] and reference it in the applicable security/privacy plan.

Restrict the use of non-organizationally owned systems or system components to process, store, or transmit organization information unless all of the following are satisfied: contractor-owned device use is documented within the contract and appropriate security and privacy plans and explicitly authorized, in writing, by the AO or designated representative; personally owned device use complies with organizational policies and directives on use of personally owned systems and components; security and privacy safeguards appropriate for the sensitivity of the data are employed; and either full-device or virtual container encryption is implemented to reduce the vulnerability of sensitive information processed, stored, or transmitted by such systems or components.
Strongly discourage the use of personally owned devices.

Before providing access to PII on any remote device, require the device user to acknowledge through a binding agreement their responsibilities to safeguard the PII accessible from the device and their awareness of and agreement to the organization's capabilities to manage the organization's PII on the device, including confiscation, in consultation with the organization's counsel if necessary to remove the PII.
Retain executed agreements with the user's access record in the [Identity Provider].
Prohibit the use of [Assignment: organization-defined network-accessible storage devices] in external systems; enforce the prohibition via [Network Access Control Point] policy.
Prohibit the use of organization-controlled portable storage devices by authorized individuals on external systems; enforce via endpoint control policy on the [Endpoint Management Platform].
Designate, by name, the individuals authorized to make information publicly accessible; record the designations in the [Ticketing System].
Train the designated individuals to ensure that publicly accessible information does not contain nonpublic information.

Review the proposed content of all information prior to posting onto the publicly accessible system to confirm that nonpublic information is not included; Network Security performs or approves this pre-posting review.

Review the content on the publicly accessible system for nonpublic information bi-weekly (no less often than every fourteen [14] days) and remove such information if discovered; record each review and its findings in the [Ticketing System].

Network Security is accountable for this procedure end to end: it documents and authorizes access methods, operates the [VPN Gateway], [Wireless Controller], [MDM Platform], and [Endpoint Management Platform] controls, maintains the VPN and remote-access configuration and Third-party access register, and performs the quarterly and bi-weekly reviews.

System Business Owners authorize mobile device and connection use, the Authorizing Official (or designated representative) provides written authorizations where required, and exceptions to any step in this procedure require Network Security review and AO approval before taking effect.
This procedure operationalizes the **Remote & Third-Party Access Standard**, which contains the full requirement text, control rationale, and applicability determinations behind each step above.
heading_statements: Document usage restrictions and connection requirements for each remote access type
Authorize each remote access type prior to allowing connections
Require callback with re-authentication when the MPLS service network cannot be used
Manage vendor logon accounts for application and turnkey systems
Verify secure configuration of all devices requiring network access
Maintain teleworking policies and procedures per NIST SP 800-46
Employ automated mechanisms to monitor and control remote access
Implement cryptographic protection for remote access sessions
Route remote access through authorized network access control points
Control privileged commands and security-relevant information via remote access
Protect information about remote access mechanisms from unauthorized use and disclosure
Provide capability to disconnect or disable remote access within one (1) hour
Define workstation use requirements for access to electronic protected health information
Establish and authorize wireless access types
Implement mandatory controls for approved wireless access
Protect wireless access with authentication and FIPS 140-compliant encryption
Disable embedded wireless capabilities not intended for use
Explicitly authorize users who may independently configure wireless networking
Select antennas and calibrate transmission power levels
Establish mobile device requirements and authorize connections
Protect information on approved mobile devices
Control mobile devices in facilities with classified systems
Establish terms and conditions for external system use
Authorize external system use before access is permitted
Restrict organization-controlled portable storage device use on external systems
Restrict use of non-organizationally owned systems and components
Prohibit storage device use on external systems

analyze: This procedure provides the step-by-step operational instructions for the Network Security team to implement the network, boundary, information flow, transmission security, and system isolation requirements defined in the Example Org Information Security Standard: Network & Boundary Protection.
Executing this procedure produces the evidence artifacts — the Firewall and segmentation rule review and the External attack-surface scan — that demonstrate continuous compliance with the Standard.

This procedure is performed by the Network Security team, on a continuous basis, across all of Example Org's network boundary devices, firewalls, proxies, gateways, internal network segments, name/address resolution services, and all systems connected to them.
Other teams (System Owners, Human Resources, the Privacy Officer, privileged administrators) participate in individual steps, but Network Security owns the process and its handoffs end to end.
- Administrative access to the [Firewall Management Console], [Proxy Management Console], [VPN Gateway], [Load Balancer], [DNS Service], [Email Gateway], [SIEM], and [Network Monitoring Tools]
- Access to the [Ticketing System] for change requests, exception records, and interconnection documentation
- Access to the [Identity Provider] for identity, session, and privileged access configuration
- Access to the [Vulnerability Scanning Tool] for compliance checks and the External attack-surface scan
- The current Example Org System Security and Privacy Plan (SSPP) and approved security and privacy architecture diagrams
- The organization-defined information flow control policies, security and privacy attribute definitions, and PII processing rules referenced by the Standard
- Written authorization from the CIO or designated representative where the Standard requires it (e.g., collaborative computing exceptions, interconnection termination orders)
- The current system and communications protection policy and procedures, and the HIPAA documentation repository

Maintain the organization-defined information flow control policies in the SSPP, and translate each policy into enforceable rules on the [Firewall Management Console], [Proxy Management Console], and [Load Balancer].
Configure deny-by-default rules at every managed interface so that information flows within the system and between connected systems occur only where an approved authorization exists.
Map each approved authorization to a named rule or policy object, and record the mapping in the [Ticketing System] so every permitted flow is traceable to an approval.
Include the resulting rule set and its approval mappings in the Firewall and segmentation rule review artifact.
Record, in the System Security and Privacy Plan, the authority to order immediate termination or suspension of any interconnection.
When an interconnection presents unacceptable risk, escalate to the Authorizing Official, who makes the risk-informed decision in consultation with the system owner.

Upon an order from the Authorizing Official, Network Security immediately disables the interconnection at the managed interface via the [Firewall Management Console] and records the action, decision, and rationale in the [Ticketing System].

Configure the organization-defined security and privacy attributes on information, source, and destination objects in the [Identity Provider] and [Firewall Management Console], and write flow control rules that evaluate those attributes as the basis for flow decisions.

Define protected processing domains in the network architecture and enforce flow control policies at the boundaries between those domains using the [Firewall Management Console] and segmentation controls.

Implement the organization-defined dynamic information flow control policies using [Network Monitoring Tools] and policy engines capable of adjusting flow decisions based on current conditions, and verify dynamic behavior during each Firewall and segmentation rule review.
Configure the [Proxy Management Console] or [Load Balancer] to decrypt TLS traffic at the boundary so flow control mechanisms can inspect it, per the organization-defined method.

Where decryption is not organization-defined for a flow, configure the boundary device to block the flow or terminate the communications session attempting to pass encrypted information through uninspected.
Log every block or termination event to the [SIEM].

Configure the organization-defined limitations on embedding data types within other data types (e.g., blocking archive-in-archive or script-in-document nesting) on the [Content Filtering Solution] at the boundary.

Configure flow control enforcement based on the organization-defined metadata (e.g., classification labels, data type tags) so that flows carrying disallowed metadata are denied at the managed interface.
Identify flows the organization defines as one-way, and implement them using hardware-based flow control mechanisms (e.g., data diodes) rather than software-only controls.
Verify during each Firewall and segmentation rule review that no software path bypasses the hardware enforcement point.
Deploy the organization-defined security or privacy policy filters for the organization-defined information flows on the [Content Filtering Solution] and [Email Gateway].

Configure each filter's failure action — block, strip, modify, or quarantine — in accordance with the organization-defined security or privacy policy, and verify the failure action fires correctly during testing.

Implement the human review workflow for the organization-defined information flows under the organization-defined conditions: route flagged items to a designated Network Security reviewer via the [Ticketing System], and require documented reviewer disposition before release.

Grant privileged administrators the capability to enable and disable policy filters under the organization-defined conditions, restricted to the privileged administrator role in the [Identity Provider].
Grant privileged administrators the capability to configure policy filters to support different security or privacy policies, with each policy variant stored as a distinct, named configuration.
Configure the organization-defined data type identifiers on the cross-domain transfer solution and validate data essential for information flow decisions against them before transfer.
Decompose transferred information into the organization-defined policy-relevant subcomponents and submit each subcomponent to the applicable policy enforcement mechanism.
Implement policy filters requiring fully enumerated formats that restrict data structure and content on each cross-domain transfer path.
Examine transferred information for the organization-defined unsanctioned information and prohibit its transfer in accordance with the organization-defined security or privacy policy.
Implement the organization-defined security or privacy policy filters on metadata for cross-domain transfers.

Configure the [Identity Provider], [VPN Gateway], and boundary devices to uniquely identify and authenticate each source and destination point — by organization, system, application, service, or individual — before permitting information transfer.
Reject transfers from unauthenticated endpoints and log the rejection to the [SIEM].
Maintain the list of organization-defined approved solutions for controlling information flow across security domains in the SSPP.
Deploy each approved solution only in its approved configuration, and verify configurations against the approved baseline during each Firewall and segmentation rule review.
Implement the organization-defined logical or physical separation mechanisms and techniques to accomplish the organization-defined required separations between information flows.

Where single-device access to platforms, applications, or data in multiple security domains is required, configure the access solution to prevent information flow between those domains, and validate the prevention controls before granting access.
Configure the cross-domain solution to modify non-releasable information using the organization-defined modification action before transfer between security domains.
Configure the cross-domain solution to parse incoming data into an internal normalized format and regenerate it consistent with its intended specification.

Configure sanitization of transferred data to minimize delivery of malicious content, command and control of malicious code, malicious code augmentation, steganography-encoded data, and spillage of sensitive information, in accordance with the organization-defined policy.
Configure the [Content Filtering Solution] to record and audit all content filtering actions and results for transfers between security domains, forwarding records to the [SIEM].
Implement redundant and independent filtering mechanisms for each data type, and document the independence of mechanisms in the architecture diagrams.
Implement a linear content filter pipeline enforced with discretionary and mandatory access controls, and document the pipeline order.

Configure monitoring to ensure content filtering mechanisms complete execution without errors and that filtering actions occur in the documented order and comply with organization-defined policy; alert on out-of-order or failed execution via the [SIEM].
Implement content filtering mechanisms using multiple processes as organization-defined.
Configure the pipeline to prevent transfer of failed content to the receiving domain.

For message-based transfers, configure the pipeline so message content is not filtered at the metadata stage, filtering metadata is validated, content is confirmed to have successfully completed filtering, and content is then transferred to the destination filter pipeline.

Implement the access policies in the [Identity Provider] so that all workforce members have appropriate access to electronic protected health information (ePHI) and workforce members without access under those policies cannot obtain it.
Maintain the authorization and supervision procedures for workforce members who work with ePHI or in locations where ePHI might be accessed, coordinated with Human Resources and the Privacy Officer.
Execute the determination procedure confirming each workforce member's access to ePHI is appropriate, using role reviews in the [Identity Provider].

On notification from Human Resources that employment or another arrangement has ended, or upon a clearance determination requiring it, disable the workforce member's access to ePHI in the [Identity Provider] and confirm removal of network paths to ePHI systems.
Maintain the policies and procedures for authorizing access to ePHI consistent with applicable subpart E requirements.

If a health care clearinghouse is part of a larger organization, implement segmentation and access controls protecting the clearinghouse's ePHI from unauthorized access by the larger organization, and include the segmentation rules in the Firewall and segmentation rule review.
Implement the procedures for granting access to ePHI — through access to a workstation, transaction, program, process, or other mechanism — via the [Identity Provider] and [Ticketing System].

Establish, document, review, and modify each user's right of access to a workstation, transaction, program, or process based on the entity's access authorization policies, recording each grant and modification in the [Ticketing System].

Document the proper functions to be performed, the manner of their performance, and the physical attributes of the surroundings of workstations (or workstation classes) that can access ePHI, and enforce the corresponding network access rules.

Require a documented authorization, recorded in the [Ticketing System], before connecting any organization-defined system component — or class of components with common characteristics or configurations — to the system.

For each internal connection, document the interface characteristics, security and privacy requirements, and the nature of the information communicated, and attach the documentation to the authorization record.

Perform security and privacy compliance checks on constituent system components using the [Vulnerability Scanning Tool] prior to establishing the internal connection; do not enable the connection until checks pass.
Review the continued need for each internal connection at least every one (1) year, and terminate connections that no longer support organizational missions or business functions.

Terminate internal system connections after the organization-defined conditions — including issuance of an order by the Chief Information Officer, Chief Information Security Officer, or senior privacy official — by disabling the connection at the managed interface and recording the termination in the [Ticketing System].

Develop, document, and disseminate the system and communications protection policy — at the organization level per ARC-AMPE — addressing purpose, scope, roles, responsibilities, management commitment, coordination among organizational entities, and compliance, consistent with applicable laws, executive orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, and guidelines.
Develop and disseminate the procedures (including this document) that facilitate implementation of the policy and its associated controls.
The designated official named in the appropriate security and privacy documents manages the development, documentation, and dissemination of the policy and procedures.

Review and update the policy and procedures at least every one (1) year and following organization-defined events, including assessment or audit findings, security or privacy incidents, and changes to applicable laws, executive orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, and guidelines.

Actively monitor for changes to applicable privacy laws, regulations, and overarching policy affecting system and communications protection, and review the policies at least every one (1) year to ensure they remain effective throughout the system's life cycle.

Maintain the policies and procedures implemented for compliance in written (electronic permitted) form, and maintain a written record of any required action, activity, or assessment — including the Firewall and segmentation rule review and the External attack-surface scan.
Retain required documentation for 6 years from the date of its creation or the date it was last in effect, whichever is later.
Make documentation available to the persons responsible for implementing the procedures to which it pertains, via the documentation repository.
Review documentation periodically and update it as needed in response to environmental or operational changes affecting the security of ePHI.

Separate user functionality, including user interface services, from system management functionality using physical or logical methods — different computers, operating system instances, CPUs, or network addresses, virtualization, separate authentication for web administrative interfaces, or isolating administrative interfaces on different domains with additional access controls.

Configure administrative interfaces so system management functionality is withheld entirely from non-privileged users — not merely greyed out — and is presented only after a session is established with administrator privileges.
Configure applications to store state information separately from other application and software data.

Isolate security functions from nonsecurity functions by means of an isolation boundary implemented via partitions and domains that controls access to and protects the integrity of the hardware, software, and firmware performing security functions.
Employ hardware separation mechanisms to implement security function isolation.
Isolate the security functions enforcing access and information flow control from nonsecurity functions and from other security functions.
Minimize the number of nonsecurity functions included within the isolation boundary containing security functions, and document the boundary contents.
When developing or procuring security functions, require implementation as largely independent modules that maximize internal cohesiveness and minimize coupling between modules.
Require security functions to be implemented as a layered structure that minimizes interactions between layers and avoids lower-layer dependence on the functionality or correctness of higher layers.

Configure systems to prevent unauthorized and unintended information transfer via shared system resources, so information produced by prior users, roles, or processes acting on their behalf is not available to current users or processes that obtain access to those resources after release.

When system processing explicitly switches between different information classification levels or security categories, apply the organization-defined procedures to prevent unauthorized information transfer via shared resources, including clearing or reassigning shared buffers, memory, and storage between processing runs.

Deploy controls protecting against — and, per NIST, optionally limiting — the organization-defined types of denial-of-service events, which per ARC-AMPE must include at minimum ICMP flood, SYN flood, slowloris, buffer overflow attack, and volume attack, informed by the latest published NIST SP 800-61 and applicable threat resources.

Employ the organization-defined controls, by type of denial-of-service event, to achieve the denial-of-service objective, configuring rate limiting, SYN cookies, and request timeouts on the [Load Balancer] and boundary devices.

Restrict the ability of individuals to launch the organization-defined denial-of-service attacks against other systems: make commonly used attack mechanisms unavailable and prohibit egress to potential target systems on specific systems or boundary devices.
Manage capacity, bandwidth, or other redundancy — through usage priorities, quotas, partitioning, or load balancing — to limit the effects of information flooding denial-of-service attacks.

Employ the organization-defined monitoring tools, informed by the latest published NIST SP 800-61, to detect indicators of denial-of-service attacks against or launched from the system, and monitor the organization-defined system resources to determine whether sufficient resources exist to prevent effective denial-of-service attacks; alert through the [SIEM].

Monitor and control communications at the external managed interfaces to the system and at the key internal managed interfaces within the system, using the [Firewall Management Console] and [Network Monitoring Tools] on a continuous basis.

Implement subnetworks for publicly accessible system components that are logically separated from internal organizational networks, ensuring traffic cannot traverse unrestricted from publicly accessible components to internal networks without inspection and authorization.
Connect to external networks or systems only through managed interfaces consisting of boundary protection devices arranged in accordance with the organizational security and privacy architecture.
Deny access to all proxies except for hosts, ports, and services that are explicitly required, and record each allowed proxy path.

Utilize stateful inspection/application firewall hardware and software, and use firewalls from at least two (2) or more different vendors at various levels within the network to reduce the possibility of compromising the entire network.

For systems with an outward-facing public web or email presence, implement and support a technical capability to detect malware in web traffic traversing the organizational boundary, including monitoring assets without deployed software agents (zero client footprint), dynamically generating actionable malware intelligence, detecting and stopping web-based and email attacks, and sending alert data to the [SIEM] as applicable.
Ensure aggregated boundary protection device information is searchable across boundary protection systems, appliances, devices, services, and applications via the [SIEM].
Run the External attack-surface scan against the external managed interfaces on a continuous basis and retain the results as an evidence artifact.
Limit the number of external network connections to the system to facilitate more comprehensive monitoring of inbound and outbound communications traffic, and document each connection in the SSPP.

Implement a managed interface for each external telecommunication service, establish a traffic flow policy for each interface, and protect the confidentiality and integrity of information transmitted across each interface.

Document each traffic flow policy exception with its supporting mission or business need and duration in the [Ticketing System]; review exceptions within every one (1) year or whenever a change in the threat environment warrants review, and remove exceptions no longer supported by an explicit mission or business need.

Prevent unauthorized exchange of control plane traffic with external networks; publish information enabling remote networks to detect unauthorized control plane traffic from internal networks; and filter unauthorized control plane traffic from external networks at the boundary devices.

Configure all managed interfaces to deny network communications traffic by default and allow it by exception, for both inbound and outbound traffic, as documented in the applicable System Security and Privacy Plan.
Record each allow exception with its justification in the [Ticketing System] and include the full rule set in the Firewall and segmentation rule review artifact.

Configure the [VPN Gateway] to prevent split tunneling for remote devices connecting to organizational systems, unless the split tunnel is securely provisioned using the organization-defined safeguards, such as sufficiently provisioned VPNs for remote connections.

Route the organization-defined internal communications traffic — including traffic bound for any untrusted external network or any network outside organizational control or the authorization boundary — through authenticated proxy servers at managed interfaces.
Document the man-in-the-middle risk introduced by the proxy implementation and the effect on VPN use in the architecture documentation.

Configure boundary devices to detect and deny outgoing communications traffic posing a threat to external systems, and audit the identity of internal users associated with denied communications by correlating [Identity Provider] and [SIEM] records.

Deploy the [DLP Solution] to prevent the exfiltration of information at the managed interfaces, and conduct exfiltration tests at the organization-defined frequency, retaining test results as evidence.
Configure managed interfaces so only incoming communications from the organization-defined authorized sources are routed to the organization-defined authorized destinations.
Reject and log all other source-destination pairs to the [SIEM].

Implement host-based boundary protection mechanisms — at minimum a host-based firewall, or HIPS/HIDS per ARC-AMPE — at the organization-defined system components, including all components capable of supporting them such as servers, workstations, and devices operating outside the organizational boundary (e.g., laptops and mobile devices).

Isolate the organization-defined information security tools, mechanisms, and support components from other internal system components by implementing physically separate subnetworks with managed interfaces.
Protect against unauthorized physical connections at the organization-defined managed interfaces, including port security and physical inspection of termination points.
Route networked, privileged accesses through a dedicated, managed interface for purposes of access control and auditing.
Configure the boundary to prevent the discovery of specific system components that represent a managed interface (e.g., suppress responses to discovery scans from untrusted sources).
Enforce adherence to protocol formats at the managed interfaces, dropping nonconforming traffic.

Configure boundary protection devices to fail in a manner that prevents systems from entering unsecure states — where system objects can be accessed in an unauthorized manner — in the event of an operational failure, and test the failure behavior.
Block inbound and outbound communications traffic between the organization-defined communication clients that are independently configured by end users and external service providers.

Provide the capability to dynamically isolate the organization-defined system components from other system components, executable on demand by Network Security via the [Firewall Management Console] or [Network Monitoring Tools].
Employ boundary protection mechanisms to isolate the organization-defined system components supporting the organization-defined missions and/or business functions.
Implement separate network addresses to connect to systems in different security domains.
Disable feedback to senders on protocol format validation failure.

For systems processing personally identifiable information, apply the organization-defined PII processing rules — per ARC-AMPE, rules ensuring compliance with the ACA, Privacy Act, and other applicable PII processing laws and regulations — at the external interfaces and key internal boundaries.
Monitor for permitted processing at those interfaces using the [DLP Solution] and [SIEM].
Document each processing exception in the [Ticketing System], and review and remove exceptions no longer supported.
Prohibit the direct connection of the organization-defined unclassified national security system to an external network without the use of the organization-defined boundary protection device.
Prohibit the direct connection of a classified national security system to an external network without the use of the organization-defined boundary protection device.
Prohibit the direct connection of the organization-defined unclassified, non-national security system to an external network without the use of the organization-defined boundary protection device.
Prohibit the direct connection of the organization-defined system to a public network.
Verify compliance with these prohibitions during each External attack-surface scan and Firewall and segmentation rule review.

Implement physically or logically separate subnetworks to isolate the organization-defined critical system components and functions from noncritical components and functions, reducing susceptibility to catastrophic or debilitating breach or compromise resulting in system failure.
Document the critical/noncritical segmentation in the architecture diagrams and validate it in the Firewall and segmentation rule review.

Protect the confidentiality and integrity of transmitted information across internal and external networks and all system components capable of transmitting information, using physical or logical means; per ARC-AMPE, encrypt any transmitted data containing sensitive information (e.g., PII, proprietary, financial, legal) using the latest published FIPS 140-compliant encryption standards.
Implement technical security measures to guard against unauthorized access to ePHI being transmitted over an electronic communications network.

Place all sensitive information in an encrypted attachment prior to sending electronic email, and encrypt email and attachments containing sensitive information transmitted outside the organization using the latest published FIPS 140-compliant encryption standards via the [Email Gateway].

Do not include the password or encryption key in the same email containing sensitive information or in a separate email; provide it to the recipient separately via text message, verbally, or another out-of-band solution, and do not use password protection of files in lieu of encryption solutions.

Implement cryptographic mechanisms to prevent unauthorized disclosure of information and detect changes to information during transmission; per ARC-AMPE, use the latest published FIPS 140-compliant encryption standards or protected distribution systems to protect PII in transit.
Maintain the confidentiality and integrity of information during preparation for transmission and during reception.
Implement cryptographic mechanisms to protect message externals unless otherwise protected by the organization-defined alternative physical controls.
Implement cryptographic mechanisms to conceal or randomize communication patterns unless otherwise protected by the organization-defined alternative physical controls.
Implement the organization-defined protected distribution system to prevent unauthorized disclosure of or detect changes to information during transmission.
Implement policies and procedures to protect ePHI from improper alteration or destruction.
Implement electronic mechanisms to corroborate that ePHI has not been altered or destroyed in an unauthorized manner.
Implement security measures to ensure electronically transmitted ePHI is not improperly modified without detection until disposed of.
Implement a mechanism to encrypt ePHI whenever deemed appropriate, per the encryption decisions documented in the SSPP.

Configure the [Identity Provider], [VPN Gateway], and application gateways to terminate the network connection associated with a communications session at the end of the session or after the defined period of inactivity: after thirty (30) minutes for privileged sessions and no longer than sixty (60) minutes for general user sessions.
Authorized management or senior security officials may terminate or suspend system-to-system interconnections; record each such action in the [Ticketing System].

Prohibit remote activation of collaborative computing devices and applications (e.g., remote meeting tools, networked white boards, cameras, microphones), with no exceptions per ARC-AMPE unless explicitly authorized in writing by the CIO or designated representative, with any authorization specifically identifying the allowed mechanisms, purpose, and the information system on which they may be used.
Configure collaborative computing devices to provide an explicit indication of use to users physically present at the devices when the devices or applications are activated.
Provide physical or logical disconnect of collaborative computing devices in a manner that supports ease of use.
Disable or remove collaborative computing devices and applications from the organization-defined systems or system components in the organization-defined secure work areas.
Configure online meeting and teleconferencing tools to provide an explicit indication of current participants.

Configure the [DNS Service] to provide additional data origin authentication and integrity verification artifacts, such as DNSSEC digital signatures and cryptographic keys, along with the authoritative name resolution data returned in response to external name/address resolution queries.

When operating as part of a distributed, hierarchical namespace, provide the means to indicate the security status of child zones and, if the child supports secure resolution services, enable verification of a chain of trust among parent and child domains.
Provide data origin and integrity protection artifacts for internal name/address resolution queries.
Configure resolving systems to request and perform data origin authentication and data integrity verification on name/address resolution responses received from authoritative sources.
Ensure the systems that collectively provide name/address resolution service for the organization are fault-tolerant and implement internal and external role separation.

Protect the authenticity of communications sessions, including protection against man-in-the-middle attacks, session hijacking, and insertion of false information into sessions, using TLS configuration baselines enforced at the [Load Balancer] and application gateways.
Invalidate session identifiers upon user logout or other session termination.
Generate a unique session identifier for each session meeting the organization-defined randomness requirements, and configure applications to recognize only system-generated session identifiers.
Only allow the use of the organization-defined certificate authorities for verification of the establishment of protected sessions, enforced via the trusted certificate store.

For the organization-defined types of failures on the indicated components, configure systems to fail to the organization-defined known system state, preserving the organization-defined system state information to facilitate restart and return to operational mode.

Verify that failure behavior prevents loss of confidentiality, integrity, or availability and does not fail to a state that could cause injury or property destruction, and test the failure behavior before production deployment.

Maintain a separate execution domain for each executing system process — for example, by assigning each process a separate address space — so inter-process communication is controlled through the security functions and one process cannot modify another's executing code.
Implement hardware separation mechanisms to facilitate process isolation.
Maintain a separate execution domain for each thread in the organization-defined multi-threaded processing.

The Network Security team is accountable for this procedure end to end, including execution of all boundary, flow control, monitoring, and review steps and production of the Firewall and segmentation rule review and External attack-surface scan artifacts.

System Owners, Human Resources, the Privacy Officer, the Authorizing Official, the CIO, the CISO, the senior privacy official, and privileged administrators participate in the specific steps that name them; exceptions to any step in this procedure require review and approval by the Network Security team lead in consultation with the CISO.

Implement the organization-defined dynamic information flow control policies using [Network Monitoring Tools] and policy engines capable of adjusting flow decisions based on current conditions, and verify dynamic behavior during each Firewall and segmentation rule review.

Configure the organization-defined limitations on embedding data types within other data types (e.g., blocking archive-in-archive or script-in-document nesting) on the [Content Filtering Solution] at the boundary.

Configure flow control enforcement based on the organization-defined metadata (e.g., classification labels, data type tags) so that flows carrying disallowed metadata are denied at the managed interface.
Deploy the organization-defined security or privacy policy filters for the organization-defined information flows on the [Content Filtering Solution] and [Email Gateway].

Configure each filter's failure action — block, strip, modify, or quarantine — in accordance with the organization-defined security or privacy policy, and verify the failure action fires correctly during testing.

Implement the human review workflow for the organization-defined information flows under the organization-defined conditions: route flagged items to a designated Network Security reviewer via the [Ticketing System], and require documented reviewer disposition before release.

Grant privileged administrators the capability to enable and disable policy filters under the organization-defined conditions, restricted to the privileged administrator role in the [Identity Provider].
Grant privileged administrators the capability to configure policy filters to support different security or privacy policies, with each policy variant stored as a distinct, named configuration.
Configure the organization-defined data type identifiers on the cross-domain transfer solution and validate data essential for information flow decisions against them before transfer.
Decompose transferred information into the organization-defined policy-relevant subcomponents and submit each subcomponent to the applicable policy enforcement mechanism.
Implement policy filters requiring fully enumerated formats that restrict data structure and content on each cross-domain transfer path.
Examine transferred information for the organization-defined unsanctioned information and prohibit its transfer in accordance with the organization-defined security or privacy policy.
Implement the organization-defined security or privacy policy filters on metadata for cross-domain transfers.
Implement the organization-defined logical or physical separation mechanisms and techniques to accomplish the organization-defined required separations between information flows.
Configure the cross-domain solution to modify non-releasable information using the organization-defined modification action before transfer between security domains.
Configure the cross-domain solution to parse incoming data into an internal normalized format and regenerate it consistent with its intended specification.

Configure sanitization of transferred data to minimize delivery of malicious content, command and control of malicious code, malicious code augmentation, steganography-encoded data, and spillage of sensitive information, in accordance with the organization-defined policy.
Configure the [Content Filtering Solution] to record and audit all content filtering actions and results for transfers between security domains, forwarding records to the [SIEM].
Implement redundant and independent filtering mechanisms for each data type, and document the independence of mechanisms in the architecture diagrams.
Implement a linear content filter pipeline enforced with discretionary and mandatory access controls, and document the pipeline order.

Configure monitoring to ensure content filtering mechanisms complete execution without errors and that filtering actions occur in the documented order and comply with organization-defined policy; alert on out-of-order or failed execution via the [SIEM].
Implement content filtering mechanisms using multiple processes as organization-defined.
Configure the pipeline to prevent transfer of failed content to the receiving domain.

For message-based transfers, configure the pipeline so message content is not filtered at the metadata stage, filtering metadata is validated, content is confirmed to have successfully completed filtering, and content is then transferred to the destination filter pipeline.

Execute the determination procedure confirming each workforce member's access to ePHI is appropriate, using role reviews in the [Identity Provider].

On notification from Human Resources that employment or another arrangement has ended, or upon a clearance determination requiring it, disable the workforce member's access to ePHI in the [Identity Provider] and confirm removal of network paths to ePHI systems.
Maintain the policies and procedures for authorizing access to ePHI consistent with applicable subpart E requirements.

If a health care clearinghouse is part of a larger organization, implement segmentation and access controls protecting the clearinghouse's ePHI from unauthorized access by the larger organization, and include the segmentation rules in the Firewall and segmentation rule review.
Implement the procedures for granting access to ePHI — through access to a workstation, transaction, program, process, or other mechanism — via the [Identity Provider] and [Ticketing System].

Establish, document, review, and modify each user's right of access to a workstation, transaction, program, or process based on the entity's access authorization policies, recording each grant and modification in the [Ticketing System].

Document the proper functions to be performed, the manner of their performance, and the physical attributes of the surroundings of workstations (or workstation classes) that can access ePHI, and enforce the corresponding network access rules.

Perform security and privacy compliance checks on constituent system components using the [Vulnerability Scanning Tool] prior to establishing the internal connection; do not enable the connection until checks pass.

Maintain the policies and procedures implemented for compliance in written (electronic permitted) form, and maintain a written record of any required action, activity, or assessment — including the Firewall and segmentation rule review and the External attack-surface scan.
Retain required documentation for 6 years from the date of its creation or the date it was last in effect, whichever is later.
Make documentation available to the persons responsible for implementing the procedures to which it pertains, via the documentation repository.
Review documentation periodically and update it as needed in response to environmental or operational changes affecting the security of ePHI.

Configure applications to store state information separately from other application and software data.

Require security functions to be implemented as a layered structure that minimizes interactions between layers and avoids lower-layer dependence on the functionality or correctness of higher layers.

Configure online meeting and teleconferencing tools to provide an explicit indication of current participants.

Configure the [DNS Service] to provide additional data origin authentication and integrity verification artifacts, such as DNSSEC digital signatures and cryptographic keys, along with the authoritative name resolution data returned in response to external name/address resolution queries.

When operating as part of a distributed, hierarchical namespace, provide the means to indicate the security status of child zones and, if the child supports secure resolution services, enable verification of a chain of trust among parent and child domains.
Provide data origin and integrity protection artifacts for internal name/address resolution queries.
Configure resolving systems to request and perform data origin authentication and data integrity verification on name/address resolution responses received from authoritative sources.
Ensure the systems that collectively provide name/address resolution service for the organization are fault-tolerant and implement internal and external role separation.
Invalidate session identifiers upon user logout or other session termination.
Generate a unique session identifier for each session meeting the organization-defined randomness requirements, and configure applications to recognize only system-generated session identifiers.
Only allow the use of the organization-defined certificate authorities for verification of the establishment of protected sessions, enforced via the trusted certificate store.
Implement hardware separation mechanisms to facilitate process isolation.
Maintain a separate execution domain for each thread in the organization-defined multi-threaded processing.

analyze: This procedure provides the step-by-step operational instructions for developing, disseminating, maintaining, and reviewing Example Org's PII processing and transparency policy and supporting documentation, and for determining, documenting, and enforcing the authority under which PII is processed.
Executing it produces and maintains the Data inventory and classification register and the Retention schedule as evidence of compliance.

Data Governance performs this procedure on Example Org's policy and documentation repositories and on all systems and processes that handle personally identifiable information (PII), including electronic protected health information (ePHI).
Other teams participate as contributors and implementers, but Data Governance owns the process and its handoffs end to end.
- Access to the [Document Management System] where policies, procedures, and HIPAA documentation are authored, published, and versioned.
- A designated PII processing and transparency policy official (see Procedure Steps) named in the appropriate security and privacy documents.
- Engagement with [Legal Counsel] or [Compliance] for review of applicable laws, regulations, and directives.
- The current Data inventory and classification register, maintained by Data Governance.
- The current Retention schedule, maintained by Data Governance.
- Access to the [Ticketing System] for tracking review tasks, updates, and event-triggered reviews.
- Access to the [Identity Provider] to verify role assignments for dissemination targets.

Data Governance drafts the organization-level PII processing and transparency policy in the [Document Management System], addressing purpose, scope, roles, responsibilities, management commitment, coordination among organizational entities, and compliance.

Data Governance engages [Legal Counsel] to confirm the policy is consistent with applicable laws, executive orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, and guidelines, and records the confirmation in the document's review history.

Data Governance submits the draft policy to the designated policy official (see below) and executive management for approval, recording the approval date and approver in the [Document Management System].

Upon approval, Data Governance publishes the policy in the [Document Management System] and disseminates it to the organization-defined personnel and roles listed in the policy's distribution section, verifying delivery through the [Ticketing System] or [Document Management System] acknowledgment tracking.
Data Governance records the published policy version and distribution list as evidence alongside the Data inventory and classification register.

Data Governance develops and documents procedures that facilitate implementation of the PII processing and transparency policy and its associated controls, including this procedure, in the [Document Management System].
Data Governance maps each procedure to the policy section and control it implements, recording the mapping in the document header.
Data Governance submits the procedures for the same approval path as the policy (designated official and executive management) and records approvals in the [Document Management System].

Data Governance disseminates the approved procedures to the personnel and roles responsible for implementing them, using the distribution mechanism in the [Document Management System], and confirms receipt.
Executive management, coordinated by Data Governance, designates an official to manage the development, documentation, and dissemination of the PII processing and transparency policy and procedures.
Data Governance records the designated official's name, title, and designation date in the policy document and in the appropriate security and privacy documents in the [Document Management System].
Data Governance updates the designation record whenever the official changes, re-publishing the affected documents and re-notifying the distribution list.
Data Governance reviews the PII processing and transparency policy and its supporting procedures at least every one (1) year, opening a review task in the [Ticketing System] to initiate the review.

Data Governance also initiates a review following organization-defined events, including assessment or audit findings, breaches or security/privacy incidents, and changes to applicable laws (including privacy laws), executive orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, and guidelines.

Data Governance actively monitors for changes to applicable privacy laws, regulations, and policies affecting PII processing and transparency, using [Legal Counsel] or [Regulatory Monitoring Service] alerts, and logs monitored changes in the [Ticketing System].

When updates are required, Data Governance revises the documents, obtains approval from the designated official and executive management, and publishes the new version in the [Document Management System].
Data Governance records each review — whether or not it produced changes — including date, reviewer, trigger, and outcome, and retains that record per the Retention schedule.

Data Governance maintains all policies, procedures, and any record of an action, activity, or assessment required to comply with the HIPAA Security Rule in written (electronic or paper) form in the [Document Management System].

Data Governance ensures every required action, activity, or assessment is documented at the time it is performed, filing the record against the relevant HIPAA control in the [Document Management System].

Data Governance verifies during the annual review that no required documentation exists only in ephemeral form (e.g., verbal decisions, unexported tickets) and migrates any such records into the [Document Management System].
Data Governance applies a six-year retention period to all HIPAA documentation, calculated from the date of its creation or the date when it was last in effect, whichever is later.
Data Governance records each HIPAA document's creation date and last-in-effect date in the Retention schedule.
Data Governance configures the [Document Management System] retention rules to prevent deletion of HIPAA documentation before its calculated retention date expires.
Data Governance verifies during the annual review that the Retention schedule entries match the actual documents and retention rules in the [Document Management System].

Data Governance grants access in the [Document Management System] to the persons responsible for implementing the procedures to which the documentation pertains, based on the role assignments in the [Identity Provider].
Data Governance reviews the access list whenever responsibilities change and updates permissions so responsible personnel always have current access.
Data Governance confirms availability during the annual review by verifying that each responsible role can retrieve its applicable documentation.
Data Governance reviews HIPAA documentation annually to determine whether environmental or operational changes affecting the security of electronic protected health information require updates.

When such changes are identified, Data Governance updates the affected documentation, obtains approval from the designated official, and publishes the revised version in the [Document Management System].
Data Governance records each periodic review and update in the document history and updates the Retention schedule's last-in-effect dates accordingly.

Data Governance identifies and documents the organization-defined authority (e.g., statute, regulation, contract, or consent) that permits each defined processing of PII, drawing on the Data inventory and classification register to enumerate processing activities.
Data Governance engages [Legal Counsel] to validate that each cited authority actually permits the processing described.

Data Governance records the authority for each processing activity in the Data inventory and classification register, linking each entry to its supporting legal or contractual source in the [Document Management System].
Data Governance reviews the documented authorities during the annual policy review and whenever monitoring identifies changes to applicable privacy laws, updating the register as needed.

Data Governance compares active PII processing activities — as enumerated in the Data inventory and classification register — against the documented authorities to identify any processing not covered by an authority.

When unauthorized processing is identified, Data Governance opens a remediation item in the [Ticketing System], notifies the owning system or business process team, and directs that the unauthorized processing be stopped or brought within an authorized basis.

Data Governance verifies with the owning team that the unauthorized processing has been stopped or authorized, and records the resolution in the [Ticketing System] and the Data inventory and classification register.
Data Governance reports unresolved unauthorized processing to the designated policy official and executive management for escalation.

Data Governance is authorized and accountable for executing every step of this procedure, including authoring, disseminating, reviewing, and retaining all policy, procedure, and HIPAA documentation, and for maintaining the Data inventory and classification register and the Retention schedule.

Executive management approves the policy and designates the policy official; [Legal Counsel] validates legal authorities; and exceptions to any step of this procedure require review and approval by the designated policy official in consultation with Data Governance.
This procedure operationalizes the **Example Org Data Protection and Privacy Standard**, which contains the full requirement text and the rationale for each control implemented above.
