analyze: This procedure provides the step-by-step operational instructions for executing the PII processing and transparency, information management and retention, PII quality, and PII inventory requirements defined in the Example Org Data Protection and Privacy Standard.
Executing this procedure produces and maintains the Data inventory and classification register and the Retention schedule as evidence of compliance.

This procedure is performed by Data Governance, with participation from the Senior Official for Privacy, Legal Counsel, [System Owners], and [Security Operations], and applies to all Example Org systems, applications, and projects that create, collect, use, disclose, store, or transmit PII (and, where applicable, PHI).
It covers the full information life cycle from collection through disposal.
- Access to the [Document Management System] where policies, procedures, and compliance records are maintained.
- Access to the [Data Catalog / Inventory Tool] used to maintain the Data inventory and classification register.
- Access to the [Ticketing System] for logging correction, deletion, and data-sharing requests.
- Access to the [Data Tagging / Policy Enforcement Tool] used to attach and enforce data tags.
- Named Senior Official for Privacy and designated Data Governance policy official, identified in the appropriate security and privacy documents.
- Current copies of applicable laws, regulations, and the Example Org Data Protection and Privacy Standard.
- Approval from the Senior Official for Privacy before any use of PII in testing, training, or research.

Data Governance drafts the organization-level PII processing and transparency policy, addressing purpose, scope, roles, responsibilities, management commitment, coordination among organizational entities, and compliance, and verifying consistency with applicable laws, executive orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, and guidelines.
Data Governance drafts supporting procedures that facilitate implementation of the policy and the associated PII processing and transparency controls.
Data Governance submits the draft policy and procedures to the Senior Official for Privacy and Legal Counsel for review, and obtains management sign-off.
Data Governance disseminates the approved policy and procedures to organization-defined personnel and roles via the [Document Management System], obtaining acknowledgment of receipt.

Data Governance designates and documents the official responsible for managing the development, documentation, and dissemination of the policy and procedures, and records that designation in the appropriate security and privacy documents.
Data Governance maintains the policy, procedures, and all required records of actions, activities, and assessments in written (electronic) form in the [Document Management System].
Data Governance retains all documentation produced under this procedure for 6 years from the date of its creation or the date it was last in effect, whichever is later.
Data Governance makes the documentation available to persons responsible for implementing the procedures to which it pertains, and to appropriate authorities upon request.

Data Governance reviews and updates the policy and procedures at least every 1 year, and additionally following organization-defined events such as assessment or audit findings, security or privacy incidents, breaches, or changes to applicable laws, regulations, or overarching policy.

Data Governance actively monitors for changes to applicable privacy laws, regulations, and overarching policy — including periodic review of documentation in response to environmental or operational changes affecting the security of electronic protected health information — and updates the policy and procedures as needed.

Data Governance verifies that the policy and procedures support cybersecurity and privacy safeguards to the greatest extent feasible throughout the system life cycle and for the information on the system, and includes operational guidance for compliance with the PII inventory control (see the PM-5 subsection below).

Data Governance determines and documents the authority that permits the processing of PII, consulting with the Senior Official for Privacy and Legal Counsel, particularly where multiple jurisdictions or sources of authority apply.

Data Governance documents the policies and procedures regarding the creation, collection, use, and disclosure of PII, identifies the applicable law governing that collection, use, and disclosure, and makes the documentation available to appropriate authorities upon request.
Data Governance restricts processing of PII to only that which is authorized under the documented authority.
Data Governance coordinates with [Training Team] to train personnel on authorized processing of PII.
Data Governance coordinates with [Security Operations] to monitor and audit organizational use of PII against the documented authority.
Data Governance attaches data tags containing the authorized processing to the organization-defined elements of PII using the [Data Tagging / Policy Enforcement Tool] [NIST 800-53 PT-2(1)].

Data Governance configures and manages enforcement of authorized processing using the organization-defined automated mechanisms in the [Data Tagging / Policy Enforcement Tool], and verifies enforcement is active [NIST 800-53 PT-2(2)].
Data Governance identifies and documents the purpose(s) for processing PII.

Where ARC-AMPE applies, authorized purposes are limited to determining eligibility for enrollment in a qualified health plan, determining eligibility for other insurance affordability programs (as defined in 45 CFR §155.300), and determining eligibility for exemptions from the individual shared responsibility provisions in Code section 5000A.

Data Governance describes the processing purpose(s) in the organization's public privacy notices and policies, and in related privacy compliance documentation such as privacy impact assessments and system of records notices, publishing via the [Privacy Notice Publication Platform].
Data Governance restricts processing of PII to only that which is compatible with the identified purpose(s).

Where ARC-AMPE applies, the Exchange may only use or disclose PII to the extent necessary to carry out functions described in 45 CFR §155.200; other functions the Secretary determines to be in compliance with the ACA and for which the individual provides consent; or other functions pursuant to the substantive and procedural requirements in 45 CFR §155.260(a)(iii).

Data Governance monitors changes in PII processing and implements mechanisms to ensure changes are made in accordance with organization-defined requirements, logging each change in the [Ticketing System].
Data Governance attaches data tags containing the processing purposes to the organization-defined elements of PII using the [Data Tagging / Policy Enforcement Tool] [NIST 800-53 PT-3(1)].
Data Governance configures the organization-defined automated mechanisms to track processing purposes of PII and verifies tracking is active [NIST 800-53 PT-3(2)].
Data Governance confirms, before any sharing, that the share is authorized, there is a need to know, and adequate assurances of protection have been provided by the sharing partner.

Data Governance enables authorized users to determine whether access authorizations assigned to a sharing partner match the information's access and use restrictions for the organization-defined information-sharing circumstances — including, per ARC-AMPE, circumstances where user discretion is required as defined in data sharing agreements such as Computer Matching Agreements or Information Exchange Agreements, consistent with 45 CFR §155.260(e).
Data Governance employs the organization-defined automated mechanisms — or, where ARC-AMPE permits, manual processes — to assist users in making information-sharing and collaboration decisions.

Data Governance employs the organization-defined automated mechanisms to enforce information-sharing decisions based on the access authorizations of sharing partners and the access restrictions on the information to be shared [NIST 800-53 AC-21(1)].
Data Governance implements and verifies that the organization's information search and retrieval services enforce the organization-defined information-sharing restrictions [NIST 800-53 AC-21(2)].

Data Governance manages and retains information within the system and information output from the system in accordance with applicable laws, executive orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, guidelines, and operational requirements, covering the full information life cycle.

Data Governance records in the Retention schedule that system output — including audit records, system reports, business and financial reports, and business records — is retained for 10 years per 45 CFR §155.1210 and 45 CFR §156.705, or in accordance with organizational policy; where NARA policy applies to federal data held by Enrollment Partners, Data Governance records that applicability in the Retention schedule.

For systems processing, storing, or transmitting PHI, Data Governance documents and retains for at least 6 years from creation or last effective date, whichever is later: decisions regarding addressable implementation specifications (including why a specification would not be reasonable and appropriate); a user's right of access to a workstation, transaction, program, or process; security incidents and their outcomes; satisfactory assurances that a business associate will safeguard PHI (recorded in a written contract or other arrangement meeting business associate agreement requirements, with documented attempts and reasons if satisfactory assurances cannot be obtained); repairs and modifications to physical components of a facility related to security (e.g., hardware, walls, doors, locks); and changes to organizational policies and procedures.

Data Governance limits the PII being processed in the information life cycle to the minimum PII elements necessary to accomplish the legally authorized purpose of collection, and records the organization-defined minimum elements in the Data inventory and classification register [NIST 800-53 SI-12(1) | ARC-AMPE SI-12(1) AE Mandatory].

Data Governance applies the organization-defined techniques, in accordance with organizational standards and applicable federal and state laws and regulations, to minimize the use of PII for research, testing, or training, and limits the creation, collection, use, and/or disclosure of PII only to the extent necessary to accomplish a specified and authorized purpose [NIST 800-53 SI-12(2) | ARC-AMPE SI-12(2) AE Mandatory].

If PII is used in the test environment, Data Governance verifies with [System Owners] that the same controls required for systems containing PII are applied to the test environment, and that synthetic PII is used to the maximum extent practicable when testing system functionality.

Data Governance obtains the Senior Official for Privacy's approval before any use of PII in testing, training, or research, and records the approval in the [Document Management System]; using synthetic or de-identified data is preferred.

At the end of the retention period recorded in the Retention schedule, Data Governance uses the organization-defined techniques to dispose of, destroy, or erase the information in a manner that prevents loss, theft, misuse, or unauthorized access [NIST 800-53 SI-12(3) | ARC-AMPE SI-12(3) AE Mandatory].
Data Governance consults the latest published NIST SP 800-88, Guidelines for Media Sanitization, when selecting disposal techniques.
Data Governance uses the latest published FIPS 140-compliant encryption standards to ensure secure deletion or destruction of PII, including originals, copies, and archived records.

Data Governance checks the accuracy, relevance, timeliness, and completeness of PII across the information life cycle at least every 1 year, recording the results against the Data inventory and classification register.
Data Governance corrects or deletes inaccurate or outdated PII identified by the check.

Data Governance maintains each individual's record in accordance with the Retention schedule regardless of that individual's activity or inactivity, and maintains a log of corrections and deletions in the [Ticketing System] so that correcting or deleting inaccurate data does not violate retention rules.

Data Governance corrects or deletes PII that is inaccurate or outdated, incorrectly determined regarding impact, or incorrectly de-identified, using the organization-defined automated mechanisms [NIST 800-53 SI-18(1)].
Data Governance employs data tags to automate the correction or deletion of PII across the information life cycle within organizational systems [NIST 800-53 SI-18(2)].
Data Governance collects PII directly from the individual wherever collection occurs [NIST 800-53 SI-18(3)].

Upon request by an individual or their designated representative, logged in the [Ticketing System], Data Governance corrects or deletes the requested PII, noting that certain PII may not be permitted to be deleted regardless of the individual's preference [NIST 800-53 SI-18(4) | ARC-AMPE SI-18(4) AE Mandatory].
If the request is denied because the organization is legally required to maintain the PII, Data Governance communicates that reason in the written denial to the individual.
Data Governance notifies the organization-defined recipients of the PII and the individuals whose PII has been corrected or deleted [NIST 800-53 SI-18(5) | ARC-AMPE SI-18(5) AE Mandatory].

Data Governance develops and updates the inventory of organizational systems at least every 1 year, and whenever there is a significant change to the inventory, recording it in the Data inventory and classification register.

Data Governance establishes, maintains, and updates — continuously or when there is a significant change to the systems, applications, and projects involved — the inventory of all systems, applications, and projects that process PII, in the Data inventory and classification register [NIST 800-53 PM-5(1) | ARC-AMPE PM-5(1) AE Mandatory].

Data Governance verifies that the policies and procedures required by PM-1 include operational guidance for compliance with the PII inventory control, updating that guidance whenever the inventory process changes.
Data Governance owns this procedure end to end, including policy development, inventory and retention schedule maintenance, quality checks, and all handoffs to participating teams.

The Senior Official for Privacy and Legal Counsel review and approve policy content, processing authority, and PII use in testing, training, and research; exceptions to any step in this procedure require their documented approval.

analyze: This procedure provides the operational steps Example Org personnel follow to protect, transport, account for, sanitize, and dispose of digital and non-digital media containing sensitive information, including PII and electronic protected health information (ePHI).

Executing this procedure implements the requirements of the Media Handling & Disposal Standard and produces the evidence — Certificates of destruction and the Media transport log — needed to demonstrate compliance.

IT Asset Management owns and executes this process end to end on a continuous basis, with participation from workforce members, facilities staff, authorized transport personnel, and [Media Sanitization Vendor] where indicated.

It applies to all digital and non-digital media (magnetic tapes, external removable hard drives, flash/thumb drives, diskettes, compact disks, digital video disks, and hard-copy documents) that store, process, or contain sensitive information at Example Org facilities or under Example Org control.
- Access to the [Asset Management System] for media inventory and control numbers
- Access to the [Ticketing System] for sanitization, disposal, and transport requests
- Access to [Identity Provider] to verify requester authorization and need to know
- Physical access authorization to media storage areas and [Controlled Areas]
- Approved sanitization equipment and FIPS-validated sanitization tools consistent with the latest published NIST SP 800-88
- Approved cross-cut shredder or contracted [Approved Shredding Vendor]
- Tamper-evident packaging, sealed packing cartons, and locked/securable transport containers
- Current risk assessment of media types and authorized information storage (see Media Access Restriction below)
- Written marking exemption approvals signed by the Chief Information Officer or designated representative
- Blank Media transport log and Certificate of destruction templates

IT Asset Management maintains this procedure and its parent policy in written (electronic) form, covering purpose, scope, roles, responsibilities, management commitment, coordination among organizational entities, and compliance, and consistent with applicable laws, regulations, and guidelines.
IT Asset Management designates the official responsible for the development, documentation, and dissemination of the media protection policy and procedures: [Policy Designation Official].
IT Asset Management disseminates the policy and this procedure to all applicable personnel and roles via [Policy Distribution Mechanism], and confirms receipt where required.

IT Asset Management reviews and updates the policy and procedures following triggering events — assessment or audit findings, security or privacy incidents, and changes to applicable laws, executive orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, or guidelines — and at least every one (1) year per ARC-AMPE.

IT Asset Management retains all versions of the policy and procedure documentation for 6 years from the date of creation or the date last in effect, whichever is later, and makes the current version available to all persons responsible for implementing the procedures.
IT Asset Management updates the documentation in response to environmental or operational changes affecting the security of electronic protected health information.

IT Asset Management records the receipt of every hardware item or electronic medium containing ePHI entering a facility in the [Asset Management System] at the point of intake, including the media control number, source, and receiving personnel.
IT Asset Management records the removal of such items from a facility in the Media transport log before release, identifying the item, the authorizing approver, the receiving party, and the purpose.
IT Asset Management records the movement of such items between areas within a facility, so that the physical location of any ePHI-bearing medium is traceable at all times.
Facilities and IT Asset Management jointly reconcile facility intake/removal records against the [Asset Management System] inventory [Reconciliation Frequency].
IT Asset Management conducts a risk assessment to determine what sensitive information, if any, may be stored on each media type and which roles are authorized with a need to know that information.

IT Asset Management restricts access to all digital and non-digital media, including media containing PII, to the authorized personnel or roles identified in the risk assessment, enforced via [Access Control Mechanism] and verified against [Identity Provider] role assignments.
IT Asset Management disables CD/DVD writers and USB ports on systems where media write capability is not required, using [Endpoint Management Tool].
IT Asset Management grants write-capability exceptions only to authorized individuals with a valid need to know, and configures each exception in compliance with the latest published NIST SP 800-88.
IT Asset Management revalidates the access and write-capability exception lists [Revalidation Frequency].
[Human Resources] notifies IT Asset Management of workforce member authorization, role changes, and terminations affecting access to ePHI.
IT Asset Management authorizes and supervises workforce member access to ePHI-bearing media only where the member's role requires it, provisioning access through [Identity Provider].
IT Asset Management reviews workforce access to ePHI-bearing media to determine it remains appropriate, and removes access when employment or other arrangements end.

IT Asset Management applies physical safeguards to all workstations that access ePHI — [Physical Safeguards, e.g., cable locks, privacy screens, locked work areas] — restricting use to authorized users.
IT Asset Management implements policies and procedures governing who may alter or destroy ePHI, and by what approved methods.

IT Asset Management enables electronic mechanisms — [Integrity Verification Mechanism, e.g., checksums, hashes, audit logging] — to corroborate that ePHI has not been altered or destroyed in an unauthorized manner.
IT Asset Management reviews integrity mechanism output for unauthorized alteration or destruction indicators and investigates any findings [Review Frequency].
IT Asset Management marks each item of system media with its distribution limitations, handling caveats, and applicable security markings.

IT Asset Management ensures every marking includes, at minimum: the creation date, the applicable information safeguarding marking based on record retention regulations, and the organization-defined contact information.
IT Asset Management labels backup tapes with the system name in addition to the minimum markings.
IT Asset Management marks media containing PII or PHI — or its container, where labeling the media itself is not practicable — consistently with ACA record retention regulations.

IT Asset Management submits requests to exempt specific media types from marking (where the media remain within [Controlled Areas]) in writing to the Chief Information Officer or designated representative, and retains the written approval in [Document Repository].

IT Asset Management stores all digital and non-digital media within [Controlled Areas], physically controlling and securely storing magnetic tapes, external removable hard drives, flash/thumb drives, diskettes, compact disks, and digital video disks.
IT Asset Management encrypts digital media using the latest published FIPS 140-compliant encryption standards before storage.

IT Asset Management stores non-digital media in secure storage such as locked cabinets or safes, stores removable media containing PII in a securable area or locked container, protects magnetic media containing PII recorded alongside other data as if all data on the media were PII, and stores surplus equipment securely while not in use.
IT Asset Management protects all stored media until it is destroyed or sanitized using approved equipment, techniques, and procedures.

IT Asset Management restricts access to media storage areas using [Assignment: organization-defined automated mechanisms] and logs all access attempts and access granted, reviewing the logs [Log Review Frequency].

The requester submits a transport request through the [Ticketing System]; IT Asset Management approves the transport and designates an identified custodian — a named individual accountable for the media for the duration of the movement.
IT Asset Management restricts all transport activities to authorized personnel and confirms the custodian's authorization against [Identity Provider].
Before moving equipment containing ePHI, IT Asset Management creates a retrievable, exact copy of the electronic protected health information, when needed, and stores the copy in [Backup Location].

IT Asset Management applies the following transport controls to digital and non-digital media containing sensitive information such as PII: encryption via a latest published FIPS 140-compliant encryption module; locked/securable containers or tamper-evident packaging carried by authorized personnel; trackable receipt by the commercial shipping carrier; and sealed packing cartons for non-digital media containing sensitive information.

The custodian documents all transport activities in the Media transport log, recording the item, media control number, origin, destination, custodian name, departure and arrival times, and any person responsible for the media at each stage.

IT Asset Management maintains the Media transport log as the accountability record of all movements of hardware and electronic media outside controlled areas, and reconciles it against the [Asset Management System] inventory [Reconciliation Frequency].
IT Asset Management reviews each sanitization or disposal request, approves it, and tracks it through the [Ticketing System] from approval through verified completion.

IT Asset Management sanitizes digital and non-digital media prior to disposal, release out of organizational control, or release for reuse, using organization-defined sanitization techniques and procedures in accordance with the latest published NIST SP 800-88 guidelines.

For media containing ePHI, IT Asset Management documents the final disposition of the information and of the hardware or media on which it is stored, and removes ePHI from electronic media before the media are made available for re-use.
IT Asset Management selects sanitization mechanisms with strength and integrity commensurate with the security category or classification of the information on the media.
IT Asset Management finely shreds hard-copy documents using approved equipment, techniques, and procedures with cross-cut shredding at a minimum, either in-house or via [Approved Shredding Vendor].

IT Asset Management sanitizes media containing PII prior to disposal, release out of the organization, or release for reuse, using the latest FIPS-validated media sanitization techniques or procedures, and disposes of or sanitizes surplus equipment in accordance with the latest published NIST SP 800-88.
IT Asset Management securely destroys or disposes of sensitive information, including PII, appropriately and reasonably and in accordance with the applicable retention schedules.
IT Asset Management verifies each completed sanitization or disposal action before closing the ticket — verifying device state, vendor certificate, or shredding output as applicable.

IT Asset Management records each sanitization and disposal action with: the name of the media recipient, the signature of the media recipient, the date/time received, the media control number and contents, movement or routing information, and — if disposed of — the date, time, and method of destruction.

IT Asset Management obtains and retains a Certificate of destruction for every destruction action performed by [Approved Shredding Vendor] or [Media Sanitization Vendor], and retains all sanitization records [Record Retention Period].

IT Asset Management tests sanitization equipment and procedures to ensure the intended sanitization is being achieved, at least every one (1) year per ARC-AMPE, using [Verification Method, e.g., sample re-verification, forensic tooling].
IT Asset Management records the test results, removes from service any equipment that fails, and remediates or replaces it before further use.
IT Asset Management applies nondestructive sanitization techniques to portable storage devices prior to connecting such devices to the system under [Assignment: organization-defined circumstances].

IT Asset Management enforces dual authorization for the sanitization of \[Assignment: organization-defined system media\]: two authorized individuals — the executing technician plus an approver designated in the [Ticketing System] — must both approve before sanitization proceeds.

IT Asset Management maintains the capability to purge or wipe information from [Assignment: organization-defined systems or system components] remotely under [Assignment: organization-defined conditions], using [Remote Wipe Mechanism], and tests that capability [Test Frequency].

IT Asset Management is authorized to perform and is accountable for every step in this procedure, including media intake, storage, transport, sanitization, disposal, documentation, and the review and maintenance of the policy and procedures it supports.

Workforce members, designated transport custodians, [Human Resources], and vendors such as [Approved Shredding Vendor] and [Media Sanitization Vendor] participate in individual steps under IT Asset Management's direction; the Chief Information Officer or designated representative approves written marking exemptions, and [Exception Approving Official] reviews and approves any exception to this procedure.
Media Handling & Disposal Standard — this Standard is the source of the full requirement text and the rationale for each control step above.

analyze: This procedure provides the step-by-step operational instructions for developing, documenting, disseminating, and maintaining the organization's system maintenance policy and supporting procedures, as required by the System Maintenance Standard.
Executing it ensures that maintenance governance documentation remains current, approved, and traceable to applicable laws, regulations, and frameworks.

Infrastructure Security performs this procedure on the organization's maintenance governance documentation (the maintenance policy and maintenance procedures) and on the systems used to author, approve, disseminate, and retain that documentation.
This procedure covers all organizational systems subject to the System Maintenance Standard.
- Designated official accountable for the maintenance policy and procedures, as defined in the System Maintenance Standard (see the "Designation of Managing Official" step below)
- Write access to [Document Management System] for storing and versioning governance documentation
- Access to [Communication/Distribution System] for disseminating approved documentation to applicable personnel
- Access to [Ticketing System] for tracking review and update tasks
- Current versions of applicable laws, executive orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, and guidelines relevant to system maintenance
- Access to recent assessment, audit, and incident records needed to inform periodic reviews
Infrastructure Security develops and documents the maintenance policy at the organization level, addressing all required elements.
Open [Document Management System] and create a new draft of the maintenance policy under Infrastructure Security ownership.
Draft the policy to address, at minimum: purpose; scope; roles and responsibilities; management commitment; coordination among organizational entities; and compliance.

Draft the policy at the organization level as required by ARC-AMPE (organization-level policy is mandatory), extending to mission/business process and/or system level only where the System Maintenance Standard calls for it.

Cross-check each policy element against applicable laws, executive orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, and guidelines, and record the sources consulted in the draft's reference section.
Submit the draft to the designated managing official (see Step 3) for review and approval.

Record the approval decision, approver, and approval date in [Document Management System], and link the approval record to the maintenance records with authorization retained as evidence for this process.
Infrastructure Security develops and documents procedures that facilitate implementation of the maintenance policy and its associated maintenance controls.
In [Document Management System], create a draft procedures document linked to the approved maintenance policy from Step 1.
Map each control and requirement in the System Maintenance Standard to a corresponding procedure section so that no control lacks an implementation procedure.

Write each procedure section as concrete operational instructions: who performs the action, what system or tool is used, in what order, and what evidence is produced (e.g., maintenance records with authorization, remote maintenance session logs).
Route the draft procedures to affected operational teams for technical review, collect feedback via [Ticketing System], and incorporate changes.
Submit the revised procedures to the designated managing official for approval, and record the approval in [Document Management System].
The organization designates a specific official to manage the development, documentation, and dissemination of the maintenance policy and procedures.

Identify the official who will manage development, documentation, and dissemination of the maintenance policy and procedures, per the organization-defined designation in the System Maintenance Standard.
Record the designation — official's name, role, and effective date — in [Document Management System] alongside the policy document.
Update the policy's Roles and Responsibilities section to name the designated official explicitly.
Communicate the designation to applicable personnel via [Communication/Distribution System] when the designation changes.
Infrastructure Security maintains this designation record as part of the maintenance records with authorization.
Infrastructure Security disseminates the approved policy and procedures to applicable personnel or roles.
After approval, publish the final policy and procedures to [Document Management System] and mark prior versions as superseded.
Identify the applicable personnel and roles from the policy's scope section.
Distribute the approved documents to those personnel via [Communication/Distribution System], and require acknowledgment of receipt where the System Maintenance Standard calls for it.
Log the distribution date, recipient list, and acknowledgments in [Document Management System].
Re-disseminate the documents to applicable personnel whenever a new version is approved following a review or update under Step 5.
Infrastructure Security reviews and updates the maintenance policy and procedures at the defined frequency and following defined trigger events.

Create a recurring review task in [Ticketing System] for the maintenance policy and procedures, scheduled at the defined review frequency — no less than every one (1) year per ARC-AMPE — and assign it to Infrastructure Security.
This review activity runs on a continuous basis between scheduled reviews as trigger events occur.

When conducting a scheduled review, read the current policy and procedures in full and verify each element against current applicable laws, executive orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, and guidelines.

In addition to scheduled reviews, initiate an out-of-cycle review whenever one of the following organization-defined events occurs: assessment or audit findings; security or privacy incidents; or changes to applicable laws, executive orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, and guidelines.

Periodically review the documentation — independently of the scheduled cycle — and update it as needed in response to environmental or operational changes affecting security (for example, new systems in scope, tooling changes, or organizational restructuring).
Draft and route any resulting changes through the same approval workflow used in Steps 1 and 2, with the designated managing official approving updates.
Record each review — scheduled or event-driven — including the reviewer, date, findings, and any resulting changes, in [Document Management System].
Re-disseminate updated documents per Step 4, and retain the review records with the maintenance records with authorization as evidence of completion.

Infrastructure Security is accountable end to end for this procedure: it develops, documents, disseminates, reviews, and updates the maintenance policy and procedures, and produces the maintenance records with authorization and remote maintenance session logs retained as evidence.
The designated managing official named in Step 3 approves the documentation and any changes to it; exceptions to this procedure require that official's review and written approval.
This procedure operationalizes the **System Maintenance Standard**, which contains the full requirement text and the rationale behind each control referenced above.

analyze: This procedure provides the step-by-step operational instructions for executing the Example Org Logging, Monitoring & Alerting Standard: selecting and generating audit records, centrally reviewing and analyzing them, alerting on failures and suspicious activity, and retaining the resulting evidence.
Executing it produces the Log source inventory and coverage report and the Alert tuning and review records that demonstrate ongoing compliance.

The Detection & Response team performs this procedure continuously across all Example Org systems, applications, databases, network devices, appliances, and services that contain or use electronic protected health information or other sensitive data, including cloud-hosted environments.
System Owners, the Authorizing Official, [Privacy Official], and other system components' custodians participate in defined steps but Detection & Response owns the process and all handoffs.
- Access to the [SIEM] with analyst and administrator roles
- Access to the [Log Management Platform] and its long-term archive/repository
- Access to the [IDS/IPS Management Console] and [Wireless IDS Console]
- Access to the [Ticketing System] for recording reviews, tuning decisions, and follow-up actions
- Access to the [Time Synchronization Service] (NTP) used for log source configuration
- The current System Security and Privacy Plan, System Security and Privacy Policy, risk assessment, and Privacy Impact Assessment
- The designated official for audit and accountability policy, documented in the System Security and Privacy Policy
- Documented legal opinion regarding system monitoring activities
- Authorizing Official acceptance of audited events for cloud environments
- System Owner approval and acceptance of audit record types
- The prior Log source inventory and coverage report

Confirm the designated official responsible for the audit and accountability policy and procedures is correctly named in the System Security and Privacy Policy; if the designation has changed, update the policy document before proceeding.
Review the audit and accountability policy and this procedure for consistency with applicable laws, regulations, directives, and Example Org's overarching security and privacy policies.

Verify the policy addresses purpose, scope, roles, responsibilities, management commitment, coordination among organizational entities, and compliance; revise any section that no longer reflects operations.
Confirm the written (electronic is acceptable) record of actions, activities, and assessments required under HIPAA is current in the designated documentation repository.

Review privacy law, regulation, and policy changes affecting audit and accountability; confirm the policy limits unnecessary or inappropriate access to PII and supports privacy throughout the system life cycle.

Update the policy and procedures at least every one (1) year, following [Organization-Defined Trigger Events], and in response to environmental or operational changes affecting the security of electronic protected health information.
Record each review and update — date, reviewer, changes made — in the Alert tuning and review records, and make the updated documents available to all personnel responsible for implementing them.
Retain all documentation produced under this procedure for 6 years from the date of creation or the date it was last in effect, whichever is later, in the designated records repository.

Derive candidate event types from the current risk assessment and organization-defined mission/business needs; coordinate with Legal, [Privacy Official], System Owners, Human Resources, and Physical Security to capture all entities requiring audit-related information in the selection criteria.

Include, at minimum, the ARC-AMPE event set: user log-on/log-off (successful and unsuccessful), configuration changes, application alerts and error messages, all system administration and privileged user activity, modification of privileges and access, account creation/modification/deletion, concurrent log-on from different workstations, and override of access control mechanisms.
For each selected event type, specify the frequency of, or situation requiring, logging, and document a rationale for why the selection is adequate to support after-the-fact incident investigations.
For cloud environments, submit the defined audited events to the Authorizing Official and obtain documented approval before enabling them.
Update the Log source inventory and coverage report to list each event type, its source component, its logging frequency/situation, and its rationale.

Re-review and update the selected event types at least every one (1) year and whenever there is a significant system modification or change in the system environment; record each review in the Alert tuning and review records.

Configure each log source so every audit record establishes: what type of event occurred, when it occurred, where it occurred, the source of the event, the outcome of the event, and the identity of any individuals, subjects, or entities associated with the event.
Configure logging of disclosures of sensitive information (including PHI and financial information) capturing the information type, date, time, receiving party, and releasing party.

Configure generation of the ARC-AMPE additional record content: session/connection/transaction/activity duration, bytes received and sent for client-server transactions, additional diagnostic messages, characteristics identifying the object or resource acted upon, individual identities of group account users, and full text of privileged commands.
Submit the defined audit record types to the System Owner and obtain documented approval and acceptance before deployment.

Compare all PII elements present in audit records against the system-defined elements in the Privacy Impact Assessment; remove or mask any element not identified as relevant and necessary, confirm any collection requiring legal authorization is legally authorized, and document the justification for PII inclusion in the audit policy.

Size audit log storage on each source system and the [Log Management Platform] to accommodate at least 90 days of retention at measured peak performance volumes; document the sizing calculation in the Log source inventory and coverage report.
Configure each log source to transfer its audit logs continuously to the [Log Management Platform], which must reside on a different system or component than the one conducting the logging.

Verify transfers are occurring by comparing source-side generation counts against received counts in the [Log Management Platform]; open a [Ticketing System] ticket for any gap and investigate before it ages out of the live window.
Configure the [SIEM] and [Log Management Platform] to alert Detection & Response in near real time upon detection of an audit logging process failure.
Upon a logging failure alert: shut down the affected system or halt processing immediately if it supports automatic shutdown; if it does not, shut it down within one (1) hour of the failure.

Configure a warning to Detection & Response when allocated audit log storage reaches [Storage Warning Threshold Percentage] of maximum capacity, and verify the warning fires correctly during the tuning tests in the Alert tuning and review records.
Configure real-time alerts for organization-defined logging failure events to the recipients documented in the System Security and Privacy Plan.

Enforce configurable network communications traffic volume thresholds on the log collection path that reflect audit log storage capacity limits; configure the collector to reject or delay traffic above the thresholds.

Maintain an alternate audit logging capability (e.g., a secondary [Log Management Platform] sink or agent-local spooling) that activates on primary logging failure; when a failure occurs and no alternate capability exists, invoke full or partial system shutdown or a degraded operational mode with limited business functionality per the documented decision matrix.
Record every failure, alert, and shutdown/degraded-mode decision in the [Ticketing System] and summarize it in the Alert tuning and review records.

Using the [SIEM], review and analyze system audit records at least every seven (7) days — no less often than weekly — for indications of inappropriate or unusual activity and its potential impact; also regularly review audit logs, access reports, and security incident tracking records.
Document each review cycle — analyst, date, queries run, findings, dispositions — in the Alert tuning and review records and the [Ticketing System].

Report review findings to the personnel and roles documented in the System Security and Privacy Plan; investigate suspicious activity or suspected violations and take appropriate action, coordinating with incident response under the Vulnerability Detection and Response rules.

Adjust the level of audit record review, analysis, and reporting whenever there is a change in risk based on law enforcement information, intelligence information, or other credible sources; record the adjustment and its justification in the Alert tuning and review records.

Integrate review, analysis, and reporting into the [SIEM] using automated mechanisms to the fullest extent possible; keep audit records from all automated security capabilities and service tools searchable, and confirm sources include systems, appliances, devices, services, and applications, including databases.

Run cross-repository correlation searches in the [SIEM] to analyze and correlate audit records across systems, appliances, devices, services, and applications for organization-wide situational awareness, and maintain centralized review capability over audit records from multiple system components.

Integrate audit record analysis with vulnerability scanning information, performance data, system monitoring information, and other defined data sources; treat this analysis as vulnerability detection subject to the Vulnerability Detection and Response rules.

Correlate audit record information with physical access monitoring data (e.g., badge/system entry logs from [Physical Access Control System]) to identify suspicious, inappropriate, unusual, or malevolent activity.
Document the permitted actions for each system process, role, and user associated with audit record review, analysis, and reporting; enforce those permissions in the [SIEM] role model.

Perform full text analysis of logged privileged commands in the dedicated [Privileged Command Analysis Component] or another system dedicated to that analysis, physically distinct from the audited systems.
Correlate nontechnical sources (e.g., HR notifications, insider-threat referrals, physical security reports) with audit record information in the [SIEM] correlation layer.

For cloud environments, document the coordination between the service provider and Example Org for audit record review, analysis, and reporting; in multi-tenant environments, document the capability and means for reviewing, analyzing, and reporting on data pertaining to Example Org as the consumer.

Verify the [Log Management Platform] provides on-demand audit record reduction and report generation supporting after-the-fact incident investigations, and that reports do not alter the original content or time ordering of records.

Confirm the capability to process, sort, and search audit records for events of interest based on organization-defined fields and selectable event criteria; exercise each search field and record the results in the Alert tuning and review records.

Confirm every log source generates time stamps from its internal system clock synchronized to the [Time Synchronization Service], mappable to UTC or GMT and accurate to within one hundred (100) milliseconds, with the UTC offset included or fixed as documented.
Verify timestamp accuracy by comparing sample log time stamps against the [Time Synchronization Service]; open a [Ticketing System] ticket to remediate any source exceeding the accuracy tolerance.

Restrict access to audit records, audit log settings, audit reports, and audit logging tools to prevent unauthorized access, modification, and deletion; configure alerts to Detection & Response upon detection of any unauthorized access, modification, or deletion attempt.
Write audit trails to hardware-enforced, write-once media (or the platform's equivalent immutable storage tier) in the long-term repository.
Store audit records in a repository that is part of a physically different system or component than the system being audited, running a different operating system than the audited component.
Enable cryptographic mechanisms (e.g., integrity hashing or signing) protecting the integrity of audit information and audit tools; verify integrity checks during each review cycle.

Restrict management of audit logging functionality to the subset of privileged users or roles defined in the System Security and Privacy Plan — individuals or roles who are not subject to audit by that system — and grant read-only audit access to a separately defined subset.
Enforce dual authorization, via the [Approval Workflow], for any movement or deletion of organization-defined audit information; no single individual may complete these operations.

Configure non-repudiation evidence for the actions defined in the System Security and Privacy Plan — at minimum the addition, modification, deletion, approval, sending, or receiving of data, and ARC-AMPE ACA eligibility and enrollment functions (applying for APTC/CSR advance payments, applying for and completing Qualified Health Plan enrollment, and related customer service) — such that irrefutable evidence ties each action to the individual or process acting on their behalf.
Retain live audit records for at least 90 days, then archive old records for ten (10) years consistent with the records retention policy, including the ACA retention rule (45 CFR §155.1210).

When an audit record is subject to a legal investigation, maintain it until released by the investigating authority; place a legal hold in the [Log Management Platform] and record the hold in the [Ticketing System].
Retain audit inspection reports, including records of corrective actions, for a minimum of three (3) years from completion of the inspection.

Ensure long-term records remain retrievable by converting records to newer formats as needed, retaining equipment capable of reading retained formats, and retaining documentation that helps personnel interpret archived records; verify retrieval by restoring a sample from archive and record the test in the Alert tuning and review records.

Enable audit record generation on all information system and network components where audit capability is deployed or available; allow authorized Detection & Response personnel to select which event types are logged by each specific component.

Update the Log source inventory and coverage report listing every generating component, its enabled event types, and its record content; investigate and close any gap between deployed components and inventoried sources.
Compile audit records from all components into a system-wide audit trail in the [SIEM], time-correlated to within [Time Correlation Tolerance] using the [Time Synchronization Service] as reference.
Normalize all component records into a standardized format (e.g., [Standardized Log Format]) at ingestion so the compiled trail is uniform.

Maintain and exercise the capability for authorized personnel to change logging on specific components based on selectable event criteria within [Logging Change Time Threshold]; log every logging change as an auditable event.
Enable auditing of user query event parameters for data sets containing personally identifiable information, capturing the querying identity and the query parameters.

Define monitoring objectives consistent with the incident response policy and procedures, and configure the [SIEM] and monitoring devices to detect attacks, indicators of potential attacks, and unauthorized local, network, and remote connections.
Document, in the System Security and Privacy Plan, the techniques and methods used to identify unauthorized use of the system.

Deploy internal monitoring capabilities and monitoring devices strategically to collect organization-determined essential information, and at ad hoc locations to track specific types of transactions of interest.

Analyze detected events and anomalies continuously; adjust the level of monitoring activity whenever there is a change in risk to organizational operations and assets, individuals, other organizations, or the Nation, recording each adjustment in the Alert tuning and review records.
Obtain and keep current the legal opinion regarding system monitoring activities; do not enable new monitoring categories affecting personnel communications before the opinion covers them.
Provide system monitoring information to the personnel and roles defined in the System Security and Privacy Plan, as needed and at the frequency documented in that Plan.
Follow all applicable rules within the FedRAMP Vulnerability Detection and Response and Incident Communication Procedure guidance for all system monitoring activities.

Operate centrally managed IDS/IPS devices at network perimeter points (including between zones) and centrally managed host-based IDS/IPS sensor agents on all networks and subnets; connect individual detection tools into the system-wide intrusion detection system via the [IDS/IPS Management Console].

For communications encrypted within a zone, use mechanisms capable of decrypting content for analysis or analyzing content before transmission or after receipt, making organization-defined encrypted traffic visible to monitoring tools.
Document, in the applicable risk assessment and System Security and Privacy Plan, every component that does not support a host-based IDS/IPS sensor, along with the compensating approach.

Configure the [SIEM] for near real-time analysis of aggregated intrusion detection information: aggregated data must be searchable, delivered in a format meeting organization-defined requirements, sourced from all network- and host-based capabilities, honor organization-directed collection rules within the requested timeframe, and retain raw intrusion detection information in an unaltered format.
Integrate intrusion detection tools into access control and flow control mechanisms so detection results can trigger enforcement.
Define and document criteria for unusual or unauthorized inbound and outbound communications activities or conditions; monitor traffic continuously against those criteria.
Test intrusion-monitoring tools and mechanisms at [IDS/IPS Test Frequency] and record each test in the Alert tuning and review records.

Employ the [Wireless IDS Console] to identify rogue wireless devices and detect attack attempts, potential compromises, and breaches — covering both external events at system boundaries and internal events within the system — and deploy intrusion detection on wireless communications traffic as it passes from wireless to wireline networks.
Implement host-based monitoring on systems, appliances, devices, services, and applications per the System Security and Privacy Plan.
Provide visibility into network traffic at external and key internal system interfaces (e.g., via [Network Packet Broker] or SPAN/tap configurations) to optimize monitoring device effectiveness.

Configure automated alerts to Detection & Response when system-generated indications of compromise occur, including the presence of malicious code, unauthorized export of information, signaling to an external information system, or potential intrusions; confirm recipients match the System Security and Privacy Plan.
Handle malicious code alerts consistent with SI-3 (malicious code protection) procedures.
Notify incident response personnel of detected suspicious events and take the documented least-disruptive actions upon detection; record the notification and action in the [Ticketing System].
Alert Detection & Response via automated mechanisms when indications of inappropriate or unusual activities with security or privacy implications occur.

Detect network services that have not been authorized or approved through the organization's authorization processes, and audit or alert Detection & Response when detected; open a [Ticketing System] ticket for each unauthorized service found.

Discover, collect, and distribute indicators of compromise from organization-defined sources (e.g., [Threat Intelligence Source]) to the defined personnel or roles, and load them into the [SIEM] detection layer.

Analyze outbound communications traffic at the external interfaces to the system and at selected interior points to discover anomalies, and analyze outbound traffic at external interfaces and interior points to detect covert exfiltration of information.
Analyze communications traffic and event patterns for the system; develop profiles representing common traffic and event patterns and use those profiles to tune system-monitoring devices.
Record each profile update and tuning change, with its rationale, in the Alert tuning and review records.
Correlate information from all monitoring tools and mechanisms employed throughout the system in the [SIEM].
Correlate information from monitoring physical, cyber, and supply chain activities to achieve integrated, organization-wide situational awareness.

Implement the additional monitoring defined for individuals identified by organization-defined sources as posing an increased level of risk, and for individuals during the defined probationary period, using the [SIEM] watchlist capability.
Implement the additional monitoring defined for privileged users, including full-session or command-level logging, and route the resulting records to the privileged command analysis capability.

The Detection & Response team is authorized to perform every step of this procedure end to end and is accountable for its outcomes, including the Log source inventory and coverage report and the Alert tuning and review records.

System Owners approve and accept audit record types, the Authorizing Official approves audited events for cloud environments, and exceptions to any step in this procedure require written approval from the Detection & Response lead in consultation with the designated audit and accountability official.

This procedure operationalizes the requirements in the *Example Org Logging, Monitoring & Alerting Standard*, which contains the full requirement text, the control rationale, and the underlying framework mappings.
heading_statements: Example Org Logging, Monitoring & Alerting Procedure
Maintain the Audit and Accountability Policy and Procedures [NIST 800-53 AU-1 | ARC-AMPE AU-1 | HIPAA 164.316(b)(1)]
Select and Document Event Types for Logging [NIST 800-53 AU-2 | ARC-AMPE AU-2]
