analyze: This procedure operationalizes Example Org's identification, authentication, and credential management controls so that every account, device, and session accessing Example Org systems is uniquely identified, appropriately authenticated, and continuously protected against credential compromise.

This procedure applies to IAM Engineering staff and any delegated system administrators who configure authentication, session, and credential controls on all Example Org information systems, including systems processing electronic protected health information (ePHI) and systems accessed by organizational, non-organizational, and non-privileged/privileged users.
It runs on a continuous basis as accounts, devices, and credentials are provisioned, used, and retired.
- Administrative access to the [Identity Provider] console and its authentication policy engine
- Access to a [Ticketing System] for logging exceptions, lockout overrides, and remediation actions
- Access to a [Mobile Device Management Platform] for mobile purge/wipe configuration
- Access to a [Configuration Management Database] or configuration baseline scanning tool
- Access to a [Password Manager] platform approved for organizational use
- Access to [Public Key Infrastructure] management tooling and trust store consoles
- Access to a [Governance, Risk, and Compliance (GRC) Platform] for policy/documentation retention
- Current approved Authentication & Credential Management Standard and applicable Security and Privacy Plan(s) (SSPP)
- Written approval from the [System Owner] or [Chief Information Security Officer] for any control exception
- Baseline reporting capability to generate the MFA enrolment report and Authentication policy configuration export
In the [Identity Provider] console, configure the account lockout policy to trigger after 5 consecutive invalid logon attempts within a 15-minute window.
Set the automatic response to lock the account for a minimum of 30 minutes or until an administrator releases it; disable automatic time-based unlock unless a documented operational exception exists.
Configure the [Identity Provider] to notify IAM Engineering via the [Ticketing System] whenever a lockout event fires.
Where an operational exception to manual release is required, document the justification and route it to the [System Owner] for approval before implementing an alternate unlock method.
Log all lockout and override events; include lockout configuration state in the Authentication policy configuration export.
In the [Mobile Device Management Platform], configure the device wipe/purge trigger to activate after 10 consecutive unsuccessful device logon attempts.
Define and apply the approved purge/wipe technique (full device wipe or container wipe) per the organization's mobile device configuration profile.
Verify the purge policy is applied to all enrolled devices via a compliance scan in the [Mobile Device Management Platform].
Capture the applied purge configuration in the Authentication policy configuration export.
Identify all systems using biometric logon in the [Identity Provider] or endpoint biometric subsystem.
Set the maximum consecutive unsuccessful biometric attempts to [Biometric Attempt Limit] in the applicable configuration console.
Confirm the limit triggers the same automatic response defined for invalid logon attempts (lockout/notification).
Record the configured value in the Authentication policy configuration export.
If alternate factors are approved for use after the primary invalid-attempt threshold is exceeded, configure them in the [Identity Provider] (e.g., a secondary verification method).
Set a separate consecutive invalid-attempt limit for the alternate factor within [Alternate Factor Attempt Window] and configure automatic lockout/notification on exceeding it.
Document which accounts/services are permitted to use alternate factors in the applicable SSPP.

Configure the pre-authentication banner on all in-scope systems to display: (a) notice that the system is a U.S. Government system or contains U.S. Government information, (b) notice that usage may be monitored, recorded, and audited, (c) notice that unauthorized use is prohibited and subject to criminal/civil penalty, and (d) notice that continued use constitutes consent to monitoring.
Configure the banner to remain on screen until the user takes explicit action (e.g., clicks "I Agree" or presses a defined key) to proceed to logon.

For publicly accessible systems, configure a banner variant that includes only the applicable monitoring/recording references and a description of authorized uses, displayed under the conditions defined for that system.
Work with the [System Owner] to determine which systems in the environment require the banner and record that determination in the applicable SSPP.

If compliance is not verified through configuration baseline checks, document in a written agreement how verification results will be produced and their periodicity, and store the agreement in the [Governance, Risk, and Compliance (GRC) Platform].
In the [Identity Provider], set the concurrent session limit to one (1) session per account and per account type by default.

For any account/account type requiring more than one concurrent session, document the justification in the applicable security and privacy plan and obtain [System Owner] approval before configuring the exception.
Verify the concurrent session setting during each configuration export and include it in the Authentication policy configuration export.

Configure endpoint and session policies (via the [Identity Provider] or endpoint management tool) to initiate a device lock after 15 minutes of inactivity, applied to both remote and internal connections.
Enable the manual lock option so users can initiate a lock before stepping away.
Configure the lock screen to display a publicly viewable image that conceals all previously visible content.
Configure the lock to remain in effect until the user re-authenticates through the established identification and authentication procedure.
Verify the inactivity timeout and lock-screen configuration in the periodic configuration export.

IAM Engineering, in coordination with the [System Owner], documents the approved functions, manner of use, and physical placement/attributes for each workstation or workstation class permitted to access ePHI.
Publish the workstation policy to affected personnel via the [Governance, Risk, and Compliance (GRC) Platform].
Review workstation configurations against the documented policy during routine compliance scans.
Define the triggering conditions for automatic session termination (inactivity period, incident response action, time-of-day restriction) in the applicable SSPP.

Configure the [Identity Provider] or application session manager to terminate sessions automatically when a defined condition occurs, including terminating electronic sessions after the configured period of inactivity.
Test termination behavior for each configured trigger and record results in the [Ticketing System].
Identify the information resources requiring authenticated access and record them in the applicable SSPP.
Configure a visible, user-accessible logout control for every communications session to those resources.
Verify logout functionality terminates the session and associated tokens immediately upon activation.
Configure the session termination flow to display the standard logout message "Your session has been terminated" upon logout.
Document this standard message text in the applicable SSPP.
Confirm the message renders correctly across supported client platforms.
Define the warning lead time (the period before termination at which the warning displays) in the applicable SSPP as [Session Expiration Warning Lead Time].
Configure the session manager to display an explicit warning message to the user at that lead time before automatic termination.
Validate the warning displays correctly in a test session and log the result.
Configure role- and identity-based access controls in the [Identity Provider] so that only authorized persons and authorized software programs can reach systems containing ePHI.
Review and reconcile the access control list against the current authorization roster on a continuous basis.
Remove or adjust access immediately upon identification of any unauthorized entry via the [Ticketing System].
Assign each user a unique username and/or numeric identifier in the [Identity Provider] at account creation; prohibit reuse of identifiers across users.
Confirm the unique identifier is used to track all logon, access, and audit events for that user.
Record identifier assignment in the account provisioning record retained in the [Governance, Risk, and Compliance (GRC) Platform].

Document the emergency access procedure describing how authorized personnel obtain necessary ePHI during an emergency, including the approval chain and the temporary credential/break-glass mechanism used.
Configure a break-glass account or emergency access role in the [Identity Provider], subject to enhanced logging and post-use review.
Test the emergency access procedure and store test evidence in the [Governance, Risk, and Compliance (GRC) Platform].
Determine, in coordination with the [System Owner], whether encryption of ePHI at rest/in transit is reasonable and appropriate for each system; document the risk-based decision.
Where implemented, configure the approved encryption mechanism to encrypt and decrypt ePHI transparently to authorized workflows.
Record the encryption configuration in the Authentication policy configuration export.

IAM Engineering drafts and maintains the identification and authentication policy and associated procedures, addressing purpose, scope, roles, responsibilities, management commitment, coordination, and applicable legal/regulatory compliance.
Designate the IAM Engineering lead as the official responsible for developing, documenting, and disseminating the policy and procedures to the personnel/roles defined in the organizational SSPP.
Disseminate the current policy and procedures to defined personnel via the [Governance, Risk, and Compliance (GRC) Platform].
Review and update the policy and procedures at least annually and following defined trigger events (audit findings, security incidents, legal/regulatory changes).
Record each review cycle and its outcome in the [Governance, Risk, and Compliance (GRC) Platform].

Maintain all authentication and credential management policies, procedures, and required action/activity/assessment records in written (which may be electronic) form in the [Governance, Risk, and Compliance (GRC) Platform].
Retain each document for 6 years from the date of creation or last effective date, whichever is later.
Make current documentation available to all personnel responsible for implementing the related procedures.
Review documentation periodically and update it as needed in response to environmental or operational changes affecting security; log each review.
Provision every organizational user (and any process acting on their behalf) with a unique identity in the [Identity Provider] before granting any local, network, or remote access.
Configure identity proofing and authentication workflows to comply with the current NIST SP 800-63 suite.
Require unique authenticators for each identity; document any authorized exception involving a shared group authenticator and its compensating controls in the applicable SSPP.
Require positive user identification (e.g., unique identifier verification) for any help desk transaction with security or privacy implications.
Include current enrollment status in the MFA enrolment report to confirm unique identity binding.
In the [Identity Provider], enforce MFA using two or more distinct factor types (something you know/have/are) for every privileged account, regardless of local, network, or remote access path.
Configure the MFA method to be phishing-resistant per current CISA guidance.
Generate the MFA enrolment report on a continuous basis and remediate any privileged account found without compliant MFA via the [Ticketing System].
Enforce phishing-resistant MFA for all non-privileged organizational account types in the [Identity Provider].
For consumer-facing accounts, strongly encourage MFA enrollment through in-product prompts even where not yet mandatory.
Track enrollment status in the MFA enrolment report and follow up on non-enrolled accounts through the [Ticketing System].

Where a shared account or authenticator exists, require each individual user to authenticate with their own unique credential in the [Identity Provider] before the system grants access to the shared resource.
Log the individual identity behind every shared-account session for audit purposes.
Periodically confirm no shared account permits access without preceding individual authentication.

Configure at least one MFA factor for both privileged and non-privileged accounts to originate from a device separate from the system being accessed (e.g., hardware token, authenticator app on a separate mobile device).
Verify the separate device meets the current published FIPS 140-compliant cryptography standard.
Apply this requirement uniformly to local, network, and remote access paths.
Record the separate-device factor type in the Authentication policy configuration export.
Configure authentication protocols for privileged and non-privileged account access to use replay-resistant mechanisms (e.g., time-based one-time passwords, cryptographic nonces, challenge-response).
Validate protocol configuration in the [Identity Provider] rejects replayed authentication attempts during a test.
Document the configured mechanism in the Authentication policy configuration export.
Identify the system accounts and services designated for single sign-on (SSO) in the applicable SSPP.
Configure the [Identity Provider] as the SSO authority for those accounts/services using an approved federation protocol.
Validate that SSO sessions inherit the applicable MFA, session timeout, and lockout controls defined elsewhere in this procedure.
Configure the [Identity Provider] to accept and electronically verify Personal Identity Verification (PIV)-compliant credentials for applicable users.
Validate the PIV certificate chain and revocation status during each verification event.
Log PIV verification outcomes for audit review.
Define the conditions under which out-of-band authentication (e.g., a call-back or secondary channel confirmation) is required, in the applicable SSPP.
Configure the out-of-band mechanism in the [Identity Provider] to trigger under those defined conditions.
Test the out-of-band flow and log results in the [Ticketing System].
Maintain a documented list of approved device types permitted to connect locally, remotely, or over the network, recorded in the applicable SSPP.
Configure network access control lists using, at minimum, MAC or IP address-based shared information to identify and authenticate approved devices before connection.
Where cryptographically based bidirectional device authentication is required, configure mutual certificate-based authentication between device and system prior to connection establishment.
Where attestation-based identification is used instead, verify the device's configuration state through the defined configuration management process before granting connection.
Record device authentication method and approved device list version in the Authentication policy configuration export.
Configure the DHCP or address-allocation service to apply standardized lease information and lease duration per the defined organizational requirements.
Configure audit logging so that lease assignment to a device is recorded at time of assignment.
Review lease audit logs on a continuous basis for anomalies.
Verify the identity of the individual, group, role, service, or device before issuing an authenticator, using the identity proofing process defined for IA-2/IA-8.
Establish initial authenticator content and confirm it meets the strength-of-mechanism requirement for its intended use.

Follow documented administrative procedures in the [Identity Provider] and [Ticketing System] for initial distribution, and for handling lost, compromised, or damaged authenticators, including revocation.
Change all default/vendor-supplied authenticators prior to first use of any account or device.
Protect authenticator content (secrets, seeds, keys) from unauthorized disclosure or modification using access-restricted storage.
Require individuals and devices to implement the protective controls specified in the applicable SSPP (e.g., not sharing credentials, securing hardware tokens).
Change the authenticator for any group or role account immediately upon a membership change.
Configure the [Identity Provider] to force an immediate authenticator change upon known or suspected compromise.
Configure a forced change of any default or vendor-supplied authenticator immediately upon system installation.
Apply the strongly recommended six-month rotation cadence to system and user account passwords where technically enforceable.
Log all forced and scheduled authenticator changes in the [Ticketing System].
Determine the applicable Certification Class for each system (Class B = IAL/AAL/FAL Level 1, Class C = Level 2, Class D = Level 3) and configure the [Identity Provider] accordingly.
Configure authentication assertions passed through third parties (e.g., browsers) to be encrypted using XML-Encryption for SAML assertions or JWE for OpenID Connect ID Tokens.
Validate assertion encryption configuration during each Authentication policy configuration export.
Confirm all authenticator management configurations comply with the current published NIST SP 800-63B.
Pair all organizational system and user account passwords with MFA consistent with the privileged/non-privileged MFA requirements above.
Strongly encourage pairing consumer account passwords with MFA through in-product enrollment prompts.

Maintain a list of commonly used, expected, or compromised passwords in the [Identity Provider] or an integrated password-check service; update the list at least annually or immediately upon suspected compromise.
Configure the [Identity Provider] to verify every new or updated password against that list before acceptance.
Ensure passwords are transmitted only over cryptographically protected channels (TLS or equivalent) between client and authentication service.
Configure password storage to use an approved salted key derivation function, preferably a keyed hash, with salting enabled to mitigate brute-force attacks.
Require immediate selection of a new permanent password upon any account recovery; treat any temporary password as requiring an immediate change with no extended lifetime.
Allow user selection of long passwords/passphrases including spaces and all printable characters; prohibit dictionary words.
Enable an automated strength-assistance tool in the password change workflow to help users select strong passwords.

Enforce minimum password length of 8 characters for consumer and all other standard accounts, and 12 characters for administrator/privileged accounts, per the current NIST SP 800-63B composition guidance.
Where organizational risk tolerance supports it, document and apply an exclusion of mobile devices from full complexity requirements.
Configure the [Public Key Infrastructure] to enforce authorized access controls on private keys before they can be used for authentication.
Map each authenticated identity to the corresponding individual's or group's account in the [Identity Provider].
Where PKI is used, validate certificates through a certification path to an accepted trust anchor, including a certificate status (revocation) check.
Maintain a local cache of revocation data to support path discovery and validation during offline or degraded connectivity.
Require developers and system installers to provide unique authenticators for each deployed component, or to change any default authenticator, prior to delivery and installation.
Verify default-authenticator status as part of the pre-deployment acceptance checklist stored in the [Ticketing System].
Classify each system's security category per the applicable SSPP.
Apply authenticator storage, transmission, and access controls proportionate to that category (e.g., stronger encryption and access restriction for higher-category systems).
Document the applied protections in the Authentication policy configuration export.
Scan application source code, configuration files, and scripts for embedded unencrypted static authenticators using the organization's code scanning tooling.
Remove or encrypt any discovered embedded static authenticator and rotate it immediately.
Log the remediation in the [Ticketing System].
Identify individuals holding accounts on multiple systems through the [Identity Provider]'s identity correlation report.
Apply defined compensating controls (e.g., unique authenticators per system, monitoring for correlated compromise) to those accounts.
Review cross-system account risk on a continuous basis.
Identify the external organizations approved to federate credentials into Example Org systems, per the applicable SSPP.
Configure federation trust relationships in the [Identity Provider] only with those approved external organizations.
Review the federation partner list periodically and remove any unapproved trust relationship.
Define the binding rules governing how identities are dynamically bound to authenticators, per the applicable SSPP.
Configure the [Identity Provider] to apply those binding rules automatically at enrollment and re-binding events.
Validate binding behavior during periodic configuration review.
Define the required biometric quality thresholds (false match/false non-match rates) applicable to Example Org biometric systems.
Configure biometric capture and matching subsystems to enforce those thresholds.
Validate configuration compliance during periodic review.
Define the maximum permitted cached-authenticator time period as [Cached Authenticator Time Limit].
Configure client and server components to purge cached authenticators after that period.
Verify cached-credential purge behavior during a configuration test.
Establish an organization-wide methodology for managing PKI trust store content across all networks, operating systems, browsers, and applications.
Apply the methodology consistently when adding, removing, or updating trusted certificate authorities in each platform's trust store.
Record trust store baseline state in the Authentication policy configuration export.
Before procuring or configuring any identity, credential, or access management product or service, confirm it appears on the current GSA-approved products/services list.
Document the approval verification in the procurement record.
Define which authenticator types require in-person or trusted-external-party issuance, per the applicable SSPP.
Route issuance of those authenticator types through the defined registration authority, requiring authorization by the defined personnel/roles before issuance.
Log each issuance event and its authorizer in the [Ticketing System].
Enable presentation attack detection (liveness detection) on all biometric authentication mechanisms.
Validate detection effectiveness during periodic testing of the biometric subsystem.
Designate the approved [Password Manager] platform for organizational password generation and management.
Configure the password manager to enforce the protective controls defined for it in the applicable SSPP (e.g., encrypted vault, master authentication with MFA).
Require users to store organizational credentials only in the approved password manager.
Configure all logon interfaces to mask authentication feedback (e.g., display asterisks/dots for typed passwords) so entered credentials are not visible on screen.
Where applicable, limit the display time of any temporarily revealed characters.
Validate masking behavior on each new or updated logon interface before release.
Configure authentication to cryptographic modules to meet applicable laws, executive orders, directives, policies, regulations, and standards.
For systems containing PII, configure encryption using the latest published FIPS 140-compliant standard.
Record cryptographic module configuration in the Authentication policy configuration export.
Provision non-organizational users (and processes acting on their behalf) with unique identities in the [Identity Provider] before granting access.
Configure identity proofing and authentication to comply with the current NIST SP 800-63-3 Digital Identity Guidelines at IAL-2/AAL-2.
Require positive identification for any help desk transaction involving a non-organizational user with security or privacy implications.
Include non-organizational account enrollment status in the MFA enrolment report.
Configure the [Identity Provider] to accept and electronically verify PIV credentials issued by other federal agencies.
Validate the certificate chain and revocation status during each verification.
Maintain a documented list of accepted external authenticators, limited to those that are NIST-compliant.
For ARC-AMPE-covered systems, confirm each external credential is certified compliant with the current NIST SP 800-63 suite by an approved accreditation authority and meets or exceeds that guidance.
Confirm any identity/credential/access management product used for this purpose is GSA-approved.
Review and update the accepted-authenticator list periodically.
Define the identity management profiles Example Org conforms to, based on identity proofing and authentication processes compliant with the current NIST SP 800-63 suite.
Configure the [Identity Provider] to enforce the defined profiles for applicable user populations.
Define the applicable PIV-I policy for accepted federated or PKI credentials.
Configure the [Identity Provider] to accept and verify credentials meeting that policy.
Define the measures required to disassociate user attributes or identifier-assertion relationships among individuals, credential service providers, and relying parties.
Configure the federation/identity architecture to apply those disassociation measures for applicable transactions.

Define the circumstances requiring re-authentication (role change, authenticator/credential change, system security category change, execution of a privileged function, fixed time period, or periodic interval) in the applicable SSPP.
Configure the [Identity Provider] or application session manager to force re-authentication automatically when each defined circumstance occurs.
At minimum, configure a fixed-time-period re-authentication requirement as defined in the SSPP.
Validate re-authentication triggers during periodic testing and log results in the [Ticketing System].

IAM Engineering owns this procedure end to end: it configures, tests, monitors, and maintains all authentication and credential controls described above, and generates the MFA enrolment report and Authentication policy configuration export on a continuous basis.

System Owners define which parts of their environment require specific controls (e.g., system use notification scope, in-scope information resources) and document exceptions in the applicable SSPP; the [Chief Information Security Officer] or [System Owner] reviews and approves any deviation from a mandatory control before IAM Engineering implements it.

analyze: Executing this procedure implements the operational controls required by the Example Org Physical & Environmental Security Standard: it limits, authorizes, monitors, and documents physical access to Example Org facilities and the electronic information systems housed within them, and it keeps the governing policy, procedures, and supporting documentation current and retrievable.

This procedure is performed by the Facilities / Physical Security team on all Example Org facilities that house electronic information systems, including data centre environments, and applies to all employees, contractors, and visitors seeking physical access to those facilities.
Facilities / Physical Security owns this process end to end; other teams participate only in the specific steps where named.
- Administrative access to the badge/access control platform used at Example Org facilities ([Badge Access Control System])
- Access to the system of record for the facility authorized-access list ([Access Control Records System])
- A ticketing system for logging access requests, visitor authorizations, repairs, and modifications ([Ticketing System])
- A system for storing and retaining policy and procedure documentation ([Document Management System])
- Identification of the official designated to manage the physical and environmental protection policy and procedures ([Designated Official])
- An approved list of acceptable forms of identification ([Assignment: organization-defined list of acceptable forms of identification])
- Current copies of the Example Org Physical & Environmental Security Standard, the disaster recovery plan, and the emergency mode operations plan
- Approval authority for access-list changes and exceptions, held by Facilities / Physical Security leadership

Confirm the physical and environmental protection policy is documented in [Document Management System] and addresses purpose, scope, roles, responsibilities, management commitment, coordination among organizational entities, and compliance.

Verify the policy and these procedures are consistent with applicable laws, executive orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, and guidelines; where a conflict is found, raise it with the [Designated Official] for resolution before proceeding.

Confirm a designated official ([Designated Official]) is named as responsible for the development, documentation, and dissemination of the policy and procedures; if the designation has changed, update the policy and record the change in [Ticketing System].

Disseminate the current policy and procedures to all applicable personnel and roles, using the distribution mechanism recorded in [Document Management System], and record the dissemination date and audience.
Ensure these procedures themselves are documented, approved, and published alongside the policy so that personnel can execute the associated physical and environmental protection controls.

On the quarterly process cycle, Facilities / Physical Security reviews the physical and environmental protection policy and procedures; additionally, complete a full review at least every one (1) year.

Trigger an out-of-cycle review following any of: assessment or audit findings; security or privacy incidents; or changes to applicable laws, executive orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, and guidelines.

Actively monitor for changes to applicable privacy laws, regulations, and overarching policy that affect physical and environmental protection, using the monitoring source recorded in [Document Management System], and review the monitoring results at least every one (1) year to confirm the policies and procedures remain effective.
Record each review — its date, reviewer (Facilities / Physical Security), findings, and any resulting updates — in [Document Management System].
Where updates are required, the [Designated Official] approves the revised policy or procedures before republishing and re-disseminating per Step 1.4.
During each review under Step 2, verify that the physical and environmental protection policy and associated controls support privacy to the greatest extent feasible throughout the system life cycle.

Verify that physical access controls, visitor procedures, and monitoring practices do not permit unnecessary or inappropriate access to Personally Identifiable Information (PII) held within the facilities or systems in scope.
Where a gap is identified, log it in [Ticketing System], assign remediation to Facilities / Physical Security, and obtain [Designated Official] approval for the remediation plan.
Apply the access-limiting policies and procedures documented under the Standard to all electronic information systems and the facilities in which they are housed.
Grant physical access only through the authorization workflow defined in Step 8; no access is permitted without a completed authorization record.

Verify on each quarterly cycle that properly authorized individuals are able to access the facilities using their issued credentials, and that unauthorized access attempts are denied and logged by the [Badge Access Control System].

Document procedures that allow facility access in support of restoration of lost data under the disaster recovery plan and emergency mode operations plan, and store them with the plans in [Document Management System].

Implement these procedures when an emergency occurs: verify the identity and role of responders against the facility authorized-access list (Step 8), grant emergency access under the documented emergency provisions, and record each emergency access event in [Ticketing System].
After the emergency, Facilities / Physical Security reconciles the emergency access events against the authorized-access list and restores normal access controls.
Maintain the physical safeguards described in the Standard — locks, controlled entry points, and monitoring — for the facility and the equipment therein.

Confirm on the quarterly cycle that entry points and equipment enclosures are intact and that no unauthorized physical access, tampering, or theft has occurred; log any findings in [Ticketing System].

Route any suspected tampering or theft incident to incident response per the coordination mechanism defined in the physical and environmental protection policy, and carry the resulting changes into the Step 2 review triggers.
Authorize physical access to the facility where a system resides based on the individual's position or role; validate each request against the requester's documented role before granting access.

For visitors, implement the visitor control procedures: escort requirements, visitor credential issuance through the [Badge Access Control System], and logging of visitor entry and exit in [Ticketing System].
Control access to software programs held at the facility for testing and revision using the same role-based validation, and record each such access grant in [Ticketing System].
Develop, obtain approval for, and maintain in [Access Control Records System] a list of individuals with authorized access to the facility where the system resides.
Issue authorization credentials for facility access through the [Badge Access Control System] only after the individual appears on the approved access list.

Review the access list detailing authorized facility access by individuals at least every six (6) months — performed on the quarterly process cycle, which satisfies this minimum — and produce the Badge access review artifact documenting the review date, reviewer, and outcomes.

Remove individuals from the facility access list when access is no longer required, and revoke their credentials in the [Badge Access Control System] as part of the same action; record the removal in [Ticketing System].

Require two forms of identification, drawn from the [Assignment: organization-defined list of acceptable forms of identification], before adding any individual to the access list or issuing credentials.

Log every repair or modification to the physical components of a facility related to security — for example hardware, walls, doors, and locks — in [Ticketing System] at the time the work is performed.
Record in each ticket the component affected, the nature of the repair or modification, the date, and the party performing the work.

Facilities / Physical Security reviews the repair and modification records on the quarterly cycle to confirm completeness and to identify any change that should trigger a policy or procedure review under Step 2.

Maintain the policies, procedures, and documentation of actions, activities, and assessments produced by this procedure — including the Badge access review and the Data centre environmental monitoring records — in written (which may be electronic) form in [Document Management System].

Retain all required documentation for 6 years from the date of its creation or the date when it last was in effect, whichever is later; configure the [Document Management System] retention settings to enforce this period before disposing of anything.

Make each document available to the persons responsible for implementing the procedures to which it pertains, using the access permissions in [Document Management System]; Facilities / Physical Security verifies this availability during the quarterly cycle.
Facilities / Physical Security performs every step of this procedure, reviews the resulting evidence artifacts, and answers for the outcome of the process end to end.

Other teams (such as system owners and visitors' sponsors) participate in individual steps where named, and exceptions to any step in this procedure require the review and approval of Facilities / Physical Security leadership in consultation with the [Designated Official].
This procedure operationalizes the *Example Org Physical & Environmental Security Standard*, which contains the underlying requirement text and the rationale for each control described above.
heading_statements: Example Org Physical & Environmental Security Operational Procedure
1. Maintain and disseminate the physical and environmental protection policy and procedures [NIST 800-53 PE-1 Low/Moderate/High | ARC-AMPE PE-1]
2. Review and update the policy and procedures [NIST 800-53 PE-1 Low/Moderate/High | ARC-AMPE PE-1 | HIPAA 164.316(b)(2)(iii) Required | ARC-AMPE PE-1]
[NIST 800-53 PE-1 Low/Moderate/High | ARC-AMPE PE-1 | HIPAA 164.316(b)(2)(iii) Required | ARC-AMPE PE-1]
3. Support privacy and limit unnecessary access to PII [ARC-AMPE PE-1]
4. Limit and authorize physical access to facilities and systems [HIPAA 164.310(a)(1)]
5. Emergency facility access for disaster recovery and emergency operations [HIPAA 164.310(a)(2)(i) Addressable]
6. Safeguard the facility and equipment from unauthorized access, tampering, and theft [HIPAA 164.310(a)(2)(ii)]
7. Role-based physical access control and visitor control [NIST 800-53 PE-2(1) | HIPAA 164.310(a)(2)(iii) Addressable]
8. Maintain the authorized facility access list and issue credentials [NIST 800-53 PE-2 Low/Moderate/High | ARC-AMPE PE-2]
9. Document repairs and modifications to facility security components [HIPAA 164.310(a)(2)(iv)]
10. Maintain, retain, and make documentation available [HIPAA 164.316(b)(1) | HIPAA 164.316(b)(2)(i) Required | HIPAA 164.316(b)(2)(ii) Required]

analyze: This procedure provides the operational instructions Endpoint Engineering follows to deploy, configure, and continuously verify malicious code protection, spam protection, memory protection, mobile code controls, and device/media restrictions across Example Org systems.

Executing it produces the evidence artifacts — the EDR deployment coverage report and the removable media policy configuration — required to demonstrate conformance to the Endpoint Protection & Device Controls Standard.

This procedure is performed by Endpoint Engineering on all organization-owned endpoints (workstations, notebook computers, mobile devices) and on system entry and exit points including firewalls, remote-access servers, email servers, web servers, and proxy servers.
It applies continuously, from initial deployment through ongoing configuration, testing, and response activities.
- Administrative access to the organization's [Endpoint Protection Platform] management console.
- Administrative access to the organization's [Email Security Gateway].
- Administrative access to the organization's [Endpoint Configuration Management Tool] for policy push and enforcement.
- Access to the [Ticketing System] for change requests, exception tracking, and incident handoffs.
- Access to the [Identity Provider] to confirm privileged-role membership for update and verification actions.
- A current copy of the applicable System Security and Privacy Plan (SSPP) for documenting alternative actions and mobile code definitions.
- Approval from Endpoint Engineering for any policy change executed under this procedure.

Endpoint Engineering identifies all system entry and exit points in scope — firewalls, remote-access servers, workstations, email servers, web servers, proxy servers, notebook computers, and mobile devices — using the [Endpoint Configuration Management Tool] inventory.
Install the malicious code protection agent from the [Endpoint Protection Platform] on every identified system, pushing via the [Endpoint Configuration Management Tool].
Verify agent installation and health on each system from the [Endpoint Protection Platform] console.
Generate the EDR deployment coverage report from the [Endpoint Protection Platform] and reconcile it against the inventory; investigate and remediate any gap on a system that reports no agent.
Retain the EDR deployment coverage report as evidence of implementation.
In the [Endpoint Protection Platform], enable the signature-based detection engine on all managed endpoints and entry/exit point systems.
Enable the non-signature-based detection engine (behavioral/heuristic analysis) alongside the signature engine on the same systems.
Confirm both engines show as active — not disabled or in passive mode — for every system in the deployment coverage report.

In the [Endpoint Protection Platform], enable automatic signature and engine updates so that protection mechanisms update as new releases become available, in accordance with organizational configuration management policies and procedures.

Restrict the ability to approve or manually trigger protection mechanism updates to users holding the privileged role in the [Identity Provider]; updates occur only when directed by such a privileged user.
Route any request for a non-standard update (delayed rollback, deferred deployment) through the [Ticketing System] as a change request reviewed and approved by Endpoint Engineering.
In the [Endpoint Protection Platform], set the scheduled scan policy for all managed systems to run at a minimum of every one (1) week.
Apply the scan schedule consistently across the full endpoint fleet via the [Endpoint Configuration Management Tool].
Review scan completion status in the [Endpoint Protection Platform] console and follow up on systems that miss their scheduled scan.
In the [Endpoint Protection Platform], enable real-time, on-access scanning of files downloaded, opened, or executed from external sources on all endpoints.

On the network entry and exit points (firewalls, email servers, web servers, proxy servers, remote-access servers), enable equivalent real-time file scanning at the [Email Security Gateway] and [Endpoint Protection Platform] network components.

Verify both endpoint-level and network-level real-time scanning are active for each system in the EDR deployment coverage report, satisfying the requirement that external-source files are scanned at both locations.
In the [Endpoint Protection Platform], set the detection response policy to **both** block and quarantine detected malicious code.
Configure the alerting policy to send a near real-time alert on every malicious code detection to the administrator and organization-defined security personnel — at minimum, [Security Operations].
Test the alert path by validating that a detection event generates the alert in the [Security Operations] alert queue.
Any action other than block-and-quarantine for a specific detection requires Endpoint Engineering approval, recorded in the [Ticketing System].
When a false positive is reported or observed, [Security Operations] or the system owner opens a ticket in the [Ticketing System] identifying the affected file, system, and detection rule.
Endpoint Engineering assesses the potential availability impact on the affected system and, if necessary, applies a narrowly scoped exclusion or rule exception in the [Endpoint Protection Platform].
Record the false positive, its analysis, and the remediation decision in the [Ticketing System]; review exclusions periodically to confirm each remains necessary.
Submit confirmed false positives to the protection vendor through its designated submission channel.
At the [Testing Frequency], Endpoint Engineering introduces a known benign test file (e.g., an industry-standard test signature) into a managed system.
Verify that the [Endpoint Protection Platform] detects the test file, blocks or quarantines it per policy, and generates the associated alert to [Security Operations].
Confirm the detection produced the expected incident reporting in the alert queue; if detection or alerting fails, open a ticket in the [Ticketing System] and remediate before the next test cycle.
Record the test outcome as evidence of mechanism verification.
In the [Endpoint Protection Platform], enable kernel-level behavioral monitoring on the organization-defined system hardware components.
Configure the policy to detect the organization-defined unauthorized operating system commands through the kernel API.
Set the response action to issue a warning, audit the command execution, and/or prevent execution of the command, per the organization-defined response for each command class.
Verify detections and audit records are flowing to the [Security Operations] alert queue.

When malicious code is detected that warrants deeper analysis, Endpoint Engineering employs the organization-defined analysis tools and techniques — including sandbox detonation and behavioral analysis in the [Endpoint Protection Platform] — to characterize the code.
Incorporate the analysis results into the organizational incident response process by attaching findings to the incident record in the [Incident Response Platform].

Incorporate the analysis results into the flaw remediation process by opening or updating the corresponding remediation item in the [Ticketing System], including any indicated patch or configuration change.

In the [Endpoint Protection Platform], enable the self-verification capability so that security and privacy functions (e.g., agent integrity, policy enforcement, scanning engine health) are checked automatically upon system startup and/or restart.
Perform verification upon command by a user with appropriate privileges (via the [Identity Provider] privileged role) whenever a manual check is needed, and on a scheduled basis at least monthly.
Confirm that scheduled and startup verifications run on all in-scope systems and that results are captured by the platform.

Configure the [Endpoint Protection Platform] to send an alert to organization-defined personnel or roles — at a minimum, the system/security administrator — whenever a security or privacy verification test fails.
Validate the alert path to the administrator and [Security Operations] queues.
When verification reveals anomalies, shut the system down, restart the system, or perform the organization-defined alternative action, as directed by Endpoint Engineering.
Under ARC-AMPE, if an alternative action (other than shutdown or restart) is selected, document that action in the applicable System Security and Privacy Plan (SSPP) before relying on it.
Record the anomaly, the action taken, and the disposition in the [Ticketing System].

Employ the automated mechanisms in the [Endpoint Protection Platform] and [Endpoint Configuration Management Tool] to orchestrate and manage security and privacy function testing across the distributed fleet, rather than per-system manual testing.
Use the central consoles to schedule tests, collect results, and track systems whose tests have not run.
Report the results of security and privacy function verification to organization-defined personnel or roles — at minimum, the system/security administrator and Endpoint Engineering leadership.
Deliver results through the reporting capability of the [Endpoint Protection Platform] and record delivery in the [Ticketing System].

Endpoint Engineering implements spam protection mechanisms at the system entry and exit points — firewalls, remote-access servers, email servers, web servers, proxy servers, workstations, notebook computers, and mobile devices — using the [Email Security Gateway] and the endpoint protection policy in the [Endpoint Protection Platform].
Configure the mechanisms to detect and act on unsolicited messages (quarantine, tag, or reject per the gateway policy).

Enable automatic updates of the spam protection mechanisms — filter rules and reputation feeds — as new releases are available, in accordance with organizational configuration management policies and procedures, at an automatic update frequency of at least every one (1) week.

Enable the learning capability of the spam protection mechanisms (e.g., Bayesian/adaptive filtering and user feedback) so the mechanisms more effectively identify legitimate communications traffic over time.
Verify in the [Email Security Gateway] console that update jobs complete successfully and that learning features are active.

Where Example Org sends email on behalf of the government as part of the business offering, implement Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting & Conformance (DMARC) on the sending domain for outgoing messages as described in DHS Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 18-01.
Confirm the DMARC DNS configuration for each sending domain: the policy is set to `p=reject` and the `rua` parameter includes `reports@dmarc.cyber.dhs.gov`.
Document DMARC compliance in the SI-08 control implementation solution description.
List the FROM: domain(s) used when emails are sent on behalf of the government in the same control implementation documentation.

In the [Endpoint Protection Platform] and via the [Endpoint Configuration Management Tool], enable exploit mitigation controls on all in-scope systems, including at a minimum data execution prevention (DEP) and address space layout randomization (ASLR).
Apply the organization-defined additional memory protection controls defined for this control set where supported by the platform.
Verify the settings are applied and not overridable by standard users, and record the applied configuration as evidence.
Endpoint Engineering defines the organization-defined prohibited media types and systems in the device control policy within the [Endpoint Protection Platform].

Configure the device control policy to restrict or prohibit the use of those media types on the organization-defined systems and system components, and retain the resulting removable media policy configuration as evidence.

Prohibit the use of personally owned media — flash drives, external hard disk drives, and other portable storage and media devices — on organization-defined systems and networks, enforced by the same device control safeguards.
Prohibit the use of portable storage devices that have no identifiable owner on organizational systems.
Prohibit the use of sanitization-resistant media in organizational systems under the device control policy.
Route any request for a media-use exception through the [Ticketing System]; Endpoint Engineering reviews and approves or denies each exception and records the decision.
Endpoint Engineering defines the acceptable and unacceptable mobile code and mobile code technologies for the system (e.g., permitted scripting environments, prohibited plugin technologies).
Under ARC-AMPE, document the acceptable and unacceptable mobile code definitions in the applicable System Security and Privacy Plan (SSPP).
Authorize, monitor, and control the use of acceptable mobile code within the system through browser/application policy and the [Endpoint Protection Platform].
Configure the [Endpoint Protection Platform] to identify the organization-defined unacceptable mobile code types on managed systems and at entry/exit points.
Configure the organization-defined corrective actions — block, alert [Security Operations], and open a ticket in the [Ticketing System] — to execute automatically upon detection.
Before any mobile code is acquired, developed, or deployed into the system, Endpoint Engineering verifies that it meets the organization-defined mobile code requirements established in the SSPP.
Record the verification and approval in the [Ticketing System] prior to deployment.
Configure web filtering and the [Endpoint Protection Platform] to prevent the download of the organization-defined unacceptable mobile code at network entry and exit points and on endpoints.

Configure the organization-defined software applications to prevent the automatic execution of mobile code, and enforce the organization-defined actions (e.g., user prompt, administrator approval) prior to any execution of mobile code.
Verify enforcement by attempting to load a known-blocked mobile code sample in a controlled test and confirming it is prevented.
Configure the environment so that permitted mobile code executes only within confined virtual machine environments.
Verify that no permitted mobile code executes outside the confined environment and that confinement settings cannot be modified by standard users.

Endpoint Engineering is accountable for this procedure end to end: it deploys, configures, tests, and reports on all malicious code protection, spam protection, memory protection, mobile code, and device control mechanisms, and it owns the handoffs to [Security Operations] and the [Incident Response Platform].

[Security Operations] and system/security administrators act on alerts and participate in testing and verification, and Endpoint Engineering reviews and approves all exceptions — false positive exclusions, media-use exceptions, alternative anomaly actions, and mobile code authorizations.

This procedure operationalizes the **Endpoint Protection & Device Controls Standard**, which contains the full requirement text, the rationale for each control, and the framework mappings ([NIST], [FedRAMP], [ARC-AMPE]) referenced above.

analyze: This procedure provides the step-by-step operational instructions Platform Security follows to establish, operate, and govern cryptographic keys, encryption at rest and in transit, certificate management, and electronic protected health information (ePHI) safeguards in accordance with the Encryption & Key Management Standard.

Platform Security performs this procedure on all Example Org systems and media that employ cryptography, store or transmit sensitive information, or handle ePHI, including keys held or encrypted by external service providers on Example Org's behalf.
- Administrative access to the organization's [Key Management Service / Hardware Security Module] and all in-scope system consoles.
- Access to the organization's [Ticketing System] for change tracking and remediation records.
- A current inventory of all systems employing cryptography, encryption endpoints, and certificate trust stores.
- An approved list of organization-defined cryptographic uses and required cryptography types per use.
- An approved certificate policy or a designated [Approved Certificate Service Provider], and where applicable, access to [PKI Provider] or prepositioned keying material channels.
- Identified external service providers that encrypt Example Org information on Example Org's behalf, with current contract and key custody documentation.
- Agreed values for all bracketed decisions in this document ([Key Recovery Deadline], [Session Inactivity Timeout], [Trust Store Review Frequency], etc.).
- Coordination contacts in [System Owner] teams, the [Privacy Officer / HIPAA Compliance function], and [Human Resources / Identity Management] for ePHI access rights.

Platform Security maintains a complete key inventory in the Key inventory and rotation log, recording for every key: unique identifier, owning system, algorithm, key length, custodian, purpose, generation and expiry dates, and storage location.

For each key, document and enforce the full lifecycle controls: key generation, distribution, storage, access, and destruction, consistent with applicable laws, directives, regulations, policies, standards, and guidelines.

Restrict access to each key to the minimum set of identities and services required, enforced through the [Key Management Service / Hardware Security Module] access policy; review access grants against the key inventory annually.
Destroy keys at end of life using the destruction method approved in the Standard, and record the destruction event, method, and operator in the Key inventory and rotation log.
Platform Security reviews the Key inventory and rotation log annually and reconciles it against live systems to confirm no unmanaged keys exist.

Before approving any cryptographic product or module for use, Platform Security verifies the product appears on the Cryptographic Module Validation Program (CMVP) validated modules list as compliant with the latest published FIPS 140 standards; record the validation certificate number in the Key inventory and rotation log entry for any keys the product manages.
Reject and replace any cryptographic product that cannot demonstrate current CMVP validation; open a remediation ticket in the [Ticketing System] with an assigned [Remediation Deadline].

Reference NIST SP 800-56A, SP 800-56B, SP 800-56C, and NIST SP 800-57 as the governing key management requirements when defining key establishment, key derivation, and key lifecycle parameters, and cite the applicable reference in each key management configuration record.

Platform Security implements a key recovery capability in the [Key Management Service / Hardware Security Module], such as escrowed key copies or key backup under dual control, for every key protecting user-accessible information.

Document the recovery workflow: the user or [Service Desk] reports the lost key, Platform Security verifies the requester's identity, and an authorized Platform Security member releases the recovered key or reissues credentials.
Test the key recovery workflow annually and record the test result in the Key inventory and rotation log.
Define and document the [Key Recovery Deadline] — the maximum time within which recovered keys or replacement access must be provided after a verified loss report.

Generate all symmetric keys within the NIST FIPS-validated or NSA-approved [Key Management Service / Hardware Security Module]; never generate symmetric keys on general-purpose endpoints or in unvalidated software.

Distribute symmetric keys only through protected channels established by the key management technology (e.g., key wrapping under a transport key); record each distribution event — key ID, recipient system, date, and channel — in the Key inventory and rotation log.
Control symmetric key material under split knowledge and dual control where a single individual would otherwise have full access to a key or its components.

Generate asymmetric key pairs using NSA-approved key management technology and processes, prepositioned keying material, DoD-approved or DoD-issued Medium Assurance PKI certificates, or DoD-approved or DoD-issued Medium Hardware Assurance PKI certificates with hardware security tokens protecting the user's private key — or, where the organization has defined its own requirements, certificates issued per those organization-defined requirements.

Where hardware security tokens are the selected mechanism, issue tokens only after identity verification, record the token serial number and assignee, and require the private key to remain non-exportable from the token.
Record each asymmetric key issuance — key ID, subject, certificate authority or issuance mechanism, assurance level, and date — in the Key inventory and rotation log.

Platform Security maintains a register of every external service provider that encrypts Example Org information on Example Org's behalf, identifying for each provider: who holds the keys, the key custody model (provider-held, customer-held, or hybrid), and the physical or logical controls protecting the key store.

Where the contract permits, require a customer-held or hybrid key model (e.g., customer-managed keys via the [Key Management Service / Hardware Security Module]) so Example Org retains physical control of its keys; document any exception and its approval in the register.

Review the provider key custody register annually against current contracts and confirm each provider's key protection controls remain in place; update the register and open tickets in the [Ticketing System] for any gaps, each with an assigned [Remediation Deadline].

Platform Security maintains the approved list of cryptographic uses (e.g., data at rest, data in transit, digital signatures, authentication) and, for each use, the type of cryptography required, in accordance with applicable laws, executive orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, and guidelines.

Map every cryptographic implementation in the environment to one of the approved uses; where a new cryptographic use is proposed, Platform Security evaluates and approves it before deployment and updates the list.

Verify during the annual review that each deployed implementation matches the cryptography type required for its use; log the verification result with the Encryption-at-rest and in-transit configuration evidence.

For each specified cryptographic use, implement at minimum the latest published FIPS 140-compliant cryptography, consistent with applicable federal laws, Executive Orders, directives, policies, regulations, and standards.

Confirm any FIPS 140-2 module in active use has a documented retirement plan, noting that FIPS 140-2 modules may remain active until September 21, 2026; schedule replacement transitions in the [Ticketing System] ahead of that date.

Apply the FedRAMP Cryptographic Module Use rules to every module selection and configuration decision; document the applicable rule and how the configuration satisfies it in the Encryption-at-rest and in-transit configuration record.
Record each module's validation status and configuration in the Encryption-at-rest and in-transit configuration evidence.

Identify all data containing sensitive information — including Personally Identifiable Information and proprietary, financial, and legal information — wherever it resides in the system, using [Data Classification / Discovery Tooling] outputs and [System Owner] attestations.

Configure encryption for every identified data store using the latest published FIPS 140-compliant encryption standards; capture the resulting settings in the Encryption-at-rest and in-transit configuration evidence.

Extend coverage to all locations where sensitive data resides — databases, file stores, backups, endpoints, and removable media — and verify no identified data store remains unencrypted; open a ticket in the [Ticketing System] with an assigned [Remediation Deadline] for any gap.

Issue public key certificates only under the organization-defined certificate policy, or obtain them from the [Approved Certificate Service Provider]; confirm the policy or provider is approved by Platform Security before any issuance.
Record every certificate issued or obtained — subject, issuer, validity period, key usage, and purpose — in the Key inventory and rotation log.
Track certificate expiry dates and renew or replace certificates before expiry; where an expiration value is not defined, apply the [Certificate Renewal Lead Time] agreed by Platform Security.

Platform Security defines and publishes the approved set of trust anchors, covering both certificates with visibility external to organizational systems and certificates related to internal system operations.
Configure the trust stores and certificate stores on all managed systems to contain only approved trust anchors; remove any anchor not on the approved list.

Review trust stores across managed systems annually against the approved anchor list, record the review results with the Encryption-at-rest and in-transit configuration evidence, and open tickets in the [Ticketing System] with an assigned [Remediation Deadline] for any unapproved anchors found.
Identify the organization-defined information at rest requiring protection; under ARC-AMPE, apply protection to all information at rest.

Implement cryptographic mechanisms enforcing both confidentiality and integrity for information at rest (ARC-AMPE requires both; NIST permits selection of one or more), and record the mechanism and scope in the Encryption-at-rest and in-transit configuration evidence.
Implement cryptographic mechanisms that prevent unauthorized disclosure and modification of the designated information at rest on the designated system components or media.

Use the latest published FIPS 140-compliant encryption standards for these mechanisms, covering — at minimum but not exclusively — Personally Identifiable Information (PII) and proprietary, financial, and legal information, in accordance with applicable federal laws, Executive Orders, directives, policies, regulations, and standards.
Verify the configuration of encryption on each in-scope component annually and refresh the Encryption-at-rest and in-transit configuration evidence with the verified settings.
Identify the organization-defined information designated for offline storage and the online storage locations where it currently resides.
Remove the designated information from online storage and transfer it to offline media; store the media in a secure physical location with access controlled and logged by Platform Security.
Record each offline transfer — data set, source system, media identifier, storage location, and operator — in the Key inventory and rotation log or the associated [Ticketing System] record.

Store all cryptographic keys in the [Key Management Service / Hardware Security Module] hardware-protected key store, or apply the organization-defined safeguards where a hardware store is not available.

Verify that no key material exists in plaintext outside the protected key store; where transient plaintext use is unavoidable (e.g., in-memory operations), confirm it is never written to disk or logs.
Include key store protection status in the annual key inventory reconciliation against the Key inventory and rotation log.

Implement technical security measures — encryption in transit using approved FIPS 140-compliant cryptography — guarding against unauthorized access to ePHI transmitted over electronic communications networks; record the in-transit settings in the Encryption-at-rest and in-transit configuration evidence.

Implement security measures that detect improper modification of ePHI in transit (e.g., authenticated encryption or integrity verification) so improperly modified ePHI is detected until disposal; document the integrity mechanism selected for each transmission path.
Verify annually that every transmission path carrying ePHI is covered by both the access-guarding and integrity measures, and refresh the in-transit configuration evidence.

Deploy a mechanism to encrypt and decrypt ePHI wherever Platform Security determines encryption is appropriate; document the determination for each ePHI system, including the decision rationale where encryption is applied and any addressable determination not to apply it.
Record the deployed encrypt/decrypt mechanism and its scope in the Encryption-at-rest and in-transit configuration evidence.

Implement technical policies and procedures on every electronic information system maintaining ePHI so that access is allowed only to persons or software programs granted access rights as specified in § 164.308(a)(4); enforce this through the [Identity Provider] and system-level access controls.
Assign a unique name and/or number for identifying and tracking user identity on each ePHI system; verify that no shared or anonymous accounts can access ePHI.
Coordinate with [Human Resources / Identity Management] to confirm access rights reflect current grants under § 164.308(a)(4), and review annually.

Establish, in coordination with the [Privacy Officer / HIPAA Compliance function], procedures for obtaining necessary ePHI during an emergency, specifying who may invoke emergency access, what ePHI may be obtained, and how access is logged and reviewed afterward.
Implement the emergency access capability (e.g., break-glass accounts with elevated logging) on each ePHI system and test it annually.
Record each emergency access invocation and its post-event review in the [Ticketing System].
Implement electronic procedures on each ePHI system that terminate an electronic session after a predetermined time of inactivity; set the timeout to the value agreed as [Session Inactivity Timeout].

Verify the session termination configuration on each ePHI system annually and record the verified settings with the Encryption-at-rest and in-transit configuration evidence or the associated system configuration records.

Platform Security is accountable for this procedure end to end, including key lifecycle management, encryption configuration verification, certificate and trust store governance, and evidence production.

[System Owners], the [Identity Provider] administrators, [Human Resources / Identity Management], and the [Privacy Officer / HIPAA Compliance function] participate in individual steps as participants; Platform Security reviews and approves any exception, and exceptions are recorded in the [Ticketing System].
