SRE makes the required equipment and supplies available at the site, or puts contracts in place supporting delivery to the site within the organization-defined time period for transfer and resumption [NIST CP-7 | FedRAMP CP-7 | ARC-AMPE CP-7 AE Mandatory].
[NIST CP-7 | FedRAMP CP-7 | ARC-AMPE CP-7 AE Mandatory]

SRE provides controls at the site — administrative, physical, and technical — equivalent to those at the primary site, and implements additional controls to protect PII in accordance with the privacy risks identified [NIST CP-7 | FedRAMP CP-7 | ARC-AMPE CP-7 AE Mandatory].
[NIST CP-7 | FedRAMP CP-7 | ARC-AMPE CP-7 AE Mandatory]

SRE prepares the site so it can serve as the operational site supporting essential mission and business functions, verifying configuration, connectivity, and access as part of the quarterly test cycle [NIST CP-7(4) High].

SRE plans and documents the course of action for circumstances that preclude returning to the primary processing site, including re-baselining operations at the alternate site, and records this plan in the ISCP [NIST CP-7(6)].

SRE develops primary and alternate telecommunications service agreements containing priority-of-service provisions in accordance with availability requirements, including RTOs, and requests Telecommunications Service Priority for all services used for national security emergency preparedness where the services are provided by a common carrier [NIST CP-8(1) Moderate/High | ARC-AMPE CP-8(1) AE Mandatory].
[NIST CP-8(1) Moderate/High | ARC-AMPE CP-8(1) AE Mandatory]

SRE obtains alternate services that reduce the likelihood of sharing a single point of failure with the primary telecommunications services [NIST CP-8(2) Moderate/High | ARC-AMPE CP-8(2) AE Mandatory].
[NIST CP-8(2) Moderate/High | ARC-AMPE CP-8(2) AE Mandatory]
SRE obtains alternate services from providers separated from the primary service providers to reduce susceptibility to the same threats [NIST CP-8(3) High].

SRE requires primary and alternate telecommunications providers to maintain contingency plans, reviews those plans to confirm they meet organizational contingency requirements, and obtains evidence of provider contingency testing and training at [Provider Evidence Frequency] [NIST CP-8(4) High].
SRE tests the alternate telecommunications services quarterly, recording call/failover test outcomes in the [Ticketing System] [NIST CP-8(5)].

SRE configures the [Backup Platform] to back up user-level information contained in the defined system components, system-level information, and system documentation (including security- and privacy-related documentation) at the documented frequencies [NIST CP-9 Low/Moderate/High].

SRE configures daily incremental backups and weekly full backups, maintaining three (3) generations of backups, at least one (1) of which is available online — a full backup plus all related incremental backups [ARC-AMPE CP-9 AE Mandatory].

SRE protects the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of backup information: restricting access to backup repositories, storing copies at the [Alternate Storage Site], and monitoring job health [NIST CP-9 | ARC-AMPE CP-9 AE Mandatory].

SRE tests backup information to verify media reliability and information integrity at least every six (6) months — quarterly under this procedure's cadence — by decrypting and transporting or transmitting a random sample of backup files from the alternate storage or backup site and comparing them to the same information at the primary processing site [NIST CP-9(1) Moderate/High | ARC-AMPE CP-9(1) AE Mandatory].
[NIST CP-9(1) Moderate/High | ARC-AMPE CP-9(1) AE Mandatory]

SRE uses a sample of backup information in the restoration of selected system functions as part of contingency plan testing, recording results in the Restore test results artifact [NIST CP-9(2) High].

SRE stores backup copies of critical system software and other security-related information in a separate facility — the [Alternate Storage Site] — or in a fire-rated container that is not collocated with the operational system [NIST CP-9(3) High].
SRE transfers system backup information to the alternate storage site within [Transfer Time Period] at [Transfer Rate], consistent with the RTO and RPO [NIST CP-9(5) High].

Where the redundant secondary system architecture is used, SRE maintains it on infrastructure not collocated with the primary system and verifies it can be activated without loss of information or disruption to operations [NIST CP-9(6)].

SRE enforces dual authorization in the [Backup Platform] for deletion or destruction of the defined backup information, requiring approval from two authorized SRE administrators before any destructive action [NIST CP-9(7)].

SRE implements cryptographic mechanisms to prevent unauthorized disclosure and modification of all backup files: encrypting PII in backups at the storage location using the methodology specified in SC-13, and applying digital signatures or cryptographic hashes to protect backup integrity, with keys managed in [Key Management Service] [NIST CP-9(8) Moderate/High | ARC-AMPE CP-9(8) AE Mandatory].
[NIST CP-9(8) Moderate/High | ARC-AMPE CP-9(8) AE Mandatory]

SRE follows the organization's policies and procedures governing receipt and removal of hardware and electronic media containing ePHI into and out of a facility, and movement of these items within the facility [HIPAA 164.310(d)(1)].

Before disposing of ePHI, or any hardware or electronic media on which it is stored, SRE executes the final disposition procedure — sanitization or destruction per the [Media Sanitization Procedure] — and records the disposition in the [Media Disposition Log] [HIPAA 164.310(d)(2)(i) Required].
Before media are made available for re-use, SRE removes all ePHI from the media using the approved sanitization method and records the sanitization event [HIPAA 164.310(d)(2)(ii) Required].
SRE records every movement of hardware and electronic media, and the person responsible for each movement, in the [Media Movement Log] [HIPAA 164.310(d)(2)(iii) Addressable].

Before moving any equipment, SRE confirms a current, retrievable, exact copy of the ePHI (and PII) on that equipment has been created and is available when needed, verifying backup job completion in the Backup job success report [HIPAA 164.310(d)(2)(iv) Addressable | ARC-AMPE CP-9 AE Mandatory].

SRE follows the organization's policies and procedures protecting ePHI from improper alteration or destruction, including the backup, integrity-checking, and dual-authorization controls defined in this procedure [HIPAA 164.312(c)(1)].

SRE enables electronic mechanisms — cryptographic hashes, digital signatures, and storage-layer integrity checks through [Key Management Service] and the [Backup Platform] — to corroborate that ePHI has not been altered or destroyed in an unauthorized manner [HIPAA 164.312(c)(2) Addressable].

Upon a disruption, compromise, or failure, SRE executes the recovery runbook to restore and reconstitute the system to a known state within the time period specified in the contingency plan or COOP, consistent with the RTO and RPO [NIST CP-10 | FedRAMP CP-10 | ARC-AMPE CP-10 AE Mandatory].
[NIST CP-10 | FedRAMP CP-10 | ARC-AMPE CP-10 AE Mandatory]

SRE performs the recovery in a trusted, secure, and verifiable manner: resetting all system parameters, reinstalling patches, reestablishing configuration settings, reinstalling application and system software, and fully testing the system before returning it to service [ARC-AMPE CP-10 AE Mandatory].

For transaction-based systems such as database management systems and transaction processing systems, SRE implements transaction recovery using transaction rollback and transaction journaling mechanisms configured in the [Database Platform] [NIST CP-10(2) Moderate/High | ARC-AMPE CP-10(2) AE Mandatory].
[NIST CP-10(2) Moderate/High | ARC-AMPE CP-10(2) AE Mandatory]

SRE restores system components within the restoration time periods defined in the service provider and organization Service Level Agreements, using configuration-controlled and integrity-protected information — versioned, checksummed images and configuration baselines — representing a known, operational state [NIST CP-10(4) High | FedRAMP CP-10(4)].

SRE protects the system components used for recovery and reconstitution — recovery images, baselines, restore tooling, and recovery environments — with access controls, integrity verification, and restricted administrative access [NIST CP-10(6)].

analyze: Executing this procedure establishes, maintains, and governs the agreements, assessments, and oversight needed to safely share information with business associates, vendors, and external service providers, and to manage the supply chain risks they introduce.

It ensures that no information exchange occurs without approved agreements, that third-party safeguards meet organizational and regulatory requirements, and that the resulting evidence is retained and reviewable.

This procedure is performed by the Third-Party Risk team on all external organizations — business associates, subcontractors, external system service providers, and supply chain partners — that create, receive, maintain, or transmit Example Org information, including electronic protected health information (ePHI) and Personally Identifiable Information (PII).
It covers the full vendor lifecycle: pre-engagement approval, agreement execution, ongoing monitoring, and termination or suspension of exchanges.
- Access to the [Contract Repository] where executed agreements and vendor records are stored
- Access to the [Vendor Management System] used to track vendor inventory, review status, and risk ratings
- Access to the [Ticketing System] for logging vendor onboarding, review, and remediation tasks
- A current inventory of all interconnections, business associates, subcontractors, and external service providers
- Designated Authorizing Official and senior cybersecurity and privacy officials empowered to approve or suspend interconnections
- Engagement of legal counsel, the senior privacy officer, and contracting officers for agreement review
- An approved supply chain risk management (SCRM) policy and SCRM plan, and a designated SCRM official
- A chartered SCRM team with the required role coverage

Before any information is shared with an external system or organization, the Third-Party Risk team identifies the appropriate agreement type for the exchange — interconnection security agreement, information exchange security agreement, memorandum of understanding or agreement, service level agreement, user agreement, non-disclosure agreement, or another organization-defined exchange agreement type.

The Third-Party Risk team drafts the agreement and documents, as part of it: the interface characteristics of each system, the security and privacy requirements and controls applicable to each system, the responsibilities of each party, and the impact level of the information communicated.

Where the exchange involves PII, the Third-Party Risk team ensures the agreement (memorandum of understanding, memorandum of agreement, letter of intent, computer matching agreement, information exchange agreement, or similar) specifically describes the PII covered and enumerates the purposes for which the PII may be used, for both internal and external parties.

The Third-Party Risk team routes the draft agreement to legal counsel, the senior privacy officer, and contracting officers for review, then obtains approval from the Authorizing Official or designated senior leadership.
The Third-Party Risk team stores the executed agreement in the [Contract Repository] and records its execution in the [Vendor Management System].
No information sharing proceeds until the applicable agreement is approved and in place.

When a proposed subsequent sharing of PII is not compatible with the purpose for which it was collected, the Third-Party Risk team blocks the sharing until additional notice is provided to the individual, their consent is obtained, and the relevant documents are updated or published.

On an annual cycle, the Third-Party Risk team reviews each information exchange agreement in the [Contract Repository] for continued validity, accuracy of interface characteristics, and continued adequacy of security and privacy requirements.

In addition to the annual review, the Third-Party Risk team triggers an out-of-cycle review whenever a significant change occurs to the system, to either organization, or to the nature of the electronic information sharing that could impact the agreement's validity or security posture.

The Third-Party Risk team updates each agreement as needed, re-obtains approvals, and records the review date and outcome in the [Vendor Management System] as part of the vendor security review records.

When an interconnection is judged to present an unacceptable level of risk, the Authorizing Official or other senior leadership — informed by senior cybersecurity or privacy officials — orders the immediate termination and/or suspension of that interconnection.

The Third-Party Risk team executes the ordered termination or suspension, notifies the connected party, documents the action and its rationale in the [Ticketing System], and updates the interconnection inventory.

Before accepting data transferred between interconnecting systems, the receiving system owner — coordinated by the Third-Party Risk team — verifies that the individuals or systems performing the transfer hold the requisite authorizations (write permissions or privileges) in the [Identity Provider] or applicable access control mechanism.
If the requisite authorizations cannot be verified, the receiving system owner rejects the transfer and escalates to the Third-Party Risk team, who records the event in the [Ticketing System].

The Third-Party Risk team identifies transitive (downstream) information exchanges by tracing, through the systems identified in the interconnection inventory, where each connected system forwards or re-shares Example Org information with other systems.
The Third-Party Risk team records each identified downstream exchange in the [Vendor Management System], including the downstream system, the data involved, and the responsible upstream party.
The Third-Party Risk team verifies or validates the controls on each identified downstream system.

Where controls cannot be verified or validated, the Third-Party Risk team takes measures to ensure the transitive exchange ceases — up to and including directing the upstream party to stop forwarding data — and documents the action in the [Ticketing System].

The Third-Party Risk team, with the security team, implements and maintains policies and procedures for authorizing access to ePHI consistent with the applicable requirements of subpart E of 45 CFR Parts 160–164.

If a health care clearinghouse is part of a larger organization, the Third-Party Risk team implements policies and procedures that protect the clearinghouse's ePHI from unauthorized access by the larger organization.

The Third-Party Risk team implements procedures for granting, establishing, documenting, reviewing, and modifying a user's right of access to ePHI — including access via a workstation, transaction, program, process, or other mechanism — based on the access authorization policies, and records access grants and reviews in the [Identity Provider] and [Vendor Management System].

Before permitting a business associate (or a business associate's subcontractor) to create, receive, maintain, or transmit ePHI on Example Org's behalf, the Third-Party Risk team obtains satisfactory assurances, in accordance with § 164.314(a), that the business associate will appropriately safeguard the information.

The Third-Party Risk team documents the satisfactory assurances through a written contract or other arrangement meeting the requirements of § 164.314(a); where an "other arrangement" is used, the Third-Party Risk team confirms it meets the requirements of § 164.504(e)(3).
The Third-Party Risk team stores the executed business associate agreement in the [Contract Repository] and logs it in the [Vendor Management System] as an executed business associate agreement.

The Third-Party Risk team, with legal counsel, ensures every business associate contract provides that the business associate will: comply with the applicable requirements of the Security Rule subpart; ensure that any subcontractors creating, receiving, maintaining, or transmitting ePHI on its behalf agree to comply by entering into a compliant contract or other arrangement; and report to Example Org any security incident of which it becomes aware, including breaches of unsecured protected health information as required by § 164.410.

The Third-Party Risk team applies the same business associate contract requirements to contracts or other arrangements between a business associate and its subcontractors as apply between Example Org and its business associates, and verifies flow-down during vendor security reviews.

Except where limited disclosures apply under § 164.504(f)(1)(ii)/(iii) or § 164.508, the Third-Party Risk team ensures a group health plan's plan documents are amended to require the plan sponsor to: implement administrative, physical, and technical safeguards reasonably and appropriately protecting the ePHI it handles on the plan's behalf; support the adequate separation required by § 164.504(f)(2)(iii) with reasonable and appropriate security measures; ensure any agent to whom it provides this information agrees to implement reasonable and appropriate security measures; and report any security incident of which it becomes aware to the group health plan.

The Third-Party Risk team requires providers of external system services to comply with organizational security and privacy requirements and to employ the [Assignment: organization-defined controls], and records this in the service contract or agreement.

The Third-Party Risk team defines and documents organizational oversight and user roles and responsibilities with regard to external system services, and includes security and privacy roles and responsibilities in the service contract or agreement.

The Third-Party Risk team employs [Assignment: organization-defined] processes, methods, and techniques to monitor control compliance by external service providers on an ongoing basis, and retains the results as vendor security review records.

The Third-Party Risk team includes language in service contracts or agreements requiring the provider to be subject to U.S. Federal laws and regulations protecting PII and to adhere to Example Org's security and privacy policies and standards consistent with 45 CFR § 155.260(b), and consults legal counsel, the senior privacy officer, and contracting officers about applicable laws, directives, policies, or regulations that may impact implementation.

Before any acquisition or outsourcing of information security services, the Third-Party Risk team conducts an organizational assessment of risk and records the assessment outcome in the [Ticketing System].

The Third-Party Risk team verifies that the acquisition or outsourcing of dedicated information security services is approved by [Assignment: organization-defined personnel or roles] before the engagement proceeds, and retains the approval with the vendor security review records.

The Third-Party Risk team requires providers of [Assignment: organization-defined external system services] to identify the functions, ports, protocols, and other services required for the use of those services, and records the provider's response in the vendor security review records.
For FedRAMP-scope engagements, the Third-Party Risk team applies this requirement to all external systems where federal customer data is processed or stored.

The Third-Party Risk team establishes, documents, and maintains trust relationships with external service providers based on [Assignment: organization-defined security and privacy requirements, properties, factors, or conditions defining acceptable trust relationships], recorded in the [Vendor Management System].

The Third-Party Risk team takes [Assignment: organization-defined actions] to verify that the interests of [Assignment: organization-defined external service providers] are consistent with and reflect organizational interests, and documents the verification results.

The Third-Party Risk team restricts the location of [Selection (one or more): information processing; information or data; system services] to [Assignment: organization-defined locations] based on [Assignment: organization-defined requirements], and records the restriction in each service contract or agreement.

For FedRAMP Certification Classes C and D, the Third-Party Risk team restricts the location of information processing, information or data, and system services as defined; for Certification Class D, the team restricts all federal customer data to the U.S., U.S. Territories, or geographic locations where there is U.S. jurisdiction.

The Third-Party Risk team verifies in no case are the safeguards afforded to sensitive information less than those mandated by state regulation, federal law, Executive Order, or other authoritative direction.
The Third-Party Risk team ensures the system's PII is processed and stored within the continental U.S., Hawaii, or U.S. Territories.

Where support, development, or IT services are to be off-shored, the Third-Party Risk team weighs that risk, documents the risk decision, and notifies CMS at least sixty (60) days prior to committing to outsourcing information system services outside the U.S.
(e.g., by contract award or services purchase).
The Third-Party Risk team restricts the geographic location of information processing and data storage to facilities located within the legal jurisdictional boundary of the United States.

For organizations processing Federal Tax Information (FTI), the Third-Party Risk team adheres to IRS Publication 1075 and notifies CMS at least sixty (60) days prior to transmitting data into an external information service environment, per the Change Notification guidance.

The Third-Party Risk team, with the security team, maintains exclusive control of cryptographic keys for encrypted material stored or transmitted through an external system, and verifies the key management arrangement is reflected in the service agreement.

The Third-Party Risk team provides for, and periodically exercises, the capability to check the integrity of information while it resides in the external system, and records the results in the vendor security review records.

The designated SCRM official develops, documents, and disseminates to [Assignment: organization-defined personnel or roles] a supply chain risk management policy — at the [Selection (one or more): organization-level; mission/business process-level; system-level] — addressing purpose, scope, roles, responsibilities, management commitment, coordination among organizational entities, and compliance, consistent with applicable laws, executive orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, and guidelines, along with procedures to facilitate implementation of the policy and associated SCRM controls.
The designated SCRM official manages the development, documentation, and dissemination of the SCRM policy and procedures, and is named in the appropriate security and privacy documents.

The SCRM official reviews and updates the SCRM policy and procedures at least every one (1) year, and following organization-defined events (e.g., assessment or audit findings; security or privacy incidents; changes to applicable laws, Executive Orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, and guidelines), and records each review in the [Document Repository].

The Third-Party Risk team maintains, in written (which may be electronic) form in the [Document Repository], the policies and procedures implemented to comply with the HIPAA Security Rule and any documented action, activity, or assessment.
The Third-Party Risk team retains these records for 6 years from the date of creation or the date when last in effect, whichever is later.

The Third-Party Risk team makes the records available to the persons responsible for implementing the procedures, and reviews them periodically and updates them as needed in response to environmental or operational changes affecting the security of ePHI.

The SCRM official develops and documents a plan for managing supply chain risks associated with the research and development, design, manufacturing, acquisition, delivery, integration, operations and maintenance, and disposal of [Assignment: organization-defined systems, system components, or system services], addressing: management, implementation, and monitoring of SCRM controls; supply chain risk tolerance; acceptable risk mitigation strategies or controls; a process for consistently evaluating and monitoring supply chain risk; approaches for implementing and communicating the plan; description and justification of mitigation measures; and associated roles and responsibilities.

The SCRM official reviews and updates the SCRM plan at least every one (1) year, or as required, to address threat, organizational, or environmental changes, and records each review in the [Document Repository].
The SCRM official protects the SCRM plan from unauthorized disclosure and modification by storing it with access controls in the [Document Repository] and restricting edit rights to the SCRM team.

The SCRM official establishes a supply chain risk management team consisting of [Assignment: organization-defined personnel, roles and responsibilities] to lead and support [Assignment: organization-defined] SCRM activities.

The SCRM official ensures the team includes personnel with diverse roles — risk executive, information technology, contracting, information security, privacy, mission or business, legal, supply chain and logistics, acquisition, business continuity, and other relevant functions — collectively knowledgeable in acquisition processes, legal practices, vulnerabilities, threats, attack vectors, and system technical aspects and dependencies.
The SCRM team refers to current NIST SCRM publications (e.g., NIST SP 800-161, NISTIR 8276) when carrying out its activities, and the charter is recorded in the [Document Repository].

Annually, the Third-Party Risk team assesses and reviews the supply chain-related risks associated with suppliers or contractors and the system, system component, or system service they provide, considering: the supplier's security and SCRM processes; foreign ownership, control or influence (FOCI); and the supplier's ability to assess subordinate second-tier and third-tier suppliers and contractors.
The Third-Party Risk team conducts these reviews itself or engages an independent third party, and retains the results as vendor security review records in the [Vendor Management System].

The Third-Party Risk team employs [Selection (one or more): organizational analysis; independent third-party analysis; organizational testing; independent third-party testing] of [Assignment: organization-defined] supply chain elements, processes, and actors associated with the system, system component, or system service, and records the method and findings.

The Third-Party Risk team establishes agreements and procedures with entities involved in the supply chain for the system, system component, or system service covering \[Selection (one or more): notification of supply chain compromises; [Assignment: organization-defined results of assessments or audits]\].
For FedRAMP-scope engagements, the Third-Party Risk team ensures the supply chain notification agreements and procedures follow the FedRAMP Incident Evaluation and Communication rules.
The Third-Party Risk team stores the executed notification agreements in the [Contract Repository] and exercises the notification procedures as part of the annual vendor security review.

The Third-Party Risk team is accountable for this process end to end: it initiates agreements, conducts vendor security reviews, maintains the vendor inventory and evidence, and coordinates all handoffs with legal counsel, contracting officers, the senior privacy officer, system owners, and the SCRM team.

The Authorizing Official or other senior leadership — informed by senior cybersecurity or privacy officials — approves agreements and interconnections and is the only authority who may order immediate termination or suspension of an interconnection; exceptions to any step of this procedure require that same official's documented approval.
This procedure operationalizes the **Business Associate & Vendor Risk Standard**, which contains the full requirement text, control mappings, and the rationale behind each step above.

analyze: This procedure defines the step-by-step actions for developing, approving, disseminating, reviewing, and protecting Example Org's information security program plan, planning policies, risk management strategy, system security and privacy plans, and HIPAA Security Rule documentation.
Executing it keeps the security program's governing documents current, approved, traceable to their framework requirements, and available to the personnel who must implement them.

This procedure is performed by the Security Program / GRC team for all organization-wide security program governance documents, system-level security and privacy plans, and HIPAA Security Rule documentation covering Example Org systems and electronic protected health information.
Other teams participate as reviewers, contributors, or approvers at the steps noted below.
- Access to the organization's [Document Repository] for storing and controlling governance documentation
- Access to the organization's [Ticketing System] for tracking reviews, approvals, and event-driven updates
- Identification of the senior official accountable for organizational risk (see Procedure Step 8)
- The current organization chart and list of organizational entities responsible for information security
- The [GRC Platform] for tracking review dates and evidence artifacts

The Security Program / GRC team drafts the organization-wide information security program plan containing an overview of security program requirements and a description of the program management controls and common controls in place or planned to meet them.
In the plan, identify and assign security roles and responsibilities, document management commitment, describe coordination among organizational entities, and state compliance obligations.
Circulate the draft plan to each organizational entity responsible for information security and incorporate their coordination feedback before finalization.

Submit the plan to the senior official accountable for the risk being incurred to organizational operations (including mission, functions, image, and reputation), organizational assets, individuals, other organizations, and the Nation, and obtain that official's documented approval.
Record the approval date and the next scheduled review date in the approved policy set with review dates retained as evidence in the [GRC Platform].
Disseminate the approved plan to organization-defined personnel and roles via the [Document Repository], and store the current version as the program plan artifact retained as evidence.
The Security Program / GRC team opens a review task in the [Ticketing System] on the annual review date recorded in the [GRC Platform].
Review the program plan against current organizational structure, controls, and requirements, and update it as needed.

In addition to the annual review, trigger an out-of-cycle review following any of these organization-defined events: system architectural or design changes, organization-wide assessment or audit findings, security or privacy incidents or breaches, and changes to applicable laws (including privacy laws), executive orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, and guidelines.
Submit each updated plan for senior official approval using the same approval path as the initial plan, and update the review date in the approved policy set with review dates.

Store the program plan in the [Document Repository] with access controls limiting read access to organization-defined personnel and roles, and write/administer access to the Security Program / GRC team.
Enable version history in the [Document Repository] so any modification is attributable to an identified user.
Review repository permissions on the plan as part of the annual plan review and remove access for personnel whose roles no longer require it.
The Security Program / GRC team maintains an appendix to the organization-wide program plan documenting each common control available for inheritance by organizational systems.
For any common control described in a separate system security plan instead of the appendix, record in the plan which separate security plan contains that control's description.
Verify the appendix and cross-references during each annual program plan review.
The Security Program / GRC team designates, by name and role, the officials responsible for the development of system information security program plans.
Record these designations in the appropriate security and privacy documents, including the program plan and the relevant system security and privacy plans.
Update the designations during the annual review or whenever a designated official's role changes.

The Security Program / GRC team actively monitors for changes to applicable privacy laws, regulations, and overarching policy that affect information security program plans, using [Legal/Regulatory Monitoring Sources] and input from [Legal/Compliance Function].
Log each identified change in the [Ticketing System] and assess whether it requires a program plan update.

During the annual review, confirm the plan remains effective and that it supports cybersecurity and privacy safeguards to the greatest extent feasible throughout each system's life cycle and for the information on that system.
The Security Program / GRC team maintains all policies and procedures implemented to comply with the HIPAA Security Rule in written (electronic permitted) form in the [Document Repository].
Maintain a written (electronic permitted) record of every action, activity, or assessment the Rule requires to be documented, stored alongside the related policy or procedure.

Retain all HIPAA Security Rule documentation for 6 years from the date of its creation or the date when it last was in effect, whichever is later; configure [Document Repository] retention rules to enforce this and verify retention settings during annual review.
Configure [Document Repository] access so HIPAA Security Rule documentation is available to those persons responsible for implementing the procedures to which the documentation pertains.

The Security Program / GRC team reviews HIPAA Security Rule documentation periodically on the cadence recorded in the [GRC Platform] and updates it as needed in response to environmental or operational changes affecting the security of electronic protected health information.

Example Org leadership appoints a senior information security officer with the mission and resources to coordinate, develop, implement, and maintain the organization-wide information security program.

Leadership identifies the security official responsible for the development and implementation of the policies and procedures required by the HIPAA Security Rule for the covered entity or business associate.
The Security Program / GRC team records both appointments in the program plan and reflects them in the org chart artifact retained as evidence; update the org chart when appointments change.

The Security Program / GRC team develops a comprehensive strategy to manage security risk to organizational operations and assets, individuals, other organizations, and the Nation associated with the operation and use of organizational systems, and privacy risk to individuals resulting from the authorized processing of personally identifiable information.
Document the strategy, obtain senior official approval, and disseminate it to organization-defined personnel via the [Document Repository].

Implement the strategy consistently across the organization by applying it as the basis for risk decisions in system planning, assessments, and authorizations, with the Security Program / GRC team accountable for consistent application.
Review and update the strategy at least every one (1) year, or as required, to address organizational changes; record each review and its outcome in the approved policy set with review dates.

The Security Program / GRC team develops an organization-level planning policy addressing purpose, scope, roles, responsibilities, management commitment, coordination among organizational entities, and compliance, and confirms it is consistent with applicable laws, executive orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, and guidelines.
Develop procedures to facilitate implementation of the planning policy and associated planning controls.
Disseminate the policy and procedures to organization-defined personnel or roles via the [Document Repository].
Record the official designated to manage the development, documentation, and dissemination of the planning policy and procedures in the appropriate security and privacy documents.

Designate officials responsible for the management of planning controls for systems, name them in the appropriate security and privacy documents, and ensure the planning policies and procedures support cybersecurity and privacy safeguards to the greatest extent feasible throughout the system's life cycle and the information on that system.

Review and update the planning policy and planning procedures at least every one (1) year and following organization-defined events: assessment or audit findings, security or privacy incidents, and changes to applicable laws (including privacy laws), executive orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, and guidelines.
Update review dates in the approved policy set with review dates.
The Security Program / GRC team implements reasonable and appropriate policies and procedures to comply with the HIPAA Security Rule standards, implementation specifications, and other requirements.
Document any changes to these policies and procedures and implement each change in accordance with the Rule, recording the change record in the [Document Repository].
Maintain policies and procedures to prevent, detect, contain, and correct security violations, coordinated with [Security Operations Function] for detection and containment activities.

Conduct an accurate and thorough assessment of the potential risks and vulnerabilities to the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of electronic protected health information held by the covered entity or business associate, and record the assessment results in the [GRC Platform].

Implement security measures sufficient to reduce identified risks and vulnerabilities to a reasonable and appropriate level, and track each risk reduction measure to closure in the [Ticketing System].

For each organizational system, the Security Program / GRC team develops a security and privacy plan using the [ARC-AMPE SSPP template], ensuring the plan is consistent with the organization's enterprise architecture.

Complete the plan so that it explicitly defines the constituent system components; describes the operational context in terms of mission and business processes; identifies the individuals that fulfill system roles and responsibilities; identifies the information types processed, stored, and transmitted; provides the security categorization with supporting rationale; describes specific threats of concern; provides the results of a privacy risk assessment for systems processing PII; describes the operational environment and any dependencies on or connections to other systems or components; provides an overview of the security and privacy requirements; identifies any relevant control baselines or overlays; describes the controls in place or planned, including rationale for tailoring decisions; includes risk determinations for security and privacy architecture and design decisions; and includes security- and privacy-related activities requiring planning and coordination with organization-defined individuals or groups.
Submit the completed plan to the authorizing official or designated representative for review and approval prior to plan implementation; record the approval in the [GRC Platform].

Distribute copies of the approved plan to organization-defined personnel, roles, or stakeholders via the [Document Repository], and communicate all subsequent plan changes to the same distribution list.

Review the plan at least every one (1) year or following significant changes, and update it to address changes to the system and its environment of operation or problems identified during plan implementation or control assessments.

Store the plan in the [Document Repository] with access controls that protect it from unauthorized disclosure and modification, and complete the review dates section of the approved policy set with review dates.

The Security Program / GRC team owns this procedure end to end: it drafts and maintains all governance documents, coordinates reviews, tracks approval dates, and answers for the completeness and currency of the approved policy set with review dates, the program plan, and the org chart.

Senior leadership (including the senior information security officer and the authorizing official) provides required approvals, and any exception to this procedure must be approved by the senior official accountable for organizational risk with the concurrence of the Security Program / GRC team.

This procedure operationalizes the 'Information Security Program Governance Standard', which contains the full requirement text, the framework mappings, and the rationale for each control described above.

analyze: This procedure provides the step-by-step operational instructions Endpoint Engineering follows to deploy, configure, and continuously verify malicious code protection, spam protection, memory protection, media restrictions, and mobile code controls across Example Org systems.
Executing this procedure satisfies the requirements of the Endpoint Protection & Device Controls Standard and produces the required evidence artifacts.

This procedure is performed by Endpoint Engineering on all Example Org system entry and exit points — including firewalls, remote access servers, workstations, email servers, web servers, proxy servers, notebook computers, and mobile devices — and on all organizational systems and networks subject to the Standard.
It runs continuously as part of ongoing endpoint operations.
- Administrative access to the [EDR Platform] management console.
- Administrative access to the [Email Security Gateway].
- Administrative access to the [Endpoint Configuration Management System] for policy push and enforcement.
- Administrative access to the [Mobile Device Management (MDM) System] for mobile device and removable media policy enforcement.
- Access to the [Ticketing System] for alert routing, exception tracking, and remediation records.
- Privileged user authorization per [Access Request System] for any manual update actions.
- Access to the applicable System Security and Privacy Plan (SSPP) repository for documentation updates.
- A current inventory of system entry and exit points maintained by Endpoint Engineering.

Endpoint Engineering maintains an inventory of all system entry and exit points, including firewalls, remote access servers, workstations, email servers, web servers, proxy servers, notebook computers, and mobile devices.
Deploy the [EDR Platform] agent to every inventoried endpoint, and deploy malicious code protection at each network entry and exit point via the [Endpoint Configuration Management System].
Enable **both** signature-based and non-signature-based (behavioral/heuristic) detection mechanisms on every deployed agent and gateway — signature-only deployment does not satisfy this requirement.
Verify agent deployment coverage against the inventory and generate the **EDR deployment coverage report**; retain this report as evidence of coverage.
Review the coverage report on a continuous basis and remediate any unprotected endpoint identified.
In the [EDR Platform] console, enable automatic signature and engine updates so that new releases are applied as they become available.

Align the update configuration with Example Org's configuration management policies and procedures; where the configuration management process defines an update window or approval gate, configure the [EDR Platform] to comply with it.
Verify on a continuous basis that endpoints are receiving updates (check last-update timestamps in the [EDR Platform] console) and escalate stale endpoints through the [Ticketing System].
In the [EDR Platform] console, configure a scheduled scan policy for all managed endpoints.
Set the scan frequency to **at least every week**; if Example Org's configuration management policy defines a more frequent [Scan Frequency], set that value instead.
Push the scan policy to all endpoints via the [Endpoint Configuration Management System] and confirm policy application status in the console.
Enable real-time protection in the [EDR Platform] policy so that files downloaded, opened, or executed from external sources are scanned as those actions occur.
Enable equivalent real-time scanning at network entry and exit points (email, web, and proxy gateways) in the [Email Security Gateway] and [Web Proxy/Gateway].
Confirm in accordance with organizational policy that no external-source file path bypasses real-time scanning, and document any approved exclusions in the [Ticketing System].
In the [EDR Platform] policy, set the on-detection action to **block** malicious code.
Configure quarantine as the companion action so detected malicious code is both blocked and quarantined, as required.
If an organization-defined alternative action is approved for a specific system, document that action and its approval in the [Ticketing System] before configuring it.
In the [EDR Platform] console, configure detection notifications to the organization-defined personnel or roles: `[Alert Recipients]`.
Configure alert delivery so that the administrator or designated security personnel receive alerts in **near real time** upon detection.
Route alerts into the [Ticketing System] so each detection generates a trackable record assigned to Endpoint Engineering.
When a suspected false positive is reported or observed, Endpoint Engineering validates the detection against the [EDR Platform] telemetry and vendor intelligence.

If confirmed as a false positive, submit an exclusion request through the [Ticketing System]; Endpoint Engineering reviews and approves or denies the exclusion, assessing the potential impact on system availability before approval.
Apply the approved exclusion via the [EDR Platform] policy, record the rationale and availability assessment in the ticket, and report the false positive to the security vendor.
Monitor quarantined or blocked legitimate files for availability impact and restore affected functionality per the approved exclusion.
In the [EDR Platform] console, configure role-based access so that update actions (engine, signature, or agent changes) can only be initiated by a privileged user.
Verify that standard users and non-privileged service accounts cannot modify or disable update settings.
Log and review privileged update actions in the [Ticketing System] or [Audit Log System].
At the organization-defined `[Testing Frequency]`, Endpoint Engineering introduces a known benign test file (e.g., an industry-standard test signature) into a managed system.

Verify that the [EDR Platform] detects the benign code and that the associated incident reporting fires — confirm the alert arrives via the configured near-real-time alert path and generates a [Ticketing System] record.
Record the test result, including detection and reporting confirmation, and retain it alongside the EDR deployment coverage report as evidence.

On the organization-defined system hardware components `[Defined System Components]`, enable kernel-level monitoring of operating system commands via the [EDR Platform] or [Host-Based Monitoring Tool].
Configure the organization-defined set of unauthorized operating system commands `[Unauthorized Command List]` for detection.
Upon detection, configure the mechanism to issue a warning, audit the command execution, and/or prevent execution of the command, per the organization-defined response `[Defined Response Action]`.
Confirm that audited command executions are written to the [Audit Log System] and reviewed by Endpoint Engineering.

When malicious code is detected and quarantined, Endpoint Engineering analyzes its characteristics and behavior using the organization-defined tools and techniques `[Malware Analysis Tools]` (e.g., sandbox detonation, behavioral analysis).
Incorporate the analysis results into the organizational incident response process by attaching findings to the incident record in the [Ticketing System].
Incorporate the results into the flaw remediation process by creating or updating remediation items (e.g., detection signatures, blocking rules, patching actions) and tracking them to closure.

Configure the [EDR Platform] and [Endpoint Configuration Management System] to run security and privacy function verification (e.g., self-tests, integrity checks, policy compliance validation) upon system startup and/or restart.
Configure verification to also run at least **monthly**, or upon command by a user with appropriate privileges; if Example Org defines a different `[Verification Frequency]`, set that value.
Verify that the correct operation of the organization-defined security and privacy functions is confirmed by each verification run, and retain verification results as evidence.
Configure the verification mechanism to alert the organization-defined personnel or roles `[Verification Alert Recipients]` when a verification test fails.
Ensure alerts are delivered at minimum to the system/security administrator, in near real time where the platform supports it.
Route failure alerts into the [Ticketing System] for assignment to Endpoint Engineering.

When anomalies are discovered during verification, Endpoint Engineering executes one of the following organization-defined actions: shut the system down, restart the system, or perform an alternative action `[Defined Alternative Action]`.
For any alternative action taken in place of shutdown or restart, document the action in the applicable System Security and Privacy Plan (SSPP) before relying on it.
Record the anomaly, the action taken, and the outcome in the [Ticketing System].

Implement automated mechanisms (e.g., the [Endpoint Configuration Management System] compliance engine) to schedule, distribute, and collect security and privacy function verification results across the distributed endpoint fleet.
Confirm that verification can be triggered and reported centrally without manual per-endpoint action.
Configure the automated verification mechanism to report results to the organization-defined personnel or roles `[Verification Results Recipients]`.
Endpoint Engineering reviews reported results on a continuous basis and escalates failures per the anomaly response steps above.
In the [Email Security Gateway], enable spam protection at the email system entry and exit points to detect unsolicited messages.
Configure the detection action (block, quarantine, tag, or the organization-defined action `[Spam Action]`) to act on detected unsolicited messages in accordance with organizational policy.
In the [Email Security Gateway], enable automatic updates of spam protection rules, filters, and reputation feeds when new releases are available.
Set the automatic update frequency to **at least every week**, or to the organization-defined `[Spam Update Frequency]` if more frequent.
Align the update configuration with Example Org's configuration management policies and procedures, and verify update currency in the gateway console on a continuous basis.
Enable the learning/training capability of the [Email Security Gateway] so the mechanism adapts to legitimate communications traffic patterns.
Periodically review false positive and false negative classifications with Endpoint Engineering and feed corrections back into the learning mechanism.

When email is sent on behalf of the government as part of the business offering, implement Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting & Conformance (DMARC) on the sending domain as described in DHS Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 18-01.
Confirm the DMARC policy is set to `p=reject`.
Document DMARC compliance in the SI-08 control implementation solution description.
List the FROM: domain(s) used when sending email on behalf of the government in that same documentation, and keep the list current as sending domains change.
Via the [Endpoint Configuration Management System], enable Data Execution Prevention (DEP) on all managed systems.
Enable Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR) on all managed systems.
Enable any additional memory-protection safeguards required by the related controls within the control set, at minimum those specified in the control set `[Related Control Set Safeguards]`.
Verify enforcement status across the fleet and record the configuration as part of the endpoint baseline.
Define the organization-defined types of system media to restrict or prohibit `[Restricted Media Types]` and the systems or system components to which the restriction applies.
Via the [MDM System] and [Endpoint Configuration Management System], implement controls that restrict or prohibit those media types on the defined systems.

Configure safeguards that prohibit the use of personally owned media — flash drives, external hard disk drives, and other portable storage and media devices — on organization-defined systems and networks.
Configure controls to prohibit the use of portable storage devices in organizational systems when such devices have no identifiable owner.
Prohibit the use of sanitization-resistant media in organizational systems.
Record the resulting removable media policy settings and export the **Removable media policy configuration** as evidence; retain it alongside the EDR deployment coverage report.
Endpoint Engineering defines the acceptable and unacceptable mobile code and mobile code technologies for Example Org systems `[Mobile Code Definitions]`.
Document the defined acceptable and unacceptable mobile code and technologies in the applicable System Security and Privacy Plan (SSPP).
Review and update the definitions whenever a new mobile code technology is proposed for use.
Establish an authorization path through the \[Ticketing System\]: any use of mobile code within a system requires Endpoint Engineering review and approval before deployment.
Monitor authorized mobile code use via the [EDR Platform] and [Web Proxy/Gateway] telemetry.
Control use by enforcing the definitions from the previous subsection in gateway and endpoint policy.
Configure the [EDR Platform] and [Web Proxy/Gateway] to detect the organization-defined unacceptable mobile code `[Unacceptable Mobile Code List]`.
Upon detection, execute the organization-defined corrective action `[Corrective Action]` (e.g., block, quarantine, alert) and record the event in the [Ticketing System].

Before mobile code is deployed in a system, Endpoint Engineering verifies that its acquisition, development, and use meet the organization-defined mobile code requirements `[Mobile Code Requirements]`.
Record the verification outcome in the authorization ticket; deployment without a recorded verification is prohibited.
In the [Web Proxy/Gateway], configure blocking rules that prevent the download of the organization-defined unacceptable mobile code.
In the [EDR Platform] policy, configure execution prevention for the same code types at the endpoint.
Verify enforcement by attempting retrieval of a known-blocked sample and confirming the block.

In the organization-defined software applications `[Defined Applications]` (e.g., browsers, office suites), disable automatic execution of mobile code via the [Endpoint Configuration Management System] baseline.
Enforce the organization-defined action prior to executing any mobile code `[Pre-Execution Action]` (e.g., user prompt, administrator approval).
Verify the configuration across the managed fleet and record it in the endpoint baseline.
For mobile code that is permitted, configure execution so it runs only within confined virtual machine (or equivalent sandbox) environments.
Verify via the [EDR Platform] that permitted mobile code is not executing outside the confined environment, and alert on any violation through the standard detection alerting path.

Endpoint Engineering is authorized to perform all steps in this procedure and is accountable for the process end to end, including configuration, verification, evidence production, and handoffs to other participating teams (e.g., [Email Security Gateway] administrators, [Ticketing System] responders).

Exceptions and alternative actions — including any SI-6 alternative action and any approved false-positive exclusion — require Endpoint Engineering review and approval, with documentation recorded in the [Ticketing System] and, where required, the applicable SSPP.

analyze: **Standard ID:** [Standard ID] **Owner:** AI Risk / Product **Applies to:** All personnel who develop, procure, integrate, deploy, operate, or decommission AI systems at Acme Health

This standard defines Acme Health's mandatory requirements for establishing and maintaining an inventory of AI systems and for conducting context, impact, and risk-mapping activities for each system across the AI lifecycle.
It applies to every AI system developed, procured, or deployed by Acme Health, in any stage from design through decommissioning.
AI Risk / Product is accountable for this process end to end.

AI Risk / Product shall maintain the AI system inventory, shall perform or coordinate every assessment step defined in this standard, shall review the outputs of those steps, and shall answer for the outcome of each.

Other teams — including Legal, Procurement, Security, and the teams that develop or deploy individual AI systems — participate in individual steps as participants named in this document, but ownership of the process and its handoffs rests with AI Risk / Product.

- **CTX-01:** AI Risk / Product shall ensure that, for each AI system in the inventory, the intended purposes, potentially beneficial uses, context-specific laws, norms and expectations, and prospective deployment settings are understood and documented, including the specific set or types of users and their expectations, and assumptions and related limitations about AI system purposes, uses, and risks across the development or product AI lifecycle.
[NIST AI RMF Map 1 | NIST AI RMF Map 1.1]

- **CTX-02:** AI Risk / Product shall ensure that potential positive and negative impacts of the AI system's uses on individuals, communities, organizations, society, and the planet are identified and documented, including the likelihood and magnitude of each identified impact (both potentially beneficial and harmful) based on expected use, past uses of AI systems in similar contexts, public incident reports, feedback from those external to the team that developed or deployed the AI system, or other data.
[NIST AI RMF Map 1.1 | NIST AI RMF Map 5 | NIST AI RMF Map 5.1]
- **CTX-03:** AI Risk / Product shall ensure that related TEVV (test, evaluation, verification, and validation) and system metrics are documented as part of establishing the system's context.

- **CTX-04:** AI Risk / Product shall ensure that interdisciplinary AI actors, competencies, skills, and capacities for establishing context reflect demographic diversity and broad domain and user experience expertise, that their participation is documented, and that opportunities for interdisciplinary collaboration are prioritized.
- **CTX-05:** AI Risk / Product shall ensure that Acme Health's mission and relevant goals for AI technology are understood and documented.
- **CTX-06:** AI Risk / Product shall ensure that the business value or context of business use is clearly defined or — in the case of assessing existing AI systems — re-evaluated.
- **CTX-07:** AI Risk / Product shall ensure that organizational risk tolerances are determined and documented.

- **CTX-08:** AI Risk / Product shall ensure that system requirements (e.g., "the system shall respect the privacy of its users") are elicited from and understood by relevant AI actors, and that design decisions take socio-technical implications into account to address AI risks.

NIST suggests, among its 13 actions for Map 1.1, maintaining awareness of industry, technical, and applicable legal standards [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 1.1 Action 1]; defining and documenting the task, purpose, minimum functionality, and benefits of the AI system [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 1.1 Action 4]; identifying whether there are non-AI or non-technology alternatives that will lead to more trustworthy outcomes [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 1.1 Action 5]; delineating the expected and acceptable AI system context of use, including social norms, impacted individuals, groups, and communities, potential positive and negative impacts, and the operational environment [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 1.1 Action 9]; and planning for risks related to human-AI configurations by documenting requirements, roles, and responsibilities for human oversight of deployed systems [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 1.1 Action 13].

NIST suggests, among its 2 actions for Map 1.2, establishing interdisciplinary teams that reflect a wide range of skills, competencies, and capabilities, verifying that team membership includes demographic diversity, broad domain expertise, and lived experiences, and documenting team composition [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 1.2 Action 1], and creating and empowering interdisciplinary expert teams to capture and engage the interdependencies of deployed AI systems and related concepts from disciplines outside of AI practice such as law, sociology, psychology, anthropology, public policy, systems design, and engineering [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 1.2 Action 2].

NIST suggests, among its 5 actions for Map 1.3, reviewing the documented system purpose from a socio-technical perspective and in consideration of societal values [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 1.3 Action 2], determining possible misalignment between societal values and stated organizational principles and code of ethics [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 1.3 Action 3], flagging latent incentives that may contribute to negative impacts [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 1.3 Action 4], and evaluating AI system purpose in consideration of potential risks, societal values, and stated organizational principles [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 1.3 Action 5].

NIST suggests, among its 3 actions for Map 1.4, documenting business value or context of business use [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 1.4 Action 1], reconciling documented concerns about the system's purpose within the business context of use against the organization's stated values, mission statements, social responsibility commitments, and AI principles [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 1.4 Action 2], and reconsidering the design, implementation strategy, or deployment of AI systems with potential impacts that do not reflect institutional values [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 1.4 Action 3].

NIST suggests, among its 6 actions for Map 1.5, utilizing existing regulations and guidelines for risk criteria, tolerance, and response established by organizational, domain, discipline, sector, or professional requirements [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 1.5 Action 1]; establishing risk tolerance levels for AI systems and allocating appropriate oversight resources to each level [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 1.5 Action 2]; establishing risk criteria in consideration of different sources of risk (e.g., financial, operational, safety and wellbeing, business, reputational, and model risks) and different levels of risk from negligible to critical [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 1.5 Action 3]; identifying the maximum allowable risk tolerance above which the system will not be deployed or will need to be prematurely decommissioned within the contextual or application setting [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 1.5 Action 4]; articulating and analyzing tradeoffs across trustworthiness characteristics and documenting them with traceable actions to inform management decisions [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 1.5 Action 5]; and reviewing uses of AI systems for "off-label" purposes, especially in settings deemed high-risk, documenting decisions, risk-related trade-offs, and system limitations [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 1.5 Action 6].

NIST suggests, among its 8 actions for Map 1.6, proactively incorporating trustworthy characteristics into system requirements [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 1.6 Action 1]; developing and standardizing practices to assess potential impacts at all stages of the AI lifecycle in collaboration with interdisciplinary experts, actors external to the team that developed or deployed the AI system, and potentially impacted communities [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 1.6 Action 3]; including potentially impacted groups, communities, and external entities (e.g., civil society organizations, research institutes, local community groups, and trade associations) in the formulation of priorities, definitions, and outcomes during impact assessment activities [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 1.6 Action 4]; conducting qualitative interviews with end users to regularly evaluate expectations and design plans related to human-AI configurations and tasks [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 1.6 Action 5]; and conducting user research to understand the individuals, groups, and communities that will be impacted by the AI, their values and context, and the role of systemic and historical biases [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 1.6 Action 8].

- **CAT-01:** AI Risk / Product shall ensure that each AI system is categorized, and that the specific tasks and methods used to implement the tasks that the AI system will support are defined (e.g., classifiers, generative models, recommenders).
[NIST AI RMF Map 2 | NIST AI RMF Map 2.1]

- **CAT-02:** AI Risk / Product shall ensure that information about the AI system's knowledge limits and how system output may be utilized and overseen by humans is documented, providing sufficient information to assist relevant AI actors when making decisions and taking subsequent actions.

- **CAT-03:** AI Risk / Product shall ensure that scientific integrity and TEVV considerations are identified and documented, including those related to experimental design, data collection and selection (e.g., availability, representativeness, suitability), system trustworthiness, and construct validation.

NIST suggests, among its 1 action for Map 2.1, defining and documenting the AI system's existing and potential learning task(s) along with known assumptions and limitations [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 2.1 Action 1].

NIST suggests, among its 6 actions for Map 2.2, documenting settings, environments, and conditions that are outside the AI system's intended use [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 2.2 Action 1]; planning and testing human-AI configurations under close to real-world conditions and documenting results [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 2.2 Action 3]; documenting dependencies on upstream data and other AI systems, including whether the specified system is an upstream dependency for another AI system or other data [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 2.2 Action 5]; and documenting connections the AI system or data will have to external networks (including the internet), financial markets, and critical infrastructure that have potential for negative externalities, as part of considering broader risk thresholds and go/no-go deployment and post-deployment decommissioning decisions [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 2.2 Action 6].

NIST suggests, among its 16 actions for Map 2.3, identifying and documenting experiment design and statistical techniques that are valid for testing complex socio-technical systems like AI [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 2.3 Action 1]; developing and applying TEVV protocols for models, the system and its subcomponents, deployment, and operation [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 2.3 Action 2]; documenting assumptions made and techniques used in data selection, curation, preparation, and analysis, including identification of constructs and proxy targets and development of indices operationalizing inherently unobservable concepts [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 2.3 Action 8]; identifying and documenting processes to understand and trace test and training data lineage and its metadata resources for mapping risks [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 2.3 Action 11]; establishing and documenting practices to check for capabilities in excess of those planned for, such as emergent properties, and to revisit prior risk management steps in light of any new capabilities [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 2.3 Action 13]; and investigating and documenting potential negative impacts related to the full product lifecycle and associated processes that may conflict with organizational values and principles [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 2.3 Action 16].
- **BEN-01:** AI Risk / Product shall ensure that AI capabilities, targeted usage, goals, and expected benefits and costs are understood in comparison with appropriate benchmarks.
- **BEN-02:** AI Risk / Product shall ensure that potential benefits of intended AI system functionality and performance are examined and documented.

- **BEN-03:** AI Risk / Product shall ensure that potential costs, including non-monetary costs, resulting from expected or realized AI errors or system functionality and trustworthiness — as connected to organizational risk tolerance — are examined and documented.
- **BEN-04:** AI Risk / Product shall ensure that targeted application scope is specified and documented based on the system's capability, established context, and AI system categorization.

- **BEN-05:** AI Risk / Product shall ensure that processes for operator and practitioner proficiency with AI system performance and trustworthiness — and relevant technical standards and certifications — are defined, assessed, and documented.
- **BEN-06:** AI Risk / Product shall ensure that processes for human oversight are defined, assessed, and documented in accordance with organizational policies from the govern function.

NIST suggests, among its 6 actions for Map 3.1, utilizing participatory approaches and engaging with system end users to understand and document AI systems' potential benefits, efficacy, and interpretability of AI task output [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 3.1 Action 1]; maintaining awareness and documentation of the individuals, groups, or communities who make up the system's internal and external stakeholders [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 3.1 Action 2]; considering performance against human baseline metrics or other standard benchmarks [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 3.1 Action 5]; and incorporating feedback from end users and potentially impacted individuals and communities about perceived system benefits [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 3.1 Action 6].

NIST suggests, among its 2 actions for Map 3.2, performing context analysis to map potential negative impacts arising from not integrating trustworthiness characteristics, engaging stakeholders external to the team that developed or deployed the AI system and potentially impacted communities to examine and document who could be harmed, what could be harmed, when harm could arise, and how harm could arise [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 3.2 Action 1], and identifying and implementing procedures for regularly evaluating the qualitative and quantitative costs of internal and external AI system failures to inform go/no-go deployment decisions throughout the AI system lifecycle [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 3.2 Action 2].

NIST suggests, among its 2 actions for Map 3.3, considering narrowing contexts for system deployment, including factors related to how outcomes may directly or indirectly affect users, groups, communities, and the environment; length of time the system is deployed in between re-trainings; geographical regions in which the system operates; dynamics related to community standards or likelihood of system misuse or abuses; and how AI system features and capabilities can be utilized within other applications or in place of other existing processes [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 3.3 Action 1], and engaging AI actors from legal and procurement functions when specifying target application scope [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 3.3 Action 2].

NIST suggests, among its 10 actions for Map 3.4, identifying and declaring AI system features and capabilities that may affect downstream AI actors' decision-making in deployment and operational settings [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 3.4 Action 1]; identifying skills and proficiency requirements for operators, practitioners, and other domain experts that interact with AI systems, and developing AI system operational documentation including information about known risks, mitigation criteria, and trustworthy characteristics [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 3.4 Action 2]; defining and developing certification procedures for operating AI systems within defined contexts of use [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 3.4 Action 4]; including operators, practitioners, and end users in AI system prototyping and testing activities under scenarios similar to deployment conditions [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 3.4 Action 5]; verifying that AI system output is interpretable and unambiguous for downstream decision-making tasks [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 3.4 Action 7]; and developing approaches to track human-AI configurations, operator, and practitioner outcomes for integration into continual improvement [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 3.4 Action 10].

NIST suggests, among its 6 actions for Map 3.5, identifying and documenting AI systems' features and capabilities that require human oversight, in relation to operational and societal contexts, trustworthy characteristics, and risks identified in Map-1 [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 3.5 Action 1]; establishing practices for AI systems' oversight in accordance with policies developed in GOVERN-1 [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 3.5 Action 2]; defining and developing training materials for relevant AI actors about AI system performance, context of use, known limitations, negative impacts, and suggested warning labels [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 3.5 Action 3]; evaluating AI system oversight practices for validity and reliability, and retesting and course correcting when oversight practices undergo extensive updates or adaptations [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 3.5 Action 5]; and verifying that model documents contain interpretable descriptions of system mechanisms, enabling oversight personnel to make informed, risk-based decisions about system risks [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 3.5 Action 6].

- **IMP-01:** AI Risk / Product shall ensure that practices and personnel for supporting regular engagement with relevant AI actors and integrating feedback about positive, negative, and unanticipated impacts are in place and documented.

NIST suggests, among its 7 actions for Map 5.2, establishing and documenting stakeholder engagement processes at the earliest stages of system formulation to identify potential impacts from the AI system on individuals, groups, communities, organizations, and society [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 5.2 Action 1]; employing methods such as value sensitive design (VSD) to identify misalignments between organizational and societal values, and system implementation and impact [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 5.2 Action 2]; incorporating quantitative, qualitative, and mixed methods in the assessment and documentation of potential impacts to individuals, groups, communities, organizations, and society [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 5.2 Action 4]; identifying a team (internal or external) that is independent of AI design and development functions to assess AI system benefits and positive and negative impacts and their likelihood and magnitude [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 5.2 Action 5]; and developing TEVV procedures that incorporate socio-technical elements and methods, and regularly reviewing and refining TEVV processes [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 5.2 Action 7].
Compliance with this standard is verified by AI Risk / Product, which is accountable for the inventory and impact assessment process end to end.

Exceptions to any requirement in this document must be approved through Acme Health's exception process and documented by AI Risk / Product, including the compensating measures in place and the risk acceptance decision.

Requirements in this standard carry the framework tags shown inline; sentences describing NIST AI RMF Playbook actions are NIST's voluntary suggestions and are not, by themselves, obligations of Acme Health unless adopted into a requirement elsewhere in Acme Health policy.
