analyze: This Standard establishes the requirements for evaluating and measuring the risks and trustworthiness characteristics of AI systems operated by Acme Health.

It applies to all AI systems in development, testing, and production at Acme Health, and to all measurement, testing, evaluation, verification, and validation (TEVV) activities performed against those systems across the AI lifecycle.

AI / ML Engineering owns the AI evaluation and measurement process described in this Standard end to end, including the selection of metrics, the execution of evaluations, the documentation of results, and the handoffs to other functions.

Domain experts, independent assessors, end users, external AI actors, and affected communities participate in individual measurement and consultation steps as specified below, but accountability for the outcome of every step rests with AI / ML Engineering.

AI / ML Engineering must select and apply approaches, methods, and metrics for measuring AI risks, starting with the most significant risks identified during the map function, and must properly document any risks or trustworthiness characteristics that will not or cannot be measured.
[NIST AI RMF Measure 1 | NIST AI RMF Measure 1.1]

NIST suggests, among its 12 actions for Measure 1.1, establishing approaches for detecting, tracking, and measuring known risks, errors, incidents, or negative impacts [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.1 Action 1]; identifying testing procedures and metrics to demonstrate whether the system is fit for purpose, functioning as claimed, and trustworthy [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.1 Action 2 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.1 Action 3]; defining acceptable limits for system performance, including course-correction suggestions when the system performs beyond those limits [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.1 Action 4]; identifying transparency metrics and accountability metrics for AI designers, developers, and deployers [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.1 Action 6 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.1 Action 7]; documenting metric selection criteria, including considered but unused metrics [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.1 Action 8]; monitoring AI system external inputs, including training data, models and components reused from other contexts, and third-party tools and resources [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.1 Action 9]; reporting metrics to inform assessments of system generalizability and reliability [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.1 Action 10]; assessing and documenting pre- versus post-deployment system performance, including existing and emergent risks [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.1 Action 11]; and documenting risks or trustworthiness characteristics identified in the Map function that will not be measured, including justification for non-measurement [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.1 Action 12].
[NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.1 Action 2 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.1 Action 3]
[NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.1 Action 6 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.1 Action 7]

AI / ML Engineering must regularly assess and update the appropriateness of AI metrics and the effectiveness of existing controls, including reports of errors and potential impacts on affected communities.

NIST suggests, among its 8 actions for Measure 1.2, assessing the external validity of all measurements [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.2 Action 1]; assessing the effectiveness of existing metrics and controls on a regular basis throughout the AI system lifecycle [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.2 Action 2]; documenting reports of errors, incidents, and negative impacts and assessing the sufficiency and efficacy of existing metrics for repairs and upgrades [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.2 Action 3]; developing new metrics when existing metrics are insufficient or ineffective [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.2 Action 4]; developing and utilizing metrics to monitor, characterize, and track external inputs, including third-party tools [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.2 Action 5]; determining the frequency and scope for sharing metrics and related information with stakeholders and impacted communities [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.2 Action 6]; utilizing stakeholder feedback processes established in the Map function to capture, act upon, and share feedback from end users and potentially impacted communities [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.2 Action 7]; and collecting and reporting software quality metrics such as rates of bug occurrence and severity, time to response, and time to repair [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.2 Action 8].

Regular assessments and updates must involve internal experts who did not serve as front-line developers for the system and/or independent assessors, with domain experts, users, external AI actors, and affected communities consulted as necessary per organizational risk tolerance.

NIST suggests, among its 8 actions for Measure 1.3, utilizing separate testing teams to enable independent decisions and course-correction for AI systems, with processes tracked and changes in performance measured and documented [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.3 Action 2]; planning and evaluating AI system prototypes with end user populations early and continuously in the AI lifecycle [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.3 Action 3]; assessing the independence and stature of TEVV and oversight AI actors to ensure they have the required levels of independence and resources to perform assurance, compliance, and feedback tasks effectively [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.3 Action 4]; evaluating the effectiveness of external stakeholder feedback mechanisms for eliciting, evaluating, and integrating input from diverse groups and for enhancing AI actor visibility and decision making regarding AI system risks [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.3 Action 6 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.3 Action 7]; and identifying and utilizing participatory approaches for assessing impacts that may arise from changes in system deployment [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.3 Action 8].
[NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.3 Action 6 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.3 Action 7]
AI / ML Engineering must evaluate AI systems for trustworthy characteristics, with test sets, metrics, and details about the tools used during TEVV documented.
[NIST AI RMF Measure 2 | NIST AI RMF Measure 2.1]

NIST suggests, among its 3 actions for Measure 2.1, leveraging existing industry best practices for transparency and documentation of all possible aspects of measurements, such as data sheets for data sets and model cards [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.1 Action 1]; regularly assessing the effectiveness of tools used to document measurement approaches, test sets, metrics, processes, and materials used [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.1 Action 2]; and updating those tools as needed [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.1 Action 3].
Evaluations involving human subjects must meet applicable requirements, including human subject protection, and must be representative of the relevant population.

NIST suggests, among its 8 actions for Measure 2.2, following human subjects research requirements, including informed consent and compensation, during dataset collection activities [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.2 Action 1]; analyzing differences between the intended and actual population of users or data subjects [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.2 Action 2]; utilizing disaggregated evaluation methods, for example by race, age, gender, ethnicity, ability, or region [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.2 Action 3]; establishing thresholds and alert procedures for dataset representativeness within the context of use [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.2 Action 4]; following intellectual property and privacy rights related to datasets and their use [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.2 Action 6]; evaluating data representativeness through investigation of known failure modes, assessment of data quality and diverse sourcing, application of public benchmarks, traditional bias testing, chaos engineering, and stakeholder feedback [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.2 Action 7]; and using informed consent for individuals providing data used in system testing and evaluation [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.2 Action 8].
AI system performance or assurance criteria must be measured qualitatively or quantitatively and demonstrated for conditions similar to the deployment setting(s), with the measures documented.

NIST suggests, among its 9 actions for Measure 2.3, conducting regular and sustained engagement with potentially impacted communities [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.3 Action 1]; regularly testing and evaluating systems in non-optimized conditions in collaboration with AI actors in user interaction and user experience roles [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.3 Action 3]; measuring AI systems prior to deployment in conditions similar to expected scenarios [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.3 Action 6]; measuring and documenting performance criteria such as validity (false positive rate, false negative rate) and efficiency (training times, prediction latency) related to ground truth within the deployment context of use [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.3 Action 7]; measuring assurance criteria such as AI actor competency and experience [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.3 Action 8]; and documenting differences between the measurement setting and the deployment environment(s) [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.3 Action 9].
The functionality and behavior of the AI system and its components, as identified in the map function, must be monitored when in production through the [Monitoring System].

NIST suggests, among its 7 actions for Measure 2.4, monitoring and documenting how metrics and performance indicators observed in production differ from those collected during pre-deployment testing, considering error propagation and feedback loop risks when differences are observed [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.4 Action 1]; monitoring for anomalies using approaches such as control limits, confidence intervals, integrity constraints, and ML algorithms [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.4 Action 3]; verifying that alerts are in place for when distributions in new input data or generated predictions differ from pre-deployment test outcomes, or when anomalies are detected [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.4 Action 4]; assessing the accuracy and quality of generated outputs against newly collected ground-truth information as it becomes available [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.4 Action 5]; and utilizing human review to track processing of unexpected data and reliability of generated outputs, warning system users when outputs may be unreliable, and verifying that human overseers have clearly defined responsibilities and training [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.4 Action 6].
The AI system to be deployed must be demonstrated to be valid and reliable, and limitations of its generalizability beyond the conditions under which it was developed must be documented.

NIST suggests, among its 15 actions for Measure 2.5, establishing or identifying and documenting approaches to measure forms of validity, including construct, internal, and external validity [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.5 Action 3]; assessing and documenting system variance using standard approaches such as confidence intervals, standard deviation, standard error, bootstrapping, or cross-validation [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.5 Action 4]; establishing or identifying and documenting robustness measures and reliability measures [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.5 Action 5 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.5 Action 6]; monitoring operating conditions for system performance outside of defined limits [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.5 Action 11]; defining post-alert actions, such as alerting relevant AI actors, requesting human review, alerting downstream users and stakeholders, tracking and mitigating error propagation, and action logging [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.5 Action 13]; logging input data and relevant system configuration information whenever there is an attempt to use the system beyond its well-defined range of system validity [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.5 Action 14]; and modifying the system over time to extend its range of system validity to new operating conditions [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.5 Action 15].
[NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.5 Action 5 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.5 Action 6]

The AI system must be evaluated regularly for safety risks identified in the map function; the system to be deployed must be demonstrated to be safe, its residual negative risk must not exceed the risk tolerance, and it must be able to fail safely — particularly if operated beyond its knowledge limits — with safety metrics reflecting system reliability and robustness, real-time monitoring, and response times for AI system failures.

NIST suggests, among its 7 actions for Measure 2.6, thoroughly measuring system performance in development and deployment contexts and under stress conditions, including stress-testing under likely scenarios such as concept drift and high load, testing under conditions similar to past known incidents or near-misses, applying chaos engineering approaches, and documenting the range of conditions under which the system has been demonstrated to fail safely [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.6 Action 1]; measuring and monitoring system performance in real-time to enable rapid response when AI system incidents are detected [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.6 Action 2]; collecting pertinent safety statistics such as out-of-range performance, incident response times, and system down time [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.6 Action 3]; documenting, practicing, and measuring incident response plans for AI system incidents, including measuring response and down times [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.6 Action 5]; and comparing documented safety testing and monitoring information with established risk tolerances on an ongoing basis [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.6 Action 6].
AI system security and resilience, as identified in the map function, must be evaluated and documented.

NIST suggests, among its 10 actions for Measure 2.7, establishing and tracking AI system security tests and metrics, such as red-teaming activities, frequency and rate of anomalous events, system down-time, incident response times, and time-to-bypass [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.7 Action 1]; using red-team exercises to actively test the system under adversarial or stress conditions and to evaluate potential mismatches between claimed and actual system performance [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.7 Action 2 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.7 Action 4]; documenting red-team exercise results as part of continuous improvement efforts [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.7 Action 3]; using countermeasures such as authentication, throttling, differential privacy, and robust ML approaches to increase the range of security conditions under which the system can return to normal function [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.7 Action 5]; verifying that third-party AI resources and personnel undergo security audits and screenings [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.7 Action 9]; and utilizing watermarking technologies as a deterrent to data and model extraction attacks [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.7 Action 10].
[NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.7 Action 2 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.7 Action 4]
Risks associated with transparency and accountability, as identified in the map function, must be examined and documented.

NIST suggests, among its 6 actions for Measure 2.8, instrumenting the system for measurement and tracking, for example by maintaining histories, audit logs, and other information usable by AI actors to review and evaluate possible sources of error, bias, or vulnerability [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.8 Action 1]; testing provided explanations for calibration with different audiences, including operators, end users, decision makers, and decision subjects, to enable recourse for consequential system decisions [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.8 Action 3]; measuring and documenting human oversight of AI systems, including the degree of oversight provided, statistics about downstream actions such as system overrides, and statistics about reported errors or complaints, time to respond, and response types [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.8 Action 4]; tracking, documenting, and measuring organizational accountability via policy exceptions and escalations and documenting "go" and "no/go" decisions made by accountable parties [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.8 Action 5]; and tracking and auditing the effectiveness of organizational mechanisms related to AI risk management, including lines of communication, roles and responsibilities, and organizational accountability roles [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.8 Action 6].
The AI model must be explained, validated, and documented, and AI system output must be interpreted within its context — as identified in the map function — to inform responsible use and governance.

NIST suggests, among its 11 actions for Measure 2.9, verifying that systems are developed to produce explainable models, post-hoc explanations, and audit logs [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.9 Action 1]; documenting AI model details including model type, data features, training algorithms, proposed uses, decision thresholds, training data, evaluation data, and ethical considerations [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.9 Action 4]; establishing, documenting, and reporting performance and error metrics across demographic groups and other segments relevant to the deployment context [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.9 Action 5]; explaining systems using a variety of methods and testing explanations according to properties such as fidelity, consistency, robustness, and interpretability [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.9 Action 6]; assessing the characteristics of system explanations according to properties such as fidelity, ambiguity, interpretability, interactivity, consistency, and resilience to attack or manipulation [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.9 Action 7]; testing the quality of system explanations with end users and other groups [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.9 Action 8]; and using transparency tools such as data statements and model cards to document explanatory and validation information [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.9 Action 11].
Privacy risk of the AI system, as identified in the map function, must be examined and documented.

NIST suggests, among its 8 actions for Measure 2.10, documenting the collection, use, management, and disclosure of personally sensitive information in datasets in accordance with privacy and data governance policies [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.10 Action 2]; quantifying privacy-level data aspects such as the ability to identify individuals or groups, for example using k-anonymity metrics, l-diversity, and t-closeness [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.10 Action 3]; establishing and documenting protocols (authorization, duration, type) and access controls for training sets or production data containing personally sensitive information [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.10 Action 4]; monitoring internal queries to production data for detecting patterns that isolate personal records [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.10 Action 5]; and using privacy-enhancing techniques such as differential privacy when publicly sharing dataset information [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.10 Action 7].
Fairness and bias, as identified in the map function, must be evaluated and the results documented.

NIST suggests, among its 24 actions for Measure 2.11, conducting fairness assessments that identify types of harms, identify across, within, and intersecting groups that might be harmed, quantify harms using general and context-specific fairness metrics, and analyze quantified harms for contextually significant differences [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.11 Action 1]; using context-specific fairness metrics to examine how system performance varies across groups, within groups, and for intersecting groups [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.11 Action 7]; defining acceptable levels of difference in performance in accordance with established organizational governance policies, business requirements, regulatory compliance, legal frameworks, and ethical standards within the context of use [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.11 Action 9]; defining the actions to be taken if disparity levels rise above acceptable levels [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.11 Action 10]; monitoring system outputs for performance or bias issues that exceed established tolerance levels [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.11 Action 13]; and evaluating practices along the lifecycle to identify potential sources of human-cognitive bias such as availability, observational, and confirmation bias [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.11 Action 22].
The environmental impact and sustainability of AI model training and management activities, as identified in the map function, must be assessed and documented.

NIST suggests, among its 6 actions for Measure 2.12, identifying and implementing key indicators of AI system energy and water consumption, efficiency, and/or GHG emissions [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.12 Action 2]; establishing measurable baselines for sustainable AI system operation in accordance with organizational policies, regulatory compliance, legal frameworks, and environmental protection and sustainability norms [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.12 Action 3]; identifying and establishing acceptable resource consumption, efficiency, and GHG emissions levels, along with actions to be taken if indicators rise above acceptable levels [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.12 Action 5]; and estimating AI system emissions levels throughout the AI lifecycle via carbon calculators or a similar process [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.12 Action 6].
The effectiveness of the employed TEVV metrics and processes in the measure function must be evaluated and documented.

NIST suggests, among its 4 actions for Measure 2.13, reviewing selected system metrics and associated TEVV processes to determine if they are able to sustain system improvements, including the identification and removal of errors [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.13 Action 1]; regularly evaluating system metrics for utility and considering descriptive approaches in place of overly complex methods [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.13 Action 2]; reviewing selected system metrics for acceptability within the end user and impacted community of interest [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.13 Action 3]; and assessing the effectiveness of metrics for identifying and measuring risks [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.13 Action 4].

AI / ML Engineering must maintain approaches, personnel, and documentation to regularly identify and track existing, unanticipated, and emergent AI risks based on factors such as intended and actual performance in deployed contexts.
[NIST AI RMF Measure 3 | NIST AI RMF Measure 3.1]

NIST suggests, among its 6 actions for Measure 3.1, comparing AI system risks with simpler or traditional models, human baseline performance, and other manual performance benchmarks [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 3.1 Action 1]; comparing end user and community feedback about deployed AI systems to internal measures of system performance [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 3.1 Action 2]; assessing the effectiveness of metrics for identifying and measuring emergent risks [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 3.1 Action 3]; measuring error response times and tracking response quality [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 3.1 Action 4]; and eliciting and tracking feedback from AI actors in user support, incident response, and support roles about the type of metrics, explanations, and other system information required for fulsome resolution of system issues, and about the adequacy of staffing and resources to perform their duties effectively and in a timely manner [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 3.1 Action 5 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 3.1 Action 6].
[NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 3.1 Action 5 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 3.1 Action 6]
Risk tracking approaches must be considered for settings where AI risks are difficult to assess using currently available measurement techniques or where metrics are not yet available.

NIST suggests, among its 3 actions for Measure 3.2, establishing processes for tracking emergent risks that may not be measurable with current approaches, including recourse mechanisms for faulty AI system outputs, bug bounties, human-centered design approaches, user-interaction and experience research, and participatory stakeholder engagement with affected or potentially impacted individuals and communities [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 3.2 Action 1]; identifying AI actors responsible for tracking emergent risks and inventorying methods [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 3.2 Action 2]; and determining and documenting the rate of occurrence and severity level for complex or difficult-to-measure risks when prioritizing new measurement approaches, allocating AI system risk management resources, evaluating AI system improvements, and making go/no-go decisions for subsequent system iterations [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 3.2 Action 3].

Feedback processes for end users and impacted communities to report problems and appeal system outcomes must be established through the [Ticketing System] and integrated into AI system evaluation metrics.

NIST suggests, among its 6 actions for Measure 3.3, measuring the efficacy of end user and operator error reporting processes [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 3.3 Action 1]; categorizing and analyzing the type and rate of end user appeal requests and results [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 3.3 Action 2]; measuring feedback activity participation rates and awareness of feedback activity availability [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 3.3 Action 3]; utilizing feedback to analyze measurement approaches and determine subsequent courses of action [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 3.3 Action 4]; evaluating measurement approaches to determine efficacy for enhancing organizational understanding of real-world impacts [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 3.3 Action 5]; and analyzing end user and community feedback in close collaboration with domain experts [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 3.3 Action 6].
Measurement approaches for identifying AI risks must be connected to deployment context(s), informed through consultation with domain experts and other end users, and documented.
[NIST AI RMF Measure 4 | NIST AI RMF Measure 4.1]

NIST suggests, among its 6 actions for Measure 4.1, supporting mechanisms for capturing feedback from system end users, including domain experts, operators, and practitioners, conducted in settings where end users can openly share their doubts and insights about AI system output in connection to their specific context of use [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 4.1 Action 1]; identifying and documenting approaches for evaluating and integrating elicited feedback from system end users, in collaboration with human-factors and socio-technical domain experts, to actively inform a process of continual improvement [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 4.1 Action 2]; utilizing end user feedback to investigate how selected metrics and measurement approaches interact with organizational and operational contexts [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 4.1 Action 4]; and identifying and implementing approaches to measure effectiveness and satisfaction with end user elicitation techniques, and documenting results [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 4.1 Action 6].

Measurement results regarding AI system trustworthiness in deployment context(s) and across the AI lifecycle must be informed by input from domain experts and relevant AI actors to validate whether the system is performing consistently as intended, and the results must be documented.

NIST suggests, among its 6 actions for Measure 4.2, integrating feedback from end users, operators, and affected individuals and communities from the Map function as inputs to assess AI system trustworthiness characteristics, ensuring both positive and negative feedback is assessed [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 4.2 Action 1]; evaluating feedback regarding end user satisfaction with, and confidence in, AI system performance, including whether output is considered valid, reliable, explainable, and interpretable [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 4.2 Action 3]; measuring the frequency of AI systems' override decisions, evaluating and documenting results, and feeding insights back into continual improvement processes [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 4.2 Action 5]; and consulting AI actors in impact assessment, human factors, and socio-technical tasks to assist with analysis and interpretation of results [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 4.2 Action 6].

Measurable performance improvements or declines — based on consultations with relevant AI actors, including affected communities, and field data about context-relevant risks and trustworthiness characteristics — must be identified and documented.

NIST suggests, among its 6 actions for Measure 4.3, developing baseline quantitative measures for trustworthy characteristics [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 4.3 Action 1]; delimiting and characterizing baseline operation values and states [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 4.3 Action 2]; utilizing qualitative approaches to augment and complement quantitative baseline measures, in close coordination with impact assessment, human factors, and socio-technical AI actors [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 4.3 Action 3]; monitoring and assessing measurements as part of continual improvement to identify potential system adjustments or modifications [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 4.3 Action 4]; performing and documenting sensitivity analysis to characterize actual and expected variance in performance after applying system or procedural updates [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 4.3 Action 5]; and documenting decisions related to the sensitivity analysis and recording the expected influence on system performance and identified risks [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 4.3 Action 6].

analyze: This standard establishes requirements for system and information integrity controls at Acme Health.
All organizational systems and system components must comply with the requirements specified herein.
The organization shall implement signature-based or non-signature-based malicious code protection mechanisms at system entry and exit points to detect and eradicate malicious code.
The organization shall implement both signature-based and non-signature-based malicious code protection mechanisms at system entry and exit points to detect and eradicate malicious code.
The organization shall automatically update malicious code protection mechanisms as new releases are available in accordance with organizational configuration management policy and procedures.
[NIST 800-53 SI-3 Low, Moderate, High | ARC-AMPE SI-3 AE Mandatory]
The organization shall update malicious code protection mechanisms only when directed by a privileged user.

The organization shall configure malicious code protection mechanisms to perform periodic scans of the system [Assignment: organization-defined frequency] and real-time scans of files from external sources at [Selection (one or more): endpoint; network entry and exit points] as the files are downloaded, opened, or executed in accordance with organizational policy.

The organization shall configure malicious code protection mechanisms to perform periodic scans of the system at least every one (1) week and real-time scans of files from external sources at endpoints and network entry and exit points as the files are downloaded, opened, or executed in accordance with organizational policy.

The organization shall configure malicious code protection mechanisms to [Selection (one or more): block malicious code; quarantine malicious code; take [Assignment: organization-defined action]] and send alert to [Assignment: organization-defined personnel or roles] in response to malicious code detection.

The organization shall configure malicious code protection mechanisms to block and quarantine malicious code and send alert to administrator or organization-defined security personnel near real-time in response to malicious code detection.
The organization shall address the receipt of false positives during malicious code detection and eradication and the resulting potential impact on the availability of the system.
[NIST 800-53 SI-3 Low, Moderate, High | ARC-AMPE SI-3 AE Mandatory]

The organization shall report malicious code scanning results to organization personnel responsible for Incident Handling in compliance with IR-4 and for Audit Review, Analysis, and Reporting in compliance with AU-6.

The organization shall test malicious code protection mechanisms [Assignment: organization-defined frequency] by introducing known benign code into the system and verify that the detection of the code and the associated incident reporting occur.

The organization shall detect [Assignment: organization-defined unauthorized operating system commands] through the kernel application programming interface on [Assignment: organization-defined system hardware components] and [Selection (one or more): issue a warning; audit the command execution; prevent the execution of the command].

The organization shall employ [Assignment: organization-defined tools and techniques] to analyze the characteristics and behavior of malicious code and incorporate the results from malicious code analysis into organizational incident response and flaw remediation processes.
The organization shall verify the correct operation of [Assignment: organization-defined security and privacy functions].
[NIST 800-53 SI-6 High | ARC-AMPE SI-6 AE Mandatory]

The organization shall perform the verification of security and privacy functions [Selection (one or more): [Assignment: organization-defined system transitional states]; upon command by user with appropriate privilege; [Assignment: organization-defined frequency]].
The organization shall perform the verification of security and privacy functions upon system startup and/or restart, upon command by a user with appropriate privileges, or at least monthly.
The organization shall alert [Assignment: organization-defined personnel or roles] to failed security and privacy verification tests.
The organization shall alert, at a minimum, the system/security administrator to failed security and privacy verification tests.
The organization shall [Selection (one or more): shut the system down; restart the system; [Assignment: organization-defined alternative action(s)]] when anomalies are discovered.

The organization shall shut the system down, restart the system, or perform another defined alternative action(s) documented in the applicable System Security and Privacy Plan (SSPP) when anomalies are discovered.
The organization shall implement automated mechanisms to support the management of distributed security and privacy function testing.
The organization shall report the results of security and privacy function verification to [Assignment: organization-defined personnel or roles].
The organization shall employ spam protection mechanisms at system entry and exit points to detect and act on unsolicited messages.
[NIST 800-53 SI-8 Moderate, High | FedRAMP SI-8 | ARC-AMPE SI-8 AE Mandatory]
The organization shall update spam protection mechanisms when new releases are available in accordance with organizational configuration management policy and procedures.
[NIST 800-53 SI-8 Moderate, High | FedRAMP SI-8 | ARC-AMPE SI-8 AE Mandatory]
The organization shall automatically update spam protection mechanisms [Assignment: organization-defined frequency].
The organization shall automatically update spam protection mechanisms at least every one (1) week.

When CSO sends email on behalf of the government as part of the business offering, the organization shall implement Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting & Conformance (DMARC) on the sending domain for outgoing messages as described in DHS Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 18-01, confirming DMARC configuration with policy=reject and the rua parameter includes reports@dmarc.cyber.dhs.gov, and documenting DMARC compliance in the SI-08 control implementation solution description including the FROM: domain(s) when emails are sent on behalf of the government.
The organization shall implement spam protection mechanisms with a learning capability to more effectively identify legitimate communications traffic.
The organization shall implement [Assignment: organization-defined controls] to protect the system memory from unauthorized code execution.
The organization shall implement, at a minimum, the related controls within this control set to protect the system memory from unauthorized code execution.

The organization shall [Selection: restrict; prohibit] the use of [Assignment: organization-defined types of system media] on [Assignment: organization-defined systems or system components] using [Assignment: organization-defined controls].

The organization shall prohibit the use of personally owned media (e.g., flash drives, external hard disk drives, and other portable storage and media devices) on organization-defined systems and networks using organization-defined security safeguards.
The organization shall prohibit the use of portable storage devices in organizational systems when such devices have no identifiable owner.
[NIST 800-53 MP-7 Low, Moderate, High | ARC-AMPE MP-7 AE Mandatory]
The organization shall prohibit the use of sanitization-resistant media in organizational systems.
The organization shall define acceptable and unacceptable mobile code and mobile code technologies.
[NIST 800-53 SC-18 Moderate, High | ARC-AMPE SC-18 AE Mandatory]
The organization shall define the acceptable and unacceptable mobile code and mobile code technologies in the applicable System Security and Privacy Plan (SSPP).
The organization shall authorize, monitor, and control the use of mobile code within the system.
[NIST 800-53 SC-18 Moderate, High | ARC-AMPE SC-18 AE Mandatory]
The organization shall identify [Assignment: organization-defined unacceptable mobile code] and take [Assignment: organization-defined corrective actions].
The organization shall prevent the download and execution of [Assignment: organization-defined unacceptable mobile code].
The organization shall verify that the acquisition, development, and use of mobile code to be deployed in the system meets [Assignment: organization-defined mobile code requirements].

The organization shall prevent the automatic execution of mobile code in [Assignment: organization-defined software applications] and enforce [Assignment: organization-defined actions] prior to executing the code.
The organization shall allow execution of permitted mobile code only in confined virtual machine environments.

analyze: **Document Owner:** IAM Engineering **Review Cycle:** At least every one (1) year, and following the events defined in Section 2 **Applicability:** All Example Org personnel, contractors, and systems that store, process, or transmit organizational information, Personally Identifiable Information (PII), or electronic protected health information (ePHI)

Example Org shall develop, document, and disseminate to applicable personnel and roles an access control policy that addresses purpose, scope, roles, responsibilities, management commitment, coordination among organizational entities, and compliance, and that is consistent with applicable laws, executive orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, and guidelines.
IAM Engineering shall develop and maintain procedures to facilitate implementation of the policy and associated access controls.
The policy shall be maintained at the organization level.
[NIST 800-53 AC-1 (Low, Moderate, High) | ARC-AMPE AC-1 | HIPAA 164.308(a)(4)(i)]
IAM Engineering shall designate an official to manage the development, documentation, and dissemination of the access control policy and procedures.
IAM Engineering is accountable for the identity lifecycle and access review process end to end, including all handoffs described in this Standard.
Other teams — including Human Resources, System Owners, and the Authorizing Official — participate in individual steps as identified below.
IAM Engineering shall assign account managers for the systems within scope of this Standard.

IAM Engineering shall review and update the access control policy and procedures at least every one (1) year and following the following events: assessment or audit findings; security or privacy incidents; and changes to applicable laws, including privacy laws, Executive Orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, and guidelines.

IAM Engineering shall actively monitor for changes to applicable privacy laws, regulations, and overarching policy that affect access control policies, and shall ensure organization, mission/business, and system access control policies remain effective.

IAM Engineering shall ensure access control policies and procedures support cybersecurity and privacy safeguards to the greatest extent feasible throughout the system's life cycle and the life cycle of the information on that system.

IAM Engineering shall maintain the policies and procedures implemented to comply with the security requirements in written (which may be electronic) form, and shall maintain a written (which may be electronic) record of any action, activity, or assessment required to be documented.
IAM Engineering shall retain required documentation for 6 years from the date of its creation or the date when it last was in effect, whichever is later.
IAM Engineering shall make documentation available to those persons responsible for implementing the procedures to which the documentation pertains.
IAM Engineering shall review documentation periodically and update it as needed in response to environmental or operational changes affecting the security of electronic protected health information.
IAM Engineering shall define and document the types of accounts allowed and specifically prohibited for use within the system.
IAM Engineering shall require organization-defined prerequisites and criteria for group and role membership.
IAM Engineering shall specify the authorized users of the system, group and role membership, and the access authorizations (i.e., privileges) and required attributes for each account.
IAM Engineering shall require approvals by organization-defined personnel or roles for requests to create accounts.
IAM Engineering shall create, enable, modify, disable, and remove accounts in accordance with organization-defined policy, procedures, prerequisites, and criteria.
IAM Engineering shall authorize access to the system based on a valid access authorization, intended system usage, and other required attributes.
IAM Engineering shall implement centralized control of user access administrator functions.
IAM Engineering shall remove or disable default user accounts and rename active default accounts.
IAM Engineering shall establish and implement a process for changing shared or group account authenticators (if deployed) when individuals are removed from the group.

IAM Engineering shall permit the use of shared and group accounts only when organization-defined conditions are met; under ARC-AMPE, these conditions are a documented and approved business need (approved in advance by the Authorizing Official) and a system security plan that describes how the accounts are used and includes compensating processes and procedures to uniquely attribute account user activities.
IAM Engineering shall monitor the use of accounts.

IAM Engineering shall monitor system accounts for atypical usage (such as access at times of day or from locations inconsistent with normal usage patterns) and report atypical usage to organization-defined personnel or roles and, if necessary, any applicable incident response team(s).

IAM Engineering shall notify account managers and organization-defined personnel or roles when accounts are no longer required, when users are terminated or transferred, and when system usage or need-to-know changes for an individual, within the following time periods:

| Event | Notification Time Period | | ------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------- | | Accounts no longer required | Within twenty-four (24) hours [ARC-AMPE AC-2] | | Users terminated or transferred | Within eight (8) hours [ARC-AMPE AC-2] | | System usage or need-to-know changes for an individual | Within eight (8) hours [ARC-AMPE AC-2] | [NIST 800-53 AC-2 (Low, Moderate, High) | ARC-AMPE AC-2]
IAM Engineering shall review accounts for compliance with account management requirements at least every ninety (90) days for all systems.
This review shall be executed as part of the quarterly access review process defined in Section 12.
IAM Engineering shall align account management processes with personnel termination and transfer processes.
IAM Engineering shall regulate the access provided to contractors and define security requirements for contractors.

IAM Engineering shall prohibit the use of guest, anonymous, and shared accounts for providing access to Personally Identifiable Information (PII), and shall provide access only to the minimum amount of PII necessary for users to perform their duties.

IAM Engineering shall implement policies and procedures to ensure that all members of the workforce have appropriate access to electronic protected health information and to prevent workforce members who do not have access from obtaining access to electronic protected health information.

IAM Engineering shall implement procedures for the authorization and/or supervision of workforce members who work with electronic protected health information or in locations where it might be accessed.
IAM Engineering shall implement procedures to determine that a workforce member's access to electronic protected health information is appropriate.

IAM Engineering shall implement policies and procedures for granting access to electronic protected health information, for example through access to a workstation, transaction, program, process, or other mechanism.

IAM Engineering shall implement policies and procedures that, based on the entity's access authorization policies, establish, document, review, and modify a user's right of access to a workstation, transaction, program, or process.

If a health care clearinghouse is part of a larger organization, IAM Engineering shall implement policies and procedures that protect the electronic protected health information of the clearinghouse from unauthorized access by the larger organization.

IAM Engineering shall support the management of system accounts using organization-defined automated mechanisms (which may include, for example, automatic notification of account managers when users are terminated or transferred, system monitoring of account usage, and notification mechanisms to report atypical account usage), implemented via the [Identity Provider].
IAM Engineering shall automatically remove or disable temporary and emergency accounts after an organization-defined time period.
IAM Engineering shall automatically disable temporary and emergency accounts after no more than ninety-six (96) hours from last use.

IAM Engineering shall disable accounts that have expired, are no longer associated with a user or individual, are in violation of organizational policy, or have been inactive for an organization-defined time period.

IAM Engineering shall disable non-consumer accounts within twenty-four (24) hours when the accounts have expired, are no longer associated with a user or individual, are in violation of organizational policy, or have been inactive for sixty (60) days.
IAM Engineering shall automatically audit account creation, modification, enabling, disabling, and removal actions.
IAM Engineering shall require that users log out when an organization-defined time period of expected inactivity is exceeded or when otherwise described as requiring logout.

IAM Engineering shall require that users log out when the time period of inactivity will exceed twenty-four (24) hours; this is a user action required in organizational user policies and is not an automated control.

IAM Engineering shall establish and administer privileged user accounts in accordance with a role-based access scheme, monitor privileged role or attribute assignments and changes to roles or attributes, and revoke access when privileged role or attribute assignments are no longer appropriate.

IAM Engineering shall establish and administer application-specific privileged user accounts in accordance with a role-based access scheme based on user responsibilities associated with application use; shall inspect administrator groups, root accounts, and other system-related accounts on demand and at least once every fourteen (14) days to ensure unauthorized accounts have not been created; and shall inspect application-specific privileged user roles every thirty (30) days.
IAM Engineering shall disable accounts of individuals within an organization-defined time period of discovery that the individual poses a significant risk.
IAM Engineering shall disable accounts of individuals within one (1) hour of discovery of an individual posing a significant risk.

IAM Engineering shall enforce approved authorizations for logical access to information and system resources in accordance with applicable access control policies, using technical policies and procedures that allow access only to those persons or software programs that have been granted access rights.
[NIST 800-53 AC-3 (Low, Moderate, High) | ARC-AMPE AC-3 | HIPAA 164.312(a)(1) (Required)]
If encryption is used as an access control mechanism, it must meet the approved and latest published FIPS 140-compliant encryption standards.
IAM Engineering shall configure operating system controls to disable public "read" and "write" access to all system-related files, objects, and directories that contain sensitive information.
IAM Engineering shall protect data stored in the information system with system access controls and encrypt data residing in non-secure areas.

When contracting with external service providers, IAM Engineering shall isolate PII, as well as software and services that receive, process, store, or transmit PII, within the service provider environment to the maximum extent possible so that other service provider customers sharing physical or virtual space cannot gain access to such data or applications.

IAM Engineering shall enforce the revocation of access authorizations resulting from changes to the security attributes of subjects and objects based on organization-defined rules governing the timing of revocations ([Revocation Timing Rules]).

IAM Engineering shall release information outside of the system only if the receiving external organization (such as a department, agency, or commercial entity not managed by the organization) provides information security and privacy safeguards commensurate with those implemented by the organization, and organization-defined controls are used to validate the appropriateness of the information designated for release.

IAM Engineering shall provide organization-defined mechanisms (including individual authentication and identification, accounting of disclosures, notice of privacy practices, request forms and application interfaces, and other mechanisms developed in consultation with the senior privacy official and legal counsel) enabling individuals to access their PII/PHI elements defined in applicable security/privacy plans, in a readable form and format, consistent with published policies, procedures, and applicable federal and state privacy requirements for processing access requests.

IAM Engineering shall implement policies and procedures that specify the proper functions to be performed, the manner in which those functions are to be performed, and the physical attributes of the surroundings of a specific workstation or class of workstations that can access electronic protected health information.
IAM Engineering shall identify and document the organization-defined duties of individuals requiring separation, and define system access authorizations to support separation of duties.

IAM Engineering shall divide critical mission functions and information system support functions (including separating information system testing functions such as user acceptance, quality assurance, and information security from production functions) among separate individuals or groups; shall ensure an independent entity — not the Business Owner, ISSO, System Developer(s)/Maintainer(s), or System Administrator(s) responsible for the system — conducts information security testing; and shall ensure audit functions are not performed by security personnel responsible for administering access control.

IAM Engineering shall employ the principle of least privilege, allowing only authorized accesses for users (or processes acting on behalf of users) that are necessary to accomplish assigned organizational tasks.
[NIST 800-53 AC-6 (Moderate, High) | FedRAMP AC-6 | ARC-AMPE AC-6]

IAM Engineering shall disable all file system access not explicitly required for system, application, and administrator functionality, and shall ensure only authorized users can access files, directories, drives, workstations, servers, network shares, ports, protocols, and services expressly required for the performance of job duties.

IAM Engineering shall provide contractors with minimal system and physical access, shall require them to agree to and support organizational security requirements, and shall assess contractors' ability to adhere to and support the organization's security policy during the contractor selection process.

IAM Engineering shall restrict the use of database management utilities to authorized database administrators, shall prevent users from accessing database data files at the logical data view, field, or field-value level, and shall implement table-level access control.

IAM Engineering shall disable all system and removable media boot access unless explicitly authorized by the organization-defined Authorizing Official for compelling operational needs; if authorized, boot access must be password protected.

IAM Engineering shall authorize access for organization-defined individuals or roles to security functions (deployed in hardware, software, and firmware) and to security-relevant information; under FedRAMP, this covers all functions not publicly accessible and all security-relevant information not publicly available, and under ARC-AMPE includes setting/modifying audit logs and auditing behavior, boundary protection system rules, access authorizations, authentication parameters, and system configurations and parameters, with the System Owner explicitly authorizing such access for authorized personnel (e.g., security administrators, system and network administrators, system security officers, system maintenance personnel, system programmers, and other privileged users).
[NIST 800-53 AC-6(1) (Moderate, High) | FedRAMP AC-6(1) | ARC-AMPE AC-6(1)]

IAM Engineering shall require that users of system accounts (or roles) with access to security functions or security-relevant information use non-privileged accounts or roles when accessing nonsecurity functions; under FedRAMP this applies to all security functions, and under ARC-AMPE, if feasible, any use of privileged accounts for such functions is audited.
[NIST 800-53 AC-6(2) (Moderate, High) | FedRAMP AC-6(2) | ARC-AMPE AC-6(2)]
IAM Engineering shall restrict privileged accounts on the system to organization-defined personnel or roles.

IAM Engineering shall review the privileges assigned to organization-defined roles and classes at an organization-defined frequency to validate the need for such privileges, and shall reassign or remove privileges as necessary to correctly reflect organizational mission and business needs.

IAM Engineering shall review the privileges assigned to all users with privileges no less often than every ninety (90) days to validate the need for such privileges, and shall reassign or remove privileges as necessary to correctly reflect organizational mission and business needs.
This review shall be executed as part of the quarterly access review process defined in Section 12.

IAM Engineering shall prevent software from executing at higher privilege levels than the users executing the software; under FedRAMP this applies to any software except software explicitly documented.
IAM Engineering shall log the execution of privileged functions.
IAM Engineering shall prevent non-privileged users from executing privileged functions.

IAM Engineering shall identify the organization-defined user actions that can be performed on the system without identification or authentication, consistent with organizational mission and business functions, and shall document and provide supporting rationale in the system security plan for those user actions not requiring identification or authentication.

IAM Engineering shall manage system identifiers by receiving authorization from organization-defined personnel or roles to assign an individual, group, role, service, or device identifier; selecting an identifier that identifies the intended individual, group, role, service, or device; and assigning the identifier to that intended party, including assigning a unique name and/or number for identifying and tracking user identity.
[NIST 800-53 IA-4 (Low, Moderate, High) | FedRAMP IA-4 | ARC-AMPE IA-4 | HIPAA 164.312(a)(2)(i) (Required)]
IAM Engineering shall prevent reuse of identifiers for an organization-defined time period.

IAM Engineering shall prevent reuse of identifiers for two (2) years, including ensuring previous identifier-based access authorizations (e.g., access to sensitive files or folders) are removed from the system before the identifier is reused.

IAM Engineering shall manage individual identifiers by uniquely identifying each individual using organization-defined characteristics identifying individual status; under FedRAMP these characteristics are contractors and foreign nationals.
[NIST 800-53 IA-4(4) (Moderate, High) | FedRAMP IA-4(4) | ARC-AMPE IA-4(4)]
IAM Engineering shall implement procedures to verify that a person or entity seeking access to electronic protected health information is the one claimed.

IAM Engineering shall identity proof users who require accounts for logical access to systems based on appropriate identity assurance level requirements as specified in applicable standards and guidelines, resolve user identities to a unique individual, and collect, validate, and verify identity evidence.

IAM Engineering shall identity proof all users who require logical access accounts — including non-privileged (i.e., consumer) accounts — to Identity Assurance Level 2 (IAL-2) or higher per the latest published NIST SP 800-63 Digital Identity Guidelines suite; for ACA Consumer Accounts, the Federal Data Services Hub (FDSH) Remote Identity Proofing (RIDP) Service may be used in lieu of otherwise meeting IAL-2.

IAM Engineering shall require that the registration process to receive an account for logical access includes supervisor or sponsor authorization, for all accounts including non-privileged (i.e., consumer) accounts.
IAM Engineering shall require that evidence of individual identification be presented to the registration authority, for all accounts including non-privileged (i.e., consumer) accounts.

IAM Engineering shall require that the presented identity evidence be validated and verified through organization-approved methods of validation and verification, which under ARC-AMPE must comply with applicable agreements with CMS, for all accounts including non-privileged (i.e., consumer) accounts.
Upon termination of individual employment, IAM Engineering shall disable system access within an organization-defined time period.
Upon termination of individual employment, IAM Engineering shall disable system access within the same day as termination.
IAM Engineering shall terminate or revoke any authenticators and credentials associated with the terminated individual.

IAM Engineering shall implement procedures for terminating access to electronic protected health information when the employment of, or other arrangement with, a workforce member ends, or as required by determinations made under the workforce clearance procedure.

IAM Engineering shall execute termination actions in a timely manner — which is essential for individuals terminated for cause — and in certain situations shall consider disabling the system accounts of individuals being terminated before notifying the individuals of the termination actions.

IAM Engineering shall conduct exit interviews that include a discussion of information security topics; under ARC-AMPE, this discussion must address non-disclosure of information security and privacy information.

IAM Engineering shall retrieve all security-related organizational system-related property (including hardware authentication tokens, system administration technical manuals, keys, identification cards, and building passes) from the terminated individual.
IAM Engineering shall retain access to organizational information and systems formerly controlled by the terminated individual.

IAM Engineering shall notify terminated individuals of applicable, legally binding post-employment requirements for the protection of organizational information, and shall require terminated individuals to sign an acknowledgment of post-employment requirements as part of the organizational termination process.

IAM Engineering shall use organization-defined automated mechanisms to notify organization-defined personnel or roles of individual termination actions and/or disable access to system resources, implemented via the [Identity Provider] integrated with the [HR System].

IAM Engineering shall review and confirm the ongoing operational need for current logical and physical access authorizations to systems and facilities when individuals are reassigned or transferred to other positions within the organization.
IAM Engineering shall initiate organization-defined transfer or reassignment actions within an organization-defined time period following the formal transfer action.
IAM Engineering shall initiate reassignment actions to ensure all system accesses no longer required (e.g., need to know) are removed or disabled within twenty-four (24) hours.
IAM Engineering shall modify access authorizations as needed to correspond with any changes in operational need due to reassignment or transfer.
IAM Engineering shall notify organization-defined personnel or roles within an organization-defined time period following transfer or reassignment. \[NIST 800-53 PS-5 (Low, Moderate, High) | ARC-AMPE

analyze: This Standard establishes Example Org's requirements for remote access, wireless access, mobile device access, external system connections, portable storage device use, and publicly accessible content, in order to protect the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of organizational information and systems.
Network Security owns this process end to end, including authorization, monitoring, documentation, and review of all remote and third-party access.

Network Security is accountable for: - Establishing, authorizing, documenting, and periodically reviewing all remote access, wireless access, mobile device, and external system connections. - Maintaining the VPN and remote-access configuration as the authoritative record of allowed connection types, configuration requirements, and usage restrictions. - Maintaining the Third-party access register as the authoritative record of external parties, external systems, and third-party agreements authorized to connect to or exchange data with organizational systems. - Coordinating with other teams (e.g., system owners, [Ticketing System] administrators, [Identity Provider] administrators) as participants in individual steps of this process, without relinquishing ownership of the overall process or its handoffs.

- Network Security must establish and document, within the VPN and remote-access configuration, usage restrictions, configuration/connection requirements, and implementation guidance for each type of remote access allowed, and must authorize each type of remote access to the system prior to allowing such connections.
[NIST 800-53 AC-17 Low/Moderate/High | ARC-AMPE AC-17 AE Mandatory]
- Network Security must employ automated mechanisms to monitor and control remote access methods.
[NIST 800-53 AC-17(1) Moderate/High | ARC-AMPE AC-17(1) AE Mandatory]

- Network Security must implement cryptographic mechanisms to protect the confidentiality and integrity of remote access sessions; encrypting remote sessions is required to protect the confidentiality and integrity of sensitive information.
[NIST 800-53 AC-17(2) Moderate/High | ARC-AMPE AC-17(2) AE Mandatory]
- Network Security must route all remote accesses through authorized and managed network access control points.
[NIST 800-53 AC-17(3) Moderate/High | ARC-AMPE AC-17(3) AE Mandatory]

- Network Security must authorize the execution of privileged commands and access to security-relevant information via remote access only in a format that provides assessable evidence, and only for [Assignment: Organization-Defined Remote Access Needs] (NIST) / for compelling operational needs, which must be defined and documented in the applicable System Security and Privacy Plan (ARC-AMPE).
The rationale for such remote access must be documented in the security plan for the system.
[NIST 800-53 AC-17(4) Moderate/High | ARC-AMPE AC-17(4) AE Mandatory]
- Network Security must protect information about remote access mechanisms from unauthorized use and disclosure.
- Network Security must provide the capability to disconnect or disable remote access to the system within [Assignment: Organization-Defined Time Period] (NIST) / within one (1) hour (ARC-AMPE).
ARC-AMPE additionally requires that network connections (system-to-system interconnections) be terminated or suspended within one (1) hour upon issuance of an order by organization-defined officials.
- Network Security must implement [Assignment: Organization-Defined Authentication Mechanisms] to authenticate [Assignment: Organization-Defined Remote Commands].

- Network Security must implement policies and procedures that specify the proper functions to be performed, the manner in which those functions are performed, and the physical attributes of the surroundings of a specific workstation or class of workstation that can access electronic protected health information.

- Network Security must establish configuration requirements, connection requirements, and implementation guidance for each type of wireless access, documented in the VPN and remote-access configuration, and must authorize each type of wireless access to the system prior to allowing such connections.
[NIST 800-53 AC-18 Low/Moderate/High | ARC-AMPE AC-18 AE Mandatory]

- Network Security must protect wireless access to the system using authentication of users and/or devices (NIST: selection of one or more) / authentication of both users and devices (ARC-AMPE), together with encryption.
ARC-AMPE additionally requires that all wireless communications be encrypted using the latest published FIPS 140-compliant encryption standards.
[NIST 800-53 AC-18(1) Moderate/High | ARC-AMPE AC-18(1) AE Mandatory]
- Network Security must disable, when not intended for use, wireless networking capabilities embedded within system components prior to issuance and deployment.
[NIST 800-53 AC-18(3) Moderate/High | ARC-AMPE AC-18(3) AE Mandatory]
- Network Security must identify and explicitly authorize users allowed to independently configure wireless networking capabilities.

- Network Security must select radio antennas and calibrate transmission power levels to reduce the probability that signals from wireless access points can be received outside of organization-controlled boundaries.

- Network Security must establish configuration requirements, connection requirements, and implementation guidance for organization-controlled mobile devices, including when such devices are outside controlled areas, and must authorize the connection of mobile devices to organizational systems.
[NIST 800-53 AC-19 Low/Moderate/High | ARC-AMPE AC-19 AE Mandatory]

- Network Security must prohibit the use of unclassified mobile devices in facilities containing systems that process, store, or transmit classified information unless specifically permitted by the authorizing official.
- Connection of unclassified mobile devices to classified systems must be prohibited.
- Connection of unclassified mobile devices to unclassified systems must require authorizing official approval.
- Use of internal or external modems or wireless interfaces within the unclassified mobile devices must be prohibited.

- Unclassified mobile devices and their stored information must be subject to random reviews/inspections by organization-defined security officials, following incident handling policy if classified information is found.
- Connection of classified mobile devices to classified systems must be restricted per organization-defined security policies.

- Network Security must employ full-device encryption or container-based encryption to protect the confidentiality and integrity of information on [Assignment: Organization-Defined Mobile Devices] (NIST) / on approved mobile devices, using the latest published FIPS 140-compliant encryption standards (ARC-AMPE).
ARC-AMPE additionally requires that information on all mobile devices containing Personally Identifiable Information (PII) be encrypted.
[NIST 800-53 AC-19(5) Moderate/High | ARC-AMPE AC-19(5) AE Mandatory]

- Network Security must establish [Assignment: Organization-Defined Terms and Conditions] and/or identify [Assignment: Organization-Defined Controls Asserted] to be implemented on external systems, consistent with the trust relationships established with other organizations owning, operating, and/or maintaining external systems, so that authorized individuals may access the system from external systems and process, store, or transmit organization-controlled information using external systems; or must prohibit the use of [Assignment: Organization-Defined Prohibited Types of External Systems].
All such determinations must be recorded in the Third-party access register.
[NIST 800-53 AC-20 Low/Moderate/High | FedRAMP AC-20 | ARC-AMPE AC-20 AE Mandatory]

- Network Security must differentiate the interrelated controls governing external access: AC-20 governs system access to and from external systems; CA-3 governs documentation of the agreement between system owners when data is exchanged between the system and an external system; SA-9 governs the responsibilities of external system owners, which are typically captured in the CA-3 agreement.

- Network Security must permit authorized individuals to use an external system to access the system or to process, store, or transmit organization-controlled information only after (a) verifying implementation of the controls required on the external system as specified in organizational security and privacy policies/plans, or (b) retaining approved system connection or processing agreements with the entity hosting the external system, recorded in the Third-party access register.
[NIST 800-53 AC-20(1) Moderate/High | ARC-AMPE AC-20(1) AE Mandatory]

- Network Security must restrict the use of non-organizationally owned systems or system components to process, store, or transmit organizational information using [Assignment: Organization-Defined Restrictions] (NIST).
- Contractor-owned devices are documented in the contract and applicable security/privacy plans and are explicitly authorized in writing by the Authorizing Official (AO) or designated representative;
- Personally owned devices comply with organizational policies on personally-owned systems;
- Appropriate security/privacy safeguards are employed for the sensitivity of the data; and
- Full-device or virtual container encryption is implemented to reduce vulnerability of information processed, stored, or transmitted by non-organizationally owned systems/components.

ARC-AMPE additionally states that use of personally owned devices is strongly discouraged, and requires that, prior to being granted access to PII on remote devices, device users acknowledge through a binding agreement their responsibility to safeguard accessible PII and their agreement to the organization's ability to manage that PII on the device, including confiscation (in consultation with organizational counsel) if necessary.
- Network Security must prohibit the use of [Assignment: Organization-Defined Network-Accessible Storage Devices] in external systems.

- Network Security must restrict the use of organization-controlled portable storage devices by authorized individuals on external systems using [Assignment: Organization-Defined Restrictions] (NIST).
ARC-AMPE specifies these restrictions must be defined in the applicable system security and privacy plans, and that such use is prohibited unless:
- The use is documented in appropriate security/privacy plans;
- The use is explicitly authorized in writing by the Authorizing Official (AO) or designated representative;
- Personally owned devices to which such storage devices are attached comply with organizational policies on personally owned systems; and
- Appropriate security/privacy safeguards are employed for the sensitivity of the data.
[NIST 800-53 AC-20(2) Moderate/High | ARC-AMPE AC-20(2) AE Mandatory]
- Network Security must prohibit the use of organization-controlled portable storage devices by authorized individuals on external systems.

- Network Security must designate individuals authorized to make information publicly accessible; train those individuals to ensure publicly accessible information does not contain nonpublic information; review proposed content prior to posting on the publicly accessible system to ensure nonpublic information is not included; and review content on the publicly accessible system for nonpublic information at [Assignment: Organization-Defined Frequency] (NIST), or bi-weekly and no less often than every fourteen (14) days (ARC-AMPE), removing such information if discovered.
[NIST 800-53 AC-22 Low/Moderate/High | ARC-AMPE AC-22 AE Mandatory]

Network Security must maintain the following evidence in support of this Standard: - **VPN and remote-access configuration** — reflecting all authorized remote access types, wireless access types, mobile device connection authorizations, usage restrictions, configuration/connection requirements, and implementation guidance described in Sections 3–5. - **Third-party access register** — reflecting all authorized external systems, third-party connections, connection/processing agreements, and restrictions on non-organizationally owned systems and portable storage devices described in Section 6–7.

Network Security must review the VPN and remote-access configuration and the Third-party access register on a quarterly basis to confirm that authorizations, configuration requirements, and third-party agreements remain accurate and continue to reflect actual remote, wireless, mobile, and external system access in use.

analyze: This Standard establishes Example Org's requirements for the processing and transparency of personally identifiable information (PII) and for the documentation obligations arising under the HIPAA Security Rule.
The Data Governance team is accountable for this process end to end, including all handoffs to participating teams.
This Standard applies to all personnel and roles designated by Data Governance.
Data Governance must develop, document, and disseminate to organization-defined personnel and roles an organization-level personally identifiable information (PII) processing and transparency policy.
NIST also permits mission/business process-level and system-level policies.

The policy must address purpose, scope, roles, responsibilities, management commitment, coordination among organizational entities, and compliance, and must be consistent with applicable laws, executive orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, and guidelines.
Data Governance must develop, document, and disseminate procedures to facilitate implementation of the PII processing and transparency policy and its associated controls.
Data Governance is designated as the official responsible for managing the development, documentation, and dissemination of the PII processing and transparency policy and procedures.
Data Governance must be named as the responsible official in the appropriate security and privacy documents.

Data Governance must review and update the PII processing and transparency policy and procedures at least every one (1) year, and following organization-defined events, including: - Assessment or audit findings; - Breaches or security/privacy incidents; and - Changes to applicable laws (including privacy laws), executive orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, and guidelines.
Data Governance must actively monitor for changes to applicable privacy laws, regulations, and policies affecting PII processing and transparency.

Data Governance must maintain the policies and procedures implemented to comply with the HIPAA Security Rule, and any record of an action, activity, or assessment required to be documented, in written (which may be electronic) form.
Data Governance must retain HIPAA documentation for 6 years from the date of its creation or the date when it was last in effect, whichever is later.
Data Governance must make HIPAA documentation available to those persons responsible for implementing the procedures to which the documentation pertains.

Data Governance must review HIPAA documentation periodically — at least annually — and update it as needed in response to environmental or operational changes affecting the security of electronic protected health information.
Data Governance must determine and document the organization-defined authority that permits the organization-defined processing of personally identifiable information (PII).
The processing of PII must be restricted to only that which is authorized.
Data Governance must maintain the following artifacts as evidence of this process:

| Artifact | Description | Owner | | ------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------- | | Data inventory and classification register | Records the organization's PII processing, including the documented authority permitting each defined processing activity (Section 6.1) | Data Governance | | Retention schedule | Records the retention obligations for documentation maintained under this Standard, including the 6-year HIPAA documentation retention period (Section 5.2) | Data Governance |

Data Governance is responsible for keeping these artifacts current as part of the annual review cycle defined in Section 4 and in response to the review triggers and update obligations defined in Sections 4 and 5.4.
