analyze: This Standard establishes requirements for audit and accountability controls within Acme Health information systems.

It defines how the organization shall generate, protect, review, and retain audit records to support security monitoring, incident response, forensic analysis, and regulatory compliance with applicable laws and regulations governing healthcare information security.

This Standard applies to all information systems and system components that process, store, or transmit electronic protected health information (ePHI) and other sensitive organizational data, including systems at the organization-level, mission/business process-level, and system-level.
This Standard covers audit event configuration, audit record content and protection, audit review and analysis, audit retention, and continuous system monitoring capabilities.
Acme Health shall designate an [Designated Official] to manage the development, documentation, and dissemination of the audit and accountability policy and procedures.
[NIST 800-53 AU-1 Low, Moderate, High | ARC-AMPE AU-1 AE Mandatory]

The [Designated Personnel or Roles] shall be responsible for implementing the audit and accountability controls defined in this Standard, reviewing audit records, responding to audit failures, and ensuring compliance with retention requirements.

Acme Health shall develop, document, and disseminate to [Designated Personnel or Roles] an audit and accountability policy at [Selection: organization-level; mission/business process-level; system-level] that addresses purpose, scope, roles, responsibilities, management commitment, coordination among organizational entities, and compliance, and is consistent with applicable laws, executive orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, and guidelines.
[NIST 800-53 AU-1 Low, Moderate, High | ARC-AMPE AU-1 AE Mandatory]

Acme Health shall develop, document, and disseminate an organization-level audit and accountability policy that addresses purpose, scope, roles, responsibilities, management commitment, coordination among organizational entities, and compliance, and is consistent with applicable laws, Executive Orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, and guidelines.

Acme Health shall develop, document, and disseminate to [Designated Personnel or Roles] procedures to facilitate the implementation of the audit and accountability policy and the associated audit and accountability controls.
[NIST 800-53 AU-1 Low, Moderate, High | ARC-AMPE AU-1 AE Mandatory]
Acme Health shall review and update the current audit and accountability policy [Review Frequency] and following [Triggering Events].
Acme Health shall review and update the current audit and accountability policy at least every one (1) year and following organization-defined events.
Acme Health shall review and update the current audit and accountability procedures [Review Frequency] and following [Triggering Events].
Acme Health shall review and update the current audit and accountability procedures at least every one (1) year and following organization-defined events.
Acme Health shall maintain the policies and procedures implemented to comply with HIPAA Security Rule in written (which may be electronic) form.
Acme Health shall maintain a written (which may be electronic) record of required actions, activities, or assessments.
Acme Health shall retain documentation for 6 years from the date of its creation or the date when it last was in effect, whichever is later.
Acme Health shall make documentation available to those persons responsible for implementing the procedures to which the documentation pertains.
Acme Health shall review documentation periodically, and update as needed, in response to environmental or operational changes affecting the security of the electronic protected health information.
Acme Health shall implement hardware, software, and/or procedural mechanisms that record and examine activity in information systems that contain or use electronic protected health information.
Acme Health shall identify the types of events that the system is capable of logging in support of the audit function: [Audit-Capable Event Types].

Acme Health shall identify the types of events that the system is capable of logging in support of the audit function: organization-defined event types based on a risk assessment of organization-defined mission/business needs.
Acme Health shall coordinate the event logging function with other organizational entities requiring audit-related information to guide and inform the selection criteria for events to be logged.
[NIST 800-53 AU-2 Low, Moderate, High | ARC-AMPE AU-2 AE Mandatory]
Acme Health shall specify the following event types for logging within the system: [Specified Event Types and Frequencies].

Acme Health shall specify the following event types for logging within the system: organization-defined event types along with organization-defined frequency or situation for each identified event type.

Acme Health shall include the following minimum set of event types for logging within the system: user log-on and log-off (successful or unsuccessful); configuration changes; application alerts and error messages; all system administration (including privileged user) activities; modification of privileges and access; account creation, modification, or deletion; concurrent log-on from different work stations; and override of access control mechanisms.
Acme Health shall provide a rationale for why the event types selected for logging are deemed to be adequate to support after-the-fact investigations of incidents.
[NIST 800-53 AU-2 Low, Moderate, High | ARC-AMPE AU-2 AE Mandatory]
Acme Health shall review and update the event types selected for logging [Review Frequency].
Acme Health shall review and update the event types selected for logging at least every one (1) year and whenever there is a significant system modification or change in the system environment.
Acme Health shall ensure that audit records contain information that establishes what type of event occurred.
[NIST 800-53 AU-3 Low, Moderate, High | ARC-AMPE AU-3 AE Mandatory]
Acme Health shall ensure that audit records contain information that establishes when the event occurred.
[NIST 800-53 AU-3 Low, Moderate, High | ARC-AMPE AU-3 AE Mandatory]
Acme Health shall ensure that audit records contain information that establishes where the event occurred.
[NIST 800-53 AU-3 Low, Moderate, High | ARC-AMPE AU-3 AE Mandatory]
Acme Health shall ensure that audit records contain information that establishes the source of the event.
[NIST 800-53 AU-3 Low, Moderate, High | ARC-AMPE AU-3 AE Mandatory]
Acme Health shall ensure that audit records contain information that establishes the outcome of the event.
[NIST 800-53 AU-3 Low, Moderate, High | ARC-AMPE AU-3 AE Mandatory]

[NIST 800-53 AU-3 Low, Moderate, High | ARC-AMPE AU-3 AE Mandatory]

Acme Health shall record disclosures of sensitive information, including Protected Health Information (PHI) and financial information, logging the information type, date, time, receiving party, and releasing party.
Acme Health shall generate audit records containing [Additional Audit Information].

Acme Health shall generate audit records containing the following additional information and event details: session, connection, transaction, or activity duration; for client-server transactions, the number of bytes received and bytes sent; additional informational messages to diagnose or identify the event; characteristics that describe or identify the object or resource being acted upon; individual identities of group account users; and full-text of privileged commands.

Acme Health shall limit personally identifiable information contained in audit records to the following elements identified in the privacy risk assessment: [PII Elements from Privacy Risk Assessment].

analyze: This Standard defines Acme Health's requirements for the governance and accountability of artificial intelligence (AI) systems across their lifecycle — from design and development through deployment, monitoring, and decommissioning.
It applies to all AI systems developed, procured, deployed, or used by or on behalf of Acme Health, including third-party AI systems.
The AI Risk / GRC team owns this process end to end and is accountable for its implementation, effectiveness, and outcomes.

Other teams (including but not limited to legal, compliance, product management, engineering, human resources, and executive leadership) participate in individual steps as described below, but AI Risk / GRC is responsible for defining, coordinating, and reviewing the overall AI governance program and for answering for its outcomes.

AI Risk / GRC must ensure that policies, processes, procedures, and practices related to mapping, measuring, and managing AI risks are in place, transparent, and implemented effectively across Acme Health.
AI Risk / GRC must ensure that legal and regulatory requirements involving AI are understood, managed, and documented.

NIST suggests, among its 3 actions for Govern 1.1, that the organization maintain awareness of the legal and regulatory considerations specific to its industry, sector, business purpose, and the application context of each deployed AI system; align its risk management efforts with applicable legal standards; and maintain policies for training and re-training staff on the legal or regulatory considerations that may affect AI-related design, development, and deployment activities.
[NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.1 Action 1 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.1 Action 2 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.1 Action 3]
AI Risk / GRC must ensure that the characteristics of trustworthy AI are integrated into Acme Health's policies, processes, procedures, and practices.

NIST suggests, among its 15 actions for Govern 1.2, that the organization define key terms and concepts related to AI systems and the scope of their purposes and intended uses; connect AI governance to existing organizational governance and risk controls; align to broader data governance policies and practices, particularly for sensitive or otherwise risky data; detail standards for experimental design, data quality, and model training; outline and document risk mapping and measurement processes and standards; detail model testing and validation processes; detail review processes for legal and risk functions; establish the frequency and detail of monitoring, auditing, and review processes; outline change management requirements; outline processes for internal and external stakeholder engagement; establish whistleblower policies for reporting serious AI system concerns; detail and test incident response plans; verify that formal AI risk management policies align with existing legal standards and industry best practices and norms; establish AI risk management policies that broadly align to AI system trustworthy characteristics; and verify that formal AI risk management policies include currently deployed and third-party AI systems.

[NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.2 Action 1 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.2 Action 2 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.2 Action 3 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.2 Action 4 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.2 Action 5 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.2 Action 6 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.2 Action 7 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.2 Action 8 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.2 Action 9 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.2 Action 10 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.2 Action 11 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.2 Action 12 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.2 Action 13 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.2 Action 14 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.2 Action 15]
AI Risk / GRC must establish processes, procedures, and practices to determine the needed level of risk management activities based on Acme Health's risk tolerance.

NIST suggests, among its 5 actions for Govern 1.3, that the organization establish policies defining mechanisms for measuring or understanding an AI system's potential impacts, including via regular impact assessments at key stages of the AI lifecycle connected to system impacts and the frequency of system updates; establish policies for measuring or understanding the likelihood of an AI system's impacts and their magnitude at key lifecycle stages; establish policies defining assessment scales for measuring potential AI system impact, whether qualitative (such as red-amber-green) or based on simulations or econometric approaches; establish policies for assigning an overall risk measurement approach, such as combining impact and likelihood; and establish policies assigning systems to uniform risk scales valid across the organization's AI portfolio while acknowledging that risk tolerance and risk levels may change over an AI system's lifecycle.

[NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.3 Action 1 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.3 Action 2 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.3 Action 3 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.3 Action 4 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.3 Action 5]
AI Risk / GRC must establish the risk management process and its outcomes through transparent policies, procedures, and other controls based on Acme Health's organizational risk priorities.

NIST suggests, among its 7 actions for Govern 1.4, that the organization establish and regularly review documentation policies addressing AI actor contact information, business justification, scope and usages, expected and potential risks and impacts, assumptions and limitations, training data description and characterization, algorithmic methodology, evaluated alternative approaches, output data description, testing and validation results, upstream and downstream dependencies, deployment/monitoring/change management plans, and stakeholder engagement plans; verify that documentation policies are standardized across the organization and remain current; establish policies for a model documentation inventory system and regularly review its completeness, usability, and efficacy; establish mechanisms to regularly review the efficacy of risk management processes; identify AI actors responsible for evaluating the efficacy of risk management processes and for course-correction; establish policies and processes regarding public disclosure of AI use and risk management material such as impact assessments, audits, and model documentation; and document and review the use and efficacy of transparency tools, following industry standards while a model is in use.

[NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.4 Action 1 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.4 Action 2 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.4 Action 3 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.4 Action 4 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.4 Action 5 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.4 Action 6 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.4 Action 7]

AI Risk / GRC must plan ongoing monitoring and periodic review of the risk management process and its outcomes, define organizational roles and responsibilities clearly, and determine the frequency of periodic review.

NIST suggests, among its 7 actions for Govern 1.5, that the organization establish policies to allocate appropriate resources and capacity for assessing AI systems' impacts on individuals, communities, and society; establish policies and procedures for monitoring and addressing AI system performance and trustworthiness, including bias and security problems, across the system lifecycle; establish policies for AI system incident response or confirm that existing incident response policies apply to AI systems; establish policies defining the organizational functions and personnel responsible for AI system monitoring and incident response; establish mechanisms enabling impacted individuals or communities to share feedback about negative AI system impacts; establish mechanisms providing recourse for impacted individuals or communities to contest problematic AI system outcomes; and establish opt-out mechanisms.

[NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.5 Action 1 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.5 Action 2 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.5 Action 3 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.5 Action 4 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.5 Action 5 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.5 Action 6 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.5 Action 7]
AI Risk / GRC must maintain mechanisms to inventory AI systems, resourced according to Acme Health's organizational risk priorities.

NIST suggests, among its 4 actions for Govern 1.6, that the organization establish policies defining the creation and maintenance of AI system inventories; establish policies defining a specific individual or team responsible for maintaining the inventory; establish policies defining which models or systems are inventoried, with preference for inventorying all models or systems, or at minimum high-risk models or systems deployed in high-stakes settings; and establish policies defining the model or system attributes to be inventoried, such as documentation, links to source code, incident response plans, data dictionaries, and AI actor contact information.
[NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.6 Action 1 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.6 Action 2 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.6 Action 3 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.6 Action 4]
AI Risk / GRC must maintain processes and procedures for decommissioning and phasing out AI systems safely and in a manner that does not increase risks or decrease Acme Health's trustworthiness.

NIST suggests, among its 4 actions for Govern 1.7, that the organization establish policies for decommissioning AI systems addressing user and community concerns and reputational risks, business continuity and financial risks, upstream and downstream system dependencies, regulatory requirements such as data retention, potential future legal or forensic investigations, and migration to a replacement system where appropriate; establish policies delineating where and for how long decommissioned systems, models, and related artifacts are stored; establish practices to track accountability and consider how decommissioning and other adaptations contribute to downstream impacts for individuals, groups, and communities; and establish policies addressing ancillary data or artifacts that must be preserved for a full understanding or execution of the decommissioned AI system, such as predictions, explanations, intermediate input feature representations, and credentials.
[NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.7 Action 1 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.7 Action 2 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.7 Action 3 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.7 Action 4]
AI Risk / GRC must ensure accountability structures are in place so that the appropriate teams and individuals are empowered, responsible, and trained for mapping, measuring, and managing AI risks.

AI Risk / GRC must document roles, responsibilities, and lines of communication related to mapping, measuring, and managing AI risks, and ensure they are clear to individuals and teams throughout Acme Health.

NIST suggests, among its 6 actions for Govern 2.1, that the organization establish policies defining AI risk management roles and responsibilities for positions directly and indirectly related to AI systems, including boards or advisory committees, senior management, AI audit functions, product and project management, AI design, development, human-AI interaction, testing and evaluation, acquisition and procurement, impact assessment, and oversight functions; establish policies promoting regular communication among AI actors participating in risk management efforts; establish policies separating AI system development functions from testing functions to enable independent course-correction; establish policies to identify, increase transparency of, and prevent conflicts of interest in AI risk management efforts; establish policies to counteract confirmation bias and market incentives that may hinder AI risk management efforts; and establish policies incentivizing AI actors to collaborate with existing legal, oversight, compliance, or enterprise risk functions.

[NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 2.1 Action 1 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 2.1 Action 2 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 2.1 Action 3 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 2.1 Action 4 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 2.1 Action 5 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 2.1 Action 6]

AI Risk / GRC must ensure that Acme Health's personnel and partners receive AI risk management training enabling them to perform their duties and responsibilities consistent with related policies, procedures, and agreements.

NIST suggests, among its 6 actions for Govern 2.2, that the organization establish policies for ongoing personnel education on applicable laws and regulations for AI systems, potential negative impacts arising from AI systems, organizational AI policies, and trustworthy AI characteristics; ensure that trainings are suitable across AI actor sub-groups, distinguishing technical roles from oversight roles; ensure that trainings comprehensively address technical and socio-technical aspects of AI risk management; verify that organizational AI policies include mechanisms for internal AI personnel to acknowledge and commit to their roles and responsibilities; verify that organizational policies address change management and include mechanisms to communicate and acknowledge substantial AI system changes; and define paths along internal and external chains of accountability to escalate risk concerns.

[NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 2.2 Action 1 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 2.2 Action 2 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 2.2 Action 3 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 2.2 Action 4 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 2.2 Action 5 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 2.2 Action 6]
Executive leadership must take responsibility for decisions about risks associated with AI system development and deployment.

NIST suggests, among its 2 actions for Govern 2.3, that organizational management declare risk tolerances for developing or using AI systems, support and actively participate in AI risk management efforts, integrate a risk and harm prevention mindset throughout the AI lifecycle as part of organizational culture, support competent risk management executives, and delegate the power, resources, and authorization to perform risk management at each appropriate level of the management chain; and that organizations establish board committees for AI risk management and oversight functions, integrated within the organization's broader enterprise risk management approach.
[NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 2.3 Action 1 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 2.3 Action 2]
AI Risk / GRC must ensure that workforce diversity, equity, inclusion, and accessibility processes are prioritized in the mapping, measuring, and managing of AI risks throughout the lifecycle.

AI Risk / GRC must ensure that decision-making related to mapping, measuring, and managing AI risks throughout the lifecycle is informed by a diverse team, including diversity of demographics, disciplines, experience, expertise, and backgrounds.

NIST suggests, among its 5 actions for Govern 3.1, that the organization define policies and hiring practices at the outset that promote interdisciplinary roles, competencies, skills, and capacity for AI efforts; define policies and hiring practices leading to demographic and domain expertise diversity, empower staff with resources and support, and facilitate staff feedback and concerns without fear of reprisal; establish policies facilitating inclusivity and the integration of new insights into existing practice; seek external expertise to supplement organizational diversity, equity, inclusion, and accessibility where internal expertise is lacking; and establish policies incentivizing AI actors to collaborate with existing nondiscrimination, accessibility and accommodation, and human resource functions, employee resource groups, and diversity, equity, inclusion, and accessibility initiatives.

[NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 3.1 Action 1 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 3.1 Action 2 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 3.1 Action 3 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 3.1 Action 4 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 3.1 Action 5]
AI Risk / GRC must maintain policies and procedures to define and differentiate roles and responsibilities for human-AI configurations and oversight of AI systems.

NIST suggests, among its 8 actions for Govern 3.2, that the organization establish policies and procedures defining and differentiating human roles and responsibilities when using, interacting with, or monitoring AI systems; establish procedures for capturing and tracking risk information related to human-AI configurations and associated outcomes; establish policies for developing proficiency standards for AI actors carrying out system operation and oversight tasks; establish specified risk management training protocols for those same actors; establish policies and procedures regarding AI actor roles and responsibilities for human oversight of deployed systems; establish policies and procedures defining human-AI configurations in relation to organizational risk tolerances and associated documentation; establish policies to enhance the explanation, interpretation, and overall transparency of AI systems; and establish policies for managing risks regarding known difficulties in human-AI configurations, human-AI teaming, and AI system user experience and interactions.

[NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 3.2 Action 1 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 3.2 Action 2 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 3.2 Action 3 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 3.2 Action 4 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 3.2 Action 5 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 3.2 Action 6 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 3.2 Action 7 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 3.2 Action 8]
Organizational teams must be committed to a culture that considers and communicates AI risk.

AI Risk / GRC must ensure that organizational policies and practices foster a critical thinking and safety-first mindset in the design, development, deployment, and uses of AI systems to minimize potential negative impacts.

NIST suggests, among its 5 actions for Govern 4.1, that the organization establish policies requiring the inclusion of oversight functions such as legal, compliance, and risk management from the outset of the system design process; establish policies promoting effective challenge of AI system design, implementation, and deployment decisions through mechanisms such as the three lines of defense, model audits, or red-teaming to minimize workplace risks such as groupthink; establish policies incentivizing a safety-first mindset and general critical thinking and review at the organizational and procedural level; establish whistleblower protections for insiders who report perceived serious problems with AI systems; and establish policies to integrate a harm and risk prevention mindset throughout the AI lifecycle.

[NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 4.1 Action 1 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 4.1 Action 2 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 4.1 Action 3 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 4.1 Action 4 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 4.1 Action 5]
Organizational teams must document the risks and potential impacts of the AI technology they design, develop, deploy, evaluate, and use, and communicate about the impacts more broadly.

NIST suggests, among its 4 actions for Govern 4.2, that the organization establish impact assessment policies and processes for AI systems it uses; align impact assessment activities with relevant regulatory or legal requirements; verify that impact assessment activities are appropriate to evaluate a system's potential negative impact and the pace of its change, and that assessments are applied on a regular basis; and utilize impact assessments to inform broader evaluations of AI system risk.
[NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 4.2 Action 1 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 4.2 Action 2 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 4.2 Action 3 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 4.2 Action 4]
AI Risk / GRC must maintain organizational practices to enable AI testing, identification of incidents, and information sharing.

NIST suggests, among its 5 actions for Govern 4.3, that the organization establish policies and procedures to facilitate and equip AI system testing; establish organizational commitment to identifying AI system limitations and sharing insights about those limitations within appropriate AI actor groups; establish policies for reporting and documenting incident response; establish policies and processes regarding public disclosure of incidents and information sharing; and establish guidelines for incident handling related to AI system risks and performance.

[NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 4.3 Action 1 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 4.3 Action 2 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 4.3 Action 3 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 4.3 Action 4 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 4.3 Action 5]
AI Risk / GRC must maintain processes for robust engagement with relevant AI actors.

AI Risk / GRC must maintain organizational policies and practices to collect, consider, prioritize, and integrate feedback from those external to the team that developed or deployed the AI system regarding the potential individual and societal impacts related to AI risks.

NIST suggests, among its 3 actions for Govern 5.1, that the organization establish AI risk management policies that explicitly address mechanisms for collecting, evaluating, and incorporating stakeholder and user feedback, which could include recourse mechanisms for faulty AI system outputs, bug bounties, human-centered design, user-interaction and experience research, and participatory stakeholder engagement with individuals and communities that may experience negative impacts; verify that stakeholder feedback is considered and addressed, including environmental concerns, across the entire population of intended users, including historically excluded populations, people with disabilities, older people, and those with limited access to the internet and other basic technologies; and clarify the organization's principles as they apply to AI systems, considering those proposed publicly, to inform external stakeholders of the organization's values, and consider publishing or adopting AI principles.
[NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 5.1 Action 1 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 5.1 Action 2 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 5.1 Action 3]

AI Risk / GRC must establish mechanisms to enable the team that developed or deployed AI systems to regularly incorporate adjudicated feedback from relevant AI actors into system design and implementation.

NIST suggests, among its 5 actions for Govern 5.2, that the organization explicitly acknowledge that AI systems, and the use of AI, present inherent costs and risks along with potential benefits; define reasonable risk tolerances for AI systems informed by laws, regulation, best practices, or industry standards; establish policies ensuring that all relevant AI actors are provided meaningful opportunities to give feedback on system design and implementation; establish policies defining how to assign AI systems to established risk tolerance levels by combining system impact assessments with the likelihood that an impact occurs, which may involve econometric evaluations, red-amber-green scales, allocation of risk management resources proportional to risk tolerance levels, and policies for approval, conditional approval, or disapproval of AI system design, implementation, and deployment; and establish policies facilitating the early decommissioning of AI systems that surpass the organization's ability to reasonably mitigate risks.

[NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 5.2 Action 1 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 5.2 Action 2 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 5.2 Action 3 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 5.2 Action 4 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 5.2 Action 5]
heading_statements: 5.4 Testing, Incident Identification, and Information Sharing (Govern 4.3)

analyze: | Field | Value | | ------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------- | | Owning Team | Security Operations | | Cadence | Continuous | | Evidence Artifacts | Incident tickets with timelines; Tabletop exercise report | | Applies To | All Example Org personnel, systems, and business processes |
This Standard establishes the mandatory requirements for Example Org's incident response capability.
It addresses the prevention, detection, containment, and correction of security violations, and the identification of and response to suspected or known security incidents.
[NIST 800-53 IR-1 | FedRAMP IR-1 | HIPAA Security Rule 164.308(a)(6)(i) | HIPAA Security Rule 164.308(a)(1)(i)]
Security Operations is accountable for this process end to end, including all handoffs between teams described in this Standard.
Other teams named in this Standard participate in individual steps but do not own the process.
Example Org must follow the FedRAMP Incident Evaluation and Communication rules in implementing the incident response controls defined in this Standard.
[FedRAMP IR-1 | FedRAMP IR-2 | FedRAMP IR-3 | FedRAMP IR-4 | FedRAMP IR-5 | FedRAMP IR-6 | FedRAMP IR-7 | FedRAMP IR-8]

Security Operations must develop, document, and disseminate to [Assignment: organization-defined personnel or roles] an incident response policy, at the organization level, that addresses purpose, scope, roles, responsibilities, management commitment, coordination among organizational entities, and compliance, and that is consistent with applicable laws, executive orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, and guidelines.
Security Operations must develop, document, and disseminate procedures to facilitate implementation of the incident response policy and the associated incident response controls.

These policies and procedures must be maintained in written (which may be electronic) form, must be made available to persons responsible for implementing the procedures, and must be reviewed periodically and updated as needed in response to environmental or operational changes affecting the security of electronic protected health information.
[HIPAA Security Rule 164.316(b)(1) | HIPAA Security Rule 164.316(b)(2)(ii) | HIPAA Security Rule 164.316(b)(2)(iii)]
Example Org must designate an official to manage the development, documentation, and dissemination of the incident response policy and procedures.
Example Org must designate officials responsible for managing incident response for systems and name them in the appropriate security and privacy documents.

Security Operations must review and update the incident response policy and the incident response procedures at least every one (1) year and following [Assignment: organization-defined events], which must include assessment or audit findings; security or privacy incidents; and changes to applicable laws, executive orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, and guidelines.

Security Operations must actively monitor for changes to applicable privacy laws, regulations, and overarching policy that affect incident response policies, and must review at least every one (1) year to ensure incident response policies and procedures remain effective.

Security Operations must ensure incident response policy and procedures support cybersecurity and privacy safeguards to the greatest extent feasible throughout the system's life cycle, and must incorporate guidance from the privacy office for handling incidents involving Personally Identifiable Information (PII).
Security Operations must retain the documentation implemented for security incident response for six (6) years from the date of creation or the date it was last in effect, whichever is later.
- **Security Operations** owns the incident response process end to end, including policy and procedure maintenance, incident handling, tracking, testing, training coordination, and reporting.

The security operations center is responsible for actions to reduce the risk that an information security and/or privacy incident will occur and to respond appropriately to each incident or breach, and maintains primary responsibility for incident detection, including internal security monitoring and analysis of network traffic and logs.

- **Information System Security Officer (ISSO)** participates in incident response coordination, including forensic malware analysis, and reviews and approves the incident response plan as defined in Section 10.
[ARC-AMPE IR-4 | NIST 800-53 IR-8 | FedRAMP IR-8 | ARC-AMPE IR-8]
- **Legal and Human Resources offices** participate in the handling of incidents involving insider threats as defined in Section 5.
- **Privacy office** provides guidance for handling incidents involving PII and participates in privacy incident and breach response as defined in Sections 10 and 11.
- **Business Owner** approves the incident response plan as defined in Section 10.
- **All personnel** must report suspected incidents as defined in Section 8.

Security Operations must provide incident response training to system users consistent with assigned roles and responsibilities within one (1) month of assuming an incident response role or responsibility or acquiring system access.
Security Operations must provide incident response training when required by system changes, and again within one (1) year of prior training.
Security Operations must review and update incident response training content every one (1) year and following [Assignment: organization-defined events/incidents].
Security Operations must formally maintain and record personnel participating in incident response training.

Training must include privacy education and awareness associated with sending sensitive information (e.g., confidential, proprietary, financial, or PII), and should include how to recognize when sensitive information such as PII is involved so personnel can coordinate with the designated (e.g., privacy) official.
Security Operations must incorporate simulated events into incident response training to facilitate the required response by personnel in crisis situations.
Security Operations must provide an incident response training environment using [Assignment: organization-defined automated mechanisms].
Security Operations must provide incident response training on how to identify and respond to a breach, including the organization's process for reporting a breach.
That breach reporting process must comply with CMS' policy and plan for preparing for and responding to a breach of PII (see AT-02 for training frequency).

Security Operations must implement an incident handling capability for incidents that is consistent with the incident response plan and includes preparation, detection and analysis, containment, eradication, and recovery.
Security Operations must coordinate incident handling activities with contingency planning activities.

Security Operations must incorporate lessons learned from ongoing incident handling activities into incident response procedures, training, and testing, and must implement the resulting changes accordingly.
Security Operations must ensure the rigor, intensity, scope, and results of incident handling activities are comparable and predictable across the organization.

Security Operations must document relevant information related to security and privacy incidents in accordance with the current organization Incident Handling and Breach Notification Standard and Procedures, inclusive of CMS reporting requirements and timelines.

Security Operations must preserve evidence through technical means, including secured storage and "write" protection of evidence media; must use sound forensics processes and utilities that support legal requirements; and must determine and follow a chain of custody for forensic evidence.

Security Operations must identify the vulnerability exploited during a security and privacy incident and implement safeguards to reduce risk and vulnerability exploit exposure, including isolating or disconnecting systems.
Security Operations must coordinate incident response activities, including forensic malware analysis, with the Information System Security Officer (ISSO).
Security Operations must maintain contact information for individuals within the organization and CMS who have incident handling responsibilities in the system Incident Response Plan.
Security Operations must support the incident handling process using [Assignment: organization-defined automated mechanisms].

Security Operations must include [Assignment: organization-defined types of dynamic reconfiguration] for [Assignment: organization-defined system components] as part of the incident response capability.
Security Operations must employ [Assignment: organization-defined dynamic response capabilities] to respond to incidents.
Security Operations must implement a configurable capability to automatically disable the system if [Assignment: organization-defined security violations] are detected.

Security Operations must identify classes of incidents and take actions in response to those incidents to ensure continuation of organizational missions and business functions, including graceful degradation; information system shutdown; fall back to manual mode/alternative technology whereby the system operates differently; employing deceptive measures; alternate information flows; or operating in a mode reserved solely for when systems are under attack.
Classes of incidents must be based on attack vector (e.g., attack via external media, the web, improper system use, loss of equipment).

Incident response policies and procedures must be aligned with business continuity processes so business continuity planners are made aware of incidents and their impacts, and Security Operations must create written guidelines for prioritizing incidents and applying appropriate responses.
Security Operations must correlate incident information and individual incident responses to achieve an organization-wide perspective on incident awareness and response.
Security Operations must implement an incident handling capability for incidents involving insider threats, ensuring close coordination with the organization's legal and human resources offices.
Security Operations must coordinate the incident handling capability for insider threats with [Assignment: organization-defined organizational entities].

Security Operations must coordinate with [Assignment: organization-defined external organizations] to correlate and share [Assignment: organization-defined incident information] to achieve a cross-organization perspective on incident awareness and more effective incident responses.
Security Operations must coordinate incident handling activities involving supply chain events with other organizations involved in the supply chain.

Security Operations must establish and maintain an integrated incident response team that can be deployed to any location identified by the organization within [Assignment: organization-defined time period].
Security Operations must analyze malicious code and/or other residual artifacts remaining in the system after the incident.
Security Operations must analyze anomalous or suspected adversarial behavior in or related to [Assignment: organization-defined environments or resources].
Security Operations must establish and maintain a security operations center.
Security Operations must manage public relations associated with an incident and employ measures to repair the reputation of the organization.
Security Operations must implement procedures to regularly review records of information system activity, such as audit logs, access reports, and security incident tracking reports.
This review runs on a continuous basis as part of the incident detection responsibility defined in Section 5.

Security Operations must test the effectiveness of the incident response capability for the system within every one (1) year using [Assignment: organization-defined tests] to determine incident response effectiveness, and must document the results.
[NIST 800-53 IR-3 Moderate, High | FedRAMP IR-3 | ARC-AMPE IR-3]
The organization's documented response to an actual incident may be used as part of an incident response capability test.
Any response capabilities not exercised during the previous actual incident response must be additionally exercised (or simulated) as part of the test.
[Assignment: organization-defined tests] may include checklists, walk-throughs, discussion-based or tabletop exercises, simulations, and comprehensive exercises.
Security Operations must test the incident response capability using [Assignment: organization-defined automated mechanisms].

Security Operations must coordinate incident response testing with organizational elements responsible for related plans, including business continuity plans, disaster recovery plans, continuity of operations plans, contingency plans, crisis communications plans, critical infrastructure plans, and occupant emergency plans.
[NIST 800-53 IR-3(2) Moderate, High | FedRAMP IR-3(2) | ARC-AMPE IR-3(2)]

Security Operations must determine the effectiveness of incident response processes, continuously improve them, and provide incident response measures and metrics that are accurate, consistent, and in a reproducible format.
Tabletop exercises conducted under this section must produce a Tabletop exercise report, which Security Operations must retain as evidence of capability testing.

Security Operations must track and document incidents, including maintaining records about each incident, its status, and other pertinent information necessary for forensics as well as evaluating incident details, trends, and handling.
Security Operations must track incidents and collect and analyze incident information using [Assignment: organization-defined automated mechanisms].
Each incident must be recorded as an incident ticket in the [Ticketing System], and incident tickets must include timelines.
Incident tickets with timelines are the evidence of record for incident tracking under this section.

Security Operations must identify and respond to suspected or known security incidents; must mitigate, to the extent practicable, the harmful effects of security incidents known to the covered entity or business associate; and must document security incidents and their outcomes.

Security Operations must require personnel to report suspected incidents to the organizational incident response capability within the timeframe established in the current organization Incident Handling Procedure.
Security Operations must report incident information to [Assignment: organization-defined authorities].

Suspected incident information must be reported to CMS within the timeframe established in the organization Incident Handling Procedure and applicable current legally binding agreements (e.g., Computer Matching Agreement, Information Exchange Agreement, Data Usage Agreement, Business Agreement, or Interconnection Security Agreement).

State Administering Entities (AEs) must report potential or confirmed security incidents within one (1) hour of discovery by completing the CMS ACA Security and Privacy Incident Response Template and notifying the CMS IT Service Desk via email to cms_it_service_desk@cms.hhs.gov or by calling 1-800-562-1963, with CMS and State AE personnel working together for the duration of the incident and CMS personnel notifying any affected federal agencies.
Security Operations must report incidents using [Assignment: organization-defined automated mechanisms] (including email, posting on web sites, and automated incident response tools and programs).
[NIST 800-53 IR-6(1) Moderate, High | FedRAMP IR-6(1) | ARC-AMPE IR-6(1)]
Security Operations must report system vulnerabilities associated with reported incidents to [Assignment: organization-defined personnel or roles].

Security Operations must provide incident information to the provider of the product or service and other organizations involved in the supply chain or supply chain governance for systems or system components related to the incident.

Example Org must require business associates (and subcontractors, via contract or other arrangement) to report to the covered entity any security incident of which they become aware, including breaches of unsecured protected health information as required by § 164.410.

Example Org must require the plan sponsor of a group health plan to report to the group health plan any security incident of which it becomes aware, in addition to implementing reasonable and appropriate administrative, physical, and technical safeguards for electronic protected health information.

Security Operations must provide an incident response support resource, integral to the organizational incident response capability, that offers advice and assistance to users of the system for the handling and reporting of incidents.

Such resources may include help desks, assistance groups, automated ticketing systems to open and track incident response tickets (implemented via the [Ticketing System]), and access to forensics services or consumer redress services when required.

For PII-related incidents, such resources may include the forensic, technical, policy, and legal expertise of Information Assurance Officers/Managers, Privacy Officers, Legal Counsel, and external or internal IT help desks.
Security Operations must increase the availability of incident response information and support using [Assignment: organization-defined automated mechanisms] to the maximum extent possible.
[NIST 800-53 IR-7(1) Moderate, High | FedRAMP IR-7(1) | ARC-AMPE IR-7(1)]

Security Operations must establish a direct, cooperative relationship between the organization's incident response capability and external providers of system protection capability, and must identify organizational incident response team members to those external providers.

Security Operations must develop an incident response plan that: - provides a roadmap for implementing the incident response capability; - describes the structure and organization of the capability; - provides a high-level approach for how the capability fits into the overall organization; - meets the unique requirements of the organization relating to mission, size, structure, and functions; - defines reportable incidents; - provides metrics for measuring the incident response capability; - defines the resources and management support needed to maintain and mature the capability; - addresses the sharing of incident information; - is reviewed and approved by the applicable Information System Security Officer (ISSO) and approved by the Business Owner at least every one (1) year; and - explicitly designates responsibility for incident response to the applicable ISSO, approved by the Business Owner.

Security Operations must distribute copies of the incident response plan to incident response personnel, including all personnel with a role or responsibility for implementing the plan (such as the CISO, CIO, ISSO, Senior Privacy Official, Incident Management/Response Team, PII Breach Response Team, Operations Centers personnel, appropriate legal officials, and public relations or communications officials).

Security Operations must update the incident response plan to address system and organizational changes or problems encountered during plan implementation, execution, or testing, at a minimum every one (1) year or when incident response event(s) demonstrate a change/update is needed to improve the plan.
Security Operations must communicate plan changes to all personnel with a role or responsibility for implementing the plan, and must protect the plan from unauthorized disclosure and modification.
Security Operations must develop and implement a Privacy Incident and Breach Response Plan.

- **Senior privacy official and legal counsel** consult on the mechanisms required by Section 8.15.
- **Supervisors and sponsors** provide registration authorization as required by Section 12.

IAM Engineering must develop, document, and disseminate to applicable personnel and roles an access control policy (at the organization, mission/business process, and/or system level) that addresses purpose, scope, roles, responsibilities, management commitment, coordination among organizational entities, and compliance, and that is consistent with applicable laws, executive orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, and guidelines.
IAM Engineering must develop, document, and disseminate procedures to facilitate implementation of the access control policy and associated access controls.
IAM Engineering is the designated official responsible for managing the development, documentation, and dissemination of the access control policy and procedures.

IAM Engineering must review and update the access control policy and procedures at [Assignment: organization-defined frequency] and following [Assignment: organization-defined events] (such as assessment or audit findings, security or privacy incidents, and changes to applicable laws, regulations, policies, standards, and guidelines).

IAM Engineering must review and update the access control policy and procedures at least every one (1) year, actively monitoring for changes to applicable privacy laws, regulations, and overarching policy that affect them.

IAM Engineering must maintain the implemented policies and procedures in written (which may be electronic) form, retain such documentation (and records of required actions, activities, or assessments) for 6 years from creation or the date last in effect (whichever is later), and make it available to those responsible for implementing the procedures.
IAM Engineering must define and document the types of accounts allowed and specifically prohibited for use within the system.
Default user accounts must be removed or disabled, and any active default accounts must be renamed.
IAM Engineering designates account managers for the systems within scope of this Standard.
IAM Engineering must require [Assignment: organization-defined prerequisites and criteria] for group and role membership.
IAM Engineering must specify the authorized users of the system, group and role membership, and the access authorizations (privileges) and required attributes for each account.
Requests to create accounts must be approved by [Assignment: organization-defined personnel or roles]; IAM Engineering performs this approval function.
Accounts must be created, enabled, modified, disabled, and removed in accordance with [Assignment: organization-defined policy, procedures, prerequisites, and criteria].
User access administrator functions must be centrally controlled.
Access to the system must be authorized based on a valid access authorization, intended system usage, and other [Assignment: organization-defined or mission-required] attributes.

Access provided to contractors must be regulated, security requirements for contractors must be defined, and contractors must be provided only minimal system and physical access contingent on their agreement to support organizational security requirements.
Users must be provided access only to the minimum amount of PII necessary to perform their duties, and the use of guest, anonymous, and shared accounts for providing access to PII is prohibited.
IAM Engineering must establish and implement a process for changing shared or group account authenticators (if deployed) when individuals are removed from the group.
Account management processes must be aligned with personnel termination and transfer processes.
The use of accounts must be monitored.

Account managers and [Assignment: organization-defined personnel or roles] must be notified within twenty-four (24) hours when accounts are no longer required, and within eight (8) hours when users are terminated or transferred or when system usage or need-to-know changes for an individual.
Accounts must be reviewed for compliance with account management requirements quarterly, and in no case less often than at least every ninety (90) days for all systems.
Account creation, modification, enabling, disabling, and removal actions must be automatically audited.

System accounts must be monitored for atypical usage (e.g., access at unusual times or from locations inconsistent with normal usage patterns), and such usage must be reported to [Assignment: organization-defined personnel or roles] and, if necessary, to applicable incident response team(s).

The management of system accounts must be supported using [Assignment: organization-defined automated mechanisms], which may include email or text notification of account managers upon user termination or transfer, system monitoring of account usage, and telephonic notification to report atypical account usage.
The [Identity Provider] must be used as the automated mechanism for account lifecycle notification and monitoring.
Temporary and emergency accounts must be automatically removed or disabled after [Assignment: organization-defined time period], and in no case later than ninety-six (96) hours from last use.

Accounts that have expired, are no longer associated with a user or individual, are in violation of organizational policy, or have been inactive must be disabled within twenty-four (24) hours of meeting those conditions; the inactivity threshold is sixty (60) days.

Users must be required to log out when the expected period of inactivity is exceeded ([Assignment: organization-defined period] per NIST; no more than twenty-four (24) hours of inactivity per ARC-AMPE, implemented as a user action in organizational user policies rather than an automated control).
For HIPAA-covered systems, electronic procedures that terminate an electronic session after a predetermined time of inactivity must be implemented.
[NIST AC-2(5) Moderate, High | ARC-AMPE AC-2(5) | HIPAA 164.312(a)(2)(iii)]
[Assignment: organization-defined] dynamic privilege management capabilities must be implemented.

Privileged user accounts must be established and administered in accordance with a role-based access scheme (including application-specific privileged accounts organized by user responsibilities), privileged role or attribute assignments and changes to them must be monitored, and access must be revoked when privileged role or attribute assignments are no longer appropriate.

Administrator groups, root accounts, and other system-related accounts must be inspected on demand and at least once every fourteen (14) days to ensure unauthorized accounts have not been created, and application-specific privileged user roles must be inspected at least every thirty (30) days.
[Assignment: organization-defined] system accounts must be created, activated, managed, and deactivated dynamically.

The use of shared and group accounts is permitted only under [Assignment: organization-defined conditions], including a documented business need approved in advance by the Authorizing Official, and a system security plan that describes how the accounts are used and includes compensating processes to uniquely attribute account user activities.
[Assignment: organization-defined circumstances and/or usage conditions] for [Assignment: organization-defined] system accounts must be enforced.
Accounts of individuals posing a significant risk must be disabled within one (1) hour of discovery that the individual poses a significant risk.
IAM Engineering must establish (and implement as needed) procedures for obtaining necessary electronic protected health information during an emergency.

Approved authorizations for logical access to information and system resources must be enforced in accordance with applicable access control policies, using technical policies and procedures that allow access only to those persons or software programs that have been granted access rights.

Procedures must be implemented for the authorization and/or supervision of workforce members who work with electronic protected health information or in locations where it might be accessed, and procedures to determine that a workforce member's access to such information is appropriate.

Policies and procedures must be implemented for granting (e.g., via workstation, transaction, program, process, or other mechanism), establishing, documenting, reviewing, and modifying user access rights based on the entity's access authorization policies.

If a health care clearinghouse is part of a larger organization, policies and procedures must be implemented that protect the clearinghouse's electronic protected health information from unauthorized access by the larger organization.

Operating system controls must be configured to disable public "read" and "write" access to system-related files, objects, and directories containing sensitive information, and data stored in the information system must be encrypted when it resides in non-secure areas (using FIPS 140-compliant encryption if encryption is used as an access control mechanism).

When contracting with external service providers, PII (and software and services that receive, process, store, or transmit PII) must be isolated within the service provider environment to the maximum extent possible so other customers sharing physical or virtual space cannot access it.
Dual authorization must be enforced for [Assignment: organization-defined privileged commands and/or other actions].

A mandatory access control policy must be enforced uniformly across covered subjects and objects, constraining subjects from passing information to unauthorized recipients, granting their privileges to others, changing security attributes, choosing security attributes for newly created or modified objects, or changing access control rules.
A discretionary access control policy must be enforced covering covered subjects and objects.
Access to [Assignment: organization-defined security-relevant information] must be prevented except during secure, non-operable system states.
A role-based access control policy must be enforced over defined subjects and objects, controlling access based on [Assignment: organization-defined roles] and users authorized to assume them.

The revocation of access authorizations resulting from changes to the security attributes of subjects and objects must be enforced, based on [Assignment: organization-defined rules] governing the timing of revocations (e.g., revocation upon next object open or access attempt).

Information must be released outside of the system only if the receiving external organization provides information security and privacy safeguards commensurate with the organization's own, and [Assignment: organization-defined controls] are used to validate the appropriateness of the information designated for release.
An audited override of automated access control mechanisms must be employed under [Assignment: organization-defined conditions] by [Assignment: organization-defined roles].
Access to data repositories containing [Assignment: organization-defined information types] must be restricted.

Applications must be required to assert, as part of installation, the access needed to defined system applications and functions; an enforcement mechanism must be provided to prevent unauthorized access; and access changes must be approved after initial installation.
An attribute-based access control policy must be enforced over defined subjects and objects, controlling access based on [Assignment: organization-defined attributes].

[Assignment: organization-defined] mechanisms (including individual authentication and identification, accounting of disclosures, notice of privacy practices, request forms and application interfaces, and other mechanisms developed in consultation with the senior privacy official and legal counsel) must be provided enabling individuals to access their PII/PHI elements defined in applicable security/privacy plans, in readable form and format, with published access request policies and procedures.

Duties of individuals requiring separation must be identified and documented, and system access authorizations must be defined to support separation of duties (e.g., via role-based access control), ensuring that personnel who administer access control functions do not also administer audit functions.

Critical mission functions, information system support functions, and information system testing functions (user acceptance, quality assurance, information security) must be divided among separate individuals or groups, with information security testing conducted by an independent entity other than the Business Owner, ISSO, system developers/maintainers, or system administrators.
The principle of least privilege must be employed, allowing only authorized accesses for users (or processes acting on behalf of users) that are necessary to accomplish assigned organizational tasks.
[NIST AC-6 Moderate, High | FedRAMP AC-6 | ARC-AMPE AC-6]

All file system, network share, port, protocol, service, and removable media/system boot access not explicitly required for system, application, and administrator functionality or authorized by the Authorizing Official for compelling operational needs must be disabled (password-protecting any authorized boot access), and only authorized users must be able to access files, directories, drives, workstations, servers, and other resources expressly required for their job duties.

The use of database management utilities must be restricted to authorized database administrators, and table-level access control must be implemented to prevent users from accessing database data files at the logical data view, field, or field-value level.

Access to [Assignment: organization-defined security functions] (deployed in hardware, software, and firmware) and security-relevant information — including setting/modifying audit logs and auditing behavior, boundary protection system rules, access authorizations, authentication parameters, and system configurations and parameters — must be authorized for [Assignment: organization-defined individuals or roles], with explicit System Owner authorization (FedRAMP defines these as all functions not publicly accessible and all security-relevant information not publicly available).
[NIST AC-6(1) Moderate, High | FedRAMP AC-6(1) | ARC-AMPE AC-6(1)]

Users of system accounts (or roles) with access to security functions or security-relevant information (all security functions per FedRAMP) must use non-privileged accounts or roles when accessing nonsecurity functions, and if feasible, any use of privileged accounts for such functions must be audited.
[NIST AC-6(2) Moderate, High | FedRAMP AC-6(2) | ARC-AMPE AC-6(2)]
Network access to [Assignment: organization-defined privileged commands] must be authorized only for compelling operational needs, and the rationale must be documented in the system security plan.
Separate processing domains must be provided to enable finer-grained allocation of user privileges.
Privileged accounts on the system must be restricted to [Assignment: organization-defined personnel or roles] (defined in the System Security and Privacy Plan).
Privileged access to the system by non-organizational users is prohibited.

The privileges assigned to [Assignment: organization-defined roles and classes] must be reviewed quarterly — and in no case less often than at least every ninety (90) days for all users with privileges — to validate the need for such privileges, and privileges must be reassigned or removed as necessary to correctly reflect organizational mission and business needs.

[Assignment: organization-defined software] (any software except software explicitly documented, per FedRAMP) must be prevented from executing at higher privilege levels than the users executing the software.
The execution of privileged functions must be logged.
Non-privileged users must be prevented from executing privileged functions.

System identifiers must be managed by receiving authorization from [Assignment: organization-defined personnel or roles] to assign an identifier, selecting an identifier that identifies the individual, group, role, service, or device, assigning the identifier to the intended party, and preventing reuse of identifiers for [Assignment: organization-defined time period].

Identifiers must not be reused for two (2) years, and previous identifier-based access authorizations (e.g., to sensitive files or folders) must be removed from the system before the identifier is reused.

A unique name and/or number must be assigned for identifying and tracking user identity, and procedures must be implemented to verify that a person or entity seeking access to electronic protected health information is the one claimed.
The use of system account identifiers that are the same as public identifiers for individual accounts is prohibited.

Individual identifiers must be managed by uniquely identifying each individual using [Assignment: organization-defined characteristics] identifying individual status, such as contractors, foreign nationals, and non-organizational users.
[NIST IA-4(4) Moderate, High | FedRAMP IA-4(4) | ARC-AMPE IA-4(4)]
Individual identifiers must be managed dynamically in accordance with an [Assignment: organization-defined dynamic identifier policy].
Coordination with [Assignment: organization-defined external organizations] for cross-organization management of identifiers is required.
Pairwise pseudonymous identifiers must be generated.
The attributes for each uniquely identified individual, device, or service must be maintained in [Assignment: organization-defined protected central storage].

Users requiring accounts for logical access to systems must be identity proofed based on appropriate identity assurance level requirements as specified in applicable standards and guidelines, user identities must be resolved to a unique individual, and identity evidence must be collected, validated, and verified.

All users requiring logical access accounts (including non-privileged/consumer accounts) must be identity proofed to Identity Assurance Level 2 (IAL-2) or higher per the latest NIST SP 800-63 suite; for ACA consumer accounts, the FDSH Remote Identity Proofing Service may be used.
The registration process to receive an account for logical access must include supervisor or sponsor authorization.
Evidence of individual identification must be presented to the registration authority.
Presented identity evidence must be validated and verified through [Assignment: organization-defined (organization-approved) methods], which must comply with applicable CMS agreements.
The validation and verification of identity evidence must be conducted in person before a designated registration authority.
A registration code or notice of proofing must be delivered through an out-of-band channel to verify the user's physical or digital address of record.
Externally-proofed identities must be accepted at [Assignment: organization-defined identity assurance level].
Upon termination of employment, system access must be disabled within the same day as termination.

Procedures must be implemented for terminating access to electronic protected health information when employment or other arrangement with a workforce member ends, or as required by access-determination procedures.
Upon termination, any authenticators and credentials associated with the individual must be terminated or revoked.
Exit interviews must be conducted that include a discussion of information security topics, including non-disclosure of information security and privacy information.

All security-related organizational system-related property (including hardware authentication tokens, technical manuals, keys, identification cards, and building passes) must be retrieved from terminated individuals.
The organization must retain access to organizational information and systems formerly controlled by the terminated individual.

Terminated individuals must be notified of applicable legally binding post-employment requirements for the protection of organizational information and must sign an acknowledgment of those requirements as part of termination.

[Assignment: organization-defined automated mechanisms] must be used to notify [Assignment: organization-defined personnel or roles] of individual termination actions and/or disable access to system resources.

When individuals are reassigned or transferred, the ongoing operational need for current logical and physical access authorizations to systems and facilities must be reviewed and confirmed, reviewing access to sensitive information such as PII to determine how permissions should change.
[Assignment: organization-defined transfer or reassignment actions] must be initiated within twenty-four (24) hours following the formal transfer action.
Reassignment actions must be initiated to ensure all system accesses no longer required (e.g., need to know) are removed or disabled within twenty-four (24) hours.
Access authorizations must be modified as needed to correspond with changes in operational need due to reassignment or transfer.
[Assignment: organization-defined personnel or roles] must be notified of personnel transfers within twenty-four (24) hours.

Policies and procedures must be implemented that specify the proper functions to be performed, the manner in which those functions are to be performed, and the physical attributes of the surroundings of workstations (or classes of workstations) that can access electronic protected health information.
IAM Engineering must execute the access review process quarterly.

Each quarterly cycle must include, at minimum: 1. **Population reconciliation.** IAM Engineering must obtain the Identity provider user export and the HR active-employee roster and reconcile the two to identify accounts that are expired, no longer associated with a user or individual, or otherwise non-compliant with Section 4 requirements. 1. **Account compliance review.** IAM Engineering must review accounts for compliance with the account management requirements in Sections 4 through 6, satisfying the review requirement in Section 5.3. 1. **Privilege review.** IAM Engineering must review the privileges assigned to all users with privileges per Section 10.10, reassigning or removing privileges as necessary. 1. **Recording and sign-off.** Each review cycle must be recorded as access review tickets with sign-off in the [Ticketing System], including findings and the disposition of each identified account or privilege.

Administrator group, root account, and other system-related account inspections (at least every fourteen (14) days) and application-specific privileged role inspections (at least every thirty (30) days) required by Section 6.6 are performed on their own cadences independent of the quarterly cycle, and their results must also be recorded in the [Ticketing System].
The evidence of record for this process is the Identity provider user export, the HR active-employee roster, and the access review tickets with sign-off produced each quarterly cycle.

IAM Engineering must retain these artifacts, together with all documentation and records of required actions, activities, or assessments under this Standard, in accordance with the retention requirements of Section 3.5.
