Facilities / Physical Security must actively monitor for changes to applicable privacy laws, regulations, and overarching policy that affect physical and environmental protection policies, and must review the policies at least every one (1) year to ensure they remain effective.

Facilities / Physical Security must ensure the physical and environmental protection policy and associated controls support privacy to the greatest extent feasible throughout the system life cycle and limit unnecessary or inappropriate access to Personally Identifiable Information (PII).

Policies and procedures must be implemented to limit physical access to electronic information systems and the facilities in which they are housed, while ensuring properly authorized access is allowed.
Facilities / Physical Security owns these policies and procedures.

Facilities / Physical Security must control and validate a person's access to facilities based on their role or function, authorizing physical access to the facility where the system resides based on position or role.

analyze: This Standard establishes the requirements for identifying, remediating, and reporting system flaws and vulnerabilities within Example Org's systems and hosted applications.
It implements the System and Information Integrity policy and the associated vulnerability management and flaw remediation controls.

Example Org must develop, document, and disseminate a system and information integrity policy to organization-defined personnel or roles that addresses: - Purpose; - Scope; - Roles and responsibilities; - Management commitment; - Coordination among organizational entities; and - Compliance.
The policy must be consistent with applicable laws, executive orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, and guidelines.
Example Org must develop, document, and disseminate procedures to facilitate implementation of the system and information integrity policy and associated controls.
This Standard and its supporting operating procedures constitute those procedures.
- Example Org must designate an official to manage the development, documentation, and dissemination of the system and information integrity policy and procedures.

- The system and information integrity policy and procedures must be reviewed and updated at an organization-defined frequency and following organization-defined events, including assessment or audit findings, security or privacy incidents, and changes to applicable laws, executive orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, and guidelines.
- The system and information integrity policy and procedures must be reviewed and updated at least every one (1) year.

- Example Org must actively monitor for changes to applicable privacy laws, regulations, and overarching policy affecting system and information integrity policies no less often than at least every one (1) year.

This Standard applies to all systems and hosted applications within Example Org's operating boundary, and to all information technology components for which a patch or work-around exists for each vendor-identified and/or CVE/CWE-identified vulnerability.
Infrastructure Security owns this process end to end and is accountable for its execution, its handoffs to other teams, and the evidence it produces.

Where Example Org systems process electronic protected health information (ePHI), the following apply: - Example Org must implement policies and procedures to protect ePHI from improper alteration or destruction.
- Example Org must implement electronic mechanisms to corroborate that ePHI has not been altered or destroyed in an unauthorized manner.

- Infrastructure Security must monitor and scan for vulnerabilities in the system and hosted applications at an organization-defined frequency and/or randomly in accordance with an organization-defined process, and when new vulnerabilities potentially affecting the system are identified and reported.

- Infrastructure Security must monitor and scan for vulnerabilities in the system and hosted applications every thirty (30) calendar days and when new vulnerabilities potentially affecting the system are identified and reported.

- Infrastructure Security must employ vulnerability monitoring tools and techniques that facilitate interoperability among tools and automate parts of the vulnerability management process by using standards for enumerating platforms, software flaws, and improper configurations; formatting checklists and test procedures; and measuring vulnerability impact.
- Infrastructure Security must employ vulnerability monitoring tools that include the capability to readily update the vulnerabilities to be scanned.
- The system vulnerabilities to be scanned must be updated prior to a new scan and when new vulnerabilities are identified and reported.
[NIST 800-53 RA-5(2) Low, Moderate, High | FedRAMP RA-5(2) | ARC-AMPE RA-5(2)]
- Infrastructure Security must follow the FedRAMP Vulnerability Detection and Response and Vulnerability Evaluation and Reporting rules for vulnerability monitoring and scanning and its enhancements.
[FedRAMP RA-5 | FedRAMP RA-5(2) | FedRAMP RA-5(3) | FedRAMP RA-5(4) | FedRAMP RA-5(5) | FedRAMP RA-5(8) | FedRAMP RA-5(11) | FedRAMP SI-2 | FedRAMP SI-2(2)]
Infrastructure Security must define the breadth and depth of vulnerability scanning coverage; the vulnerability scan must fully cover the ACA boundary and all its components.
Infrastructure Security must determine information about the system that is discoverable and take organization-defined corrective actions.
- Infrastructure Security must implement privileged access authorization to organization-defined system components for organization-defined vulnerability scanning activities.

- Infrastructure Security must implement privileged access authorization to all components that support authentication for all scans; if automated scanning tool functionality is used, it must perform credentialed scans, and credentials must be compliant with organizational policy to the extent possible.
- Infrastructure Security must analyze vulnerability scan reports and results from vulnerability monitoring.
- Infrastructure Security must compare the results of multiple vulnerability scans using organization-defined automated mechanisms.

- Infrastructure Security must review historic audit logs to determine if a vulnerability identified in an organization-defined system has been previously exploited within an organization-defined time period.
- Infrastructure Security must correlate the output from vulnerability scanning tools to determine the presence of multi-vulnerability and multi-hop attack vectors.
- Infrastructure Security must establish a public reporting channel for receiving reports of vulnerabilities in organizational systems and system components.
[NIST 800-53 RA-5(11) Low, Moderate, High | FedRAMP RA-5(11) | ARC-AMPE RA-5(11)]
- Infrastructure Security must make raw results from vulnerability scanning tools available to the organization in an unaltered format.
- Infrastructure Security must incorporate vulnerability scan findings and weaknesses into the Plan of Action and Milestones (POA&M).

- Infrastructure Security must provide timely responses to informational requests and scheduled Information Security and Privacy Continuous Monitoring (ISCM) submission requirements to CMS as applicable; ACA Administering Entities must deliver vulnerability scans to CMS quarterly on 31 January, 30 April, 31 July, and 31 October.

- Infrastructure Security must share information obtained from the vulnerability monitoring process and control assessments with organization-defined personnel or roles (at minimum, affected/related stakeholders) to help eliminate similar vulnerabilities in other systems.
Each scan cycle must produce and retain scan results with remediation SLAs, documenting each identified vulnerability, its severity, and its assigned remediation deadline per Section 5.2.
- Example Org must identify, report, and correct system flaws.
- Infrastructure Security must test software and firmware updates related to flaw remediation for effectiveness and potential side effects before installation.
- Security-relevant software and firmware updates must be installed within an organization-defined time period of the release of the updates.
- Security-relevant software and firmware updates must be installed within thirty (30) days of the release of the updates.
- Flaw remediation must be incorporated into the organizational configuration management process.

- Example Org must apply flaw remediation requirements to all information technology components for which a patch or work-around exists for each vendor-identified and/or CVE/CWE-identified vulnerability.
- Infrastructure Security must provide timely responses, as defined by the CISO, to informational requests for organizational flaw (e.g., patch) status and posture information.
Infrastructure Security must remediate legitimate vulnerabilities within organization-defined response times in accordance with an organizational assessment of risk.

Legitimate vulnerabilities identified during vulnerability scanning must be remediated within the following timeframes, in accordance with the organization's assessment of risk: [ARC-AMPE RA-5 | ARC-AMPE SI-2]

| Severity | Remediation Timeframe | | -------- | --------------------------------- | | Critical | Within fifteen (15) calendar days | | High | Within thirty (30) calendar days | | Moderate | Within ninety (90) calendar days | | Low | Within one (1) year |
Example Org must measure the time between flaw identification and flaw remediation, and establish organization-defined benchmarks for taking corrective actions.
The severity-based timeframes in Section 5.2 constitute the benchmarks against which remediation performance is measured.
Infrastructure Security must record these measurements as the patch compliance report.

- Example Org must determine if system components have applicable security-relevant software and firmware updates installed using automated mechanisms at least monthly, and must use automated mechanisms for updating security-relevant software and firmware to the maximum extent possible.
[NIST 800-53 SI-2(2) Moderate, High | FedRAMP SI-2(2) | ARC-AMPE SI-2(2)]
- Example Org must employ automated patch management tools to facilitate flaw remediation to organization-defined system components.
[NIST 800-53 SI-2(4) | FedRAMP SI-2 (per ARC-AMPE SI-2 discussion) | ARC-AMPE SI-2(4)]

- Example Org must patch on at least a monthly basis to ensure all systems within the purview of the organization are up to date with the most current security patches, including a validation period on any lower-tier information technology environment before production servers receive the patch.
- Example Org must install organization-defined security-relevant software and firmware updates automatically to organization-defined system components.
Previous versions of software and firmware components must be removed after updated versions have been installed, for all upgraded/replaced components that are no longer required for operation.
Example Org must conduct root cause analysis to identify underlying causes of issues or failures, develop actions to address the root cause, and implement and monitor those actions for effectiveness.

If a security patch will not be applied to an information technology component, or a legacy component no longer maintained by the vendor remains in use, Infrastructure Security must conduct a risk analysis and document the risk-based decision through the configuration management process in the form of written authorization from the organization's Chief Information Officer (CIO) or designee (e.g., the system data owner or CISO).
- Example Org must receive system security alerts, advisories, and directives from organization-defined external organizations on an ongoing basis.
- Infrastructure Security must generate internal security alerts, advisories, and directives as deemed necessary.

- Infrastructure Security must disseminate security alerts, advisories, and directives to organization-defined personnel or roles, elements, and/or external organizations, at a minimum to system security personnel and administrators with configuration/patch-management responsibilities.
- Security directives must be implemented in accordance with established time frames, or the issuing organization must be notified of the degree of noncompliance.
- Example Org must follow the FedRAMP Addressing FedRAMP Communication rules for security alerts, advisories, and directives.
- Security alert and advisory information must be broadcast throughout the organization using organization-defined automated mechanisms.

- The policies and procedures implemented to comply with this Standard must be maintained in written (which may be electronic) form, and Example Org must maintain a written (which may be electronic) record of any action, activity, or assessment required to be documented.
- Required documentation must be retained for 6 years from the date of its creation or the date when it last was in effect, whichever is later.
- Documentation must be made available to those persons responsible for implementing the procedures to which the documentation pertains.
- Documentation must be reviewed periodically and updated as needed in response to environmental or operational changes affecting the security of electronic protected health information.
This process is expected to produce, at minimum, the following artifacts, owned and maintained by Infrastructure Security:

| Artifact | Description | | ---------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Scan results with remediation SLAs | Raw and analyzed vulnerability scan results (per Section 4.7 and 4.8) with each finding mapped to its severity-based remediation deadline (Section 5.2) | | Patch compliance report | Measurements of time between flaw identification and flaw remediation against the established benchmarks (Section 5.3), demonstrating monthly patching status across all in-scope systems |
All artifacts are subject to the retention and availability requirements in Section 7.

analyze: This Standard establishes the requirements for protecting Example Org's facilities, physical infrastructure, systems, and information assets from unauthorized physical access, tampering, theft, and environmental hazards.
It is issued under the authority of Example Org's information security program and is consistent with applicable laws, Executive Orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, and guidelines.

This Standard applies to all facilities in which Example Org electronic information systems reside, all personnel and visitors granted physical access to those facilities, all workstations that access electronic protected health information, and all system components, media, and output devices located within or moving through those facilities.

The **Facilities / Physical Security team** owns this Standard and the processes it defines end to end, including execution, review, evidence production, and coordination with other participating teams.

The Facilities / Physical Security team shall coordinate with the organizational incident response capability, the privacy office and/or the senior official for privacy, and authorized maintenance personnel as specified in the individual requirements below.

4.1 The Facilities / Physical Security team shall develop, document, and disseminate to applicable personnel or roles an organization-level physical and environmental protection policy that addresses purpose, scope, roles, responsibilities, management commitment, coordination among organizational entities, and compliance, and is consistent with applicable laws, Executive Orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, and guidelines.
The policy may be developed at the mission/business process level or system level.

4.2 The Facilities / Physical Security team shall develop, document, and disseminate procedures to facilitate the implementation of the physical and environmental protection policy and the associated physical and environmental protection controls.
4.3 An organization-defined official shall be designated to manage the development, documentation, and dissemination of the physical and environmental protection policy and procedures.
Under ARC, this official must be documented in the organization's System Security and Privacy Policy.

4.4 The Facilities / Physical Security team shall review and update the current physical and environmental protection policy and procedures at least every one (1) year and following organization-defined events (e.g., assessment or audit findings, security or privacy incidents, and changes to applicable laws, Executive Orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, and guidelines).

4.5 The Facilities / Physical Security team shall actively monitor for changes to applicable privacy laws, regulations, and overarching policy that affect physical and environmental protection policies, and review at least annually to ensure the policies and procedures remain effective.

4.6 The physical and environmental protection policy and associated controls must support privacy to the greatest extent feasible throughout the system's life cycle, and limit unnecessary or inappropriate access to Personally Identifiable Information (PII).

4.7 The Facilities / Physical Security team shall implement policies and procedures to limit physical access to electronic information systems and the facilities in which they are housed, while ensuring properly authorized access is allowed.
4.8 The Facilities / Physical Security team shall implement policies and procedures to safeguard the facility and the equipment therein from unauthorized physical access, tampering, and theft.

4.9 The Facilities / Physical Security team shall implement policies and procedures to document repairs and modifications to the physical components of a facility that are related to security (e.g., hardware, walls, doors, and locks).
5.1 The Facilities / Physical Security team shall develop, approve, and maintain a list of individuals with authorized access to the facility where the system resides.
5.2 The Facilities / Physical Security team shall issue authorization credentials for facility access.
5.3 The Facilities / Physical Security team shall review the access list detailing authorized facility access by individuals at least every six (6) months.
5.4 The Facilities / Physical Security team shall remove individuals from the facility access list when access is no longer required.
5.5 Physical access to the facility where the system resides shall be authorized based on position or role.
5.6 Two forms of identification from [Assignment: organization-defined list of acceptable forms of identification] shall be required for visitor access to the facility where the system resides.

5.7 Unescorted access to the facility where the system resides shall be restricted to personnel with security clearances, formal access authorizations, a need for access to all information contained within the system, or [Assignment: organization-defined physical access authorizations].

6.1 The Facilities / Physical Security team shall enforce physical access authorizations at entry and exit points to the facility where the system resides by verifying individual access authorizations before granting access and controlling ingress and egress using [Assignment: organization-defined physical access control systems or devices] and/or guards.
6.2 The Facilities / Physical Security team shall maintain physical access audit logs for entry or exit points.
6.3 Access to areas within the facility designated as publicly accessible shall be controlled by implementing [Assignment: organization-defined physical access controls or security safeguards].
6.4 Visitors shall be escorted and visitor activity controlled in [Assignment: organization-defined circumstances].
6.5 The Facilities / Physical Security team shall secure keys, combinations, and other physical access devices.
6.6 The Facilities / Physical Security team shall inventory [Assignment: organization-defined physical access devices] every ninety (90) days.

6.7 Combinations and keys shall be changed at least every one (1) year or earlier as required by a security-relevant event, and/or when keys are lost, combinations are compromised, or when individuals possessing the keys or combinations are transferred or terminated.
6.8 Access to the data center/facility shall be controlled using door and window locks, security personnel, or physical authentication devices (e.g., biometrics and smart card/PIN combination).

6.9 Servers shall be stored and operated in physically secure environments and access granted to explicitly authorized personnel only; access to grounds/facilities shall be restricted to authorized persons only.

6.11 Physical access authorizations to the system, in addition to the facility physical access controls, shall be enforced at [Assignment: organization-defined physical spaces].

6.12 Security checks shall be performed at [Assignment: organization-defined frequency] at the physical perimeter of the facility or system for exfiltration of information or removal of system components.
6.13 Guards shall be employed to control [Assignment: organization-defined physical access points] to the facility where the system resides 24 hours per day, 7 days per week.
6.14 Lockable physical casings shall be used to protect [Assignment: organization-defined system components] from unauthorized physical access.

6.15 [Assignment: organization-defined anti-tamper technologies] shall be employed to detect and/or prevent physical tampering or alteration of [Assignment: organization-defined hardware components] within the system.
6.16 Access shall be limited using physical barriers.
6.17 Access control vestibules shall be employed at [Assignment: organization-defined locations].

6.18 The Facilities / Physical Security team shall establish (and implement as needed) procedures that allow facility access in support of restoration of lost data under the disaster recovery plan and emergency mode operations plan in the event of an emergency.
7.1 The Facilities / Physical Security team shall implement physical safeguards for all workstations that access electronic protected health information to restrict access to authorized users.

7.2 The Facilities / Physical Security team shall implement policies and procedures that specify the proper functions to be performed, the manner in which those functions are to be performed, and the physical attributes of the surroundings of a specific workstation or class of workstation that can access electronic protected health information.

8.1 Physical access to [Assignment: organization-defined system distribution and transmission lines] within organizational facilities shall be controlled using [Assignment: organization-defined security controls or safeguards].

8.2 The Facilities / Physical Security team shall disable any physical ports (e.g., wiring closets and patch panels) not in use.
8.3 Physical access to output from [Assignment: organization-defined output devices] shall be controlled to prevent unauthorized individuals from obtaining the output.
[NIST PE-5 Moderate/High | ARC PE-5 AE Mandatory]
8.4 Individual identity shall be linked to receipt of output from output devices.
9.1 The Facilities / Physical Security team shall monitor physical access to the facility where the system resides to detect and respond to physical security incidents.

9.2 The Facilities / Physical Security team shall review physical access logs at least monthly (every thirty [30] days) and upon occurrence of organization-defined events or potential indications of events.
9.3 The Facilities / Physical Security team shall coordinate results of reviews and investigations with the organizational incident response capability.
9.4 Physical access to the facility where the system resides shall be monitored using physical intrusion alarms and surveillance equipment.
[NIST PE-6(1) Moderate/High | ARC PE-6(1) AE Mandatory]

9.5 [Assignment: organization-defined classes or types of intrusions] shall be recognized and [Assignment: organization-defined response actions] initiated using [Assignment: organization-defined automated mechanisms].

9.6 Video surveillance shall be employed of [Assignment: organization-defined operational areas], video recordings reviewed at [Assignment: organization-defined frequency], and recordings retained for [Assignment: organization-defined time period].
9.7 Physical access to the system, in addition to facility physical access monitoring, shall be monitored at [Assignment: organization-defined physical spaces].
10.1 The Facilities / Physical Security team shall maintain visitor access records to the facility where the system resides for at least one (1) year.
10.2 The Facilities / Physical Security team shall review visitor access records at least monthly (every thirty [30] days).
10.3 Anomalies in visitor access records shall be reported to [Assignment: organization-defined personnel or roles].

10.4 At a minimum, visitor access records must include the name and organization of the person visiting, the visitor's signature, form of identification, date of access, time of entry and departure, purpose of visit, and the name and organization of the person visited.
10.5 The policy for collection and retention of visitor access records shall be reviewed by the privacy office and/or the senior official for privacy.
10.6 Visitor access records shall be maintained and reviewed using [Assignment: organization-defined automated mechanisms].
10.7 Personally identifiable information contained in visitor access records shall be limited to the elements identified in the privacy risk assessment.
11.1 Power equipment and power cabling for the system shall be protected from damage and destruction.
[NIST PE-9 Moderate/High | ARC PE-9 AE Mandatory]

11.2 Only authorized maintenance personnel shall be permitted to access infrastructure assets, including power generators; heating, ventilation, and air conditioning (HVAC) systems; cabling; and wiring closets.
11.3 Redundant power cabling paths that are physically separated by [Assignment: organization-defined distance] shall be employed.
11.4 Automatic voltage controls shall be employed for [Assignment: organization-defined critical system components].
11.5 The capability of shutting off power to [Assignment: organization-defined system or individual system components] in emergency situations shall be provided.
[NIST PE-10 Moderate/High | ARC PE-10 AE Mandatory]
11.6 Emergency shutoff switches or devices shall be placed in [Assignment: organization-defined location] by system or system component to facilitate access for authorized personnel.
[NIST PE-10 Moderate/High | ARC PE-10 AE Mandatory]
11.7 The emergency power shutoff capability shall be protected from unauthorized activation.
[NIST PE-10 Moderate/High | ARC PE-10 AE Mandatory]
11.8 A main power switch or emergency cut-off switch shall be implemented and maintained, prominently marked and protected by a cover, for data centers, servers, and mainframe rooms.

12.1 An uninterruptible power supply shall be provided to facilitate an orderly shutdown of the system and/or transition of the system to long-term alternate power in the event of a primary power source loss.
[NIST PE-11 Moderate/High | ARC PE-11 AE Mandatory]
12.2 Emergency power equipment shall be tested on a schedule that complies with manufacturer recommendations and local, state, and federal requirements, and no less often than every three (3) years.

12.3 An alternate power supply for the system, activated manually or automatically, that can maintain minimally required operational capability in the event of an extended loss of the primary power source shall be provided.

12.4 An alternate power supply shall be provided that is self-contained, not reliant on external power generation, and capable of maintaining minimally required or full operational capability in the event of an extended loss of the primary power source.

13.1 Automatic emergency lighting for the system shall be employed and maintained that activates in the event of a power outage or disruption and that covers emergency exits and evacuation routes within the facility.

13.2 Emergency lighting equipment shall be tested on a schedule that complies with manufacturer recommendations and local, state, and federal requirements, and no less often than every three (3) years.
13.3 Emergency lighting shall be provided for all areas within the facility supporting essential mission and business functions.
14.1 Fire detection and suppression systems that are supported by an independent energy source shall be employed and maintained.
14.2 Fire protection equipment shall be tested on a schedule that complies with manufacturer recommendations and local, state, and federal requirements, and no less often than every three (3) years.

14.3 Fire detection systems shall be employed that activate automatically and notify [Assignment: organization-defined personnel or roles] and [Assignment: defined emergency responders] in the event of a fire.
[NIST PE-13(1) Moderate/High | ARC PE-13(1) AE Mandatory]

14.4 Fire suppression systems shall be employed that activate automatically and notify [Assignment: organization-defined personnel or roles] and [Assignment: organization-defined emergency responders], and an automatic fire suppression capability shall be employed when the facility is not staffed on a continuous basis.

14.5 The facility shall undergo fire protection inspections by authorized and qualified inspectors at [Assignment: organization-defined frequency], and identified deficiencies shall be resolved within [Assignment: organization-defined time period].

15.1 Temperature, humidity, and pressure levels within the facility where the system resides shall be maintained at acceptable levels — under ARC, at acceptable vendor-specified levels consistent with the ASHRAE document *Thermal Guidelines for Data Processing Environments* (NIST 800-53 also permits radiation or other organization-defined environmental controls).
15.2 Environmental control levels shall be monitored at [Assignment: organization-defined frequency].
The Facilities / Physical Security team shall retain the resulting Data centre environmental monitoring records as evidence of compliance with this requirement.

15.3 When environmental control alerts occur, the alert level shall be evaluated and the prescribed guidelines for that level followed, component management alerted of possible loss of service and/or media, and damage reported, remedial action provided, and the contingency plan implemented if necessary.
15.4 [Assignment: organization-defined automatic environmental controls] shall be employed in the facility to prevent fluctuations potentially harmful to the system.

15.5 Environmental control monitoring shall be employed that provides an alarm or notification of changes potentially harmful to personnel or equipment to [Assignment: organization-defined personnel or roles].
16.1 The system shall be protected from damage resulting from water leakage by providing master shutoff or isolation valves that are accessible, working properly, and known to key personnel.

16.2 Water damage protection equipment shall be tested on a schedule that complies with manufacturer recommendations and local, state, and federal requirements, and no less often than every three (3) years.
16.3 The presence of water near the system shall be detected and [Assignment: organization-defined personnel or roles] alerted using [Assignment: organization-defined automated mechanisms].
17.1 All system components entering and exiting the facility shall be authorized and controlled.
17.2 Records of the system components shall be maintained.

17.3 The Facilities / Physical Security team shall implement policies and procedures that govern the receipt and removal of hardware and electronic media containing electronic protected health information into and out of a facility, and the movement of these items within the facility.

17.4 The Facilities / Physical Security team shall implement policies and procedures to address the final disposition of electronic protected health information, and/or the hardware or electronic media on which it is stored.
17.5 Procedures shall be implemented for removal of electronic protected health information from electronic media before the media are made available for re-use.
17.6 A record shall be maintained of the movements of hardware and electronic media and any person responsible therefor.
17.7 A retrievable, exact copy of electronic protected health information shall be created, when needed, before movement of equipment.
18.1 The Facilities / Physical Security team shall determine and document the alternate work sites allowed for use by employees.

18.2 [Assignment: organization-defined controls] shall be employed at alternate work sites; under ARC, these controls should be defined in the appropriate System Security and Privacy Plan (SSPP).

18.3 The effectiveness of controls at alternate work sites shall be assessed.
[NIST PE-17 Moderate/High | ARC PE-17 AE Mandatory]
18.4 A means shall be provided for employees to communicate with information security and privacy personnel in case of incidents.
[NIST PE-17 Moderate/High | ARC PE-17 AE Mandatory]

19.1 System components shall be positioned within the facility to minimize potential damage from [Assignment: organization-defined physical and environmental hazards] and to minimize the opportunity for unauthorized access.

20.2 Required documentation shall be retained for 6 years from the date of its creation or the date when it last was in effect, whichever is later.

This Standard establishes the mandatory requirements for security and privacy awareness, literacy, and role-based training at Example Org, together with the associated personnel security requirements for position risk designation, screening, and workforce access authorization.

It applies to all members of the Example Org workforce, including management, senior executives, employees, contractors, and other individuals working on behalf of the organization who access, use, manage, or develop organizational systems.
The Security Awareness team is accountable for this process end to end, including delivery, tracking, content maintenance, reporting, and handoffs to other participating teams.

Security Awareness must develop, document, and disseminate to applicable personnel or roles an organization-level security and privacy awareness and training policy that addresses purpose, scope, roles, responsibilities, management commitment, coordination among organizational entities, and compliance, and that is consistent with applicable laws, executive orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, and guidelines.
The policy may be maintained at the organization, mission/business process, or system level.
Security Awareness must develop, document, and disseminate procedures to facilitate implementation of the awareness and training policy and the associated awareness and training controls.

Security Awareness must designate an official [Assignment: organization-defined official] to manage the development, documentation, and dissemination of the awareness and training policy and procedures, and must name these officials in the appropriate security and privacy documents.

Security Awareness must review and update the awareness and training policy and the associated procedures at least every one (1) year and following organization-defined events, such as assessment or audit findings; security or privacy incidents; and changes to applicable laws (including privacy laws), executive orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, and guidelines.

Security Awareness must actively monitor for changes to applicable privacy laws, regulations, and overarching policy that affect awareness and training policies, and must ensure awareness and training policies and procedures support cybersecurity and privacy safeguards throughout the system's life cycle and the information on that system.

Example Org must incorporate security and privacy roles and responsibilities into organizational position descriptions, including role-based training requirements, with position descriptions developed in consultation with the organization's security and privacy officers.
Example Org must implement a security awareness and training program for all members of the workforce, including management.

Security Awareness must provide security and privacy literacy training to all system users (including managers, senior executives, and contractors) as part of initial training for new users and at least every one (1) year thereafter.

Security Awareness must provide literacy training when required by system changes or following organization-defined events (e.g., assessment or audit findings; security or privacy incidents; changes to applicable laws, executive orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, and guidelines).

Security Awareness must develop and implement an information security and privacy education and awareness training program for all employees and individuals working on behalf of the organization who access, use, manage, or develop systems.
The training must address an individual's responsibilities associated with sending sensitive information in email.

Security Awareness must provide privacy training, before granting access to organizational systems and networks, to all employees and contractors who work on systems that collect, maintain, store, use, or disclose PII.
Security Awareness must update literacy training and awareness content at least once every one (1) year and following organization-defined events.
Security Awareness must incorporate lessons learned from internal or external security incidents or breaches into literacy training and awareness techniques.

Security Awareness must employ techniques to increase the security and privacy awareness of system users, including phishing email tests and other organization-defined awareness techniques (defined in the applicable security and privacy plan).
Phishing email tests must be executed through the [Phishing Simulation Platform].
Security Awareness must provide practical exercises in literacy training that simulate events and incidents.

Security Awareness must provide literacy training on recognizing and reporting potential indicators of insider threat, including how to communicate employee and management concerns regarding potential insider threat indicators through appropriate organizational channels in accordance with established organizational policies and procedures.

Security Awareness must provide literacy training on recognizing and reporting potential and actual instances of social engineering and social mining, including how to recognize and report, through appropriate organizational and defined channels (e.g., applicable security and privacy plans), potential attempts to trick an individual into revealing information or taking an action that can be used to breach, compromise, or otherwise adversely impact a system.

Security Awareness must provide literacy training on recognizing suspicious communications and anomalous behavior in organizational systems using organization-defined indicators of malicious code, including how to recognize and report, through appropriate organizational and defined channels (e.g., applicable security and privacy plans), potentially suspicious email or web communications (e.g., unexpected emails, emails with strange or poor grammar, or emails from an unfamiliar sender appearing to be from a known sponsor or contractor) and anomalous behaviors in systems.

Security Awareness must provide literacy training on the advanced persistent threat (APT), including techniques for recognizing suspicious emails, use of removable systems in non-secure settings, the potential targeting of individuals at home, and the various ways APTs can infiltrate the organization (e.g., through websites, emails, advertisement pop-ups, articles, and social engineering).
Security Awareness must provide literacy training on the cyber threat environment and reflect current cyber threat information in system operations.

Security Awareness must provide role-based security and privacy training to personnel with significant information security and privacy roles and responsibilities before authorizing access to the system or information or performing assigned duties, and at least every one (1) year thereafter.

Security Awareness must provide role-based training when required by system changes, when an employee enters a new position that requires additional role-specific training, and following significant changes to the system or the system environment.

Security Awareness must disable, through the [Identity Provider], the user accounts of personnel with significant information security and privacy roles and responsibilities who have not completed the required role-based training within the mandated timeframes, until they have met their role-based training requirement.
Security Awareness must update role-based training content at least every one (1) year and following organization-defined events or significant changes to the system or system environment.
Security Awareness must incorporate lessons learned from internal or external security incidents or breaches into role-based training.

Security Awareness must provide [Assignment: organization-defined personnel or roles] with initial and recurring [Assignment: organization-defined frequency] training in the employment and operation of environmental controls.

Security Awareness must provide [Assignment: organization-defined personnel or roles] with initial and recurring [Assignment: organization-defined frequency] training in the employment and operation of physical security controls.
Security Awareness must provide practical exercises in security and privacy training that reinforce training objectives.

Security Awareness must provide organizational personnel (including vendors, contractors, and employees) with initial training, and at least every one (1) year thereafter, in the employment and operation of personally identifiable information processing and transparency controls.

Security Awareness must develop and implement a privacy education and awareness training program for all employees and individuals working on behalf of the organization involved in managing, using, and/or processing PII.

The program must: - include responsibilities associated with sending PII in email; - ensure privacy communications and training are job-specific and commensurate with the employee's responsibilities; - complete initial training on privacy responsibilities before permitting access to organizational information and systems, with annual refresher training thereafter; - ensure additional or advanced training is commensurate with increased responsibilities or changes in duties; - include acceptable rules of behavior and the consequences of not following them in both initial and refresher training; and - ensure training addresses the rules for telework and other authorized remote access programs.
Security Awareness must provide periodic security updates (security reminders) to workforce members.
Example Org must implement procedures for guarding against, detecting, and reporting malicious software.
Example Org must implement procedures for monitoring log-in attempts and reporting discrepancies.
Example Org must implement procedures for creating, changing, and safeguarding passwords.

Example Org must implement policies and procedures to ensure that all workforce members have appropriate access to electronic protected health information and to prevent workforce members without such access from obtaining it.
Example Org must implement procedures for the authorization and/or supervision of workforce members who work with electronic protected health information or in locations where it might be accessed.

Example Org must screen individuals prior to authorizing access to the system, and must implement procedures to determine that a workforce member's access to electronic protected health information is appropriate.

Example Org must implement procedures for terminating access to electronic protected health information when employment or other arrangement with a workforce member ends, or as required by clearance determinations.
Example Org must assign a risk designation to all organizational positions.

Example Org must establish screening criteria for individuals filling positions, including explicit information security role appointment requirements (e.g., training and security clearances), and must factor whether the workforce member will work with PII into the screening criteria.
Example Org must review and update position risk designations at least every one (1) year or whenever a position's duties are changed, revised, or realigned.
Example Org must ensure that all individuals with significant security responsibilities possess, at a minimum, a background investigation.

Example Org must rescreen individuals in accordance with organization-defined conditions and frequency [Assignment: organization-defined rescreening conditions and frequency], in accordance with the organizational Personnel Security Policy and anytime an individual changes position, consistent with PS-2 for the new position.
Example Org must conduct background investigations in a manner commensurate with organizational Personnel Security policy and guidance prior to employment.

For prospective and existing employees accessing ACA-sensitive information or PII, Example Org must meet personnel suitability standards based on a valid need-to-know (which cannot be assumed from position or title) and favorable background check results, with the background check including, at a minimum, contacting provided references and the local law enforcement agency or agencies.

Example Org must not permit employees and contractors access to information systems until they have been vetted in accordance with organizational policy and have signed the appropriate access agreements.

Example Org must verify that individuals accessing a system processing, storing, or transmitting classified information are cleared and indoctrinated to the highest classification level of the information to which they have access on the system.

Example Org must verify that individuals accessing a system processing, storing, or transmitting types of classified information requiring formal indoctrination are formally indoctrinated for all relevant types of information to which they have access on the system.

Example Org must ensure individuals accessing information requiring special protective measures have valid access authorizations demonstrated by assigned official government duties and satisfy [Assignment: organization-defined additional personnel screening criteria].

Example Org must verify that individuals accessing a system processing, storing, or transmitting organization-defined information types meet [Assignment: organization-defined citizenship requirements].

Security Awareness must document and monitor information security and privacy training activities, including security and privacy awareness training and specific role-based security and privacy training.
Training delivery and completion must be tracked in the [Learning Management System].
Security Awareness must produce, at the conclusion of each annual training cycle, a Training completion report and Phishing simulation results as evidence of program execution.
Security Awareness must retain individual training records for [Assignment: organization-defined retention period], and for a minimum of five (5) years after completing a specific training course.

Example Org must maintain the policies and procedures implemented to comply with the HIPAA Security Rule in written (which may be electronic) form, and must maintain a written (which may be electronic) record of any action, activity, or assessment required to be documented.
Example Org must retain HIPAA-required documentation for 6 years from the date of its creation or the date when it last was in effect, whichever is later.
Example Org must make HIPAA documentation available to those persons responsible for implementing the procedures to which the documentation pertains.
Example Org must review HIPAA documentation periodically and update it as needed in response to environmental or operational changes affecting the security of electronic protected health information.

The Security Awareness team is accountable for the outcomes of every requirement in this Standard, including the production and retention of the Training completion report and Phishing simulation results, the annual review and update of the awareness and training policy and procedures, and the coordination of handoffs with other participating teams (including personnel screening, system ownership, and access management functions) for requirements that those teams execute on Security Awareness's behalf.

analyze: **Standard ID:** STD-AIGOV-001 **Owner (end to end):** AI Risk / GRC **Applies to:** All Acme Health personnel, teams, and partners who design, develop, deploy, evaluate, procure, use, oversee, or decommission AI systems. **Audience:** Acme Health security, IT, risk, compliance, and engineering staff who implement and audit against this document.
This Standard establishes Acme Health's requirements for governing and accounting for artificial intelligence (AI) systems across their lifecycle.
AI Risk / GRC is accountable for this process end to end, including its handoffs to other participating teams.

Other teams (e.g., Legal, Compliance, Engineering, Clinical Operations, Executive Leadership) participate in individual steps as specified below, but AI Risk / GRC owns the process and answers for its outcome.
AI Risk / GRC shall ensure that legal and regulatory requirements involving AI are understood, managed, and documented.

Acme Health must, for Govern 1.1, maintain awareness of the applicable legal and regulatory considerations and requirements specific to industry, sector, and business purpose, as well as the application context of the deployed AI system (Action 1); aligning risk management efforts with applicable legal standards (Action 2); and maintaining policies for training and re-training organizational staff about necessary legal or regulatory considerations that may impact AI-related design, development, and deployment activities (Action 3).
[NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.1 Action 1 | Govern 1.1 Action 2 | Govern 1.1 Action 3]
AI Risk / GRC shall ensure that the characteristics of trustworthy AI are integrated into Acme Health's organizational policies, processes, procedures, and practices.

NIST suggests, among its 15 actions for Govern 1.2, defining key terms and concepts related to AI systems and the scope of their purposes and intended uses (Action 1); connecting AI governance to existing organizational governance and risk controls (Action 2); aligning to broader data governance policies and practices, particularly the use of sensitive or otherwise risky data (Action 3); detailing standards for experimental design, data quality, and model training (Action 4); outlining and documenting risk mapping and measurement processes and standards (Action 5); detailing model testing and validation processes (Action 6); detailing review processes for legal and risk functions (Action 7); establishing the frequency of and detail for monitoring, auditing, and review processes (Action 8); outlining change management requirements (Action 9); outlining processes for internal and external stakeholder engagement (Action 10); establishing whistleblower policies to facilitate reporting of serious AI system concerns (Action 11); detailing and testing incident response plans (Action 12); verifying that formal AI risk management policies align to existing legal standards and industry best practices and norms (Action 13); establishing AI risk management policies that broadly align to AI system trustworthy characteristics (Action 14); and verifying that formal AI risk management policies include currently deployed and third-party AI systems (Action 15).

[NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.2 Action 1 | Govern 1.2 Action 2 | Govern 1.2 Action 3 | Govern 1.2 Action 4 | Govern 1.2 Action 5 | Govern 1.2 Action 6 | Govern 1.2 Action 7 | Govern 1.2 Action 8 | Govern 1.2 Action 9 | Govern 1.2 Action 10 | Govern 1.2 Action 11 | Govern 1.2 Action 12 | Govern 1.2 Action 13 | Govern 1.2 Action 14 | Govern 1.2 Action 15]
AI Risk / GRC shall maintain processes, procedures, and practices to determine the needed level of risk management activities based on the organization's risk tolerance.

NIST suggests, among its 5 actions for Govern 1.3, establishing policies to define mechanisms for measuring or understanding an AI system's potential impacts, for example via regular impact assessments at key stages in the AI lifecycle connected to system impacts and frequency of system updates (Action 1); establishing policies to define mechanisms for measuring or understanding the likelihood of an AI system's impacts and their magnitude at key stages in the AI lifecycle (Action 2); establishing policies that define assessment scales for measuring potential AI system impact, which may be qualitative such as red-amber-green (RAG) or may entail simulations or econometric approaches (Action 3); establishing policies for assigning an overall risk measurement approach for an AI system or its important components, for example via multiplication or combination of a mapped risk's impact and likelihood (Action 4); and establishing policies to assign systems to uniform risk scales that are valid across the organization's AI portfolio, acknowledging that risk tolerance and risk levels may change over the lifecycle of an AI system (Action 5).
[NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.3 Action 1 | Govern 1.3 Action 2 | Govern 1.3 Action 3 | Govern 1.3 Action 4 | Govern 1.3 Action 5]
AI Risk / GRC shall establish the risk management process and its outcomes through transparent policies, procedures, and other controls based on organizational risk priorities.

NIST suggests, among its 7 actions for Govern 1.4, establishing and regularly reviewing documentation policies addressing information such as AI actor contact information, business justification, scope and usages, expected and potential risks and impacts, assumptions and limitations, description and characterization of training data, algorithmic methodology, evaluated alternative approaches, description of output data, testing and validation results, down- and up-stream dependencies, plans for deployment, monitoring, and change management, and stakeholder engagement plans (Action 1); verifying that documentation policies for AI systems are standardized across the organization and remain current (Action 2); establishing policies for a model documentation inventory system and regularly reviewing its completeness, usability, and efficacy (Action 3); establishing mechanisms to regularly review the efficacy of risk management processes (Action 4); identifying AI actors responsible for evaluating efficacy of risk management processes and approaches and for course-correction based on results (Action 5); establishing policies and processes regarding public disclosure of the use of AI and risk management material such as impact assessments, audits, model documentation, and validation and testing results (Action 6); and documenting and reviewing the use and efficacy of different types of transparency tools and following industry standards at the time a model is in use (Action 7).
[NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.4 Action 1 | Govern 1.4 Action 2 | Govern 1.4 Action 3 | Govern 1.4 Action 4 | Govern 1.4 Action 5 | Govern 1.4 Action 6 | Govern 1.4 Action 7]

AI Risk / GRC shall plan ongoing monitoring and periodic review of the risk management process and its outcomes, shall clearly define organizational roles and responsibilities for those activities, and shall determine the frequency of periodic review ([Review Frequency]).

NIST suggests, among its 7 actions for Govern 1.5, establishing policies to allocate appropriate resources and capacity for assessing impacts of AI systems on individuals, communities, and society (Action 1); establishing policies and procedures for monitoring and addressing AI system performance and trustworthiness, including bias and security problems, across the lifecycle of the system (Action 2); establishing policies for AI system incident response, or confirming that existing incident response policies apply to AI systems (Action 3); establishing policies to define organizational functions and personnel responsible for AI system monitoring and incident response activities (Action 4); establishing mechanisms to enable the sharing of feedback from impacted individuals or communities about negative impacts from AI systems (Action 5); establishing mechanisms to provide recourse for impacted individuals or communities to contest problematic AI system outcomes (Action 6); and establishing opt-out mechanisms (Action 7).
[NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.5 Action 1 | Govern 1.5 Action 2 | Govern 1.5 Action 3 | Govern 1.5 Action 4 | Govern 1.5 Action 5 | Govern 1.5 Action 6 | Govern 1.5 Action 7]
AI Risk / GRC shall maintain mechanisms to inventory AI systems, and shall resource those mechanisms according to organizational risk priorities.

NIST suggests, among its 4 actions for Govern 1.6, establishing policies that define the creation and maintenance of AI system inventories (Action 1); establishing policies that define a specific individual or team that is responsible for maintaining the inventory (Action 2); establishing policies that define which models or systems are inventoried, with preference to inventorying all models or systems or, minimally, high risk models or systems, or systems deployed in high-stakes settings (Action 3); and establishing policies that define model or system attributes to be inventoried, for example documentation, links to source code, incident response plans, data dictionaries, and AI actor contact information (Action 4).
[NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.6 Action 1 | Govern 1.6 Action 2 | Govern 1.6 Action 3 | Govern 1.6 Action 4]

AI Risk / GRC shall maintain processes and procedures for decommissioning and phasing out AI systems safely and in a manner that does not increase risks or decrease the organization's trustworthiness.

NIST suggests, among its 4 actions for Govern 1.7, establishing policies for decommissioning AI systems that typically address user and community concerns and reputational risks, business continuity and financial risks, up- and downstream system dependencies, regulatory requirements such as data retention, potential future legal, regulatory, security, or forensic investigations, and migration to the replacement system if appropriate (Action 1); establishing policies that delineate where and for how long decommissioned systems, models, and related artifacts are stored (Action 2); establishing practices to track accountability and consider how decommission and other adaptations or changes in system deployment contribute to downstream impacts for individuals, groups, and communities (Action 3); and establishing policies that address ancillary data or artifacts that must be preserved for fulsome understanding or execution of the decommissioned AI system, for example predictions, explanations, intermediate input feature representations, and usernames and passwords (Action 4).
[NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.7 Action 1 | Govern 1.7 Action 2 | Govern 1.7 Action 3 | Govern 1.7 Action 4]

AI Risk / GRC shall document roles, responsibilities, and lines of communication related to mapping, measuring, and managing AI risks, and shall ensure they are clear to individuals and teams throughout the organization.

NIST suggests, among its 6 actions for Govern 2.1, establishing policies that define the AI risk management roles and responsibilities for positions directly and indirectly related to AI systems, including but not limited to boards of directors or advisory committees, senior management, AI audit functions, product management, project management, AI design, AI development, human-AI interaction, AI testing and evaluation, AI acquisition and procurement, impact assessment functions, and oversight functions (Action 1); establishing policies that promote regular communication among AI actors participating in AI risk management efforts (Action 2); establishing policies that separate management of AI system development functions from AI system testing functions to enable independent course-correction of AI systems (Action 3); establishing policies to identify, increase the transparency of, and prevent conflicts of interest in AI risk management efforts (Action 4); establishing policies to counteract confirmation bias and market incentives that may hinder AI risk management efforts (Action 5); and establishing policies that incentivize AI actors to collaborate with existing legal, oversight, compliance, or enterprise risk functions in their AI risk management activities (Action 6).
[NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 2.1 Action 1 | Govern 2.1 Action 2 | Govern 2.1 Action 3 | Govern 2.1 Action 4 | Govern 2.1 Action 5 | Govern 2.1 Action 6]

AI Risk / GRC shall ensure that the organization's personnel and partners receive AI risk management training to enable them to perform their duties and responsibilities consistent with related policies, procedures, and agreements.

NIST suggests, among its 6 actions for Govern 2.2, establishing policies for personnel addressing ongoing education about applicable laws and regulations for AI systems, potential negative impacts that may arise from AI systems, organizational AI policies, and trustworthy AI characteristics (Action 1); ensuring that trainings are suitable across AI actor sub-groups, for AI actors carrying out technical tasks such as developers and operators as compared to AI actors in oversight roles such as legal, compliance, and audit (Action 2); ensuring that trainings comprehensively address technical and socio-technical aspects of AI risk management (Action 3); verifying that organizational AI policies include mechanisms for internal AI personnel to acknowledge and commit to their roles and responsibilities (Action 4); verifying that organizational policies address change management and include mechanisms to communicate and acknowledge substantial AI system changes (Action 5); and defining paths along internal and external chains of accountability to escalate risk concerns (Action 6).
[NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 2.2 Action 1 | Govern 2.2 Action 2 | Govern 2.2 Action 3 | Govern 2.2 Action 4 | Govern 2.2 Action 5 | Govern 2.2 Action 6]
Acme Health executive leadership shall take responsibility for decisions about risks associated with AI system development and deployment.

NIST suggests, among its 2 actions for Govern 2.3, that organizational management declare risk tolerances for developing or using AI systems, support AI risk management efforts and play an active role in such efforts, integrate a risk and harm prevention mindset throughout the AI lifecycle as part of organizational culture, support competent risk management executives, and delegate the power, resources, and authorization to perform risk management to each appropriate level throughout the management chain (Action 1); and that organizations establish board committees for AI risk management and oversight functions and integrate those functions within the organization's broader enterprise risk management approaches (Action 2).
[NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 2.3 Action 1 | Govern 2.3 Action 2]

AI Risk / GRC shall ensure that decision-making related to mapping, measuring, and managing AI risks throughout the lifecycle is informed by a diverse team, including diversity of demographics, disciplines, experience, expertise, and backgrounds.

NIST suggests, among its 5 actions for Govern 3.1, defining policies and hiring practices at the outset that promote interdisciplinary roles, competencies, skills, and capacity for AI efforts (Action 1); defining policies and hiring practices that lead to demographic and domain expertise diversity, empowering staff with necessary resources and support, and facilitating the contribution of staff feedback and concerns without fear of reprisal (Action 2); establishing policies that facilitate inclusivity and the integration of new insights into existing practice (Action 3); seeking external expertise to supplement organizational diversity, equity, inclusion, and accessibility where internal expertise is lacking (Action 4); and establishing policies that incentivize AI actors to collaborate with existing nondiscrimination, accessibility and accommodation, and human resource functions, employee resource groups (ERGs), and diversity, equity, inclusion, and accessibility (DEIA) initiatives (Action 5).
[NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 3.1 Action 1 | Govern 3.1 Action 2 | Govern 3.1 Action 3 | Govern 3.1 Action 4 | Govern 3.1 Action 5]
AI Risk / GRC shall maintain policies and procedures that define and differentiate roles and responsibilities for human-AI configurations and oversight of AI systems.

NIST suggests, among its 8 actions for Govern 3.2, establishing policies and procedures that define and differentiate the various human roles and responsibilities when using, interacting with, or monitoring AI systems (Action 1); establishing procedures for capturing and tracking risk information related to human-AI configurations and associated outcomes (Action 2); establishing policies for the development of proficiency standards for AI actors carrying out system operation tasks and system oversight tasks (Action 3); establishing specified risk management training protocols for AI actors carrying out system operation tasks and system oversight tasks (Action 4); establishing policies and procedures regarding AI actor roles and responsibilities for human oversight of deployed systems (Action 5); establishing policies and procedures defining human-AI configurations, meaning configurations where AI systems are explicitly designated and treated as team members in primarily human teams, in relation to organizational risk tolerances and associated documentation (Action 6); establishing policies to enhance the explanation, interpretation, and overall transparency of AI systems (Action 7); and establishing policies for managing risks regarding known difficulties in human-AI configurations, human-AI teaming, and AI system user experience and user interactions (UI/UX) (Action 8).
[NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 3.2 Action 1 | Govern 3.2 Action 2 | Govern 3.2 Action 3 | Govern 3.2 Action 4 | Govern 3.2 Action 5 | Govern 3.2 Action 6 | Govern 3.2 Action 7 | Govern 3.2 Action 8]

AI Risk / GRC shall maintain organizational policies and practices that foster a critical thinking and safety-first mindset in the design, development, deployment, and uses of AI systems to minimize potential negative impacts.

NIST suggests, among its 5 actions for Govern 4.1, establishing policies that require inclusion of oversight functions — legal, compliance, and risk management — from the outset of the system design process (Action 1); establishing policies that promote effective challenge of AI system design, implementation, and deployment decisions via mechanisms such as the three lines of defense, model audits, or red-teaming, to minimize workplace risks such as groupthink (Action 2); establishing policies that incentivize safety-first mindset and general critical thinking and review at an organizational and procedural level (Action 3); establishing whistleblower protections for insiders who report on perceived serious problems with AI systems (Action 4); and establishing policies to integrate a harm and risk prevention mindset throughout the AI lifecycle (Action 5).
[NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 4.1 Action 1 | Govern 4.1 Action 2 | Govern 4.1 Action 3 | Govern 4.1 Action 4 | Govern 4.1 Action 5]

Organizational teams that design, develop, deploy, evaluate, and use AI technology shall document the risks and potential impacts of that technology, and shall communicate about those impacts more broadly; AI Risk / GRC owns and accounts for this documentation and communication process end to end.

NIST suggests, among its 4 actions for Govern 4.2, establishing impact assessment policies and processes for AI systems used by the organization (Action 1); aligning organizational impact assessment activities with relevant regulatory or legal requirements (Action 2); verifying that impact assessment activities are appropriate to evaluate the potential negative impact of a system and how quickly a system changes, and that assessments are applied on a regular basis (Action 3); and utilizing impact assessments to inform broader evaluations of AI system risk (Action 4).
[NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 4.2 Action 1 | Govern 4.2 Action 2 | Govern 4.2 Action 3 | Govern 4.2 Action 4]
AI Risk / GRC shall maintain organizational practices that enable AI testing, identification of incidents, and information sharing.

NIST suggests, among its 5 actions for Govern 4.3, establishing policies and procedures to facilitate and equip AI system testing (Action 1); establishing organizational commitment to identifying AI system limitations and sharing of insights about limitations within appropriate AI actor groups (Action 2); establishing policies for reporting and documenting incident response (Action 3); establishing policies and processes regarding public disclosure of incidents and information sharing (Action 4); and establishing guidelines for incident handling related to AI system risks and performance (Action 5).
[NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 4.3 Action 1 | Govern 4.3 Action 2 | Govern 4.3 Action 3 | Govern 4.3 Action 4 | Govern 4.3 Action 5]

AI Risk / GRC shall maintain organizational policies and practices to collect, consider, prioritize, and integrate feedback from those external to the team that developed or deployed the AI system regarding the potential individual and societal impacts related to AI risks.

NIST suggests, among its 3 actions for Govern 5.1, establishing AI risk management policies that explicitly address mechanisms for collecting, evaluating, and incorporating stakeholder and user feedback that could include recourse mechanisms for faulty AI system outputs, bug bounties, human-centered design, user-interaction and experience research, and participatory stakeholder engagement with individuals and communities that may experience negative impacts (Action 1); verifying that stakeholder feedback is considered and addressed, including environmental concerns and across the entire population of intended users, including historically excluded populations, people with disabilities, older people, and those with limited access to the internet and other basic technologies (Action 2); and clarifying the organization's principles as they apply to AI systems, considering those which have been proposed publicly, to inform external stakeholders of the organization's values, and considering publishing or adopting AI principles (Action 3).
[NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 5.1 Action 1 | Govern 5.1 Action 2 | Govern 5.1 Action 3]

AI Risk / GRC shall establish mechanisms that enable the team that developed or deployed AI systems to regularly incorporate adjudicated feedback from relevant AI actors into system design and implementation.

NIST suggests, among its 5 actions for Govern 5.2, explicitly acknowledging that AI systems and the use of AI present inherent costs and risks along with potential benefits (Action 1); defining reasonable risk tolerances for AI systems informed by laws, regulation, best practices, or industry standards (Action 2); establishing policies that ensure all relevant AI actors are provided with meaningful opportunities to provide feedback on system design and implementation (Action 3); establishing policies that define how to assign AI systems to established risk tolerance levels by combining system impact assessments with the likelihood that an impact occurs, often entailing some combination of econometric evaluations of impacts and impact likelihoods, red-amber-green (RAG) scales for impact severity and likelihood, policies for allocating risk management resources along established risk tolerance levels with higher-risk systems receiving more risk management resources and oversight, and policies for approval, conditional approval, and disapproval of the design, implementation, and deployment of AI systems (Action 4); and establishing policies facilitating the early decommissioning of AI systems that surpass an organization's ability to reasonably mitigate risks (Action 5).
[NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 5.2 Action 1 | Govern 5.2 Action 2 | Govern 5.2 Action 3 | Govern 5.2 Action 4 | Govern 5.2 Action 5]
Compliance with this Standard is audited by AI Risk / GRC, which owns this process end to end and answers for its outcome.
Deviations shall be reported to AI Risk / GRC and tracked to resolution.

The "NIST suggests" statements in this document reflect NIST's voluntary suggested actions from the NIST AI RMF Playbook and are not requirements of Acme Health; the tagged requirement statements in Sections 2 through 18 are binding on the personnel and teams to whom they are addressed.
