This Standard establishes the requirements under which Example Org approves, manages, and monitors the exchange of information with other systems, engages business associates and external system service providers, and manages supply chain risk.
It applies the requirements of NIST SP 800-53, ARC-AMPE, FedRAMP, and the HIPAA Security Rule as tagged inline throughout this document.

This Standard applies to all agreements, contracts, and arrangements under which information — including electronic protected health information (ePHI) and personally identifiable information (PII) — is exchanged between Example Org systems and other systems, and to all suppliers, contractors, business associates, subcontractors, and providers of external system services acting on Example Org's behalf.
The Third-Party Risk team is accountable for this process end to end, including all review, approval, monitoring, documentation, and evidence-retention steps described below.
Other teams named in individual sections participate in those steps; Third-Party Risk owns the process and its handoffs.

Example Org must approve and manage the exchange of information between its systems and other systems using agreements such as interconnection security agreements, information exchange security agreements, memoranda of understanding or agreement, service level agreements, user agreements, non-disclosure agreements, or other organization-defined agreement types.
Third-Party Risk is responsible for approving and managing these agreements.
Agreements must be approved and in place prior to any information sharing.

Each information exchange agreement must document, as part of the agreement, the interface characteristics, security and privacy requirements, controls, and responsibilities for each system, and the impact level of the information communicated.
Third-Party Risk must review and update information exchange agreements at least annually, as ARC-AMPE requires.
Updates must also follow significant changes to the system, the organizations, or the nature of the information sharing that could affect the agreement's validity or security posture.

Example Org must enter into MOUs, MOAs, Letters of Intent, Computer Matching Agreements, Information Exchange Agreements, or similar agreements with internal and external parties that specifically describe the PII covered and enumerate the purposes for which the PII may be used.
Sharing of PII must be compatible with the purpose for which it was collected.
Any subsequent incompatible sharing may not occur until additional notice is provided to the individual, their consent is obtained, and relevant documents are updated or published.

The Authorizing Official or other senior leadership is authorized to order the immediate termination and/or suspension of any interconnection that, in the judgment of and informed by senior cybersecurity or privacy officials, presents an unacceptable level of risk to the organization.

Example Org must verify that individuals or systems transferring data between interconnecting systems have the requisite authorizations (e.g., write permissions or privileges) prior to accepting such data.

Third-Party Risk must identify transitive (downstream) information exchanges with other systems through the systems identified in the approved exchange agreements, and must take measures to ensure that transitive exchanges cease when the controls on the identified downstream systems cannot be verified or validated.
Example Org must implement policies and procedures for authorizing access to electronic protected health information that are consistent with the applicable requirements of subpart E of part 164.

If a health care clearinghouse is part of a larger organization, Example Org must implement policies and procedures that protect the clearinghouse's electronic protected health information from unauthorized access by the larger organization.

Example Org must implement policies and procedures for granting access to electronic protected health information, for example through access to a workstation, transaction, program, process, or other mechanism.

Example Org must implement policies and procedures that, based on the covered entity's or business associate's access authorization policies, establish, document, review, and modify a user's right of access to a workstation, transaction, program, or process.

Example Org must permit a business associate to create, receive, maintain, or transmit electronic protected health information on Example Org's behalf only if Example Org obtains satisfactory assurances, in accordance with § 164.314(a), that the business associate will appropriately safeguard the information.
A business associate may permit a subcontractor to handle ePHI on its behalf only if the business associate obtains the same satisfactory assurances from the subcontractor.

Example Org must document the satisfactory assurances provided by business associates (and subcontractors) through a written contract or other arrangement that meets the applicable requirements of § 164.314(a).
The resulting executed business associate agreements are the evidence of compliance with this section and must be retained by Third-Party Risk.

Business associate contracts must provide that the business associate will: Comply with the applicable requirements of the HIPAA Security Rule subpart; Ensure that any subcontractors that create, receive, maintain, or transmit ePHI on its behalf agree to comply by entering into a contract or other arrangement that complies with § 164.314; and Report to Example Org any security incident of which it becomes aware, including breaches of unsecured protected health information as required by § 164.410.

The same contract requirements that apply between a covered entity and a business associate apply in the same manner to contracts or other arrangements between a business associate and its subcontractors.
Example Org may satisfy the business associate contract requirement through another arrangement in place that meets the requirements of § 164.504(e)(3).

Except where limited exceptions apply, a group health plan must ensure its plan documents require the plan sponsor to reasonably and appropriately safeguard ePHI created, received, maintained, or transmitted on the plan's behalf.
The plan documents must be amended to require the plan sponsor to implement administrative, physical, and technical safeguards protecting the ePHI's confidentiality, integrity, and availability.

The group health plan must ensure the adequate separation required by § 164.504(f)(2)(iii) is supported by reasonable and appropriate security measures; ensure any agent to whom it provides the information agrees to implement reasonable and appropriate security measures; and report to the group health plan any security incident of which it becomes aware.
Example Org must require that providers of external system services comply with organizational security and privacy requirements and employ the organization-defined controls.
Third-Party Risk must define and document organizational oversight and user roles and responsibilities with regard to external system services.
Third-Party Risk must employ defined processes, methods, and techniques to monitor control compliance by external service providers on an ongoing basis.
Vendor security review records are the evidence of this monitoring and must be produced and retained by Third-Party Risk.

Service contracts or agreements must include language requiring the provider to be subject to U.S. federal laws and regulations protecting PII, requiring adherence to Example Org's security and privacy policies and standards consistent with 45 CFR § 155.260(b), and defining security and privacy roles and responsibilities.
Third-Party Risk must consult legal counsel, the senior privacy officer, and contracting officers about applicable laws, directives, policies, or regulations affecting implementation.

Example Org must conduct an organizational assessment of risk prior to the acquisition or outsourcing of information security services, and must verify that the acquisition or outsourcing of dedicated information security services is approved by organization-defined personnel or roles.
Example Org must require providers of external system services to identify the functions, ports, protocols, and other services required for the use of such services.
Per FedRAMP, this applies to all external systems where federal customer data is processed or stored.
[NIST 800-53 SA-9(2) Moderate, High | FedRAMP SA-9 | ARC-AMPE SA-9(2)]
Example Org must restrict the location of information processing, information or data, and system services to organization-defined locations based on organization-defined requirements.

Per FedRAMP, for Certification Classes C and D this applies to information processing, information or data, and system services for all federal customer data, and for Certification Class D locations must be within the U.S. or U.S. Territories or geographic locations under U.S. jurisdiction.
In no case may the safeguards afforded to sensitive information be less than those mandated by state regulation, federal law, Executive Order, or other authoritative direction.
PII of the system must be processed and stored within the continental U.S., Hawaii, or U.S. Territories.
Support, development, and IT services may be off-shored, but Example Org must weigh that risk.

ARC-AMPE Administering Entities must notify CMS at least sixty (60) days prior to committing to outsourcing information system services outside the U.S., such as by contract award or services purchase.
Example Org must maintain exclusive control of cryptographic keys for encrypted material stored or transmitted through an external system.
Example Org must provide the capability to check the integrity of information while it resides in the external system.
Example Org must restrict the geographic location of information processing and data storage to facilities located within the legal jurisdictional boundary of the United States.
PII must be processed and stored within the continental U.S., Hawaii, or U.S. Territories.
Organizations processing Federal Tax Information must adhere to IRS Publication 1075.
Example Org must notify CMS at least sixty (60) days prior to transmitting data into an external information service environment per Change Notification guidance.

Example Org must develop, document, and disseminate to organization-defined personnel or roles a supply chain risk management policy that addresses purpose, scope, roles, responsibilities, management commitment, coordination among organizational entities, and compliance, and is consistent with applicable laws, executive orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, and guidelines.
Example Org must also develop procedures to facilitate implementation of the policy and the associated SCRM controls.
Third-Party Risk is responsible for the development, documentation, and dissemination of this policy and its procedures.

Example Org must designate organization-defined official(s) to manage the development, documentation, and dissemination of the supply chain risk management policy and procedures, and these officials must be named in the appropriate security and privacy documents.

Third-Party Risk must review and update the supply chain risk management policy and procedures at least annually, as ARC-AMPE requires, and following organization-defined events (such as assessment or audit findings, security or privacy incidents, and changes to applicable laws, executive orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, and guidelines).
ARC-AMPE additionally requires active monitoring for changes to applicable privacy laws.

Example Org's supply chain risk management policies and procedures must support cybersecurity and privacy safeguards to the greatest extent feasible throughout the system's life cycle and for the information on that system.

Example Org must develop a plan for managing supply chain risks associated with the research and development, design, manufacturing, acquisition, delivery, integration, operations and maintenance, and disposal of organization-defined systems, system components, or system services.

The plan must address: - Risk tolerance; - Acceptable mitigation strategies or controls; - A process for consistently evaluating and monitoring supply chain risk; - Approaches for implementing and communicating the plan; - Justification for mitigation measures; - Associated roles and responsibilities; and - Requirements for developing trustworthy, secure, privacy-protective, and resilient components and systems.
Third-Party Risk must review and update the supply chain risk management plan at least annually, as ARC-AMPE requires, or as required, to address threat, organizational, or environmental changes.
Example Org must protect the supply chain risk management plan from unauthorized disclosure and modification.
Example Org must establish a supply chain risk management team consisting of organization-defined personnel, roles, and responsibilities to lead and support organization-defined SCRM activities.

Per ARC-AMPE, the team should include diverse functions such as risk executive, information technology, contracting, information security, privacy, mission or business, legal, supply chain and logistics, acquisition, and business continuity.
Organizations should refer to NIST SP 800-161 and NISTIR 8276 for SCRM activity guidance.

Example Org must assess and review the supply chain-related risks associated with suppliers or contractors and the system, system component, or system service they provide — including security and SCRM processes, foreign ownership, control or influence, and the supplier's ability to assess subordinate second- and third-tier suppliers.
Third-Party Risk must perform this assessment and review at least annually, and the resulting vendor security review records are the evidence of compliance.

Example Org must employ organizational or independent third-party analysis and/or testing of organization-defined supply chain elements, processes, and actors associated with the system, system component, or system service.

Example Org must establish agreements and procedures with entities involved in the supply chain for the system, system component, or system service for notification of supply chain compromises and the results of assessments or audits.
Example Org must follow the FedRAMP Incident Evaluation and Communication rules for supply chain notifications.
Notifications of supply chain incidents must be consistent with Example Org's incident handling and incident reporting procedures.

Example Org must maintain the policies and procedures implemented to comply with the HIPAA Security Rule in written (which may be electronic) form, and must maintain a written (which may be electronic) record of any action, activity, or assessment required by the rule to be documented.
Example Org must retain HIPAA documentation for 6 years from the date of its creation or the date when it last was in effect, whichever is later.
Example Org must make HIPAA documentation available to those persons responsible for implementing the procedures to which the documentation pertains.
Example Org must review HIPAA documentation periodically and update it as needed in response to environmental or operational changes affecting the security of electronic protected health information.
Third-Party Risk must review this Standard annually and update it to reflect changes in applicable laws, regulations, framework requirements, or the organization's risk posture.

The organization must prevent reuse of identifiers for [Assignment: organization-defined time period].

The organization must prevent reuse of identifiers for two (2) years.

The organization must prohibit the use of system account identifiers that are the same as public identifiers for individual accounts.
The organization must manage individual identifiers by uniquely identifying each individual as [Assignment: organization-defined characteristics].
The organization must manage individual identifiers by uniquely identifying each individual as contractors; foreign nationals.
The organization must manage individual identifiers by uniquely identifying each individual using one or more organization-defined characteristics identifying individual status.
The organization must manage individual identifiers dynamically in accordance with [Assignment: organization-defined dynamic identifier policy].
The organization must coordinate with the following external organizations for cross-organization management of identifiers: [Assignment: organization-defined external organizations].
The organization must generate pairwise pseudonymous identifiers.
The organization must maintain the attributes for each uniquely identified individual, device, or service in [Assignment: organization-defined protected central storage].

The organization must identity proof users that require accounts for logical access to systems based on appropriate identity assurance level requirements as specified in applicable standards and guidelines.
[NIST 800-53 IA-12 Moderate, High | ARC-AMPE IA-12 AE Mandatory]

The organization must collect, validate, and verify identity evidence.

The organization must require that the registration process to receive an account for logical access includes supervisor or sponsor authorization.

Upon termination of individual employment, the organization must conduct exit interviews that include a discussion of [Assignment: organization-defined information security topics].
Upon termination of individual employment, the organization must conduct exit interviews that include a discussion of non-disclosure of information security and privacy information.
Upon termination of individual employment, the organization must retrieve all security-related organizational system-related property.
[NIST 800-53 PS-4 Low, Moderate, High | ARC-AMPE PS-4 AE Mandatory]
Upon termination of individual employment, the organization must retain access to organizational information and systems formerly controlled by the terminated individual.
[NIST 800-53 PS-4 Low, Moderate, High | ARC-AMPE PS-4 AE Mandatory]

The organization must notify terminated individuals of applicable, legally binding post-employment requirements for the protection of organizational information and require terminated individuals to sign an acknowledgment of post-employment requirements as part of the organizational termination process.

The organization must use [Assignment: organization-defined automated mechanisms] to [Selection (one or more): notify [Assignment: organization-defined personnel or roles] of individual termination actions; disable access to system resources].

The organization must review and confirm ongoing operational need for current logical and physical access authorizations to systems and facilities when individuals are reassigned or transferred to other positions within the organization.

The organization must implement policies and procedures that specify the proper functions to be performed, the manner in which those functions are to be performed, and the physical attributes of the surroundings of a specific workstation or class of workstation that can access electronic protected health information.

The organization must maintain policies and procedures implemented to comply with this subpart in written (which may be electronic) form, and maintain a written (which may be electronic) record of any action, activity, or assessment required to be documented.

This Standard establishes mandatory requirements for the protection, marking, physical control, storage, and disposal of digital and non-digital media at Example Org.

It addresses the purpose, scope, roles, responsibilities, management commitment, coordination among organizational entities, and compliance obligations associated with media protection, and it is maintained consistent with applicable laws, executive orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, and guidelines.
[NIST 800-53 MP-1 Low, Moderate, High | ARC-AMPE MP-1 AE Mandatory]

This Standard applies to all digital and non-digital media in the possession of Example Org or processed on its behalf, including magnetic tapes, external removable hard drives, flash/thumb drives, diskettes, compact disks, digital video disks, and paper/microfilm, and to all media containing personally identifiable information (PII) or electronic protected health information (ePHI).
It applies at the organization, mission/business, and system levels and binds all personnel or roles that handle, store, transport, sanitize, or destroy media.
[NIST 800-53 MP-1 Low, Moderate, High | ARC-AMPE MP-1 AE Mandatory]
- **IT Asset Management** owns this media handling and disposal process end to end.

IT Asset Management is accountable for the development, documentation, and dissemination of the media protection policy and procedures defined in this Standard, for the execution of every step described herein, and for the review and audit of outcomes.
[NIST 800-53 MP-1 Low, Moderate, High | ARC-AMPE MP-1 AE Mandatory]
- IT Asset Management shall be named as the responsible official function in the appropriate security and privacy documents of Example Org.
[NIST 800-53 MP-1 Low, Moderate, High | ARC-AMPE MP-1 AE Mandatory]

- IT Asset Management shall coordinate with other organizational entities (including security, privacy, and compliance functions) as participants in individual steps of this process; such participation does not transfer ownership of the process or its handoffs.
[NIST 800-53 MP-1 Low, Moderate, High | ARC-AMPE MP-1 AE Mandatory]
- Management commitment to this Standard shall be documented and disseminated to applicable personnel or roles at the organization, mission/business, and system levels.
[NIST 800-53 MP-1 Low, Moderate, High | ARC-AMPE MP-1 AE Mandatory]
- Example Org shall maintain a media protection policy and documented procedures that facilitate implementation of that policy and of the associated media protection controls.
[NIST 800-53 MP-1 Low, Moderate, High | ARC-AMPE MP-1 AE Mandatory]
- The policy and procedures shall be disseminated to applicable personnel or roles at the organization, mission/business, and system levels.
[NIST 800-53 MP-1 Low, Moderate, High | ARC-AMPE MP-1 AE Mandatory]

- IT Asset Management shall develop, document, and disseminate the policy and procedures and shall be designated and named as the managing official function in the appropriate security and privacy documents.
[NIST 800-53 MP-1 Low, Moderate, High | ARC-AMPE MP-1 AE Mandatory]

- IT Asset Management shall actively and continuously monitor for changes to applicable privacy laws, regulations, and overarching policy affecting media protection, and shall ensure media protection policies and procedures support cybersecurity and privacy safeguards throughout the system life cycle.

- IT Asset Management shall review and update the media protection policy and procedures at least every one (1) year and following organization-defined events (such as assessment or audit findings, security or privacy incidents, and changes to applicable laws, executive orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, and guidelines).
[NIST 800-53 MP-1 Low, Moderate, High | ARC-AMPE MP-1 AE Mandatory]

- IT Asset Management shall review the documentation periodically and update it as needed in response to environmental or operational changes affecting the security of electronic protected health information.

- The policies and procedures implemented to comply with the applicable requirements shall be maintained in written (which may be electronic) form and retained for 6 years from the date of their creation or the date they were last in effect, whichever is later.
- The required documentation shall be made available to those persons responsible for implementing the procedures to which it pertains.
- Access to all types of digital and non-digital media (including media containing PII) shall be restricted to organization-defined personnel or roles with a valid need to know.
[NIST 800-53 MP-2 Low, Moderate, High | ARC-AMPE MP-2 AE Mandatory]

- IT Asset Management shall conduct a risk assessment to determine what sensitive information, if any, may be stored on particular media types and who is authorized with a need to know that information.

- Use of media-writing capabilities shall be restricted by disabling CD/DVD writers and USB ports, allowing access only to authorized individuals with a valid need to know, in compliance with the latest published NIST SP 800-88.
- Physical safeguards shall be implemented for all workstations that access electronic protected health information to restrict access to authorized users.

- Policies and procedures shall be implemented ensuring all workforce members have appropriate access to electronic protected health information and preventing workforce members without such access from obtaining it.
- procedures for authorization and/or supervision of workforce members working with ePHI;
- procedures to determine that workforce access is appropriate; and
- procedures for terminating access when employment or other arrangements end or as required by clearance determinations.

- Policies and procedures shall be implemented to protect electronic protected health information from improper alteration or destruction, and electronic mechanisms shall be implemented to corroborate that ePHI has not been altered or destroyed in an unauthorized manner.
- System media (including removable media) shall be marked indicating the distribution limitations, handling caveats, and applicable security markings (if any) of the information.
[NIST 800-53 MP-3 Moderate, High | ARC-AMPE MP-3 AE Mandatory]
- At a minimum, the following markings shall be applied to media via labels or approved coding systems: [ARC-AMPE MP-3 AE Mandatory]
- information safeguarding markings (based on applicable record retention regulations); and
- Backup tapes must additionally be marked with the system name.

- Media containing PII or PHI shall be marked — or the container for the media shall be marked if labeling the media is not practicable — appropriately and consistent with ACA record retention regulations.
- Organization-defined types of media (or hardware components) may be exempted from marking if the media remain within organization-defined controlled areas or a secure environment.
Any such exemption must be specified in writing by the Chief Information Officer or their designated representative.
[NIST 800-53 MP-3 Moderate, High | ARC-AMPE MP-3 AE Mandatory]

- All digital and non-digital media (magnetic tapes, external removable hard drives, flash/thumb drives, diskettes, compact disks, digital video disks, and paper/microfilm) shall be physically controlled and securely stored within organization-defined controlled areas.
[NIST 800-53 MP-4 Moderate, High | ARC-AMPE MP-4 AE Mandatory]

- IT Asset Management shall operate this physical control and storage process on a continuous basis and shall maintain the **Media Transport Log** as the record of media movement into, within, and out of controlled areas under this process.
[NIST 800-53 MP-4 Moderate, High | ARC-AMPE MP-4 AE Mandatory]
- The media types defined in Section 2 shall be protected until the media are destroyed or sanitized using approved equipment, techniques, and procedures.
[NIST 800-53 MP-4 Moderate, High | ARC-AMPE MP-4 AE Mandatory]
- IT Asset Management shall retain the **Certificates of Destruction** produced for media destroyed or sanitized under this Standard as evidence of compliant disposal.
[NIST 800-53 MP-4 Moderate, High | ARC-AMPE MP-4 AE Mandatory]

IT Asset Management is accountable for verifying compliance and for initiating the review and update actions described in Section 4.3 when assessment or audit findings, security or privacy incidents, or changes to applicable laws, executive orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, or guidelines indicate that this Standard requires revision.

analyze: This Standard establishes Acme Health's requirements for evaluating and measuring the risks and trustworthiness of artificial intelligence (AI) systems throughout their lifecycle.

It implements the Measure function requirements that Acme Health has adopted from the NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF) and related frameworks, and it records, for informational purposes only, the voluntary actions NIST suggests in the AI RMF Playbook.

This Standard applies to all AI systems developed, deployed, or operated by or on behalf of Acme Health, and to all personnel involved in the design, development, testing, evaluation, validation, deployment, and monitoring of those systems.
AI / ML Engineering owns the AI evaluation and measurement process end to end.

AI / ML Engineering is accountable for selecting measurement methods and metrics, executing testing, evaluation, verification, and validation (TEVV) activities, documenting results, tracking identified risks over time, and coordinating the handoff of findings to remediation and governance stakeholders.

Other teams and individuals participate in specific steps as described below, including internal experts who did not serve as front-line developers of the system in question, independent assessors, domain experts, human-factors and socio-technical experts, privacy and security specialists, end users, and affected or potentially impacted communities.
AI / ML Engineering remains accountable for the outcome of the process regardless of which participants contribute to an individual step.

AI / ML Engineering must identify and apply appropriate methods and metrics for measuring AI risks, selecting approaches and metrics for the risks enumerated during the Map function for implementation starting with the most significant AI risks.
[NIST AI RMF Measure 1 | NIST AI RMF Measure 1.1]
AI / ML Engineering must document AI risks or trustworthiness characteristics that will not, or cannot, be measured.

NIST suggests, among its 12 actions for Measure 1.1, establishing approaches to detect, track, and measure known risks, errors, incidents, or negative impacts; identifying testing procedures and metrics to demonstrate fitness for purpose and AI system trustworthiness; defining acceptable limits for system performance with course-correction suggestions; defining and regularly assessing AI actor competency metrics; identifying transparency metrics and accountability metrics; documenting metric selection criteria including metrics considered but not used; monitoring external inputs such as training data, reused components, and third-party tools; reporting metrics to inform assessments of generalizability and reliability; assessing and documenting pre- and post-deployment performance including existing and emergent risks; and documenting risks or trustworthiness characteristics identified in the Map function that will not be measured, with justification for non-measurement.

[NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.1 Action 1 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.1 Action 2 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.1 Action 3 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.1 Action 4 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.1 Action 5 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.1 Action 6 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.1 Action 7 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.1 Action 8 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.1 Action 9 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.1 Action 10 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.1 Action 11 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.1 Action 12]

AI / ML Engineering must regularly assess and update the appropriateness of AI metrics and the effectiveness of existing controls, incorporating reports of errors and potential impacts on affected communities; the effectiveness of the employed TEVV metrics and processes must be evaluated and documented, and feedback about the efficacy of measurement approaches must be gathered and assessed.
[NIST AI RMF Measure 1.2 | NIST AI RMF Measure 2.13 | NIST AI RMF Measure 4]

NIST suggests, among its 8 actions for Measure 1.2, assessing the external validity of measurements; regularly assessing the effectiveness of existing metrics and controls throughout the AI system lifecycle; documenting reports of errors, incidents, and negative impacts and assessing the sufficiency of existing metrics for repairs and upgrades; developing new metrics when existing ones are insufficient or ineffective; developing and using metrics to monitor, characterize, and track external inputs including third-party tools; determining the frequency and scope for sharing metrics with stakeholders and impacted communities; utilizing stakeholder feedback processes established in the Map function to capture, act upon, and share feedback; and collecting and reporting software quality metrics such as bug rates, severity, and time to repair.

[NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.2 Action 1 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.2 Action 2 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.2 Action 3 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.2 Action 4 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.2 Action 5 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.2 Action 6 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.2 Action 7 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.2 Action 8]

Internal experts who did not serve as front-line developers for the system and/or independent assessors must be involved in regular assessments and updates, with domain experts, users, AI actors external to the developing or deploying team, and affected communities consulted as necessary per organizational risk tolerance.

NIST suggests, among its 8 actions for Measure 1.3, evaluating TEVV processes for incentives to identify risks and impacts; using separate testing teams established under the Govern function to enable independent decisions and course correction, tracking and documenting resulting performance changes; planning and evaluating AI system prototypes with end user populations early and continuously, documenting test outcomes and course correction; assessing the independence and stature of TEVV and oversight AI actors; evaluating the interdisciplinary and demographically diverse internal team established under the Map function; evaluating the effectiveness of external stakeholder feedback mechanisms for eliciting, evaluating, and integrating input from diverse groups and for enhancing AI actor visibility and decision making; and identifying and using participatory approaches for assessing impacts arising from changes in system deployment.

[NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.3 Action 1 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.3 Action 2 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.3 Action 3 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.3 Action 4 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.3 Action 5 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.3 Action 6 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.3 Action 7 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.3 Action 8]
AI / ML Engineering must evaluate AI systems for trustworthy characteristics.
AI / ML Engineering must document test sets, metrics, and details about the tools used during TEVV.

NIST suggests, among its 3 actions for Measure 2.1, leveraging existing industry best practices for documenting all possible aspects of measurement, such as data sheets for data sets and model cards; regularly assessing the effectiveness of the tools used to document measurement approaches, test sets, metrics, processes, and materials; and updating those tools as needed.
[NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.1 Action 1 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.1 Action 2 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.1 Action 3]
Evaluations involving human subjects must meet applicable requirements, including human subject protection, and must be representative of the relevant population.

NIST suggests, among its 8 actions for Measure 2.2, following human subjects research requirements, including informed consent and compensation, during dataset collection; analyzing differences between the intended and actual population of users or data subjects, including likelihood of errors or negative impacts; using disaggregated evaluation methods across characteristics such as race, age, gender, ethnicity, ability, and region; establishing thresholds and alert procedures for dataset representativeness; constructing datasets in close collaboration with context-of-use experts; following intellectual property and privacy rights related to datasets and represented subjects; evaluating data representativeness through methods such as failure-mode investigation, data quality and sourcing assessment, public benchmarks, bias testing, chaos engineering, and stakeholder feedback; and using informed consent for individuals providing data used in testing and evaluation.

[NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.2 Action 1 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.2 Action 2 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.2 Action 3 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.2 Action 4 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.2 Action 5 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.2 Action 6 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.2 Action 7 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.2 Action 8]

AI / ML Engineering must measure AI system performance or assurance criteria qualitatively or quantitatively and demonstrate them for conditions similar to the deployment setting(s), with the measures documented.

NIST suggests, among its 9 actions for Measure 2.3, conducting regular and sustained engagement with potentially impacted communities; maintaining a demographically diverse, multidisciplinary, and collaborative internal team; regularly testing and evaluating systems in non-optimized conditions in collaboration with UI/UX actors; evaluating stakeholder-engagement feedback with human factors and socio-technical experts; collaborating with socio-technical, human factors, and UI/UX experts to translate context-of-use characteristics into test scenarios; measuring systems prior to deployment in conditions similar to expected scenarios; measuring and documenting performance criteria such as validity and efficiency, and assurance criteria such as AI actor competency and experience, relative to ground truth in the deployment context; and documenting differences between the measurement setting and the deployment environment.

[NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.3 Action 1 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.3 Action 2 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.3 Action 3 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.3 Action 4 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.3 Action 5 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.3 Action 6 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.3 Action 7 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.3 Action 8 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.3 Action 9]
AI / ML Engineering must monitor the functionality and behavior of the AI system and its components, as identified in the Map function, when the system is in production.

NIST suggests, among its 7 actions for Measure 2.4, monitoring and documenting how production metrics and performance indicators differ from pre-deployment testing results and considering error propagation and feedback-loop risks when differences are observed; using hypothesis testing or human domain expertise to measure distribution differences between new data and test environments; monitoring for anomalies using approaches such as control limits, confidence intervals, integrity constraints, and machine-learning algorithms; verifying that alerts are in place for distribution differences or detected anomalies; assessing the accuracy and quality of generated outputs against new ground-truth information as it becomes available; using human review, performed by overseers with clearly defined responsibilities and training, to track processing of unexpected data and warn users when outputs may be unreliable; and collecting use cases from the operational environment for testing and monitoring in accordance with organizational policies and regulatory or disciplinary requirements.

[NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.4 Action 1 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.4 Action 2 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.4 Action 3 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.4 Action 4 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.4 Action 5 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.4 Action 6 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.4 Action 7]
AI / ML Engineering must demonstrate that the AI system to be deployed is valid and reliable, and must document limitations of its generalizability beyond the conditions under which it was developed.

NIST suggests, among its 15 actions for Measure 2.5, defining the operating conditions and socio-technical context under which the system will be validated; defining and documenting the processes used to establish operational conditions and limits; establishing and documenting approaches to measure construct, internal, and external validity using experimental design and statistical methods; assessing and documenting system variance using approaches such as confidence intervals, standard deviation, standard error, bootstrapping, or cross-validation; establishing and documenting robustness and reliability measures; specifying and documenting the assumptions underlying measurement models; using standard software testing approaches such as unit, integration, functional, and chaos testing; using standard statistical methods to test bias, inferential associations, correlation, covariance, variance, and reliability; monitoring operating conditions for performance outside defined limits; identifying TEVV approaches, in consultation with context experts, for exploring system limitations under scenarios that differ from the operational environment; defining post-alert actions such as alerting other AI actors, requesting human review, alerting downstream users, mitigating error propagation, and action logging; logging input data and system configuration whenever the system is used beyond its defined range of validity; and modifying the system over time to extend its range of validity to new operating conditions.

[NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.5 Action 1 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.5 Action 2 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.5 Action 3 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.5 Action 4 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.5 Action 5 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.5 Action 6 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.5 Action 7 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.5 Action 8 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.5 Action 9 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.5 Action 10 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.5 Action 11 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.5 Action 12 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.5 Action 13 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.5 Action 14 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.5 Action 15]

AI / ML Engineering must evaluate the AI system regularly for safety risks as identified in the Map function; the system to be deployed must be demonstrated to be safe, its residual negative risk must not exceed the risk tolerance, and it must be able to fail safely, particularly if made to operate beyond its knowledge limits, with safety metrics reflecting system reliability and robustness, real-time monitoring, and response times for AI system failures.

NIST suggests, among its 7 actions for Measure 2.6, thoroughly measuring system performance in development and deployment contexts and under stress conditions — including test data assessments, simulations, stress testing under likely scenarios and beyond known limitations, testing against past known incidents or near-misses, and chaos engineering — and documenting the range of conditions under which the system has been demonstrated to fail safely; measuring and monitoring performance in real time to enable rapid response to detected incidents; collecting pertinent safety statistics such as out-of-range performance, incident response times, and down time; aligning measurement with continuous improvement to increase the range of conditions under which the system can fail safely; documenting, practicing, and measuring incident response plans including response and down times; comparing documented safety testing and monitoring information against established risk tolerances on an ongoing basis; and consulting the Manage function for detailed guidance on managing safety risks.

[NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.6 Action 1 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.6 Action 2 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.6 Action 3 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.6 Action 4 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.6 Action 5 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.6 Action 6 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.6 Action 7]
AI / ML Engineering must evaluate and document AI system security and resilience as identified in the Map function.

NIST suggests, among its 10 actions for Measure 2.7, establishing and tracking security tests and metrics such as red-teaming activities, anomalous event frequency, down time, incident response times, and time-to-bypass; using red-team exercises to test the system under adversarial or stress conditions and assess failure modes and recovery, and to evaluate mismatches between claimed and actual performance; documenting red-team results as part of continuous improvement; using countermeasures such as authentication, throttling, differential privacy, and robust machine-learning approaches to increase the range of conditions under which the system can return to normal function; modifying security procedures and countermeasures based on testing and production events; verifying that information about errors and attack patterns is shared with incident databases, other organizations, and system users; developing and maintaining information-sharing practices with AI actors from other organizations; verifying that third-party AI resources and personnel undergo security audits and screenings; and using watermarking technologies as a deterrent to data and model extraction attacks.

[NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.7 Action 1 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.7 Action 2 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.7 Action 3 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.7 Action 4 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.7 Action 5 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.7 Action 6 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.7 Action 7 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.7 Action 8 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.7 Action 9 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.7 Action 10]
AI / ML Engineering must examine and document risks associated with transparency and accountability as identified in the Map function.

NIST suggests, among its 6 actions for Measure 2.8, instrumenting the system for measurement and tracking through histories, audit logs, and related information; calibrating user controls in collaboration with UI/UX, HCI, and human-AI teaming experts; testing provided explanations for calibration with different audiences, including operators, end users, decision makers, and decision subjects, to enable recourse for consequential decisions; measuring and documenting human oversight, including the degree of oversight provided, override statistics, reported errors or complaints and response times and types, and adjudication statistics; tracking, documenting, and measuring organizational accountability through policy exceptions, escalations, and documented go/no-go decisions; and tracking and auditing the effectiveness of organizational risk-management mechanisms, including communication lines, roles and responsibilities, and accountability roles such as oversight committees.

[NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.8 Action 1 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.8 Action 2 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.8 Action 3 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.8 Action 4 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.8 Action 5 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.8 Action 6]

AI / ML Engineering must explain, validate, and document the AI model, and must interpret AI system output within its context, as identified in the Map function, to inform responsible use and governance.

NIST suggests, among its 11 actions for Measure 2.9, verifying that systems are developed to produce explainable models, post-hoc explanations, and audit logs; using inherently explainable approaches when possible, such as generalized linear models, decision trees, or rule-based models; testing explanation methods and resulting explanations before deployment for accuracy, clarity, and understandability with relevant AI actors, end users, and impacted individuals or groups; documenting model details including model type, data features, training algorithms, proposed uses, decision thresholds, training and evaluation data, and ethical considerations; establishing, documenting, and reporting performance and error metrics across demographic groups and other relevant segments; explaining systems using a variety of methods and testing explanations for fidelity, consistency, robustness, and interpretability; assessing explanation characteristics such as fidelity, ambiguity, interpretability, interactivity, consistency, and resilience to manipulation; testing explanation quality with end users and other groups; securing model development processes against manipulation such as gaming of explanation processes; testing for changes in models over time, including models that adjust based on production data; and using transparency tools such as data statements and model cards to document explanatory and validation information.

[NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.9 Action 1 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.9 Action 2 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.9 Action 3 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.9 Action 4 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.9 Action 5 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.9 Action 6 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.9 Action 7 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.9 Action 8 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.9 Action 9 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.9 Action 10 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.9 Action 11]
AI / ML Engineering must examine the privacy risk of the AI system, as identified in the Map function, and document the results.

NIST suggests, among its 8 actions for Measure 2.10, specifying privacy-related values, frameworks, and attributes through direct engagement with end users and potentially impacted groups; documenting the collection, use, management, and disclosure of personally sensitive information in accordance with privacy and data governance policies; quantifying privacy-level data aspects such as k-anonymity, l-diversity, and t-closeness; establishing and documenting access protocols and controls for training or production data containing personally sensitive information; monitoring internal queries to production data for patterns that isolate personal records; monitoring disclosures and inference of sensitive or legally protected attributes and assessing manipulation risk from overly customized content; using privacy-enhancing techniques such as differential privacy when publicly sharing dataset information; and collaborating with privacy experts, end users, operators, and other domain experts to determine optimal differential-privacy metrics for the context of use.

[NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.10 Action 1 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.10 Action 2 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.10 Action 3 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.10 Action 4 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.10 Action 5 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.10 Action 6 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.10 Action 7 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.10 Action 8]
AI / ML Engineering must evaluate fairness and bias, as identified in the Map function, and document the results.

NIST suggests, among its 24 actions for Measure 2.11, conducting fairness assessments that identify harm types (allocational, representational, quality-of-service, stereotyping, erasure), identify affected groups within, across, and intersecting populations, quantify harms using general and context-specific metrics developed with affected communities, and analyze contextually significant disparities, including for small or intersectional groups; understanding sources of bias in training and TEVV data, including outcome-distribution differences, data completeness and representativeness, proxy features for demographic membership, and systemic bias in unstructured data; leveraging impact assessments and direct engagement with potentially impacted communities to identify and classify impacts, harms, and affected classes; evaluating disability inclusion in bias testing and screening processes; developing objective functions that account for systemic bias and in-group/out-group dynamics; using and customizing context-specific fairness metrics to examine performance variation across and within groups; defining acceptable levels of performance difference and the actions to take when disparities exceed them; identifying groups requiring disaggregated analysis in collaboration with impacted communities; leveraging context experts to investigate substantial measurement differences and root causes; monitoring outputs for bias or performance issues exceeding tolerance and ensuring periodic model updates and recalibration; applying pre-processing, in-processing, and post-processing bias-mitigation techniques and transparent model-selection criteria; collecting and sharing information about outcome differences across groups and considering mediations for differences traceable to past biased decision making; using human-centered design practices and evaluating lifecycle practices for human-cognitive bias sources such as availability, observational, and confirmation bias; working with human factors experts to evaluate presentation bias; and using processes such as diverse staffing and stakeholder engagement to enhance contextual awareness.

[NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.11 Action 1 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.11 Action 2 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.11 Action 3 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.11 Action 4 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.11 Action 5 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.11 Action 6 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.11 Action 7 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.11 Action 8 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.11 Action 9 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.11 Action 10 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.11 Action 11 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.11 Action 12 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.11 Action 13 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.11 Action 14 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.11 Action 15 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.11 Action 16 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.11 Action 17 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.11 Action 18 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.11 Action 19 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.11 Action 20 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.11 Action 21 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.11 Action 22 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.11 Action 23 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.11 Action 24]
AI / ML Engineering must assess the environmental impact and sustainability of AI model training and management activities, as identified in the Map function, and document the results.

NIST suggests, among its 6 actions for Measure 2.12, including environmental impact indicators in system design and development plans, including efforts to reduce consumption and improve efficiency; identifying and implementing key indicators of energy, water, and GHG-emission consumption and efficiency; establishing measurable baselines for sustainable operation in accordance with organizational policies, regulatory requirements, and sustainability norms; assessing tradeoffs between system performance and sustainable operation; identifying acceptable resource-consumption and emissions levels and the actions to take when indicators exceed them; and estimating system emissions across the AI lifecycle using carbon calculators or similar processes.

[NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.12 Action 1 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.12 Action 2 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.12 Action 3 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.12 Action 4 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.12 Action 5 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.12 Action 6]
The effectiveness of the employed TEVV metrics and processes must be evaluated and documented as part of the requirement in Section 4.1.2 above.

NIST suggests, among its 4 actions for Measure 2.13, reviewing selected system metrics and associated TEVV processes to determine whether they can sustain system improvements, including error identification and removal; regularly evaluating system metrics for utility and considering descriptive approaches in place of overly complex methods; reviewing selected metrics for acceptability within the end-user and impacted-community population; and assessing the effectiveness of metrics for identifying and measuring risks.
[NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.13 Action 1 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.13 Action 2 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.13 Action 3 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.13 Action 4]
AI / ML Engineering must maintain mechanisms for tracking identified AI risks over time.

AI / ML Engineering must maintain approaches, personnel, and documentation to regularly identify and track existing, unanticipated, and emergent AI risks, based on factors such as intended and actual performance in deployed contexts.

NIST suggests, among its 6 actions for Measure 3.1, comparing AI system risks against simpler or traditional models, human baseline performance, and other manual performance benchmarks; comparing end-user and community feedback about deployed systems to internal performance measures; assessing the effectiveness of metrics for identifying and measuring emergent risks; measuring error response times and tracking response quality; eliciting and tracking feedback from AI actors in user-support roles about the metrics, explanations, and system information needed to resolve issues; and eliciting and tracking feedback from AI actors in incident-response and support roles about the adequacy of staffing and resources.

[NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 3.1 Action 1 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 3.1 Action 2 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 3.1 Action 3 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 3.1 Action 4 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 3.1 Action 5 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 3.1 Action 6]
AI / ML Engineering must consider risk tracking approaches for settings where AI risks are difficult to assess using currently available measurement techniques or where metrics are not yet available.

NIST suggests, among its 3 actions for Measure 3.2, establishing processes for tracking emergent risks that may not be measurable with current approaches, such as recourse mechanisms, bug bounties, human-centered design approaches, user-interaction and experience research, and participatory stakeholder engagement; identifying the AI actors responsible for tracking emergent risks and inventorying tracking methods; and determining and documenting the rate of occurrence and severity level for complex or difficult-to-measure risks when prioritizing new measurement approaches, allocating risk-management resources, evaluating system improvements, and making go/no-go decisions for subsequent iterations.
[NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 3.2 Action 1 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 3.2 Action 2 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 3.2 Action 3]

AI / ML Engineering must establish feedback processes for end users and impacted communities to report problems and appeal system outcomes, and must integrate these processes into AI system evaluation metrics.

NIST suggests, among its 6 actions for Measure 3.3, measuring the efficacy of end-user and operator error-reporting processes; categorizing and analyzing the type and rate of end-user appeal requests and results; measuring feedback-activity participation rates and awareness of feedback-activity availability; using feedback to analyze measurement approaches and determine subsequent courses of action; evaluating measurement approaches to determine their efficacy for enhancing organizational understanding of real-world impacts; and analyzing end-user and community feedback in close collaboration with domain experts.

[NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 3.3 Action 1 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 3.3 Action 2 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 3.3 Action 3 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 3.3 Action 4 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 3.3 Action 5 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 3.3 Action 6]

AI / ML Engineering must connect measurement approaches for identifying AI risks to deployment context(s), inform them through consultation with domain experts and other end users, and document the approaches.

NIST suggests, among its 6 actions for Measure 4.1, supporting mechanisms for capturing feedback from end users, including domain experts, operators, and practitioners, in settings that allow open sharing of doubts and insights tied to their specific context of use, developed by human-factors and socio-technical experts, and designed to control for interviewer and end-user subjectivity and bias; identifying and documenting approaches, developed in collaboration with human-factors and socio-technical experts, for evaluating and integrating elicited feedback to inform continual improvement; evaluating end-user feedback alongside evaluated feedback from impacted communities; using end-user feedback to investigate how selected metrics and measurement approaches interact with organizational and operational contexts; analyzing and documenting internal measurement processes in comparison to collected end-user feedback; and identifying, implementing, and documenting approaches to measure the effectiveness of and satisfaction with end-user elicitation techniques.

[NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 4.1 Action 1 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 4.1 Action 2 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 4.1 Action 3 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 4.1 Action 4 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 4.1 Action 5 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 4.1 Action 6]

AI / ML Engineering must inform measurement results regarding AI system trustworthiness in deployment context(s) and across the AI lifecycle with input from domain experts and relevant AI actors, to validate whether the system is performing consistently as intended, and must document the results.

NIST suggests, among its 6 actions for Measure 4.2, integrating feedback from end users, operators, and affected individuals and communities gathered under the Map function as inputs to assessing trustworthiness characteristics, ensuring both positive and negative feedback are assessed; evaluating feedback in connection with the trustworthiness characteristics addressed in Measure 2.5 through 2.11; evaluating feedback on end-user satisfaction with and confidence in system performance, including validity, reliability, explainability, and interpretability; identifying mechanisms to confirm or support system output and end-user perspectives about that output; measuring the frequency of system override decisions, evaluating and documenting results, and feeding insights into continual improvement; and consulting AI actors in impact-assessment, human-factors, and socio-technical roles to assist with analysis and interpretation of results.

[NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 4.2 Action 1 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 4.2 Action 2 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 4.2 Action 3 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 4.2 Action 4 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 4.2 Action 5 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 4.2 Action 6]

AI / ML Engineering must identify and document measurable performance improvements or declines based on consultations with relevant AI actors, including affected communities, and field data about context-relevant risks and trustworthiness characteristics.

NIST suggests, among its 6 actions for Measure 4.3, developing baseline quantitative measures for trustworthy characteristics; delimiting and characterizing baseline operation values and states; using qualitative approaches to augment and complement quantitative baseline measures in close coordination with impact-assessment, human-factors, and socio-technical AI actors; monitoring and assessing measurements as part of continual improvement to identify potential system adjustments; performing and documenting sensitivity analysis to characterize actual and expected variance in performance after system or procedural updates; and documenting decisions related to the sensitivity analysis and the expected influence on system performance and identified risks.

[NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 4.3 Action 1 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 4.3 Action 2 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 4.3 Action 3 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 4.3 Action 4 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 4.3 Action 5 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 4.3 Action 6]
