This standard defines the requirements for treating AI risks and responding to AI-related incidents and errors at Acme Health.
It applies to all AI systems in development, deployment, and post-deployment operation.
The AI Risk / Incident Response team is accountable for this process end to end, including all handoffs described in this document.
Other teams may participate in individual steps as identified herein.

The AI Risk / Incident Response team must determine whether the AI system achieves its intended purposes and stated objectives, and must make a determination as to whether its development or deployment should proceed.

NIST suggests, among its 5 actions for Manage 1.1, considering trustworthiness characteristics when evaluating AI systems' negative risks and benefits [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 1.1 Action 1], utilizing TEVV outputs from the MAP and MEASURE functions when considering risk treatment [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 1.1 Action 2], regularly tracking and monitoring negative risks and benefits throughout the AI system lifecycle, including in post-deployment monitoring [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 1.1 Action 3], regularly assessing and documenting system performance relative to trustworthiness characteristics and tradeoffs between negative risks and opportunities [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 1.1 Action 4], and evaluating tradeoffs in connection with real-world use cases and impacts as enumerated in MAP function outcomes [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 1.1 Action 5].
The AI Risk / Incident Response team must prioritize treatment of documented AI risks based on impact, likelihood, and available resources or methods.

NIST suggests, among its 3 actions for Manage 1.2, assigning risk management resources relative to established risk tolerance, such that AI systems with lower risk tolerances receive greater oversight, mitigation, and management resources [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 1.2 Action 1], documenting AI risk tolerance determination practices and resource decisions [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 1.2 Action 2], and regularly reviewing risk tolerances and re-calibrating, as needed, in accordance with information from AI system monitoring and assessment [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 1.2 Action 3].

The AI Risk / Incident Response team must develop, plan, and document responses to AI risks deemed high priority (as identified by the MAP function), with risk response options including mitigating, transferring, avoiding, or accepting.

NIST suggests, among its 5 actions for Manage 1.3, observing regulatory and established organizational, sector, discipline, or professional standards and requirements for applying risk tolerances within the organization [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 1.3 Action 1], documenting procedures for acting on AI system risks related to trustworthiness characteristics [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 1.3 Action 2], prioritizing risks involving physical safety, legal liabilities, regulatory compliance, and negative impacts on individuals, groups, or society [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 1.3 Action 3], identifying risk response plans and resources and organizational teams for carrying out response functions [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 1.3 Action 4], and storing risk management and system documentation in an organized, secure repository that is accessible by relevant AI actors and appropriate personnel [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 1.3 Action 5].
The AI Risk / Incident Response team must document negative residual risks (the sum of all unmitigated risks) to both downstream acquirers of AI systems and end users.

NIST suggests, among its 3 actions for Manage 1.4, documenting residual risks within risk response plans, denoting risks that have been accepted, transferred, or subject to minimal mitigation [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 1.4 Action 1], establishing procedures for disclosing residual risks to relevant downstream AI actors [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 1.4 Action 2], and informing relevant downstream AI actors of requirements for safe operation, known limitations, and suggested warning labels as identified in MAP 3.4 [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 1.4 Action 3].

The AI Risk / Incident Response team must take into account the resources required to manage AI risks, along with viable non-AI alternative systems, approaches, or methods, to reduce the magnitude or likelihood of potential impacts.

NIST suggests, among its 6 actions for Manage 2.1, planning and implementing risk management practices in accordance with established organizational risk tolerances [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 2.1 Action 1], verifying risk management teams are resourced to carry out functions, including establishing processes for considering methods that are not automated, semi-automated, or other procedural alternatives for AI functions, enhancing AI system transparency mechanisms for AI teams, enabling exploration of AI system limitations by AI teams, and identifying, assessing, and cataloging past failed designs and negative impacts or outcomes to avoid known failure modes [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 2.1 Action 2], identifying resource allocation approaches for managing risks in systems deemed high-risk, that self-update (adaptive, online, reinforcement self-supervised learning or similar), that are trained without access to ground truth (unsupervised, semi-supervised learning or similar), or with high uncertainty or where risk management is insufficient [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 2.1 Action 3], regularly seeking and integrating external expertise and perspectives to supplement organizational diversity (e.g., demographic, disciplinary), equity, inclusion, and accessibility where internal capacity is lacking [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 2.1 Action 4], enabling and encouraging regular, open communication and feedback among AI actors and internal or external stakeholders related to system design or deployment decisions [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 2.1 Action 5], and preparing and documenting plans for continuous monitoring and feedback mechanisms [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 2.1 Action 6].
The AI Risk / Incident Response team must apply mechanisms in place to sustain the value of deployed AI systems.

NIST suggests, among its 4 actions for Manage 2.2, establishing risk controls considering trustworthiness characteristics, including data management, quality, and privacy controls (e.g., minimization, rectification or deletion requests) as part of organizational data governance policies; machine learning and end-point security countermeasures (e.g., robust models, differential privacy, authentication, throttling); business rules that augment, limit, or restrict AI system outputs within certain contexts; utilizing domain expertise related to deployment context for continuous improvement and TEVV across the AI lifecycle; development and regular tracking of human-AI teaming configurations; model assessment and test, evaluation, validation and verification (TEVV) protocols; use of standardized documentation and transparency mechanisms; software quality assurance practices across the AI lifecycle; and mechanisms to explore system limitations and avoid past failed designs or deployments [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 2.2 Action 1], establishing mechanisms to capture feedback from system end users and potentially impacted groups while the system is in deployment, including feedback about how changes in system deployment (e.g., introducing new technology, decommissioning algorithms and models, adapting system, model or algorithm) may create negative impacts that are not visible along the AI lifecycle [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 2.2 Action 2], reviewing insurance policies, warranties, or contracts for legal or oversight requirements for risk transfer procedures [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 2.2 Action 3], and documenting risk tolerance decisions and risk acceptance procedures [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 2.2 Action 4].
The AI Risk / Incident Response team must follow procedures to respond to and recover from a previously unknown risk when it is identified.

NIST suggests, among its 7 actions for Manage 2.3, having protocols, resources, and metrics in place for continual monitoring of AI systems' performance, trustworthiness, and alignment with contextual norms and values [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 2.3 Action 1], establishing and regularly reviewing treatment and response plans for incidents, negative impacts, or outcomes [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 2.3 Action 2], establishing and maintaining procedures to regularly monitor system components for drift, decontextualization, or other AI system behavior factors [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 2.3 Action 3], establishing and maintaining procedures for capturing feedback about negative impacts [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 2.3 Action 4], verifying contingency processes to handle any negative impacts associated with mission-critical AI systems, and to deactivate systems [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 2.3 Action 5], enabling preventive and post-hoc exploration of AI system limitations by relevant AI actor groups [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 2.3 Action 6], and decommissioning systems that exceed risk tolerances [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 2.3 Action 7].

The AI Risk / Incident Response team must maintain and apply mechanisms to supersede, disengage, or deactivate AI systems that demonstrate performance or outcomes inconsistent with intended use, with responsibilities assigned and understood.

NIST suggests, among its 8 actions for Manage 2.4, regularly reviewing established procedures for AI system bypass actions, including plans for redundant or backup systems to ensure continuity of operational and/or business functionality [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 2.4 Action 1], regularly reviewing system incident thresholds for activating bypass or deactivation responses [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 2.4 Action 2], applying change management processes to understand the upstream and downstream consequences of bypassing or deactivating an AI system or AI system components [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 2.4 Action 3], applying protocols, resources, and metrics for decisions to supersede, bypass, or deactivate AI systems or AI system components [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 2.4 Action 4], preserving materials for forensic, regulatory, and legal review [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 2.4 Action 5], conducting internal root cause analysis and process reviews of bypass or deactivation events [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 2.4 Action 6], decommissioning and preserving system components that cannot be updated to meet criteria for redeployment [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 2.4 Action 7], and establishing criteria for redeploying updated system components, in consideration of trustworthiness characteristics [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 2.4 Action 8].

The AI Risk / Incident Response team must document risk treatments for identified and measured AI risks — including response and recovery plans and communication plans — and must monitor them regularly.

The AI Risk / Incident Response team must implement post-deployment AI system monitoring plans, including mechanisms for capturing and evaluating input from users and other relevant AI actors, appeal and override, decommissioning, incident response, recovery, and change management.

NIST suggests, among its 9 actions for Manage 4.1, establishing and maintaining procedures to monitor AI system performance for risks and negative and positive impacts associated with trustworthiness characteristics [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 4.1 Action 1], performing post-deployment TEVV tasks to evaluate AI system validity and reliability, bias and fairness, privacy, and security and resilience [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 4.1 Action 2], evaluating AI system trustworthiness in conditions similar to the deployment context of use, and prior to deployment [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 4.1 Action 3], establishing and implementing red-teaming exercises at a prescribed cadence, and evaluating their efficacy [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 4.1 Action 4], establishing procedures for tracking dataset modifications such as data deletion or rectification requests [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 4.1 Action 5], establishing mechanisms for regular communication and feedback between relevant AI actors and internal or external stakeholders to capture information about system performance, trustworthiness, and impact [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 4.1 Action 6], sharing information about errors, near-misses, and attack patterns with incident databases, other organizations with similar systems, and system users and stakeholders [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 4.1 Action 7], responding to and documenting detected or reported negative impacts or issues in AI system performance and trustworthiness [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 4.1 Action 8], and decommissioning systems that exceed established risk tolerances [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 4.1 Action 9].

The AI Risk / Incident Response team must integrate measurable activities for continual improvement into AI system updates, including regular engagement with interested parties, including relevant AI actors.

NIST suggests, among its 5 actions for Manage 4.2, integrating trustworthiness characteristics into protocols and metrics used for continual improvement [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 4.2 Action 1], establishing processes for evaluating and integrating feedback into AI system improvements [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 4.2 Action 2], assessing and evaluating alignment of proposed improvements with relevant regulatory and legal frameworks [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 4.2 Action 3], assessing and evaluating alignment of proposed improvements connected to the values and norms within the context of use [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 4.2 Action 4], and documenting the basis for decisions made relative to tradeoffs between trustworthiness characteristics, system risks, and system opportunities [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 4.2 Action 5].

The AI Risk / Incident Response team must communicate incidents and errors to relevant AI actors, including affected communities, and must follow and document processes for tracking, responding to, and recovering from incidents and errors.

NIST suggests, among its 5 actions for Manage 4.3, establishing procedures to regularly share information about errors, incidents, and negative impacts with relevant stakeholders, operators, practitioners, and users, and impacted parties [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 4.3 Action 1], maintaining a database of reported errors, near-misses, incidents, and negative impacts including date reported, number of reports, assessment of impact and severity, and responses [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 4.3 Action 2], maintaining a database of system changes, reason for change, and details of how the change was made, tested, and deployed [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 4.3 Action 3], maintaining version history information and metadata to enable continuous improvement processes [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 4.3 Action 4], and verifying that relevant AI actors responsible for identifying complex or emergent risks are properly resourced and empowered [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 4.3 Action 5].

analyze: **Standard ID:** STD-REMOTE-001 **Owning Team:** Network Security **Classification:** Internal — Mandatory Compliance

This Standard establishes mandatory requirements for all remote access to Example Org systems, wireless access, mobile device access, third-party (vendor) access, and access to Example Org systems from external systems.
It applies to all Example Org personnel, contractors, and third parties who access Example Org systems remotely, and to all systems that permit such access.
Network Security is accountable for this process end to end, including authorization, monitoring, disconnection capability, recertification, and evidence retention.

| Role | Responsibility | | ------------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Network Security | Owns this Standard end to end: authorizes remote access types, maintains the VPN and remote-access configuration and the Third-party access register, monitors remote access methods, executes disconnection and connection-termination actions, recertifies vendor-assigned User IDs, and conducts the quarterly review defined in Section 11. | | System Business Owner | Authorizes the use of mobile devices per Section 9 and documents remote access rationale in the applicable System Security and Privacy Plan (SSPP). | | Authorizing Official (AO) or designated representative | Provides written authorization where required for portable storage device use on external systems and for non-organizationally owned systems and components per Section 10. | | Device users | Comply with all device configuration, encryption, and acknowledgment requirements in Sections 5, 9, and 10. |

3.1 Network Security must establish and document usage restrictions, configuration/connection requirements, and implementation guidance for each type of remote access allowed, and must authorize each type of remote access to the system prior to allowing such connections.
These authorizations, restrictions, and requirements must be recorded in the VPN and remote-access configuration.

3.2 For organizations supporting remote access (including teleworking), Network Security must follow the latest published NIST SP 800-46 guidelines by establishing policies and procedures that define: forms of permitted remote access; types of devices permissible for remote access; types of access granted to remote users; and handling of remote user account provisioning.
3.3 For remote access solutions (e.g., e-authentication), Network Security must follow the latest published NIST SP 800-63.

3.4 Network Security must require callback capability with re-authentication to verify connections from authorized locations when the Multi-Protocol Label Switching (MPLS) service network cannot be used.

4.1 For application systems and turnkey systems that require the vendor to log on, Network Security must assign the vendor a User ID and password, require entry through the standard authentication process, authorize and log access to such systems, and recertify vendor-assigned User IDs within every one (1) year.
4.2 All vendor-assigned User IDs, the systems they access, their authorization status, and recertification outcomes must be recorded in the Third-party access register maintained by Network Security.

5.1 Network Security must ensure all computers and devices that require network access to an Example Org network or system — whether government furnished equipment (GFE), contractor furnished equipment (CFE), or personal — are securely configured to, at a minimum: - have up-to-date system patches; - run current anti-virus software; - run a host-based intrusion detection system; - have functionality providing automatic execution of code disabled; and - employ the latest published FIPS 140-compliant encryption standards.
6.1 Network Security must employ automated mechanisms to monitor and control remote access methods.

6.2 Network Security must implement cryptographic mechanisms to protect the confidentiality and integrity of remote access sessions; encrypting remote sessions protects the confidentiality and integrity of sensitive information.
6.3 Network Security must route remote accesses through authorized and managed network access control points.

6.4 Network Security must authorize the execution of privileged commands and access to security-relevant information via remote access only in a format that provides assessable evidence and for compelling operational needs, and the rationale for remote access must be documented in the security plan for the system.

6.5 Network Security must define what constitutes a compelling operational need for remote execution of privileged commands and access to security-relevant information, and must document these definitions in the applicable System Security and Privacy Plan (SSPP).
6.6 Network Security must protect information about remote access mechanisms from unauthorized use and disclosure.
6.7 Network Security must provide the capability to disconnect or disable remote access to the system within an organization-defined time period.
The defined time period is one (1) hour.
6.8 Network Security must terminate or suspend network connections (i.e., a system-to-system interconnection) within one (1) hour upon issuance of an order by organization-defined officials.
6.9 Network Security must implement organization-defined mechanisms to authenticate organization-defined remote commands.

7.1 Network Security must implement policies and procedures that specify the proper functions to be performed, the manner in which those functions are to be performed, and the physical attributes of the surroundings of a specific workstation or class of workstation that can access electronic protected health information.

8.1 Network Security must establish configuration requirements, connection requirements, and implementation guidance for each type of wireless access, and must authorize each type of wireless access to the system prior to allowing such connections.
These requirements and authorizations must be recorded in the VPN and remote-access configuration.

8.2 If wireless access is explicitly approved, Network Security must disable wireless device service set identifier (SSID) broadcasting and implement the following wireless restrictions and access controls: - encryption protection is enabled; - access points are placed in secure areas; - access points are shut down when not in use (e.g., nights, weekends); - a stateful inspection firewall is implemented between the wireless network and the wired infrastructure; - Media Access Control (MAC) address authentication is utilized; - static IP addresses (not Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) are utilized; - personal firewalls are utilized on all wireless clients; - file sharing is disabled on all wireless clients; - intrusion detection agents are deployed on the wireless side of the firewall; - wireless activity is monitored and recorded with records reviewed on a regular basis (as defined in applicable security/privacy plans); and - the implementation adheres to the latest published IEEE 802.11 Wireless Local Area Network (WLAN) standard.
8.3 Network Security must protect wireless access to the system using authentication of users and devices and encryption.
8.4 Network Security must ensure all communications via the wireless access device are encrypted using the latest published FIPS 140-compliant encryption standards.
8.5 Network Security must disable, when not intended for use, wireless networking capabilities embedded within system components prior to issuance and deployment.
8.6 Network Security must identify and explicitly authorize the users allowed to independently configure wireless networking capabilities.

8.7 Network Security must select radio antennas and calibrate transmission power levels to reduce the probability that signals from wireless access points can be received outside of organization-controlled boundaries.

9.1 Network Security must establish configuration requirements, connection requirements, and implementation guidance for organization-controlled mobile devices, to include when such devices are outside of controlled areas, and must authorize the connection of mobile devices to organizational systems.
9.2 The System Business Owner must authorize the use of mobile devices.
9.3 Only organization-owned mobile devices and software may be used to process, access, and store Personally Identifiable Information (PII).

9.4 Network Security must ensure mobile devices are configured to protect the storage and transmission of information on the device and must implement scanning of the device using a virus protection application.
9.5 Network Security must employ full-device encryption or container-based encryption to protect the confidentiality and integrity of information on organization-defined (approved) mobile devices.
9.6 Full-device or container encryption on mobile devices must use the latest published FIPS 140-compliant encryption standards.
9.7 Information on all mobile devices that contain Personally Identifiable Information (PII) must be encrypted.

9.8 Before device users are provided access to Personally Identifiable Information (PII) on remote devices, Network Security must require them to acknowledge through a binding agreement their responsibilities to safeguard the PII accessible from the device and that they are aware of and [remainder of this requirement was truncated in the source material and must be completed against the source before publication].

10.1 Network Security must either establish organization-defined terms and conditions and identify organization-defined controls asserted to be implemented on external systems — consistent with the trust relationships established with other organizations owning, operating, and/or maintaining external systems — allowing authorized individuals to (1) access the system from external systems and (2) process, store, or transmit organization-controlled information using external systems; or prohibit the use of organization-defined prohibited types of external systems.

10.2 The defined terms and conditions for external system use must address, at a minimum: - the types of applications that can be accessed from external information systems; - the maximum FIPS 199 security category of information that can be processed, stored, and transmitted; - how other users of the external information system will be prevented from accessing federal information; - the use of Virtual Private Network (VPN) and stateful inspection firewall technologies; - the use of and protection against the vulnerabilities of wireless technologies; - the maintenance of adequate physical security controls; - the use of virus and spyware protection software; and - how often the security capabilities of installed software are to be updated.

10.3 The interrelated controls must be differentiated as follows: AC-20 describes system access to and from external systems; CA-3 describes documentation of an agreement between the respective system owners when data is exchanged between the CSO and an external system; and SA-9 describes the responsibilities of external system owners, which would typically be captured in the agreement required by CA-3.

10.4 Authorized individuals may use an external system to access the system or to process, store, or transmit organization-controlled information only after either verification of the implementation of controls on the external system as specified in the organization's security and privacy policies and security and privacy plans, or retention of approved system connection or processing agreements with the organizational entity hosting the external system.
Network Security must verify these conditions and must record the verification or retained agreements in the Third-party access register.
[NIST AC-20(1) Moderate, High | FedRAMP AC-20(1) | ARC-AMPE AC-20(1)]
10.5 Network Security must restrict the use of organization-controlled portable storage devices by authorized individuals on external systems using organization-defined restrictions.

10.6 The restrictions on the use of organization-controlled portable storage devices on external systems must be defined in the applicable system security and privacy plans, and such use may be permitted only when: - the use is documented within appropriate security/privacy plans; - the use is explicitly authorized, in writing, by the Authorizing Official (AO) or designated representative; - personally owned devices to which the portable storage devices are to be attached comply with organization policies and directives on use of personally owned systems and components; and - security and privacy safeguards appropriate for the sensitivity of the data are employed.

10.7 Network Security must restrict the use of non-organizationally owned systems or system components to process, store, or transmit organizational information using organization-defined restrictions, unless: - the use of contractor-owned devices is documented within the contract and appropriate security and privacy plans and explicitly authorized, in writing, by the Authorizing Official (AO) or designated representative; - the use of personally owned devices complies with organizational policies and directives on use of personally-owned systems and components; - security and privacy safeguards appropriate for the sensitivity of the data are employed; and - either full-device or virtual container encryption is implemented to reduce the vulnerability of sensitive information processed, stored, or transmitted by non-organizationally owned systems or system components.
10.8 The use of personally owned devices must be strongly discouraged.

11.1 Network Security must review the VPN and remote-access configuration and the Third-party access register quarterly to confirm that all authorized remote access types, vendor-assigned User IDs, external system agreements, and disconnection capabilities remain accurately documented and compliant with this Standard.

11.2 The following artifacts constitute the evidence of record for this Standard and must be retained and produced upon audit: - VPN and remote-access configuration; and - Third-party access register.

11.3 Findings from the quarterly review must be remediated by Network Security within [Remediation Deadline], and unresolved findings must be escalated to the Authorizing Official or designated representative.

This Standard establishes the requirements for the protection, handling, transport, sanitization, and disposal of digital and non-digital media at Example Org.

It addresses the full media lifecycle — from receipt into a facility through final destruction or release out of organizational control — and ensures that media containing sensitive information, including electronic protected health information (ePHI) and personally identifiable information (PII), is protected against unauthorized access, alteration, disclosure, and destruction.

This Standard applies to all digital and non-digital system media owned, controlled, or processed by Example Org, including magnetic tapes, external removable hard drives, flash/thumb drives, diskettes, compact disks, digital video disks, and hard-copy documents, and to all personnel and roles that handle such media.

**IT Asset Management** is accountable for this process end to end, including receipt and removal of media, movement of media within facilities, transport accountability, sanitization and disposal actions, and the production and retention of the evidence artifacts defined in this Standard (Certificates of destruction and the Media transport log).
**IT Asset Management** must designate official(s) to manage the development, documentation, and dissemination of the media protection policy and procedures.

Example Org must develop, document, and disseminate to applicable personnel or roles an organization-level media protection policy that addresses purpose, scope, roles, responsibilities, management commitment, coordination among organizational entities, and compliance, and that is consistent with applicable laws, executive orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, and guidelines.
Example Org must develop, document, and disseminate procedures to facilitate implementation of the media protection policy and the associated media protection controls.

The media protection policy and procedures must be reviewed and updated following organization-defined events (such as assessment or audit findings, security or privacy incidents, and changes to applicable laws, executive orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, and guidelines).
This review must occur at least every one (1) year.

The media protection policies and procedures must be maintained in written (which may be electronic) form, retained for 6 years from the date of creation or the date they were last in effect (whichever is later), made available to persons responsible for implementing the procedures, and reviewed and updated periodically in response to environmental or operational changes affecting the security of electronic protected health information.

IT Asset Management must implement policies and procedures that govern the receipt and removal of hardware and electronic media containing electronic protected health information into and out of a facility, and the movement of these items within the facility.
Access to digital and non-digital media (including all types of media containing PII) must be restricted to organization-defined authorized personnel or roles.

Use of media write capabilities must be restricted by disabling CD/DVD writers and USB ports, allowing access only to authorized individuals with a valid need to know, in compliance with the latest published NIST SP 800-88.
A risk assessment must be conducted to determine what sensitive information, if any, can be stored on certain media types and who is authorized with a need to know that information.

Policies and procedures must be implemented ensuring all workforce members have appropriate access to electronic protected health information and preventing workforce members without such access from obtaining it, including: - procedures for authorization and/or supervision of workforce members; [HIPAA 164.308(a)(3)(ii)(A)] - procedures to determine that workforce access is appropriate; and [HIPAA 164.308(a)(3)(ii)(B)] - procedures for terminating access when employment or other arrangements end.
Physical safeguards must be implemented for all workstations that access electronic protected health information to restrict access to authorized users.

Policies and procedures must be implemented to protect electronic protected health information from improper alteration or destruction, and electronic mechanisms must be implemented to corroborate that it has not been altered or destroyed in an unauthorized manner.
System media must be marked indicating the distribution limitations, handling caveats, and applicable security markings (if any) of the information.
At a minimum, markings must include: - creation date; - information safeguarding markings (based on applicable record retention regulations); and - organization-defined contact information,

with backup tapes also labeled with the system name, and media containing PII or PHI (or its container, if labeling the media is not practicable) marked consistently with ACA record retention regulations.
Specific types of media may be exempted from marking if the media remain within organization-defined controlled areas or secure environments.
Such exemptions must be specified in writing by the Chief Information Officer or their designated representative.

Digital and non-digital media (including magnetic tapes, external removable hard drives, flash/thumb drives, diskettes, compact disks, and digital video disks) must be physically controlled and securely stored within organization-defined controlled areas.
Stored system media must be protected until the media are destroyed or sanitized using approved equipment, techniques, and procedures.
- Digital media must be encrypted using the latest published FIPS 140-compliant encryption standards.
- Non-digital media must be stored in secure storage such as locked cabinets or safes.
- Removable media containing PII must be stored in a securable area or locked container.
- Magnetic media containing PII recorded alongside other data must be protected as if all data on the media were PII.
- Surplus equipment must be stored securely while not in use.
Access to media storage areas must be restricted, and access attempts and access granted must be logged using [Assignment: organization-defined automated mechanisms].

Digital and non-digital media containing sensitive information (such as PII) must be protected and controlled during transport outside of controlled areas using organization-defined controls such as: - a latest published FIPS 140-compliant encryption module; - locked/securable containers or tamper-evident packaging transported via authorized personnel; - a trackable receipt by the commercial shipping carrier; and - sealed packing cartons for non-digital media containing sensitive information.

Accountability for system media must be maintained during transport outside of controlled areas, including maintaining a record of the movements of hardware and electronic media and of any person responsible for them.
IT Asset Management must record these movements in the Media transport log.
Activities associated with the transport of system media must be documented.
Activities associated with the transport of system media must be restricted to authorized personnel.
An identified custodian must be employed during transport of system media outside of controlled areas.
A retrievable, exact copy of electronic protected health information must be created, when needed, before movement of equipment.

Digital and non-digital system media must be sanitized prior to disposal, release out of organizational control, or release for reuse using organization-defined sanitization techniques and procedures in accordance with the latest published NIST SP 800-88 guidelines.

For electronic protected health information, this includes addressing the final disposition of the information and the hardware or media on which it is stored, and removing ePHI from electronic media before the media are made available for re-use.
Sanitization mechanisms must be employed with the strength and integrity commensurate with the security category or classification of the information.
- Hard-copy documents must be finely shredded using approved equipment, techniques, and procedures with cross-cut shredding at a minimum.
- Media containing PII must be sanitized prior to disposal, release out of the organization, or release for reuse using the latest FIPS-validated media sanitization techniques or procedures.
- Surplus equipment must be disposed of or sanitized in accordance with the latest published NIST SP 800-88.
Media sanitization and disposal actions must be reviewed, approved, tracked, documented, and verified.
Sensitive information, including PII, must be securely destroyed or disposed of appropriately and reasonably and in accordance with retention schedules.

Media-related sanitization records must contain: - the name of the media recipient; - the signature of the media recipient; - the date/time received; - the media control number and contents; - movement or routing information; and - if disposed of, the date, time, and method of destruction.
IT Asset Management must produce a Certificate of destruction for each disposal action and retain it as evidence of the sanitization and disposal process.
Sanitization equipment and procedures must be tested to ensure that the intended sanitization is being achieved.
This testing must occur within every one (1) year.
Nondestructive sanitization techniques must be applied to portable storage devices prior to connecting such devices to the system under [Assignment: organization-defined circumstances].
Dual authorization must be enforced for the sanitization of [Assignment: organization-defined system media].

The capability must be provided to purge or wipe information from [Assignment: organization-defined systems or system components] \[Selection: remotely; under [Assignment: organization-defined conditions]\].
This process runs on a continuous basis and must produce and retain the following evidence artifacts:

| Artifact | Produced By | Associated Requirements | | -------------------------- | ------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- | | Certificate of destruction | IT Asset Management | Media sanitization and disposal actions (Section 9.3, 9.4) | | Media transport log | IT Asset Management | Transport accountability and documentation (Section 8.2) |
Compliance with this Standard is mandatory for all personnel and roles within scope.
Exceptions must be documented and approved in accordance with the organization's exception management process.
Violations may result in disciplinary action in accordance with organizational policy.

analyze: This standard defines Acme Health's requirements for governing, and being accountable for, the risks of artificial intelligence (AI) systems.
As a healthcare organization, Acme Health is subject to legal and regulatory requirements involving AI, and this standard establishes how those obligations are understood, managed, and documented.
This standard applies to all AI systems that Acme Health designs, develops, deploys, evaluates, uses, or procures, including third-party AI systems and currently deployed systems.
AI Risk / GRC is accountable for this standard and for the AI risk management process it defines, end to end.
AI Risk / GRC owns every step, review, handoff, and outcome described in this document; other teams named below participate in individual steps as participants.
Statements in this document introduced by "NIST suggests" restate voluntary suggested actions from the NIST AI RMF Playbook.
They are suggestions from NIST, not requirements of this standard, and impose no obligation on Acme Health.
All other requirement statements are binding on the teams to which they are addressed.

| Field | Value | |---|---| | Standard owner | AI Risk / GRC | | Applies to | All AI systems designed, developed, deployed, evaluated, used, or procured by Acme Health, including third-party and currently deployed systems | | Periodic review frequency | [Review Frequency] |

Acme Health shall maintain policies, processes, procedures, and practices related to mapping, measuring, and managing AI risks that are in place, transparent, and implemented effectively across the organization.
AI Risk / GRC shall own these policies, processes, procedures, and practices and shall answer for their effectiveness.
Acme Health shall ensure that legal and regulatory requirements involving AI are understood, managed, and documented.
AI Risk / GRC shall perform and document this understanding and management, and shall answer for its outcome.

NIST suggests, among its 3 actions for Govern 1.1, maintaining awareness of the applicable legal and regulatory considerations and requirements specific to industry, sector, and business purpose, as well as the application context of the deployed AI system [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.1 Action 1], aligning risk management efforts with applicable legal standards [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.1 Action 2], and maintaining policies for training (and re-training) organizational staff about necessary legal or regulatory considerations that may impact AI-related design, development, and deployment activities [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.1 Action 3].
Acme Health shall integrate the characteristics of trustworthy AI into organizational policies, processes, procedures, and practices.
AI Risk / GRC shall own and maintain this integration.

NIST suggests, among its 15 actions for Govern 1.2, defining key terms and concepts related to AI systems and the scope of their purposes and intended uses [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.2 Action 1], connecting AI governance to existing organizational governance and risk controls [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.2 Action 2], aligning to broader data governance policies and practices, particularly the use of sensitive or otherwise risky data [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.2 Action 3], detailing standards for experimental design, data quality, and model training [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.2 Action 4], outlining and documenting risk mapping and measurement processes and standards [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.2 Action 5], detailing model testing and validation processes [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.2 Action 6], detailing review processes for legal and risk functions [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.2 Action 7], establishing the frequency of and detail for monitoring, auditing, and review processes [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.2 Action 8], outlining change management requirements [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.2 Action 9], outlining processes for internal and external stakeholder engagement [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.2 Action 10], establishing whistleblower policies to facilitate reporting of serious AI system concerns [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.2 Action 11], detailing and testing incident response plans [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.2 Action 12], verifying that formal AI risk management policies align to existing legal standards and industry best practices and norms [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.2 Action 13], establishing AI risk management policies that broadly align to AI system trustworthy characteristics [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.2 Action 14], and verifying that formal AI risk management policies include currently deployed and third-party AI systems [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.2 Action 15].
Acme Health shall maintain processes, procedures, and practices to determine the needed level of risk management activities based on the organization's risk tolerance.
AI Risk / GRC shall own these processes and shall answer for their outcome.

NIST suggests, among its 5 actions for Govern 1.3, establishing policies to define mechanisms for measuring or understanding an AI system's potential impacts, for example via regular impact assessments at key stages in the AI lifecycle, connected to system impacts and frequency of system updates [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.3 Action 1], establishing policies to define mechanisms for measuring or understanding the likelihood of an AI system's impacts and their magnitude at key stages in the AI lifecycle [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.3 Action 2], establishing policies that define assessment scales for measuring potential AI system impact, which may be qualitative such as red-amber-green (RAG) or may entail simulations or econometric approaches [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.3 Action 3], establishing policies for assigning an overall risk measurement approach for an AI system or its important components, for example via multiplication or combination of a mapped risk's impact and likelihood (risk ≈ impact x likelihood) [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.3 Action 4], and establishing policies to assign systems to uniform risk scales that are valid across the organization's AI portfolio, such as documentation templates, while acknowledging that risk tolerance and risk levels may change over the lifecycle of an AI system [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.3 Action 5].
The AI risk management process and its outcomes shall be established through transparent policies, procedures, and other controls based on Acme Health's organizational risk priorities.
AI Risk / GRC shall own the establishment of these policies, procedures, and controls.

NIST suggests, among its 7 actions for Govern 1.4, establishing and regularly reviewing documentation policies that address information related to AI actor contact information, business justification, scope and usages, expected and potential risks and impacts, assumptions and limitations, description and characterization of training data, algorithmic methodology, evaluated alternative approaches, description of output data, testing and validation results including explanatory visualizations and information, down- and up-stream dependencies, plans for deployment, monitoring, and change management, and stakeholder engagement plans [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.4 Action 1], verifying that documentation policies for AI systems are standardized across the organization and remain current [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.4 Action 2], establishing policies for a model documentation inventory system and regularly reviewing its completeness, usability, and efficacy [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.4 Action 3], establishing mechanisms to regularly review the efficacy of risk management processes [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.4 Action 4], identifying AI actors responsible for evaluating efficacy of risk management processes and approaches and for course-correction based on results [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.4 Action 5], establishing policies and processes regarding public disclosure of the use of AI and risk management material such as impact assessments, audits, model documentation, and validation and testing results [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.4 Action 6], and documenting and reviewing the use and efficacy of different types of transparency tools and following industry standards at the time a model is in use [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.4 Action 7].

Ongoing monitoring and periodic review of the AI risk management process and its outcomes shall be planned, organizational roles and responsibilities for these activities shall be clearly defined, and the frequency of periodic review shall be determined and documented ([Review Frequency]).
AI Risk / GRC shall own the monitoring and periodic review of this process and its outcomes, and shall answer for the results.

NIST suggests, among its 7 actions for Govern 1.5, establishing policies to allocate appropriate resources and capacity for assessing impacts of AI systems on individuals, communities, and society [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.5 Action 1], establishing policies and procedures for monitoring and addressing AI system performance and trustworthiness, including bias and security problems, across the lifecycle of the system [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.5 Action 2], establishing policies for AI system incident response, or confirming that existing incident response policies apply to AI systems [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.5 Action 3], establishing policies to define organizational functions and personnel responsible for AI system monitoring and incident response activities [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.5 Action 4], establishing mechanisms to enable the sharing of feedback from impacted individuals or communities about negative impacts from AI systems [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.5 Action 5], establishing mechanisms to provide recourse for impacted individuals or communities to contest problematic AI system outcomes [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.5 Action 6], and establishing opt-out mechanisms [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.5 Action 7].
Acme Health shall maintain mechanisms to inventory AI systems, resourced according to organizational risk priorities.
AI Risk / GRC shall own and maintain the AI system inventory and shall answer for its completeness.

NIST suggests, among its 4 actions for Govern 1.6, establishing policies that define the creation and maintenance of AI system inventories [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.6 Action 1], establishing policies that define a specific individual or team that is responsible for maintaining the inventory [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.6 Action 2], establishing policies that define which models or systems are inventoried, with preference to inventorying all models or systems or, minimally, high-risk models or systems or systems deployed in high-stakes settings [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.6 Action 3], and establishing policies that define model or system attributes to be inventoried, such as documentation, links to source code, incident response plans, data dictionaries, and AI actor contact information [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.6 Action 4].

AI Risk / GRC shall own processes and procedures for decommissioning and phasing out AI systems safely and in a manner that does not increase risks or decrease Acme Health's trustworthiness, and shall answer for the outcome of every decommissioning and phase-out.

NIST suggests, among its 4 actions for Govern 1.7, establishing policies for decommissioning AI systems that typically address user and community concerns and reputational risks, business continuity and financial risks, up- and downstream system dependencies, regulatory requirements such as data retention, potential future legal, regulatory, security, or forensic investigations, and migration to the replacement system if appropriate [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.7 Action 1], establishing policies that delineate where and for how long decommissioned systems, models, and related artifacts are stored [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.7 Action 2], establishing practices to track accountability and consider how decommissioning and other adaptations or changes in system deployment contribute to downstream impacts for individuals, groups, and communities [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.7 Action 3], and establishing policies that address ancillary data or artifacts that must be preserved for fulsome understanding or execution of the decommissioned AI system, such as predictions, explanations, intermediate input feature representations, and usernames and passwords [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.7 Action 4].
Acme Health shall maintain accountability structures so that the appropriate teams and individuals are empowered, responsible, and trained for mapping, measuring, and managing AI risks.
AI Risk / GRC shall own these accountability structures end to end.
Roles, responsibilities, and lines of communication related to mapping, measuring, and managing AI risks shall be documented and clear to individuals and teams throughout Acme Health.
AI Risk / GRC shall own the documentation of these roles, responsibilities, and lines of communication, and shall answer for keeping them clear across the organization.

NIST suggests, among its 6 actions for Govern 2.1, establishing policies that define the AI risk management roles and responsibilities for positions directly and indirectly related to AI systems, including but not limited to boards of directors or advisory committees, senior management, AI audit functions, product management, project management, AI design, AI development, human-AI interaction, AI testing and evaluation, AI acquisition and procurement, impact assessment functions, and oversight functions [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 2.1 Action 1], establishing policies that promote regular communication among AI actors participating in AI risk management efforts [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 2.1 Action 2], establishing policies that separate management of AI system development functions from AI system testing functions to enable independent course-correction of AI systems [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 2.1 Action 3], establishing policies to identify, increase the transparency of, and prevent conflicts of interest in AI risk management efforts [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 2.1 Action 4], establishing policies to counteract confirmation bias and market incentives that may hinder AI risk management efforts [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 2.1 Action 5], and establishing policies that incentivize AI actors to collaborate with existing legal, oversight, compliance, or enterprise risk functions in their AI risk management activities [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 2.1 Action 6].

Acme Health's personnel and partners shall receive AI risk management training to enable them to perform their duties and responsibilities consistent with related policies, procedures, and agreements.
AI Risk / GRC shall own this training and shall answer for its outcome.

NIST suggests, among its 6 actions for Govern 2.2, establishing policies for personnel addressing ongoing education about applicable laws and regulations for AI systems, potential negative impacts that may arise from AI systems, organizational AI policies, and trustworthy AI characteristics [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 2.2 Action 1], ensuring that trainings are suitable across AI actor sub-groups, for AI actors carrying out technical tasks such as developers and operators as compared to AI actors in oversight roles such as legal, compliance, and audit [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 2.2 Action 2], ensuring that trainings comprehensively address technical and socio-technical aspects of AI risk management [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 2.2 Action 3], verifying that organizational AI policies include mechanisms for internal AI personnel to acknowledge and commit to their roles and responsibilities [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 2.2 Action 4], verifying that organizational policies address change management and include mechanisms to communicate and acknowledge substantial AI system changes [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 2.2 Action 5], and defining paths along internal and external chains of accountability to escalate risk concerns [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 2.2 Action 6].
Executive leadership shall take responsibility for decisions about the risks associated with AI system development and deployment.

NIST suggests, among its 2 actions for Govern 2.3, that organizational management declare risk tolerances for developing or using AI systems, support AI risk management efforts and play an active role in such efforts, integrate a risk and harm prevention mindset throughout the AI lifecycle as part of organizational culture, support competent risk management executives, and delegate the power, resources, and authorization to perform risk management to each appropriate level throughout the management chain [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 2.3 Action 1], and that organizations establish board committees for AI risk management and oversight functions and integrate those functions within the organization's broader enterprise risk management approaches [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 2.3 Action 2].
Acme Health shall prioritize workforce diversity, equity, inclusion, and accessibility processes in the mapping, measuring, and managing of AI risks throughout the AI lifecycle.
AI Risk / GRC shall own the integration of these processes into AI risk management.

Decision-making related to mapping, measuring, and managing AI risks throughout the lifecycle shall be informed by a diverse team, including diversity of demographics, disciplines, experience, expertise, and backgrounds.

NIST suggests, among its 5 actions for Govern 3.1, defining policies and hiring practices at the outset that promote interdisciplinary roles, competencies, skills, and capacity for AI efforts [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 3.1 Action 1], defining policies and hiring practices that lead to demographic and domain expertise diversity, empowering staff with necessary resources and support, and facilitating the contribution of staff feedback and concerns without fear of reprisal [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 3.1 Action 2], establishing policies that facilitate inclusivity and the integration of new insights into existing practice [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 3.1 Action 3], seeking external expertise to supplement organizational diversity, equity, inclusion, and accessibility where internal expertise is lacking [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 3.1 Action 4], and establishing policies that incentivize AI actors to collaborate with existing nondiscrimination, accessibility and accommodation, and human resource functions, employee resource groups (ERGs), and diversity, equity, inclusion, and accessibility (DEIA) initiatives [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 3.1 Action 5].
Acme Health shall maintain policies and procedures that define and differentiate roles and responsibilities for human-AI configurations and oversight of AI systems.
AI Risk / GRC shall own these policies and procedures.

NIST suggests, among its 8 actions for Govern 3.2, establishing policies and procedures that define and differentiate the various human roles and responsibilities when using, interacting with, or monitoring AI systems [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 3.2 Action 1], establishing procedures for capturing and tracking risk information related to human-AI configurations and associated outcomes [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 3.2 Action 2], establishing policies for the development of proficiency standards for AI actors carrying out system operation tasks and system oversight tasks [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 3.2 Action 3], establishing specified risk management training protocols for AI actors carrying out system operation tasks and system oversight tasks [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 3.2 Action 4], establishing policies and procedures regarding AI actor roles and responsibilities for human oversight of deployed systems [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 3.2 Action 5], establishing policies and procedures defining human-AI configurations (configurations where AI systems are explicitly designated and treated as team members in primarily human teams) in relation to organizational risk tolerances, and associated documentation [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 3.2 Action 6], establishing policies to enhance the explanation, interpretation, and overall transparency of AI systems [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 3.2 Action 7], and establishing policies for managing risks regarding known difficulties in human-AI configurations, human-AI teaming, and AI system user experience and user interactions (UI/UX) [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 3.2 Action 8].
Acme Health's organizational teams shall maintain a commitment to a culture that considers and communicates AI risk.
AI Risk / GRC shall own the cultivation and measurement of this culture.

Acme Health's organizational policies and practices shall foster a critical thinking and safety-first mindset in the design, development, deployment, and uses of AI systems to minimize potential negative impacts.

NIST suggests, among its 5 actions for Govern 4.1, establishing policies that require inclusion of oversight functions (legal, compliance, risk management) from the outset of the system design process [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 4.1 Action 1], establishing policies that promote effective challenge of AI system design, implementation, and deployment decisions via mechanisms such as the three lines of defense, model audits, or red-teaming to minimize workplace risks such as groupthink [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 4.1 Action 2], establishing policies that incentivize safety-first mindset and general critical thinking and review at an organizational and procedural level [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 4.1 Action 3], establishing whistleblower protections for insiders who report on perceived serious problems with AI systems [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 4.1 Action 4], and establishing policies to integrate a harm and risk prevention mindset throughout the AI lifecycle [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 4.1 Action 5].

Acme Health's organizational teams shall document the risks and potential impacts of the AI technology they design, develop, deploy, evaluate, and use, and shall communicate about the impacts more broadly.
AI Risk / GRC shall own the process for this documentation and communication and shall answer for its outcome.

NIST suggests, among its 4 actions for Govern 4.2, establishing impact assessment policies and processes for AI systems used by the organization [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 4.2 Action 1], aligning organizational impact assessment activities with relevant regulatory or legal requirements [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 4.2 Action 2], verifying that impact assessment activities are appropriate to evaluate the potential negative impact of a system and how quickly a system changes, and that assessments are applied on a regular basis [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 4.2 Action 3], and utilizing impact assessments to inform broader evaluations of AI system risk [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 4.2 Action 4].
Acme Health shall maintain organizational practices that enable AI testing, identification of incidents, and information sharing.
AI Risk / GRC shall own these practices and shall answer for their outcome.

NIST suggests, among its 5 actions for Govern 4.3, establishing policies and procedures to facilitate and equip AI system testing [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 4.3 Action 1], establishing organizational commitment to identifying AI system limitations and sharing of insights about limitations within appropriate AI actor groups [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 4.3 Action 2], establishing policies for reporting and documenting incident response [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 4.3 Action 3], establishing policies and processes regarding public disclosure of incidents and information sharing [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 4.3 Action 4], and establishing guidelines for incident handling related to AI system risks and performance [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 4.3 Action 5].
Acme Health shall maintain processes for robust engagement with relevant AI actors.
AI Risk / GRC shall own these engagement processes end to end.

Acme Health shall maintain organizational policies and practices to collect, consider, prioritize, and integrate feedback from those external to the team that developed or deployed the AI system regarding the potential individual and societal impacts related to AI risks.
AI Risk / GRC shall own these policies and practices and shall answer for their outcome.

NIST suggests, among its 3 actions for Govern 5.1, establishing AI risk management policies that explicitly address mechanisms for collecting, evaluating, and incorporating stakeholder and user feedback, which could include recourse mechanisms for faulty AI system outputs, bug bounties, human-centered design, user-interaction and experience research, and participatory stakeholder engagement with individuals and communities that may experience negative impacts [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 5.1 Action 1], verifying that stakeholder feedback is considered and addressed, including environmental concerns, and across the entire population of intended users, including historically excluded populations, people with disabilities, older people, and those with limited access to the internet and other basic technologies [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 5.1 Action 2], and clarifying the organization's principles as they apply to AI systems, considering those which have been proposed publicly, to inform external stakeholders of the organization's values, and considering publishing or adopting AI principles [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 5.1 Action 3].

Acme Health shall establish mechanisms that enable the team that developed or deployed AI systems to regularly incorporate adjudicated feedback from relevant AI actors into system design and implementation.
AI Risk / GRC shall own the adjudication of feedback and the handoff of adjudicated feedback to the developing or deploying team, and shall answer for the outcome.

NIST suggests, among its 5 actions for Govern 5.2, explicitly acknowledging that AI systems, and the use of AI, present inherent costs and risks along with potential benefits [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 5.2 Action 1], defining reasonable risk tolerances for AI systems informed by laws, regulation, best practices, or industry standards [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 5.2 Action 2], establishing policies that ensure all relevant AI actors are provided with meaningful opportunities to provide feedback on system design and implementation [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 5.2 Action 3], establishing policies that define how to assign AI systems to established risk tolerance levels by combining system impact assessments with the likelihood that an impact occurs, often entailing some combination of econometric evaluations of impacts and impact likelihoods, red-amber-green (RAG) scales for impact severity and likelihood, policies for allocating risk management resources along established risk tolerance levels with higher-risk systems receiving more risk management resources and oversight, and policies for approval, conditional approval, and disapproval of the design, implementation, and deployment of AI systems [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 5.2 Action 4], and establishing policies facilitating the early decommissioning of AI systems that surpass an organization's ability to reasonably mitigate risks [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 5.2 Action 5].
